components.name: Parmesan
components.explain:
On an American menu, Parmesan is a generic word. In the United States Parmesan is defined by a federal standard of identity, a granular grating cheese cured at least ten months, wherever it is made. In the European Union it is the other way round: since a 2008 ruling of the European Court of Justice, only Parmigiano Reggiano may be sold as parmesan.

Parmigiano Reggiano is made only around Parma, Reggio Emilia and Modena, with no preservatives, and is inspected at twelve months.

The Eggs Sardou prints Parmesan creamed spinach. The kitchen may use Parmigiano Reggiano, the Grana Padano already on the Caesar, or a domestic Parmesan; until the chef says which, call it Parmesan and nothing grander.

card.front: Does Parmesan on the Eggs Sardou mean Parmigiano Reggiano?
card.back: Not necessarily: in the US Parmesan is a generic name for a hard grating cheese, wherever it is made. Ask the kitchen which cheese goes into the creamed spinach.

producer.who: Parmesan, cheese and maker not printed
producer.where: As sourced: Parmigiano Reggiano is from Parma, Reggio Emilia and Modena; American Parmesan may come from anywhere
producer.history:
The word Parmesan means different things on either side of the Atlantic. In the European Union, a 2008 ruling of the European Court of Justice held that only Parmigiano Reggiano, the protected cheese of Parma, Reggio Emilia, Modena and parts of Mantua and Bologna, may be sold as parmesan. Its rules are strict: cows fed on fresh fodder and hay, no silage, no preservatives, dairies that make nothing else, and inspection at twelve months.

In the United States, Parmesan is a generic name. The federal standard of identity describes a granular cheese with a hard, brittle rind that grates readily, at most 32 per cent moisture and cured at least ten months; it says nothing about where the cheese is made.

So when an American menu prints Parmesan, as Brennan's does in the creamed spinach of the Eggs Sardou, it promises a hard grating cheese, not a particular one. The kitchen may use Parmigiano Reggiano, the Grana Padano it buys for the Caesar and the Shells & Cheese, which has its own card, or a domestic Parmesan. A server should know the difference and find out which.
facts: A 2008 European Court of Justice ruling reserves the name parmesan in the EU for Parmigiano Reggiano.
In the United States Parmesan is a generic name defined by a federal standard of identity, not by place.
The US standard asks for a granular, readily grated cheese, at most 32 per cent moisture, cured at least ten months.
Parmigiano Reggiano is made around Parma, Reggio Emilia and Modena and inspected at twelve months.
Parmigiano Reggiano allows no preservatives and no silage in the cows' feed.
notes: Say Parmesan creamed spinach, as printed; never upgrade it to Parmigiano Reggiano unless the kitchen confirms it.
Guests who ask whether it is the real thing deserve the honest answer: in America Parmesan is a general name, and you will check which cheese.
The Creamed Spinach side may share the Sardou's spinach, but that is an inference; confirm at lineup.
Dairy and other dietary questions about the spinach go to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Creamed spinach finished with Parmesan, a hard grating cheese in the Italian style; I can check with the kitchen exactly which one tonight.
askKitchen: Is the Parmesan in the Sardou spinach Parmigiano Reggiano, Grana Padano or a domestic Parmesan?

components.name: Albert Boxler
components.explain:
Albert Boxler is a small family domaine in Niedermorschwihr, a village in the hills above Colmar in Alsace, and one of the region's most admired small estates. It is known above all for grand cru wines from two granite hillsides, the Brand and the Sommerberg, and our list carries a run of them in Riesling and Pinot Gris, with names such as Wibthal, Eckberg and Dudenstein on the labels, beside a Gewurztraminer, Muscat and an Edelzwicker blend.

The bottle in our pairings is the Pinot Gris 2020, the domaine's Pinot Gris without a grand cru name: rich, smoky and spiced, a classic partner for duck and foie gras. Whether it carries a touch of sweetness is for the sommelier, since 2020 came the year before Alsace made a dryness indication compulsory.

card.front: What is Albert Boxler known for, and where is it?
card.back: A small family domaine in Niedermorschwihr, above Colmar in Alsace, admired for grand cru wines from two granite hills, the Brand and the Sommerberg. We pour its Pinot Gris 2020.

producer.history:
Albert Boxler is a small family domaine in Niedermorschwihr, a village in the hills above Colmar, and the wine list counts it among the most admired small estates of Alsace. No source gives its founding or its generations, so they are not told here.

Its reputation rests on two grand crus, the Brand and the Sommerberg. Both are granite, the old crystalline rock of the Vosges, where many other Alsace crus lie on limestone, marl or sandstone. Each of the fifty-one Alsace grand crus is an appellation of its own, with its own rules.

Our list shows how finely the domaine divides its ground. Beside the Brand and the Sommerberg it prints labels named Wibthal, Eckberg and Dudenstein, in Riesling and in Pinot Gris, with a Gewurztraminer, Muscat and an Edelzwicker, the Alsace name for a blend. The Rieslings are described as intense, dry and mineral.

The bottle in our pairings is the Pinot Gris 2020, the domaine's Pinot Gris without a grand cru name. Alsace Pinot Gris is fuller and more aromatic than Italian Pinot Grigio, and with foie gras it is a classic of the region. The 2020 came the year before Alsace made a dryness indication compulsory, so whether it carries a touch of sweetness is a question for the sommelier.

components.name: Château Meyney
components.explain:
Château Meyney is an estate in Saint-Estèphe, the northernmost of the Médoc's four great villages, near the Gironde estuary. It is not one of the 1855 classed growths; Saint-Estèphe's are led by the second growths Cos d'Estournel and Montrose. The village is known for firm, savoury reds: its gravel is shallow and sits on clay that holds water, so the vines suffer less in drought and the wine has more flesh and more grip.

We pour La Chapelle de Meyney, the château's second wine, made from younger vines. It is Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and a little Petit Verdot, aged in French oak, part of it new; the exact mix of each vintage is for the sommelier. Ours is the 2018: blackcurrant, cedar and tobacco, the value bottle for the hanger steak with béarnaise.

card.front: What is La Chapelle de Meyney?
card.back: The second wine of Château Meyney in Saint-Estèphe, from younger vines: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and a little Petit Verdot, firm and savoury. Meyney is not one of the 1855 classed growths.

Château Meyney is an estate in Saint-Estèphe, the northernmost of the four great villages of the Médoc, near the Gironde estuary. It is not one of the classed growths of 1855: Saint-Estèphe holds five, led by the second growths Cos d'Estournel and Montrose, and Meyney stands outside that list.

Saint-Estèphe is known for firm, structured, savoury reds, and the Codex explains why. The gravel there is shallower than in Pauillac and sits on clay that holds water, so the vines suffer less in drought and give wines with more flesh and more grip.

Our bottle is La Chapelle de Meyney, the château's second wine. A second wine is made from the younger vines and the lots that do not go into the grand vin. Recent vintages have been about two thirds Cabernet Sauvignon, with Merlot and a little Petit Verdot, aged about twelve months in French oak, part of it new; the blend moves with the vintage, and the 2018 mix is for the sommelier. Ours is the 2018: blackcurrant and plum, cedar, tobacco and earth, with the firm tannin that cuts through béarnaise and egg yolk. It is the value bottle for the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak.

components.name: Château Haut-Bages Libéral
components.explain:
Château Haut-Bages Libéral is one of the eighteen fifth growths of the 1855 classification, in Pauillac, the village of three first growths. Its largest parcel lies beside Château Latour, and the estate has been certified organic and biodynamic since 2019. Haut is French for high, and Bages is the plateau in the south of Pauillac.

The wine is about three quarters Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, aged in French oak with part new barrels: firm, fresh Pauillac. Ours is the 2018, blackcurrant, graphite and cedar, the fair-priced way into classed growth Pauillac on our list, for the Chateaubriand, a steak or lamb, decanted about an hour ahead.

card.front: What makes Haut-Bages Libéral a good story at the table?
card.back: A Pauillac fifth growth whose largest parcel lies beside Château Latour, certified organic and biodynamic: classed growth Pauillac at a fair price.

producer.where: Pauillac, Médoc, Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Château Haut-Bages Libéral is one of the eighteen fifth growths of the 1855 classification, in Pauillac, the village that holds three of the five first growths. Its name joins haut, French for high, to Bages, the plateau in the south of Pauillac that also names Lynch-Bages. Where the name Libéral comes from is a question for the sommelier.

Its largest vineyard parcel lies beside Château Latour, in the south of the commune. The estate has been certified organic and biodynamic since 2019, and as of October 2026 it is run by Claire Villars-Lurton.

The wine is Pauillac in a firm, fresh style: about three quarters Cabernet Sauvignon and a quarter Merlot, aged fourteen to eighteen months in French oak, about 40 percent of it new. Ours is the 2018: blackcurrant, graphite and cedar, ripe fruit and firm, polished tannin, decanted about an hour ahead. On our list it sits below the Talbot, the fair-priced way into classed growth Pauillac, and it suits the Roasted Chateaubriand, a steak or lamb.

components.name: Château Mouton Rothschild
components.explain:
Château Mouton Rothschild, in Pauillac, was bought by Nathaniel de Rothschild in 1853 and ranked a second growth in 1855. Baron Philippe de Rothschild campaigned for half a century until a decree of 1973, signed by Jacques Chirac as minister of agriculture, made it a first growth: the only promotion ever made to the list. The motto changed to Premier je suis, second je fus, Mouton ne change: first I am, second I was, Mouton does not change.

Since the 1945 vintage every label has carried a different artist's work, Picasso and Warhol among them. Baron Philippe also founded Opus One with Robert Mondavi. Ours is the 2005: opulent, Cabernet-led Pauillac for a milestone.

card.front: What sets Mouton Rothschild apart among the first growths?
card.back: The only estate promoted in the 1855 classification, in 1973, and since the 1945 vintage a different artist’s label every year.

producer.who: Château Mouton Rothschild, the Pauillac first growth promoted in 1973
producer.where: Pauillac, Médoc, Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Château Mouton Rothschild is the Pauillac estate that changed the 1855 classification. Nathaniel de Rothschild bought it in 1853, two years before the ranking, and in 1855 it was placed among the second growths. Its old motto answered the slight: Premier ne puis, second ne daigne, Mouton suis. First I cannot be, second I do not deign to be, Mouton I am.

Baron Philippe de Rothschild campaigned for half a century to change the rank, and in 1973 a decree signed by Jacques Chirac, then minister of agriculture, made Mouton a first growth: the only promotion ever made to the red list. The motto became Premier je suis, second je fus, Mouton ne change: first I am, second I was, Mouton does not change.

Since the 1945 vintage each label has carried a work by a different artist, Braque, Picasso, Warhol, Bacon and Hockney among them, paid in wine rather than money. Baron Philippe also joined Robert Mondavi to found Opus One in Napa, first vintage 1979, which is on our list too.

The wine is Cabernet Sauvignon dominant, with Merlot and Cabernet Franc: cassis liqueur, cigar box and sweet oak, the most opulent of the Pauillac firsts. The list carries it in many vintages; the one to name is the 2005.

components.name: Château Margaux
components.explain:
Château Margaux is one of the four original first growths of 1855, with Lafite, Latour and Haut-Brion, and the only first growth that shares its name with its village and appellation, in the southern Médoc. Thomas Jefferson named it among Bordeaux's four first-quality growths in 1787, long before the classification. The wine is Cabernet Sauvignon led, from gravel croupes, famous for perfume before power: violets, rose and silky tannin.

Pavillon Rouge is its second wine, and Pavillon Blanc, all Sauvignon Blanc, is sold as Bordeaux Blanc because Margaux is a red-only appellation. Our list holds thirteen vintages of the grand vin; the 2007 is the gentlest priced.

card.front: Château Margaux or a Margaux: what is the difference?
card.back: Margaux is the village and appellation in the southern Médoc; Château Margaux is its first growth, perfumed and silky. Pavillon Rouge is the château’s second wine.

Château Margaux is one of the four original first growths of the 1855 classification, with Lafite, Latour and Haut-Brion, and the only one that shares its name with its village and appellation: Margaux, in the southern Médoc. Its vineyard lies on gravel croupes, low rises of deep gravel, in the commune of Margaux.

Its reputation is older than the classification. Thomas Jefferson, touring Bordeaux in 1787 as the American minister to France, named it among the four growths of first quality, the same four that 1855 placed at the top. The neoclassical château, built in the early nineteenth century, is the house on the label.

The wine is Cabernet Sauvignon led, with Merlot, Petit Verdot and Cabernet Franc, and it is famous for perfume before power: violets, rose and cool graphite on the silkiest tannin in the Médoc. Pavillon Rouge is the second wine. Pavillon Blanc, all Sauvignon Blanc, is sold as Bordeaux Blanc, because the Margaux appellation is for red wine only.

Our list carries the grand vin in thirteen vintages from 1990 to 2018. The 2007 is the gentlest priced, and the Pavillon Rouge 2010 sits on the same page.

components.name: Château Lafite Rothschild
components.explain:
Château Lafite Rothschild is one of the four original first growths of 1855, listed first among them. Its gravel rises lie in northern Pauillac, running to the Saint-Estèphe boundary, facing Cos d'Estournel across the Jalle de Breuil. Baron James de Rothschild bought it in 1868, and the family owns it still, with Duhart-Milon in Pauillac and L'Évangile in Pomerol, both on our list.

Lafite is the most reserved and perfumed of the firsts: cedar, graphite and pencil shavings over restrained cassis. Carruades de Lafite is the second wine. Ours is the 2004, for a milestone dinner; the sommelier decants it.

card.front: Who bought Lafite in 1868, and what is its style?
card.back: Baron James de Rothschild. Lafite is the most reserved and perfumed first growth: cedar, graphite and cassis. Carruades de Lafite is its second wine.

Château Lafite Rothschild is one of the four original first growths of 1855, listed first among them. Its gravel rises lie in the north of Pauillac and run to the Saint-Estèphe boundary; across the little stream of the Jalle de Breuil, which marks the commune line, stands Cos d'Estournel.

In the eighteenth century it belonged to the Marquis de Ségur, who also owned Latour and said his heart was at Calon. Baron James de Rothschild bought Lafite in 1868, and the family has owned it since. The same family owns Duhart-Milon, a Pauillac fourth growth, and L'Évangile in Pomerol, and makes the Légende range; all three names are on our list.

Lafite is the most reserved and perfumed of the firsts: cedar, graphite and pencil shavings over restrained cassis, built on finesse rather than weight. Carruades de Lafite, named for the Carruades plateau parcels, is the second wine.

The list carries Lafite in many vintages from 1989, with a 2007 magnum. The one to name is the 2004, for a milestone dinner, opened and decanted by the sommelier.

components.name: Château Latour
components.explain:
Château Latour is one of the four original first growths of 1855, in southern Pauillac at the Saint-Julien border. Its heart is L'Enclos, a walled block of deep gravel beside the Gironde; fruit from outside it goes to the second wine, Les Forts de Latour. The estate is named for an old fortified tower; the tower on the label is a seventeenth century dovecote raised on that site.

Latour is the most structured first growth, dense and slow, and since the 2012 vintage it has released its wines only when it judges them ready. We carry the 2005 and, among our Birth Year bottles, a 1946, the year Brennan's opened.

card.front: Why does our list hold a Château Latour 1946?
card.back: Brennan’s opened in 1946, and Latour 1946 is the grandest of the four Birth Year bottles: a first growth Pauillac, opened and judged by the sommelier.

producer.who: Château Latour, the powerful first growth of Pauillac
producer.where: Pauillac, Médoc, Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Château Latour is one of the four original first growths of 1855, in the south of Pauillac where the commune meets Saint-Julien. Its heart is L'Enclos, the walled block of deep gravel beside the Gironde. Fruit from outside the Enclos goes to the second and third wines: Les Forts de Latour, first released with the 1966 vintage, and Pauillac de Latour. The Grand Clos of Léoville Las Cases runs up to it from Saint-Julien, and Pichon Lalande faces it across the road.

The estate takes its name from an old fortified tower that once watched the river. The round tower on the label is a seventeenth century dovecote raised on that site. In the eighteenth century Latour, like Lafite, belonged to the Marquis de Ségur.

Latour is the most structured of the firsts: dense, austere in youth and famous for holding its shape in weak vintages. With the 2012 vintage it left the en primeur system, and it now releases its wines only when it judges them ready. It has been owned by the Pinault family since 1993.

We carry the 2005 and, among the Selections from our Birth Year, a 1946, the year Brennan's opened.

components.name: Château Cos d'Estournel
components.explain:
Château Cos d'Estournel is a second growth of 1855 in Saint-Estèphe, a commune with no first growth, which it leads with Montrose. In the early nineteenth century Louis Gaspard d'Estournel sold much of his wine into India and the East, and built a cellar crowned with pagodas to say so; the estate is still nicknamed the Maharajah of Saint-Estèphe.

The wine is Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, the most exotic Saint-Estèphe: dark spice, sandalwood and black fruit. Ours is the 2015 in magnum, a grand bottle for a beef celebration.

Château Lassègue is a Saint-Émilion estate on the Right Bank of Bordeaux, and the bottle we pour is its second wine, Les Cadrans de Lassègue, first made in 2008. A second wine is the château’s own wine from younger vines and the lots that do not go into the grand vin, made by the same team at a gentler price. Les Cadrans is mainly Merlot with Cabernet Franc from the estate’s younger vines and foothill blocks, aged a few months in French oak, and it takes its name from the sundials, cadrans, on the château’s front.

The label says Saint-Émilion Grand Cru, an appellation, not a rank. It is our gentlest priced Bordeaux: soft, red cherry and plum, ready now.

components.name: Château Bellegrave
components.explain:
Château Bellegrave is a small family estate in the south west of Pomerol, the Right Bank appellation beside Saint-Émilion known for plush Merlot. Jean Bouldy bought it in 1951, and the third generation of the Bouldy family runs it, as of October 2026. The vines grow on clay and gravel and are farmed organically, with ECOCERT certification in 2009; the blend is about three parts Merlot to one of Cabernet Franc.

Pomerol has never classified its châteaux, so the label carries no rank. On our list Bellegrave is the gentle way into Pomerol: black cherry, plum and cocoa, soft and supple, and a natural partner for the duck.

At the table it is the Merlot lover’s bottle, decanted thirty to forty-five minutes ahead, as its card says, and a natural partner for the duck.

components.name: Château Cheval Blanc
components.explain:
Château Cheval Blanc, the white horse, is the most famous estate in Saint-Émilion. It lies in the far north west of the appellation, hard against Pomerol, on gravel, sand and clay; its land was separated from Château Figeac in 1832. It breaks the Right Bank’s rules twice: gravel where limestone is expected, and Cabernet Franc, in near-equal parts with Merlot, where Merlot is expected. The result is floral and silky: violets, red plum and sweet spice.

Cheval Blanc and Ausone held the top rank alone for decades; in 2021 both announced they would not enter the 2022 revision. Our 2008 was made when it was ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé A.

card.front: What makes Cheval Blanc different from most Saint-Émilion?
card.back: Gravel instead of limestone, and Cabernet Franc in near-equal parts with Merlot: floral, silky and perfumed. It withdrew from the classification before the 2022 revision.

Château Cheval Blanc, the white horse, is the most famous estate in Saint-Émilion. It lies in the far north west of the appellation, hard against the boundary with Pomerol, on gravel, sand and clay rather than the limestone most of Saint-Émilion is known for. Its land was separated from Château Figeac in 1832, and the two still share their gravel rise as neighbours, not one estate.

It breaks the Right Bank’s other rule too. Where Saint-Émilion is Merlot country, Cheval Blanc grows Cabernet Franc, called Bouchet by older growers there, in near-equal parts with Merlot. That is the root of its style: floral and exotic rather than stony, violets, red plum and sweet spice on a satin texture. Its second wine is Le Petit Cheval.

In 2021 both announced they would not enter the 2022 revision, objecting to its criteria, so the estate now stands outside the classification. Our 2008 was made when it was ranked A, as our list prints it.

Its 1947 is among the most celebrated Bordeaux of the twentieth century, and in the film Sideways a 1961 Cheval Blanc is the bottle the hero has saved. The list carries vintages from 1990 to 2020.

components.name: Pétrus
components.explain:
Pétrus is the most famous wine of Pomerol and among the most prized in the world. It comes from a small outcrop of blue clay, the buttonhole, at the high point of the Pomerol plateau, and it is Merlot, effectively the whole blend: truffle, dark plum and iron, deep without weight. Pomerol has never been classified, so Pétrus carries no rank at all, and the label reads Pétrus alone, without Château. It was long run by the Moueix family of Libourne.

We list two mature vintages, 1980 and 1989; the 1989 belongs to the celebrated pair of 1989 and 1990. The sommelier opens every bottle.

card.back: Pomerol has never been classified, so its most famous wine has no rank: blue clay at the high point of the plateau, almost all Merlot, labelled Pétrus without Château.

The blue clay is a small outcrop, not the soil of the whole plateau, which is part of why nothing else in Pomerol tastes quite like it.

Pétrus was long run by the Moueix family of Libourne. The Moueix name also stands behind Trotanoy, La Fleur-Pétrus and, in Napa, Christian Moueix’s Dominus, all on our list; a family name is not one owner, so never say one company makes them all.

The style is Merlot at maximum depth without weight: truffle, dark plum and iron. Our bottles are mature. The 1980 is forty-six years old, and the 1989 belongs to the celebrated pair of 1989 and 1990. Every bottle that old is its own, so the sommelier opens it.

components.name: Château Trotanoy
components.explain:
Château Trotanoy is a small estate on the western slope of the Pomerol plateau, on clay over gravel; its name is said to come from trop ennui, the trouble of working that soil. It is a Moueix property, as of October 2026, and the Codex calls it long regarded as the closest thing to Pétrus in the Moueix stable: Merlot with a little Cabernet Franc, dark, dense and mineral. Like all Pomerol, it is unclassified.

Our bottle is a 1946, one of four Selections from our Birth Year, made from vines that stood before the great frost of 1956. When the Moueix family came to the estate is not confirmed, so never say they made it.

card.back: Eighty-year-old Pomerol from a Moueix estate, one of our four Birth Year bottles. Pomerol is unclassified, so never call it a first growth, and never say the Moueix family made the 1946.

The two share a history as well as a soil: the Cheval Blanc vineyard was sold out of Figeac in 1832, and they have been different estates ever since. components.name: Château Canon
components.explain:
Château Canon is a walled vineyard on the limestone plateau just west of the town of Saint-Émilion, with old quarry cellars beneath it. The Codex calls it the teaching wine for limestone plateau Saint-Émilion: Merlot with Cabernet Franc, chalky and precise, red cherry, orange peel and fine tannin. It is ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé B. The Wertheimer family of Chanel bought it in 1996; they also own Rauzan-Ségla in Margaux, on our list. It is not Canon-la-Gaffelière.

Our bottle is a 1946, the gentlest priced of our four Birth Year bottles, made fifty years before the Chanel purchase: never say Chanel made it.

card.back: The Wertheimer family of Chanel. Our 1946 was made fifty years before, so never say Chanel made it. Canon is limestone plateau Saint-Émilion, not Canon-la-Gaffelière.

Château Troplong Mondot is a Saint-Émilion estate on one of the highest points of the appellation’s limestone plateau, on the Right Bank of Bordeaux. The wine list ranks it Premier Grand Cru Classé, printed with the B of the tier below the A estates. components.name: Château Haut-Brion
components.explain:
Château Haut-Brion stands on gravel mounds now inside the suburbs of Pessac, on the edge of the city of Bordeaux. In 1855 it was the one estate outside the Médoc ranked among the first growths, and the Graves classification of 1959 lists it again, for its red. In 1663 the London diarist Samuel Pepys wrote of drinking a wine called Ho Bryan, naming the property rather than its region. Clarence Dillon, an American financier, bought it in 1935, and Domaine Clarence Dillon has held it since; ownership can change.

We pour two: the red 2002, the gentlest priced first growth on our list, smoky and silky, and the white 2019, Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc, one of the rarest and most expensive dry whites in Bordeaux. Let the sommelier lead with both.

card.front: What makes Haut-Brion the exception among the 1855 first growths?
card.back: It is the only one outside the Médoc, on gravel in Pessac, in the Graves. Pepys drank its Ho Bryan in 1663; we pour the red 2002 and the rare white 2019.

producer.who: Château Haut-Brion, the first growth of the Graves, in Pessac; we pour its red 2002 and its rare white 2019
producer.where: Pessac, Pessac-Léognan, Graves, Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Château Haut-Brion lies on gravel mounds that the city of Bordeaux has grown around: its vines now stand inside the suburbs of Pessac. The Codex dates the estate to 1533. In 1663 the London diarist Samuel Pepys wrote of drinking a French wine called Ho Bryan with a good taste of its own, naming the property rather than the region, often taken as the moment a Bordeaux estate began to sell wine on its own name.

When the brokers ranked the red wines for the Paris Exposition of 1855, by the prices they fetched, Haut-Brion was the one estate outside the Médoc placed among the four first growths, with Lafite, Latour and Margaux; Mouton joined them in 1973. The Graves drew up its own classification in 1953 and 1959 and lists Haut-Brion again for its red, the only estate in both. Since 1987 its appellation has been Pessac-Léognan, carved out of the northern Graves.

Clarence Dillon, an American financier, bought it in 1935, and Domaine Clarence Dillon has held it since; the Dillon family bought La Mission Haut-Brion, across the road, in 1983. The red blends Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc: smoke, warm gravel and tobacco. The white, Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc, is one of the rarest and most expensive dry whites in Bordeaux. The second wine, printed on our list as Bahans Haut-Brion, has been called Le Clarence de Haut-Brion since the 2007 vintage.

components.name: Château Carbonnieux
components.explain:
Château Carbonnieux is an estate at Léognan in Pessac-Léognan, the northern part of the Graves just south of the city of Bordeaux. When the Graves drew up its own classification, reds in 1953 and whites in 1959, Carbonnieux was listed for both colours, one of the handful of estates classified for white, and the white is the wine it is known for.

That white blends Sauvignon Blanc, for freshness and citrus, with Sémillon, for body and the beeswax notes that grow with age, and it is raised in barrel.

Ours is the 2016, our anchor for white Bordeaux: grapefruit, lemon curd, beeswax and a little toast, ten years on and still fresh. It sits on the same page as the Haut-Brion Blanc at a far gentler price, and suits the redfish or the crab claws.

card.front: What is Château Carbonnieux classified for, and what is it best known for?
card.back: A classed growth of the Graves for both red and white, in Pessac-Léognan. Its white, Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon raised in barrel, is the famous one; ours is the 2016.

producer.history:
Château Carbonnieux is one of the classed growths of the Graves, the gravel country that runs south from the city of Bordeaux along the left bank of the Garonne. Its vineyards are at Léognan, in the northern Graves, which became an appellation of its own, Pessac-Léognan, in 1987.

The classification of 1855 left the Graves out, Haut-Brion apart, so the Graves drew up its own list: reds in 1953, whites in 1959. The list has a single tier and records which colour each estate is classified for. Carbonnieux is classified for both, one of the handful of estates listed for white, and the white is the wine it is known for.

That white follows the Graves recipe: Sauvignon Blanc for freshness and citrus, Sémillon for body, texture and the beeswax and honey notes that come with age, raised in barrel. It is crisp and citrusy young and rounds out in bottle, which is why a ten year old white Bordeaux belongs on a list.

Our list prints the 2016 at $160 and the 2022 at $190, and a separate white, L'Enclos de Carbonnieux 2021, at $75. How that wine relates to the château, and the estate's own history and family, are questions for the sommelier.

components.name: Piedrasassi
components.explain:
Piedrasassi is the small Syrah label of the winemaker Sashi Moorman and his wife Melissa Sorongon, made in Lompoc in Santa Barbara County since 2003. They make Syrah the Northern Rhône way: savoury, peppery and fresh rather than ripe and heavy. Moorman also co-founded Sandhi, whose Chardonnay is on our white pages.

Ours comes from the Bien Nacido Vineyard in the Santa Maria Valley, a grower's vineyard cooled by Pacific fog that sells fruit to many producers, and a name for cool-climate California Syrah since Qupé bottled it. The 2021, $80, is black cherry, black pepper, smoked meat and olive, medium in body with lively acidity: the red for a Rhône lover, lamb or the hanger steak. Rim Rock, from the Arroyo Grande Valley, sits beside it at the same price.

card.back: Sashi Moorman and Melissa Sorongon, in Lompoc. Ours is from the Bien Nacido Vineyard, in the Santa Maria Valley: savoury, peppery, Northern Rhône in style.

components.name: Penfolds
components.explain:
Penfolds, founded at Magill near Adelaide in 1844, is Australia's most famous wine house: a great blender that draws fruit from across South Australia and matures it in American oak for long life. Its wines carry bin numbers, house codes rather than a classification.

Grange is the legend. Max Schubert, then its chief winemaker, studied Bordeaux in 1950, made the first experimental Grange from Shiraz in 1951, kept making it in secret after the board ordered it stopped in 1957, and saw it reinstated with the 1960. We print it in four vintages, the 2004 at $650 the oldest.

Bin 389, Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz, is matured partly in barrels that held the previous vintage of Grange, hence Baby Grange: our 2019 at $145 is the gentler way into the house.

card.front: Why is Penfolds Bin 389 called Baby Grange?
card.back: It matures partly in barrels that held the previous vintage of Grange, Max Schubert's Shiraz first made in 1951. We print Bin 389 2019 at $145 and Grange from $650.

producer.history:
Penfolds is Australia's most famous wine name. Dr Christopher Rawson Penfold and Mary Penfold founded it in 1844 at Magill, on the edge of Adelaide, and it grew into the great blender of South Australia, drawing fruit from regions such as the Barossa, Coonawarra and McLaren Vale and maturing it in American oak, for structure and long life rather than the voice of one vineyard. Its wines carry bin numbers, house codes from the cellar, not a legal classification.

Grange is the legend. Max Schubert, Penfolds' chief winemaker, toured Europe in 1950 studying Bordeaux and came home wanting a wine that would live for decades. Without enough Cabernet or French oak, he used Shiraz and new American oak hogsheads and made the first experimental vintage in 1951. The board ordered him to stop after showings in 1957; he made the 1957, 1958 and 1959 in secret, and the wine was reinstated with the 1960. It was labelled Grange Hermitage into the late 1980s, Hermitage being an old Australian name for Shiraz.

Bin 389, Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz, is matured in American oak, partly in barrels that held the previous vintage of Grange, hence its nickname, Baby Grange.

We print both: Bin 389 2019 at $145, and Grange in four vintages, the 2004 at $650, twenty-two years old, then 2009 and 2010 at $875 and 2011 at $775.

components.name: Château Musar
components.explain:
Château Musar is Lebanon's legendary red. Gaston Hochar founded it in 1930 and his son Serge made it world famous, keeping it going through fifteen years of civil war with only two vintages missed. The grapes grow high in the Bekaa Valley, between two mountain ranges; the wine is made and aged at Ghazir, north of Beirut.

The red blends Cabernet Sauvignon, Cinsault and Carignan, is aged in oak and bottle and released around seven years after the harvest. It is unfiltered, wild, savoury and individual, a wine people love or cannot get past.

We print five Musar wines; ours, the 2003 at $285, is dried cherry, fig, spice, leather and incense, silky with lively acidity, for lamb, game or cheese.

card.front: Where do Château Musar's grapes grow, and where is the wine made?
card.back: In Lebanon's high Bekaa Valley; the wine is made and aged at Ghazir, north of Beirut. Gaston Hochar founded it in 1930 and his son Serge made it famous.

producer.history:
Château Musar is the great name of Lebanese wine. Gaston Hochar founded it in 1930, and his son Serge Hochar made it world famous. The grapes grow in the Bekaa Valley, a high plateau between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges at around a thousand metres, where altitude gives cool nights against the summer heat; the wine is made and aged in the cellars at Ghazir, north of Beirut, near the coast.

Musar kept making wine through fifteen years of civil war, missing only two vintages, with the fruit trucked over the mountains to the cellar.

The red is Cabernet Sauvignon, Cinsault and Carignan, aged in oak and then in bottle and released around seven years after the harvest. It is unfiltered and, by modern standards, high in volatile acidity, with a wild, savoury edge: drinkers either love it or cannot get past it, so a first-time guest should be told.

Our list prints five Musar wines: the red in 1994 at $400, 1995 at $450, 1997 and 2003 at $285, and the younger Hochar red 2020 at $90. Ours, the 2003 at $285, bin 33512, is twenty-three years old: dried cherry, fig, spice, leather and incense, silky, with lively acidity.

components.name: Domaine Fichet
components.explain:
Domaine Fichet is a family estate at Igé in the northern Mâconnais. The family traces its vines back to a Stéphus Fichet in 1408; the modern estate dates to 1976 and Francis Fichet, and his son Pierre-Yves joined in 1988, with Olivier two years later.

Château London is a reputed slope of Igé that other growers bottle too. Jean-Claude Boisset says the name comes from its original owner, who lived on the rue Landon in Paris: no castle and no English link. Fichet makes it mostly in stainless steel; the 2023 had about a tenth in older oak.

On our printed card it is the dinner tasting white, poured with the Louisiana BBQ Lobster; confirm the pour at lineup.

producer.history:
Domaine Fichet is a family estate in Igé, a village of the northern Mâconnais, based in the hamlet of Martoret. The family traces its winegrowing back to the Middle Ages, to a Stéphus Fichet who was growing vines in 1408. The modern estate dates to 1976 and Francis Fichet. The estate's tourism listing says he left the village cooperative to make his own wine; Wine Anorak has his first grapes still going to the Igé cooperative, so tell the start simply as 1976.

Pierre Yves joined his father in 1988; Olivier followed in 1990. By Wine Anorak's 2024 account Pierre-Yves looks after the vines and Olivier makes the wine, the estate is certified sustainable (HVE), and two of its blocks, La Cra and La Frasière, are farmed organically.

Château London is not Fichet's invention but a reputed slope of Igé, which Domaine des Roches and Jean-Claude Boisset also bottle. Boisset's account of the name is the one to tell: its original owner lived on the rue Landon in Paris, and over time Landon became London. So there is no castle, and nothing to do with England.

Fichet's Château London comes from old vines; a listing of the 2018 gives the oldest as 86 years old. Wine Anorak found the 2023 about nine parts stainless steel to one part older oak, a little barrel for roundness beside the freshness of the steel. How the 2024 we pour was made is a question for the sommelier.

components.name: Domaine du Roc des Boutires
components.explain:
Domaine du Roc des Boutires is a small Pouilly-Fuissé estate in the shadow of the Roche de Solutré, the limestone rock that stands over the appellation. Its name joins the rock to Aux Bouthières, the climat at its heart, promoted to premier cru in 2020; a boutière was an old track mule drivers used to carry oil and wine.

The Parinet family of Château du Moulin-à-Vent, in Beaujolais, bought its grapes from 2011 and the domaine in 2016, and the wine is made at Romanèche-Thorins, which the appellation allows.

Our En Bertilionne 2020 comes from one small, high parcel facing east-south-east, aged partly in barrel: round, textured Chardonnay for the crab claws.

card.front: Where does the name Roc des Boutires come from?
card.back: From the Roche de Solutré, the rock over Pouilly-Fuissé, and the Aux Bouthières climat; a boutière was an old mule track for carrying oil and wine.

producer.who: Domaine du Roc des Boutires, a small Pouilly-Fuissé estate beneath the Roche de Solutré

producer.history:
Domaine du Roc des Boutires is a small estate in Pouilly-Fuissé, the best known appellation of the Mâconnais, lying in the shadow of the Roche de Solutré, the great limestone rock that stands over the vineyards. Its importer explains the name as terroir and tradition together: the rock, and the climat of Aux Bouthières at the estate's heart. In old French, a boutière was a secondary road that mule drivers used to carry oil and wine through remote country. Aux Bouthières was one of the twenty-two sites promoted to premier cru in 2020.

The vines are Chardonnay on a strip of Jurassic limestone, mostly planted in the early 1970s. The present chapter began with the Parinet family, owners of Château du Moulin-à-Vent in Beaujolais since 2009: they bought the estate's grapes as must from 2011 and the domaine itself in 2016. With no cellar in the village, the grapes travel to Romanèche-Thorins, one of the villages the Pouilly-Fuissé rules allow to make the wine.

En Bertilionne, our bottle, comes from a single small plot high on the slope, at about 350 metres, facing east-south-east on limestone with marl. It is aged partly in barrel, the share changing with the vintage, and the 2020 now has several years in bottle.

components.name: Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon
components.explain:
Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon, the heirs of Count Lafon, is the Mâconnais estate of the Lafon family of Domaine des Comtes Lafon in Meursault. Dominique Lafon bought a small domaine at Milly-Lamartine in September 1999 and brought organic and biodynamic farming with him. It grew to Uchizy and Chardonnay in 2003, Viré-Clessé in 2009, and Saint-Véran and Pouilly-Fuissé in 2014.

Milly added Lamartine to its name in 1902, for the poet Alphonse de Lamartine, its one-time mayor, who owned an estate there.

Our Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine 2023 is the Lafon name at a gentler price: round pear and lemon with a chalky freshness for the crab and corn omelette.

card.front: Whose estate is Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon?
card.back: The Mâconnais estate of the Lafon family of Meursault, bought at Milly-Lamartine in 1999 and farmed biodynamically. We pour its Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine.

producer.history:
Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon, the heirs of Count Lafon, is the Mâconnais estate of the Lafon family, whose Domaine des Comtes Lafon in Meursault is one of the great names of white Burgundy. The Meursault domaine goes back to Jules Lafon, who built it after his marriage in 1894.

In September 1999 Dominique Lafon, by then in charge in Meursault, bought a small domaine at Milly-Lamartine and brought organic and biodynamic farming with him. The estate grew in steps: Uchizy and Chardonnay in 2003, Viré-Clessé in 2009, and Saint-Véran and Pouilly-Fuissé in 2014. A merchant calls it the baby brother of the Meursault domaine.

Milly itself carries a famous name. The poet Alphonse de Lamartine, whose family house there dates to 1705, was mayor of the village and owned an estate there, and in 1902 Lamartine was added to the village's name.

Our bottle is the village Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine. The estate's named Milly parcel, the Clos du Four, faces east and is raised with native yeasts in large barrels; how our village wine was made is a question for the sommelier.

components.name: Jean-Paul & Benoît Droin
components.explain:
Jean-Paul & Benoît Droin is a Chablis family estate whose growers can be traced with certainty to 1620; Benoît is counted the fourteenth generation. His father Jean-Paul joined in 1965 and built the modern reputation. Benoît, at the domaine since 1999 and in full charge since 2014, has moved away from new oak, keeping tank for some wines and a share of barrel for others.

The family holds five of the seven grands crus. Our Vaillons 2023 is its premier cru blended from five climats on the left bank of the Serein: lemon and chalk with a little more depth than village Chablis.

card.front: How many of the seven Chablis grands crus does the Droin family hold?
card.back: Five: Blanchot, Valmur, Vaudésir, Grenouilles and Les Clos. We pour their Vaillons premier cru; the list also carries Valmur, Vaudésir and Hommage à Louis.

producer.who: Jean-Paul and Benoît Droin, father and son of a Chablis family traced to 1620
producer.where: Chablis, Burgundy, France
producer.founded: A family of Chablis growers since at least 1620
producer.history:
The Droin family have been growers in Chablis for centuries. Benoît Droin can trace his winemaking ancestors with certainty to 1620, and a record of 1547 may take the family back further; he is counted the fourteenth generation.

His father, Jean-Paul, joined the estate in 1965 and built its modern reputation. Benoît joined in 1999 and took full charge when Jean-Paul retired in 2014. He has steered the cellar away from new oak: the Petit Chablis, the Chablis and some premiers and grands crus are made in tank, others see a quarter to a half in barrel, and new oak in the grands crus stops at about a tenth.

The estate holds five of the seven Chablis grands crus, Blanchot, Valmur, Vaudésir, Grenouilles and Les Clos, with a spread of premiers crus. Its Hommage à Louis is a single parcel where Les Clos meets Valmur, named by the family for an ancestor, Louis.

Vaillons, our bottle, blends five climats within the premier cru, Epinottes, Roncières, Séchet, Chatains and Beugnons, on the left bank of the Serein. In 2022 about a fifth of it saw oak and the rest stayed in tank. Young it shows white flowers and iodine; with age, oyster shell.

components.name: Domaine René et Vincent Dauvissat
components.explain:
Domaine René et Vincent Dauvissat, now known as Domaine Vincent Dauvissat, is the family domaine that stands with Raveneau at the top of Chablis. Robert Dauvissat was among the first growers to bottle his own Chablis, in 1931; his son René built the reputation from about 1950, and René's son Vincent worked beside him from 1976 and took the lead in 1989.

The two great families are linked by marriage: Robert's daughter Andrée married François Raveneau. The wines age in old barrels, including the small Chablis feuillette, and taste of stone rather than wood.

Our Les Preuses 2015, from a block planted in 1970, has years in bottle: the grandest bottle for the oysters.

card.front: How are the Dauvissat and Raveneau families of Chablis linked?
card.back: By marriage: Andrée Dauvissat, René's sister, married François Raveneau, who founded his domaine in 1948. They remain separate estates, together at the top of Chablis.

producer.who: Domaine René et Vincent Dauvissat, now Domaine Vincent Dauvissat, a reference estate of Chablis
producer.where: Chablis, Burgundy, France
producer.founded: 1931, when Robert Dauvissat began bottling his own Chablis (one source says the 1920s)
producer.history:
The Dauvissat family's domaine is one of the two reference estates of Chablis, named again and again beside Raveneau; Clive Coates places it near the Raveneau brothers at the top of the Chablis hierarchy.

Its modern story starts in 1931, when Robert Dauvissat was among the first growers to bottle his own Chablis. His son René began around 1950 and built the estate's reputation, adding grand and premier cru parcels. René's son Vincent worked beside his father from 1976 and took the lead in 1989, and the fourth generation, Ghislain, joined in 2013. A merchant says the domaine was previously called René et Vincent Dauvissat and is now run entirely by Vincent; our list prints the 2015 under the old name and the 2023s as Vincent Dauvissat.

The family is tied to its great neighbour by marriage: Robert's daughter Andrée married François Raveneau, and the domaine he founded in 1948 drew on Dauvissat parcels. The two estates are separate, as is Jean et Sébastien Dauvissat, another branch of the wider family.

Dauvissat holds the grands crus Les Clos and Les Preuses and premiers crus including La Forest, Séchet and Vaillons. The wines age in old barrels, including the feuillette, the small traditional Chablis cask, over a long élevage, so they gain texture without tasting of oak. Les Preuses, our bottle, comes from a single block planted in 1970; Decanter finds it perhaps less powerful but more elegant than Les Clos.

components.name: Domaine François Raveneau
components.explain:
Domaine François Raveneau is the name Chablis collectors ask for first. François Raveneau founded it in 1948, joining vines he bought to parcels from his wife's family, the Dauvissats, and was the first in his family to bottle at the estate. His sons Jean-Marie and Bernard followed him; since 2020 and 2021 their children, Isabelle and Maxime, have run it.

The wines are raised in barrels and feuillettes with little or no new oak. Montée de Tonnerre, our bottle, is the domaine's biggest wine and its flagship, from Chapelot and Pied d'Aloup beside the grand cru slope: intense, stony Premier Cru with real grip.

card.front: Who founded Domaine Raveneau, and how is it tied to Dauvissat?
card.back: François Raveneau, in 1948, with vines of his own and parcels from his wife's family, the Dauvissats. The two great Chablis estates are linked by that marriage.

producer.who: Domaine François Raveneau, the cult family domaine of Chablis
producer.where: Chablis, Burgundy, France
producer.history:
Domaine François Raveneau is the name Chablis collectors ask for first; a Decanter profile calls its wine Chablis' greatest. It is a family domaine through and through.

François Raveneau founded it in 1948, joining vineyards he bought to parcels from the family of his wife, Andrée Dauvissat. He was the first of his family to bottle at the estate instead of selling grapes to merchants, and by Decanter's account he bottled at the domaine from the 1960s. His son Jean-Marie joined him in 1978, and the estate passed to Jean-Marie and his brother Bernard; the sources differ on the year.

A new generation has since taken over. Bernard retired at the start of 2020 in favour of his daughter Isabelle, who had joined in 2010, and Jean-Marie in 2021 in favour of his son Maxime, who had joined in 2017. The two are first cousins.

The wines are raised in barrels and feuillettes with little or no new wood, so the stone of Chablis comes first. Montée de Tonnerre is the biggest cuvée and the flagship, from parcels in Chapelot, at the foot of the slope, and Pied d'Aloup, at the top. Only in a very large vintage is Chapelot bottled on its own; by Isabelle Raveneau's account the last time was 2018. She calls Montée de Tonnerre a very sapid, grippy wine.

components.name: Domaine Louis Michel
components.explain:
Domaine Louis Michel, labelled Louis Michel & Fils, is the Chablis family estate best known for making every wine without oak. The domaine dates to 1850. Louis Michel brought it to prominence, followed by his son Jean-Loup, and then by Jean-Loup's nephew Guillaume Gicqueau-Michel, who came to Chablis in 2007.

Until about 1970 the wines were made in old oak; by 1980 the barrels were gone and everything was made in stainless steel, the grands crus included, so the wines taste of chalk and lemon rather than wood.

We pour its village Chablis and a Montmains Premier Cru half-bottle: crisp, mineral partners for the redfish and the crab.

card.front: What sets Domaine Louis Michel apart in Chablis?
card.back: No oak at all: since about 1980 every wine, the grands crus included, is made in stainless steel. We pour its village Chablis and a Montmains Premier Cru half-bottle.

components.name: JM Sélèque
components.explain:
JM Sélèque is a family grower in Pierry, a premier cru village just south of Épernay known for its Meunier. Henri Sélèque, who came to France from Poland, planted the first vines in 1965 and sold his first bottles in 1969; his son Richard took over in 1975. Henri’s grandson Jean-Marc came home in 2008 after working in the Napa and Yarra valleys, and has moved the vines to organic farming, partly biodynamic since 2010, without seeking certification.

Our bottle is Solessence, his blend of seven villages: led by Chardonnay, with Meunier and a little Pinot Noir, part fermented in oak, with a perpetual reserve and very little sugar. At $100 it is one of the gentlest prices among our grower bottles, and a first pick for the Fried Pickles.

components.name: Pierre Paillard
components.explain:
Pierre Paillard is a family grower in Bouzy, a Grand Cru village of the Montagne de Reims famous for its Pinot Noir. The Paillards have made wine there for more than two hundred years, since an ancestor, Antoine Paillard, became a winegrower in Bouzy in the second half of the eighteenth century. Benoît Paillard, son of Pierre, ran the cellar from 1973, and Benoît’s sons, the brothers Antoine and Quentin, the eighth generation, took over from him in the 2010s. They farm only Bouzy Grand Cru vines, organically.

Our bottle is Les Parcelles XVIII, about 70 percent Pinot Noir and 30 percent Chardonnay, built on the 2018 harvest with reserve wine and finished Extra Brut: 0 to 6 grams of sugar per liter in the finished wine. The Roman numeral is that base year. It is the sweet spot bottle for the Louisiana Oysters.

card.front: What does the XVIII on Pierre Paillard Les Parcelles mean?
card.back: The base harvest, 2018, topped up with reserve wine. It is Grand Cru Champagne from Bouzy, about 70 percent Pinot Noir, and very dry.

What all agree on is more than two hundred years of winemaking in one of the most famous Pinot Noir villages of Champagne, a Grand Cru on the Montagne de Reims.

Benoît Paillard, son of Pierre, ran the cellar from 1973, and his sons, the brothers Antoine and Quentin, the eighth generation, took the domaine over from him in the 2010s; sources give different years. They farm only Bouzy Grand Cru vines, mostly Pinot Noir with Chardonnay, organically, with composts and plant infusions instead of synthetic sprays, and in the cellar they leave out chaptalisation, enzymes and cold stabilisation.

Les Parcelles is their non-vintage Grand Cru, a blend of the family’s Bouzy parcels. The XVIII is built on the 2018 harvest with reserve wine, about 70 percent Pinot Noir and 30 percent Chardonnay, and finished Extra Brut, a finished wine sugar category rather than a stated dosage. La Grande Récolte, the vintage-dated wine, sits beside it on our list.

components.name: Chartogne-Taillet
components.explain:
Chartogne-Taillet is a family grower in Merfy, a village on the Massif de Saint-Thierry north-west of Reims, where the Taillets have grown vines for centuries; an ancestor, Fiacre Taillet, kept a register of his life, his vines and the events of his day. Alexandre Chartogne, who worked with Anselme Selosse, took over from his parents in 2006 and is known for bottling single parcels apart, such as Les Barres, ungrafted Meunier planted in 1952 in deep sand over chalk.

Our bottle is the Rosé Brut: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, coloured with a little red wine from Merfy Pinot Noir, dry and savoury. It is the sweet spot bottle for the Steak Tartare Cannoli, and our list carries Cuvée Saint Anne and two single parcels beside it.

card.front: What is unusual about the Les Barres vines at Chartogne-Taillet?
card.back: They are ungrafted Meunier, planted in 1952 in sand almost three metres deep over chalk, where phylloxera struggles. Alexandre Chartogne bottles the parcel on its own.

Chartogne-Taillet is a family grower in Merfy, a quiet village on the southern slopes of the Massif de Saint-Thierry, north-west of Reims; Decanter calls it the only récoltant-manipulant, a grower who makes its own wine, in the village. The Taillet family has grown vines in Merfy for centuries, and an ancestor, Fiacre Taillet, kept a register of his life, his work and the events of his day. The Chartogne-Taillet name joins two families by marriage.

Alexandre Chartogne worked with Anselme Selosse in Avize before taking over from his parents, Philippe and Elisabeth, in 2006, when he was in his early twenties. He set out to show what Merfy’s soils say: sand and clay over chalk, the sand in Les Barres almost three metres deep. Les Barres is a parcel of ungrafted Meunier planted in 1952, the sand credited with keeping phylloxera away; Orizeaux, on more chalky ground, is another of his single-parcel bottlings.

Cuvée Sainte Anne, which our list prints as Saint Anne, is the blend that introduces the estate and the village. The rosé, our bottle, joins Pinot Noir and Chardonnay and takes its colour from a little red wine made from Merfy Pinot Noir; published blends differ, so the proportions are the sommelier’s to give.

components.name: Larmandier-Bernier
components.explain:
Larmandier-Bernier is a family grower in Vertus, the premier cru village at the southern end of the Côte des Blancs. The house began with the marriage of Philippe Larmandier and Elisabeth Bernier in 1971: she brought her Vertus vineyards, and they built their cellar there. Pierre Larmandier took over in 1988 and, with his wife Sophie, gave up herbicides in 1992 and farmed the whole estate biodynamically from 1999, fermenting with the grapes’ own yeasts. Their sons, Arthur and then Georges, have worked with them since 2017.

Our bottle is Longitude, a Premier Cru Blanc de Blancs named for its four villages, Vertus, Oger, Avize and Cramant, which lie close to the fourth meridian. A perpetual reserve begun in 2004 adds depth, and a very low dosage keeps it bone dry: the sweet spot bottle for the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters.

card.front: Why is Larmandier-Bernier’s Champagne called Longitude?
card.back: Its Chardonnay comes from four Côte des Blancs villages, Vertus, Oger, Avize and Cramant, which lie close to the fourth meridian. It is a biodynamic grower’s Premier Cru Blanc de Blancs.

components.name: Jacques Selosse
components.explain:
Jacques Selosse is the Avize estate, in a Grand Cru village of the Côte des Blancs, that changed modern Champagne. Jacques Selosse founded the domaine with his wife in 1949. Their son Anselme trained at the wine school in Beaune, joined in 1974 and took over in 1980, and made Champagne the way Burgundy makes white wine, fermenting and ageing it in oak barrels from his own grand cru vines. A generation of growers, Alexandre Chartogne among them, learned from him. His solera wine, Substance, was first called Origine.

Our bottle is Initial, a Grand Cru Blanc de Blancs blended from three consecutive harvests from Avize, Cramant and Oger; our list prints its disgorgement date, 10.16.23. Rare and intense, it wants a white-wine glass and time to open.

card.front: Why do growers call Anselme Selosse their teacher?
card.back: Taking over in Avize in 1980, he made Champagne like white Burgundy, fermenting in oak barrels, and a generation of growers, Alexandre Chartogne among them, trained with him or followed him.

Jacques Selosse created the domaine in Avize, a Grand Cru village of the Côte des Blancs, with his wife in 1949, and in 1964 he made wine from part of his own grapes for the first time. Their son Anselme studied at the Lycée viticole de Beaune, came home in 1974 to try his ideas on his father’s vines, and took the domaine over in 1980 with his wife, Corinne.

What Anselme brought back from Burgundy changed Champagne. He fermented and aged his wines in oak barrels, as a great white Burgundy domaine would, from his own grand cru vines in Avize, Cramant and Oger. In the mid-1980s he began a solera on the model of Jerez, a store of wine refreshed with every harvest; first called Origine, it is now Substance. Growers across the region followed him, and Alexandre Chartogne of Merfy worked with him before taking over his own family estate.

The family welcomes guests at Les Avisés, a hotel and restaurant above the cellars in Avize, and Anselme’s son, Guillaume Selosse, also makes small lots under his own name. Initial, our bottle, is the Grand Cru Blanc de Blancs that opens the range, blended from three consecutive harvests.

components.name: Tribaut-Schloesser
components.explain:
Tribaut-Schloesser is a family Champagne house in Romery, a village near Hautvillers close to the Marne valley. Its first bottles were made in 1929, and the guides tell the founding two ways: Hachette credits René Schloesser, a Luxembourger married to a Champagne grower, while Sommeliers International tells of the union of Jean Tribaut and Suzanne Schloesser. The brand took the Tribaut-Schloesser name in 1950, and the third generation took négociant status, so the house may buy grapes as well as grow them.

Our bottle is Origine, a Meunier-led Brut with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir and some oak-aged reserve wine: fresh pear, plum and a touch of brioche. It comes as a half-bottle, the right size for two at the Roost Bar with the Creole Spiced Nuts.

components.name: Veuve Fourny et Fils
components.explain:
Veuve Fourny et Fils is a family house in Vertus, the premier cru village at the southern end of the Côte des Blancs. The Fourny family has grown vines in Vertus since 1856 and, by Hachette, made Champagne since 1930. The name means the widow Fourny and sons: Madame Fourny kept the house going and gave it her name, and her sons Emmanuel and Charles-Henry, the fifth generation, took over in 1993. They make low-dosage wines from parcels across the Vertus premier cru, among them the tiny walled Clos Faubourg Notre-Dame.

We carry two half-bottles: the Premier Cru Blanc de Blancs Extra Brut, all Vertus Chardonnay and bone dry, for the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters, and the Premier Cru Rosé Brut, for the Steak Tartare Cannoli. It has nothing to do with Veuve Clicquot.

card.front: Who is the widow in Veuve Fourny et Fils?
card.back: Madame Fourny, who kept the Vertus house going and gave it her name; her sons Emmanuel and Charles-Henry took over in 1993. It is not Veuve Clicquot.

producer.history:
The Fourny family has grown vines in Vertus, the premier cru village at the southern end of the Côte des Blancs, since 1856, and by Hachette’s account has made Champagne since 1930. The house’s own story names three people it inherited from: Albert, the grandfather, his son Roger, and Madame Veuve Fourny, the widow who kept the house going and gave the brand her name. Veuve is French for widow, and et Fils means and sons.

Her sons, Emmanuel and Charles-Henry Fourny, took over in 1993 as the fifth generation: Emmanuel as oenologist, in the vines and the cellar, and Charles-Henry running the house, with their mother’s support. They work many lieux-dits in the Vertus premier cru and aim for the purest expression of grape and place, with low dosage. Their rarest vineyard is the Clos Faubourg Notre-Dame, a tiny walled plot in Vertus that they bottle on its own.

Our two half-bottles show the range at its simplest: the Blanc de Blancs Extra Brut, all Vertus Chardonnay, and the Premier Cru Rosé Brut, whose blend and colouring the sommelier confirms. The list’s bigger bottles, Monts de Vertus and the Vinothèque MV2000 magnum, are the collector’s end.

components.name: Pierre Péters
components.explain:
Pierre Péters is a family grower in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, the Grand Cru village of the Côte des Blancs most famous for Chardonnay. The family has been in the village since the nineteenth century; Camille Péters began bottling the estate’s own Champagne early in the twentieth century, the family bought plots in Les Chétillons in 1930, and the first bottles under the Pierre Péters name followed in 1946. The wines draw on a perpetual reserve, a store of older wines topped up every harvest, whose oldest layer goes back to 1988; Rodolphe Péters took over from his father, François, in 2008.

Our bottle is the Cuvée de Réserve in magnum: all Grand Cru Chardonnay, mostly Le Mesnil with Oger, Cramant and Avize, chalky and creamy, ten to twelve glasses for a celebrating table.

card.front: What is the perpetual reserve in Pierre Péters Cuvée de Réserve?
card.back: A store of older wines, its oldest layer from 1988, topped up each harvest and blended back for depth. The Cuvée de Réserve is all Grand Cru Chardonnay from the Côte des Blancs.

Camille Péters began bottling the estate’s own Champagne early in the twentieth century, and in 1930 the family bought plots in Les Chétillons, a lieu-dit of Le Mesnil that became its most famous wine, bottled on its own since 1971.

Camille died in 1944, and the first bottles labelled Pierre Péters followed in 1946. Pierre passed the estate to his second son, François, in 1967, and François’s son Rodolphe, the sixth generation, worked on the blends from 2000 and took over in 2008. The house keeps a perpetual reserve, a store of older wines topped up with each harvest, and its oldest layer goes back to 1988.

components.name: Louis Roederer and Cristal
components.explain:
Louis Roederer is a family Champagne house in Reims that dates itself to 1776 and takes its name from Louis Roederer, who inherited the firm in 1833. In 1876 it created Cristal for Tsar Alexander II of Russia, in a clear, flat-bottomed bottle; after the Russian monarchy fell in 1917 the wine vanished, and the house made it again for sale from 1945.

Roederer’s strength is its own vineyards: Cristal and the other vintage wines come only from them, and the 2012 Cristal was the first made wholly from biodynamically farmed grapes. Collection is the house blend that replaced Brut Premier; its number counts the harvests, so 244 is built on 2019 with a perpetual reserve.

We pour Collection 244 at $120 and Cristal 2015 at $775: one house, two very different occasions. Keep the clear Cristal bottle out of the light.

card.front: Why is Cristal in a clear bottle, and who was it made for?
card.back: It was created in 1876 for Tsar Alexander II of Russia, who wanted a clear bottle. Louis Roederer of Reims still bottles Cristal in clear glass, so keep it out of the light.

producer.who: Louis Roederer, the family Champagne house in Reims that makes Cristal

producer.history:
Louis Roederer dates itself to 1776, to a Reims wine business that traded at first as Dubois Père et Fils. Louis Roederer, born in 1809, joined his uncle’s firm in 1827, inherited it in 1833 and gave it his own name.

In 1876 the house created Cristal for Tsar Alexander II of Russia, in a clear, flat-bottomed bottle; the story told is that the Tsar feared assassination and wanted nothing hidden in the glass. When the Russian monarchy fell in 1917 the wine disappeared, and Roederer made it again for sale from 1945.

Camille Olry-Roederer ran the house from 1932, after her husband Léon died, until the mid-1970s, and bought vineyards in the best villages whenever she could. Those vines are the house’s signature: Cristal and the other vintage wines are made only from Roederer’s own vineyards, and the 2012 Cristal was the first made entirely from biodynamically farmed grapes. The house describes itself as family owned.

Its non-vintage is Collection, which replaced Brut Premier. The number counts the house’s harvests: Collection 244 is built on 2019, Roederer’s 244th, blended with a perpetual reserve begun in 2012 and a little oak-aged wine. Cristal 2015 is 60 percent Pinot Noir and 40 percent Chardonnay.

components.name: Veuve Clicquot and the widow
components.explain:
Veuve Clicquot was founded in Reims in 1772 by Philippe Clicquot, a textile merchant. When his son died in 1805, the son’s widow, Barbe-Nicole Clicquot Ponsardin, took over at 27: veuve is French for widow. The house credits her with the first vintage Champagne in 1810, the riddling table in 1816, which gathers the yeast in the neck of the bottle so it can be removed, and the first blended rosé in 1818.

Yellow Label, whose label merchants date to 1877, is the house Brut: Pinot Noir-led with Meunier and Chardonnay and a large share of reserve wine, round, toasty and generous. The label looks orange; the house calls it yellow.

At $155 it is the name many guests ask for first, so know it well and say yes with confidence.

card.front: What does Veuve mean, and what is the widow Clicquot credited with?
card.back: Veuve is French for widow. Barbe-Nicole Clicquot, widowed in 1805, is credited with the riddling table in 1816 and the first blended rosé in 1818.

producer.who: Veuve Clicquot, the Reims house named for the widow Clicquot
producer.where: Reims, Champagne, France

producer.history:
Veuve Clicquot was founded in Reims in 1772 by Philippe Clicquot, a textile merchant. When his son died in 1805, the son’s widow, Barbe-Nicole Clicquot Ponsardin, took over the house at 27 and renamed it Veuve Clicquot Ponsardin: veuve is French for widow.

The house credits her with three firsts: a vintage Champagne in 1810; the riddling table in 1816 (one merchant adds her cellar master, Antoine-Aloys de Muller), which gathers the yeast in the neck of the bottle so it can be removed; and in 1818 a rosé made by blending red wine from Bouzy into the Champagne, the method most houses still use. The house quotes her line that black grapes give the finest white wines, and Pinot Noir is still its heart.

The yellow label dates from 1877, when, by a merchant's account, it was registered as a trademark for a British market that wanted dry wine. Retailers describe the wine as Pinot Noir-led, with Meunier and Chardonnay from many crus and a large share of reserve wine. The prestige La Grande Dame, named for her, began with the 1962 vintage and was released in 1972 for the bicentenary.

In 2010 divers off the Åland Islands raised bottles of Veuve Clicquot from a nineteenth-century wreck in the Baltic. Louis Vuitton bought the house in 1986, the year before LVMH was formed.

components.name: Charles Heidsieck, Champagne Charlie
components.explain:
Charles Heidsieck was founded in Reims in 1851 by Charles-Camille Heidsieck, whom a New York paper named Champagne Charlie after he took his wine to America from 1852. In 1862, collecting debts in the South, he was arrested in Union-held New Orleans and held for months, at Fort Jackson, Louisiana, by most accounts, before his release.

In 1867 he bought chalk cellars, crayères, under Reims; they still age the wines. The style rests on reserve wine: the Brut Réserve, which our list prints as Réserve Brut, carries around 40 percent older reserve wines and at least three years on its lees, so it tastes rich, nutty and toasty.

Piper-Heidsieck is a separate house with the same family name and, since 2011, the same owner.

card.front: Which Champagne founder was arrested in New Orleans? Why is his Brut Réserve rich?
card.back: Charles-Camille Heidsieck, Champagne Charlie, arrested in Union-held New Orleans in 1862. His house's Brut Réserve carries around 40 percent older reserve wines and long ageing on its lees.

producer.who: Charles Heidsieck, the Reims house of Champagne Charlie

producer.history:
Charles Heidsieck was founded in Reims in 1851 by Charles-Camille Heidsieck, then about 29. Two other houses carry the Heidsieck name, Piper-Heidsieck and Heidsieck & Co Monopole, and they are separate.

He sailed to the United States in 1852 and was among the first to sell his own Champagne there; a New York paper named him Champagne Charlie. The Civil War nearly ruined him. Going south in 1862 to collect debts, he was arrested in Union-held New Orleans, suspected over letters or a French consular pouch he carried, and held for months, at Fort Jackson, Louisiana, by most accounts (one says Fort Pickens in Florida). He was freed, in November 1862 by one account, after appeals that several accounts say reached President Lincoln, and went home sick and bankrupt.

In 1867 he bought chalk crayères beneath Reims rather than vineyards. They still age the house’s wines, and one source says they became part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2015.

The style rests on reserve wine. The Brut Réserve, printed on our list as Réserve Brut, blends about 60 crus with around 40 percent reserve wines, averaging about ten years old, and spends at least three years on its lees. EPI, the Descours family group, bought the house with Piper-Heidsieck from Rémy Cointreau in 2011.

components.name: Armand de Brignac, the Ace of Spades
components.explain:
Armand de Brignac, the Ace of Spades, is made by the Cattier family of Chigny-les-Roses on the Montagne de Reims, who have owned vines there since 1763. By the family’s account the name came from a character in a novel, registered decades before it was used.

Brut Gold was released in 2006 and reached the world that October in Jay-Z’s video Show Me What You Got. A company led by Jay-Z bought the brand in 2014 and sold half to Moët Hennessy in 2021.

The bottle is the show: metallised gold with a pewter ace of spades applied by hand. Inside, about 40 percent each Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with 20 percent Meunier, from three harvests: ripe, round and creamy. Present it label out, and ice it well; the gold bottle hides the wine and chills slowly.

card.front: Who makes Armand de Brignac, and why is it called Ace of Spades?
card.back: The Cattier family of Chigny-les-Roses, who have owned vines there since 1763. The nickname comes from the pewter ace of spades on its metallised gold bottle.

producer.history:
Armand de Brignac is a young brand made by an old family. The Cattiers have owned vines at Chigny-les-Roses, on the Montagne de Reims, since 1763, and began bottling their own Champagne after Jean Cattier came home wounded from the front in 1916 (one source says 1918). By the family’s own account, the name Armand de Brignac was registered in the late 1940s or early 1950s, taken from a character in a novel, and then lay unused.

In the early 2000s the family and Sovereign Brands of New York built a prestige cuvée around it, and Brut Gold was released in 2006. It reached a world audience that October in Jay-Z’s video Show Me What You Got, after his public break with Cristal. A company led by Jay-Z bought the brand from Sovereign Brands in November 2014, and in February 2021 he sold half of it to Moët Hennessy.

The bottle is the signature: metallised gold, with a French pewter ace of spades label applied and polished by hand, hence the nickname Ace of Spades. Brut Gold blends about 40 percent Pinot Noir, 40 percent Chardonnay and 20 percent Meunier from three harvests, and it ages in the Cattier cellars, about 30 metres down and among the deepest in Champagne.

components.name: Dom Pérignon and the plénitudes
components.explain:
Dom Pérignon is the prestige vintage Champagne of Moët & Chandon, named for Dom Pierre Pérignon, the Benedictine monk of the abbey of Hautvillers who died in 1715. He was a pioneer of quality, not the inventor of Champagne. The name came to Moët in a 1927 dowry, and the first vintage, 1921, was launched in 1936.

It is always a vintage and always Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. The house holds that each vintage passes through three peaks it calls plénitudes, and releases some vintages again at the later ones: the first after at least eight years on the lees, P2 after many more, P3 after decades.

Our P2 2006, at $1260, is the same 2006 kept about fifteen years on its lees before disgorging, by a retailer's account: deeper and toastier than the first release.

card.front: What does P2 mean on a Dom Pérignon?
card.back: Plénitude 2: the same vintage released a second time, after many more years on its lees. Ours is the 2006, deeper and toastier than the first release.

producer.who: Dom Pérignon, the prestige vintage Champagne of Moët & Chandon
producer.where: Épernay, Champagne, France; named for the monk of the abbey of Hautvillers
producer.founded: First vintage 1921, launched by Moët & Chandon in 1936
producer.history:
Dom Pérignon takes its name from Dom Pierre Pérignon, the Benedictine monk of the abbey of Hautvillers, near Épernay, who died in 1715. He was a pioneer of quality; contrary to the popular myth, he did not discover the Champagne method.

The name first belonged to Champagne Mercier, which never used it. It came to Moët & Chandon in 1927 as part of a dowry, when Francine Durand-Mercier married Comte Paul Chandon-Moët. Moët launched Dom Pérignon as its prestige cuvée in 1936 with the 1921 vintage, which sailed to New York on the SS Normandie. Until the 1943 vintage it was Moët vintage Champagne moved into the special bottle after long cellaring.

It is always a vintage, always Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, drawn from grand cru villages and, by most accounts, one premier cru, Hautvillers. The house holds that each vintage passes through three peaks, plénitudes, and releases some vintages again at the later ones: the first after at least eight years on the lees, P2 after roughly twelve to fifteen years or more, and P3 after decades. The late releases were sold as Oenothèque until 2014, when they became Plénitude. A retailer gives our 2006 P2 about fifteen years on its lees.

The name came to Moët & Chandon in 1927, in the dowry of Francine Durand-Mercier on her marriage to Comte Paul Chandon-Moët.
The first vintage, 1921, was launched in 1936 and sailed to New York on the SS Normandie.
Always vintage and always Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; sources name Hautvillers as the only premier cru beside the grands crus.
The house sees three peaks, plénitudes, in a vintage’s life: the first after at least eight years on the lees, P2 after many more, P3 after decades.
The late releases were called Oenothèque until 2014, when they were renamed Plénitude.
A retailer gives the 2006 P2 about fifteen years on its lees before it was disgorged.

P2 is not a different wine: it is the same 2006, disgorged later after many more years on its lees. Say so plainly when a guest asks.
Never say Dom Pérignon invented Champagne; say the monk was a pioneer of quality.
Dom Pérignon is Moët & Chandon’s prestige wine, not a separate old house; the list also holds Dom Pérignon Rosé 2009 for a guest who wants pink.

components.name: Salon, one wine only
components.explain:
Salon makes one wine: Chardonnay from the grand cru village of Le Mesnil-sur-Oger in the Côte des Blancs, from a single year, and only in years the house declares. Eugène-Aimé Salon made his first vintage, 1905, for his own use; the first sold was 1921, and by one account Maxim’s in Paris was its only commercial outlet until the 1950s.

The grapes come from the house’s own one-hectare Jardin de Salon and about nineteen village parcels. The wine is made without malolactic fermentation, keeping its sharp acidity, and rests about ten years before release. In undeclared years the fruit goes to Delamotte, its sister house, also on our list.

Salon has belonged to Laurent-Perrier since 1988 or 1989. Our 2013 is $2080: serve it in a white-wine glass and let it open.

card.front: What makes Salon unlike any other Champagne house?
card.back: It makes one wine only: Chardonnay from Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, from a single year, made only in declared years and rested about a decade. The first vintage sold was 1921.

He made his first vintage, 1905, for his own use, bought a hectare of vines in Le Mesnil in 1911, and sold his first commercial vintage, 1921. Fermentation has been in stainless steel since Laurent-Perrier arrived, and the malolactic fermentation is blocked to keep the wine’s sharp acidity. Each vintage rests about ten years before release.
