components.name: Nicolas Feuillatte, the growers’ Champagne
components.explain:
Nicolas Feuillatte is the brand of a growers’ cooperative group at Chouilly, near Épernay. The Centre Vinicole de la Champagne, a group of cooperatives, was founded in 1972 so growers could pool their wine and their sales. Nicolas Feuillatte, a Parisian who built a business in the United States importing African coffee, launched his own Champagne in 1976, and in 1986 the brand passed to the Centre Vinicole.

At the end of 2021 the cooperative merged with Castelnau’s to form Terroirs et Vignerons de Champagne, about 6,000 growers. The house blend, Réserve Exclusive Brut, which our list prints as Réserve, is 40 percent Pinot Noir, 40 percent Meunier and 20 percent Chardonnay: fresh, fruity and easy.

Our half-bottle is $65, a Champagne for two at brunch and the pick for the Eggs Hussarde.

card.front: Who makes Nicolas Feuillatte Champagne?
card.back: The Centre Vinicole de la Champagne at Chouilly, a growers’ cooperative group founded in 1972, which has carried the brand since 1986. Our half-bottle Réserve is fresh and fruity, for two at brunch.

Nicolas Feuillatte is a Champagne brand with two beginnings. The cooperative came first: the Centre Vinicole de la Champagne, a group of cooperatives, was founded in 1972, under Henri Macquart, so that growers could pool their wine and their sales; its home is at Chouilly.

The man was born in Paris in 1926 and built a business in the United States importing African coffee. Back in France, he bought the Domaine de Bouleuse, a vineyard in the Ardre valley near Reims, and in 1976 launched a Champagne under his own name, at first for American friends. In 1986 the brand passed to the Centre Vinicole: one source says he sold it, the house says the two joined forces. Feuillatte died in August 2014, aged 88.

At the end of 2021 the cooperative merged with the one behind Champagne Castelnau to form Terroirs et Vignerons de Champagne, a group of about 6,000 growers at the time.

The house blend, Réserve Exclusive Brut, is 40 percent Pinot Noir, 40 percent Meunier and 20 percent Chardonnay, aged three to four years in the cellars; our list prints it simply as Réserve. components.name: Paul Bara
components.explain:
Paul Bara is a family grower in Bouzy, a grand cru village of the Montagne de Reims famous for Pinot Noir. The family has been in Bouzy since 1833 by most sources, and Paul Bara was the first to sell Champagne under his own name, from the 1950s. As a récoltant-manipulant it makes Champagne only from its own grand cru vines, mostly Pinot Noir, so the wines are full and red-fruited. It belongs to the Club Trésors de Champagne, whose Special Club wines must pass a tasting panel twice.

On Birthday Bubbles we pour its rosé in a half-bottle: about 80 percent Pinot Noir, part of it Bouzy’s own still red wine for colour, and 20 percent Chardonnay. The bottle list adds the Extra Brut and the Special Club white and rosé.

card.front: What makes Paul Bara’s rosé taste of Bouzy?
card.back: It is grand cru Pinot Noir from a Bouzy family grower, coloured with Bouzy Rouge, the village’s own still red wine, with about 20 percent Chardonnay.

Paul Bara was the first of the family to sell Champagne under his own name, from the 1950s. He was also Bouzy’s historian, the author of a book on the village’s people and wines, and an early exporter to the United States.

The estate is a récoltant-manipulant, a grower that makes Champagne only from its own vines: grand cru Bouzy in many small parcels, mostly Pinot Noir with some Chardonnay, and by one guide a little in Verzenay.

The style is Pinot Noir-led and red-fruited. The house belongs to the Club Trésors de Champagne, whose Special Club wines are made only in exceptional years and must pass a tasting panel twice, as base wine and as finished Champagne.

Its Brut Rosé Grand Cru, sold in some markets as the Grand Rosé, is about 80 percent Pinot Noir, including some 12 percent Bouzy Rouge, the village’s still red wine, and 20 percent Chardonnay: ripe, juicy red fruit with a fine bead.

components.name: Weingut Hexamer
components.explain:
Weingut Hexamer is a family estate at Meddersheim on the Nahe, the small Riesling region between the Mosel and the Rhine. Its best known vineyard is the Meddersheimer Rheingrafenberg: the village name first, then the site, as German labels do.

Hexamer makes Riesling both dry and sweet. Our list prints its Altenberg Kabinett 2023, a Rheingrafenberg Trocken 2021, which is dry, and the Rheingrafenberg Spätlese 2010 we pour with the World Famous Bananas Foster. Spätlese means late harvest, riper grapes picked later; this one is sweet.

At sixteen years the fruit has turned to honey, baked apple and apricot, with a little petrol and spice, and the acidity is still bright. Sweet enough for the caramel and rum, sharp enough to cut the butter: the value bottle for that dessert.

card.front: Who is Hexamer, and why does its 2010 Spätlese suit Bananas Foster?
card.back: A family estate at Meddersheim on the Nahe. Its mature Rheingrafenberg Spätlese is sweet and honeyed, with acidity bright enough to cut the butter.

producer.who: Weingut Hexamer, a family estate at Meddersheim on the Nahe

producer.history:
Weingut Hexamer is a family estate at Meddersheim, a village on the Nahe, the small Riesling region between the Mosel and the Rhine. Its best known vineyard is the Meddersheimer Rheingrafenberg; the first word names the village and the second the vineyard, as German labels do.

The Nahe is its own region, with an unusual patchwork of soils, and its Riesling sits between the fine acidity of the Mosel and a fuller, stonier depth. Hexamer works across the ladder: our list prints its Meddersheimer Altenberg Kabinett 2023, its Rheingrafenberg Trocken 2021, which is dry, and the Rheingrafenberg Spätlese 2010 we pour with dessert.

Spätlese means late harvest: riper grapes, picked later. The word fixes ripeness at harvest, not how sweet the finished wine is; this one is made sweet. At sixteen years the fruit has turned to honey, baked apple and apricot, with a little petrol and spice, the marks of mature Riesling, and the acidity that lets Riesling age is still bright.

That acidity is why it works with the World Famous Bananas Foster, flambéed tableside in brown sugar, butter and rum: sweet enough for the caramel, sharp enough to cut the butter, so the dessert tastes lighter. It is the house's value bottle for that dessert.

components.name: Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé
components.explain:
Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé is the great family domaine of Chambolle-Musigny, where the family has held vines since the fifteenth century. It is by far the largest owner of Musigny, the most perfumed of the great Côte de Nuits grand crus, and it also holds Bonnes-Mares and the premier cru Les Amoureuses.

Only the oldest Musigny vines go into the Vieilles Vignes; wine from the younger Musigny vines is sold as Chambolle-Musigny Premier Cru. The style is reserved and firm when young, and the Chambolle perfume arrives only after a decade or more in bottle.

Our bottle is the Musigny Vieilles Vignes 2012, bin 22537, one of the famous names on the red Burgundy pages; the list also carries the domaine’s Bonnes-Mares and Chambolle-Musigny Premier Cru. Recommend decanting, and bring the sommelier.

card.front: What does Vieilles Vignes mean on de Vogüé’s Musigny?
card.back: Old vines: only the domaine’s oldest Musigny vines go into it. Wine from its younger Musigny vines is sold as Chambolle-Musigny Premier Cru.

producer.history:
Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé is the historic domaine of Chambolle-Musigny. The family has held vines in the village since the fifteenth century, and the domaine carries the name of Comte Georges de Vogüé.

Its fame rests on Musigny, the grand cru at the southern end of Chambolle, above the Clos de Vougeot, often called the most perfumed ground in the Côte de Nuits. De Vogüé is by far its largest owner, with roughly two thirds of the vineyard, including all of the parcel called Les Petits Musigny. The domaine also holds Bonnes-Mares, the grand cru that straddles Chambolle-Musigny and Morey-Saint-Denis, and Les Amoureuses, the premier cru just below Musigny that is most often argued for promotion.

The grand vin is the Musigny Vieilles Vignes, from the oldest vines; younger Musigny vines go into the Chambolle-Musigny Premier Cru. Musigny is also the one Côte de Nuits grand cru allowed to make white wine, and de Vogüé is the source of that white: after replanting, the domaine declassified it to Bourgogne Blanc from the 1994 vintage. Whether the white carries the Musigny name again today is a question for the sommelier.

The wines are reserved and tightly wound when young, built on structure rather than early charm, and their Chambolle perfume arrives only with a decade or more in bottle.

components.name: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti
components.explain:
The Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, which guests call DRC, is in Vosne-Romanée and for many collectors the most celebrated wine estate in the world. It owns two grand crus outright, Romanée-Conti and La Tâche, both monopoles, holds parcels of Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant, Grands-Échezeaux and Échezeaux, farms Corton, and makes the whites Le Montrachet and Corton-Charlemagne.

The Romanée-Conti vineyard takes its name from the Prince de Conti, who bought it in 1760. The domaine dates from 1869, and since 1942 it has been run as a société civile by the de Villaine and Leroy families. Its reds are made with whole bunches and long ageing in new oak: perfume and lift rather than weight.

We carry the Échezeaux 2015, La Tâche 2012 and Romanée-Conti 2014 among many vintages. Recognise the request, confirm the bottle and bring the sommelier.

card.front: Which two grand crus does the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti own outright?
card.back: Romanée-Conti and La Tâche, both monopoles. Our Échezeaux comes from a grand cru the domaine shares with other owners, in the commune of Flagey-Échezeaux.

producer.history:
The Domaine de la Romanée-Conti takes its name from its most famous vineyard, which carries the name of the Prince de Conti, who bought it in 1760. The domaine dates from 1869, when Jacques-Marie Duvault-Blochet bought Romanée-Conti, and since 1942 it has been run as a société civile by the de Villaine and Leroy families.

It owns two grand crus entire, Romanée-Conti and La Tâche, both monopoles. La Tâche is the larger: it was enlarged in 1933, when part of the neighbouring Les Gaudichots was absorbed after litigation. The domaine also holds parcels of Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant, Grands-Échezeaux and Échezeaux, a parcel of Le Montrachet, and Corton, leased from 2009, with Corton-Charlemagne from 2019.

Romanée-Conti’s last harvest from ungrafted vines was 1945; it was replanted in 1947, and no wine was made from it again until the early 1950s.

The reds are made with whole bunches and long ageing in new oak that the fruit absorbs completely, and the style is perfume and lift rather than weight. So little is made that the wines are sold in very small allocations.

components.name: Domaine Armand Rousseau
components.explain:
Domaine Armand Rousseau is the family domaine at the head of nearly every list for Gevrey-Chambertin. Armand Rousseau built it in the early twentieth century, and in the 1930s it was among the estates that pioneered bottling and selling under their own name, when most Burgundy still left the cellar in cask for a merchant.

Its grand crus include Chambertin, Chambertin-Clos de Bèze, the walled monopole Clos des Ruchottes, Mazis-Chambertin and Charmes-Chambertin. It also holds the largest share of the premier cru Clos Saint-Jacques, which many rank beside the grand crus. The grapes are destemmed, and the wines are deep and savoury, built on tannin and length.

Our bottle is the Clos Saint-Jacques 2019, bin 23651. It is young: suggest a decant and bring the sommelier.

card.front: Why does Rousseau’s Clos Saint-Jacques sell at grand cru prices?
card.back: A premier cru many rank beside Gevrey’s grand crus; Rousseau holds the largest share among its five owners, and was among the pioneers of estate bottling in the 1930s.

producer.history:
Domaine Armand Rousseau carries the name of the man who built it in Gevrey-Chambertin in the early twentieth century. In the 1930s it was one of the estates that pioneered domaine bottling: it bottled and sold wine under its own name when most Burgundy still left the cellar in cask for a merchant to raise and label. His son Charles Rousseau carried the domaine on.

The holdings read like a map of Gevrey’s best ground. There are parcels of Chambertin and Chambertin-Clos de Bèze, the two crus at the head of the village’s nine grand crus; the Clos des Ruchottes, a walled monopole inside Ruchottes-Chambertin; and Mazis-Chambertin and Charmes-Chambertin. There is also the premier cru Clos Saint-Jacques, routinely argued to deserve grand cru rank. It has five owners, and Rousseau holds the largest share.

The grapes are destemmed. The result is deep, savoury Gevrey, built on tannin and length rather than sweetness, and slow to open.

components.name: Domaine Coudert
components.explain:
Domaine Coudert is the family estate behind the Clos de la Roilette, a vineyard in Fleurie, one of the ten crus of Beaujolais, on the cru’s border with Moulin-à-Vent. The grape is Gamay.

Fleurie is usually the floral, graceful cru, but the Clos de la Roilette gives a firmer, darker wine than most Fleurie, with the depth to age. On our list the wine goes by the name of the clos; Coudert is the family’s name. The list also carries a Moulin-à-Vent under the Domaine Coudert name.

Our bottle is the Clos de la Roilette Fleurie 2023, bin 34574: the value red with the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. Served lightly chilled, its gentle tannin stays calm with the Creole sauce, the tasso and the spice.

card.front: Who makes our Clos de la Roilette Fleurie, and where is the clos?
card.back: The Coudert family. The clos lies in Fleurie on its border with Moulin-à-Vent, and gives a firmer, darker wine than most Fleurie.

Fleurie is the cru Beaujolais lovers think of for floral grace. The Clos de la Roilette is known for something else: a firmer, deeper and darker Fleurie than most, with the structure to age. Our list also carries a Moulin-à-Vent under the Domaine Coudert name.

When the Couderts came to the clos, whether it is still walled or wholly theirs, and how the wine is made, with whole bunches or not and in what vessels it rests, are not in our sources; those are questions for the sommelier.

On our list it is a value bottle with a clear job. Lightly chilled, its gentle tannin and bright fruit stay fresh against tomato, Creole spice and smoky tasso: the easy red for a brunch table.

components.name: Fattoria di Fèlsina
components.explain:
Fattoria di Fèlsina is a Chianti Classico estate at Castelnuovo Berardenga, on the warm southern edge of the zone northeast of Siena, where the Chianti hills meet the Crete Senesi. The Codex dates it from 1966.

It is a Sangiovese house. Its Chianti Classico is all Sangiovese, fermented in steel and aged about a year in medium-size Slavonian casks. Rancia, a single vineyard on a former monastic site, is bottled on its own as a Riserva and is the reference for southern Chianti Classico.

Our list prints four: the Chianti Classico 2022 at $90, our easy Italian red for a mixed table; Rancia Riserva 2019 and 2020 at $165, the serious step up; and Maestro Raro, which the list calls their Cabernet, among the Super Tuscans.

card.front: Where is Fèlsina, and what is Rancia?
card.back: A Chianti Classico estate at Castelnuovo Berardenga, the warm southern edge of the zone near Siena. Rancia is its single vineyard Sangiovese, bottled as a Riserva: the step up from its $90 Chianti Classico.

producer.history:
Fattoria di Fèlsina farms at Castelnuovo Berardenga, the southern extremity of Chianti Classico, northeast of Siena, where the zone meets the clay hills of the Crete Senesi. Chianti Classico is the historic heart of Chianti between Florence and Siena, and this corner is warmer and drier than the northern communes. Fèlsina's Sangiovese is firm, savoury and mineral, with oak in support rather than for flavour. The Codex dates the estate from 1966.

Fèlsina is a Sangiovese house. Its Chianti Classico is all Sangiovese, fermented in stainless steel and aged about twelve months in medium-size Slavonian oak casks; in some markets it is labelled Berardenga. Rancia, a parcel on a former monastic site, is bottled on its own as a Chianti Classico Riserva and is the reference for southern Chianti Classico. Fontalloro, pure Sangiovese from parcels on both sides of the DOCG boundary, must be labelled IGT for geography alone, and Colonia, a Gran Selezione, is the estate's most structured wine.

Our list prints four: the Chianti Classico 2022 at $90, the Rancia Riserva 2019 and 2020 at $165 each, and Maestro Raro 2019, which the wine list calls their Cabernet, among the Super Tuscans.

components.name: Produttori del Barbaresco
components.explain:
Produttori del Barbaresco is the growers' co-operative of the village of Barbaresco, in the Langhe hills of Piedmont: some fifty grower families who bring their Nebbiolo to one cellar. It was founded in 1958 on roots going back to 1894, and its members farm a large share of the commune, including Asili, Rabajà and Ovello.

The method is traditional: large Slavonian oak, no new barriques. Its classic Barbaresco is blended across its members' vineyards; in strong years it also bottles up to nine single vineyard Riservas, and in poor years none, so every parcel goes into the one Barbaresco.

Our list prints the Barbaresco 2020 at $95, our Nebbiolo under $100, and four single vineyards from 2019, Asili, Montefico, Ovello and Rabajà, at $185 each.

card.front: What is the Produttori del Barbaresco?
card.back: The village co-operative of Barbaresco, founded in 1958: about fifty grower families and traditional large casks. A classic blended Barbaresco, with single vineyard Riservas such as Asili only in strong vintages.

producer.history:
Barbaresco is a small village in the Langhe hills of Piedmont, and its wine, like Barolo, is Nebbiolo. The Produttori del Barbaresco is the village's growers' co-operative: some fifty member families who bring their grapes to one cellar. It was founded in 1958 on roots going back to 1894, and the Codex calls it a parish co-operative that out-ages estates. Its members farm a large share of the commune, including the great vineyards Asili, Rabajà, Montestefano and Ovello.

The style is traditional: large Slavonian oak casks, no new barriques and a consistent house character. The classic Barbaresco is blended across the members' vineyards. In strong vintages the co-operative also bottles single vineyard Riservas from nine named crus: Asili, Rabajà, Montestefano, Ovello, Pora, Paje, Muncagota, Montefico and Rio Sordo. In weaker years no cru is made and every parcel goes into the one Barbaresco, which is why the Codex calls it the cleanest illustration of declassification. A Langhe Nebbiolo takes declassified fruit.

Our list prints the Barbaresco 2020 at $95, under the name Cantina Produttori Barbaresco, and four 2019 single vineyards at $185: Asili, Montefico, Ovello and Rabajà.

components.name: Tenuta San Guido
components.explain:
Tenuta San Guido is the Incisa della Rocchetta family estate at Bolgheri, on the Tuscan coast. In the 1940s Mario Incisa della Rocchetta planted Cabernet on stony slopes at Castiglioncello di Bolgheri because he wanted a wine in the Bordeaux manner for his own table. That wine, Sassicaia, was first sold with the 1968 vintage, as a humble table wine, and is regarded as the first Super Tuscan. Since 2013 it has had a denomination of its own, Bolgheri Sassicaia, the only Italian DOC held by a single estate.

Our list prints Guidalberto 2022 at $150, the estate's younger Cabernet and Merlot, and Sassicaia from 2018 at $515, with 2019 and 2020 at $545: Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc, elegant rather than heavy.

card.front: Why does Sassicaia matter?
card.back: It is the first Super Tuscan: Cabernet planted at Bolgheri by Mario Incisa della Rocchetta, first sold with the 1968 vintage. Since 2013 it has its own DOC, Bolgheri Sassicaia, the only one in Italy held by a single estate.

producer.history:
Tenuta San Guido is the Incisa della Rocchetta family estate at Bolgheri, on the Tuscan coast south of Livorno. In the 1940s Mario Incisa della Rocchetta, its founder, planted Cabernet on stony inland slopes at Castiglioncello di Bolgheri, reputedly from cuttings of Lafite, because he wanted a wine in the Bordeaux manner for himself. For years it was made only for the family table.

Sassicaia was first sold with the 1968 vintage, as a humble table wine, because Italian law had no better category for a Cabernet of that ambition. Giacomo Tachis, the oenologist the estate shared with Antinori, made it. It is regarded as the first Super Tuscan, and the law caught up in stages: the 1992 Goria law created the IGT tier, the Bolgheri DOC was rewritten in 1994 to admit red wines, with Sassicaia as its own denomination inside Bolgheri, and in 2013 Bolgheri Sassicaia became a DOC in its own right, the only one in Italy held by a single estate.

Sassicaia is Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc, aged in French barriques: restrained and aromatic, cedar and herbs over fruit. Guidalberto, Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot first released in the 2000s, is the younger red, and Le Difese the entry wine.

Our list prints Guidalberto 2022 at $150 and Sassicaia 2018 at $515, with the 2019 and 2020 at $545.

components.name: Il Poggione
components.explain:
Il Poggione is the Franceschi family's estate at Sant'Angelo in Colle, a hamlet in the warm southern sector of Montalcino, in Tuscany. It has been in the family since the late 1800s and is one of the largest single holdings in that corner of the zone.

Its Brunello di Montalcino is all Sangiovese, as the law requires, aged in large oak casks in the traditional way: ripe, generous southern fruit, consistent rather than showy. Its Riserva, Vigna Paganelli, comes from an old planting, and its Rosso di Montalcino is the teaching example of Rosso as a real wine.

Ours is the Brunello 2018 at $198: the classic, fairly priced Brunello on our list, and a reliable red for steak.

card.front: Who makes our Il Poggione Brunello, and where?
card.back: The Franceschi family, in the family since the late 1800s, at Sant'Angelo in Colle in the warm south of Montalcino. All Sangiovese, aged in large casks: classic, generous Brunello.

Montalcino is a hill town south of Siena, and its great red, Brunello di Montalcino, is made only from Sangiovese and aged for years before release: five years for the regular wine, six for a Riserva. Il Poggione lies at Sant'Angelo in Colle, a hamlet in the warm southern sector of the zone rather than a denomination of its own, and it is one of the largest single holdings there. The Franceschi family has held it since the late 1800s, which makes it one of the historic names of Brunello.

The style is traditional. The Brunello is aged in large oak casks, and the southern sun gives ripe, generous fruit: plum and cherry over sweet tobacco, consistent rather than showy. The Riserva, Vigna Paganelli, comes from an old planting, and the Rosso di Montalcino, released much younger, is the Codex's teaching example of Rosso as a real wine.

Il Poggione is not Poggio Antico, another Montalcino estate, and not Il Marroneto, another Brunello on our page.

Ours is the Brunello di Montalcino 2018 at $198, bin 17832: the classic, fairly priced Brunello on the list, and a reliable red for steak.

components.name: Bartolo Mascarello
components.explain:
Bartolo Mascarello is a small family cellar in the village of Barolo, in the Langhe hills of Piedmont, dated by the Codex to 1919. It is the traditionalist standard of the Barolo Wars, and it refuses single-cru bottling on principle: it makes one Barolo, blended from Cannubi, San Lorenzo and Rué in Barolo with Rocche dell'Annunziata in La Morra, fermented in cement and aged in large old casks, never barriques. Its hand-drawn label, No barrique, no Berlusconi, puts the philosophy in four words.

Our list prints that one Barolo, as Barolo/La Morra, in nine vintages from 2011 to 2021, $260 to $850; ours is the 2017 at $340.

card.front: Why does Bartolo Mascarello make only one Barolo?
card.back: Tradition: it blends four vineyards in Barolo and La Morra into one wine, ages it in large old casks and refuses single-cru bottling. Hence Barolo/La Morra on our list.

producer.who: Bartolo Mascarello, the small traditional family cellar in the village of Barolo
producer.where: Barolo, Langhe, Piedmont, Italy
producer.founded: 1919, as the Codex records
producer.history:
Barolo is Nebbiolo from a handful of villages in the Langhe hills of Piedmont, and Bartolo Mascarello is a small family cellar in the village of Barolo itself, dated by the Codex to 1919. It holds parcels in Cannubi, San Lorenzo and Rué in the commune of Barolo, and in Rocche dell'Annunziata in La Morra. Cannubi is one of the oldest named sites in the Langhe: a bottle carried its name in 1752.

In the Barolo Wars the modernists turned to short macerations and new barriques; the traditionalists, Bartolo Mascarello among them with Rinaldi and Giacomo Conterno, kept long macerations and large Slavonian casks. Mascarello is the standard of that camp. It makes one Barolo, blended from all four sites, fermented in cement and aged in large old botti, and it refuses single-cru bottling on principle: there is no Cannubi to ask for. Its hand-drawn label, No barrique, no Berlusconi, made the philosophy famous, and the Codex records Maria Teresa Mascarello continuing the single blend. Its other wines include a Dolcetto d'Alba and a Freisa.

It is no relation to Giuseppe Mascarello, a separate family whose Monprivato is also on our list.

Our list prints the Barolo, as Barolo/La Morra, in nine vintages from 2011 to 2021, $260 to $850; ours is the 2017 at $340.

components.name: Gaja
components.explain:
Gaja is the family winery in the village of Barbaresco, in Piedmont, dated by the Codex to 1859. Angelo Gaja made it world famous and took Barbaresco from a lesser Barolo to a wine priced above it. From the 1960s Gaja put single vineyard names on Barbaresco labels, Sorì San Lorenzo first, then Sorì Tildìn and Costa Russi. From the 1996 vintage they were labelled Langhe, so Barbera could be blended in, and they returned to Barbaresco with 2013. The style is polished: French oak, low yields, rigorous selection.

Ours is the flagship Barbaresco 2012 at $380, with age on it. The list also prints the three crus as Langhe, and Darmagi, a Langhe Cabernet.

card.front: What did Angelo Gaja do for Barbaresco?
card.back: He made it world famous: single vineyard bottlings beginning in the 1960s, polished Nebbiolo in French oak, priced above Barolo. Ours is the family's flagship Barbaresco 2012.

producer.history:
Gaja is the family winery in the village of Barbaresco, in the Langhe hills of Piedmont, dated by the Codex to 1859. Angelo Gaja made it one of the most famous names in Italian wine and took Barbaresco from the lesser neighbour of Barolo to a wine priced above it.

From the 1960s, beginning with Sorì San Lorenzo, Gaja put single vineyard names on Barbaresco labels, bottling Sorì San Lorenzo, Sorì Tildìn and Costa Russi on their own in a region that blended by tradition. Sorì is Piedmontese for a south-facing slope, and Tildìn was Angelo's grandmother Clotilde. From the 1996 vintage the three were labelled Langhe Nebbiolo, so Barbera could be blended in; with 2013, a return the Codex credits to Angelo's daughter Gaia, they went back to Barbaresco. Darmagi, Cabernet planted in the Langhe, is named for his father's dismay.

The style is polished: low yields, rigorous selection and French oak, dark-fruited Nebbiolo with international reach. The house later bought land in Barolo and in Tuscany, and the Gaja name is also on Pieve Santa Restituta in Montalcino and Ca' Marcanda near Bolgheri.

Ours is the flagship Barbaresco 2012 at $380, bin 16332, all Nebbiolo from the family's vineyards in the village.

Sorì means a south-facing slope in Piedmontese; Sorì Tildìn is named for Angelo Gaja's grandmother Clotilde.

The Gaja name is also on Pieve Santa Restituta and Ca' Marcanda in Tuscany, and on IDDA, Angelo Gaja's Etna partnership with Alberto Graci.
Ours: Barbaresco 2012, $380, bin 16332, printed simply Gaja on the Barbaresco page.

Guests ask if it is Barolo. The honest answer: no, Barbaresco, the neighbouring village; same grape, Nebbiolo.
The crus on our list say Langhe because of their vintages, 2010 and 2011: they are still the single vineyards of Barbaresco.
Pieve Santa Restituta and Ca' Marcanda are Gaja's Tuscan wines, not Barbaresco; IDDA is a Sicilian partnership.
Do not say who runs the winery today; the sources name Angelo Gaja and his daughter Gaia, not the present arrangement.
producer.sayIt: Gaja is the name that put Barbaresco on the world's tables: polished Nebbiolo, rose and cherry, with fourteen years of age.

components.name: Biondi Santi (Tenuta Greppo)
components.explain:
Biondi Santi is the family credited with creating Brunello di Montalcino, at Tenuta Greppo outside the Tuscan hill town of Montalcino. In the nineteenth century Ferruccio Biondi Santi propagated a Sangiovese selection called Brunello; the rules that Brunello be pure Sangiovese and age five years, six for a Riserva, descend from what the house was already doing. The wines are pale, high-toned and built on acidity, aged in large old Slavonian casks, and old Riservas are called back to the cellar to be topped up and recorked.

In December 2016 the EPI group of the Descours family, which also owns Piper-Heidsieck and Rare, acquired the majority. Ours is the Annata 2012 at $425.

card.front: Why is Biondi Santi called the inventor of Brunello?
card.back: The family is credited with creating it at Tenuta Greppo in the nineteenth century: Ferruccio Biondi Santi propagated the Brunello selection of Sangiovese. Ours is the Annata 2012.

producer.history:
Biondi Santi is the family credited with creating Brunello di Montalcino, at Tenuta Greppo, outside the hill town of Montalcino south of Siena. In the nineteenth century Ferruccio Biondi Santi propagated a selection of Sangiovese known locally as Brunello, the little dark one, and his late-1800s bottlings are the reference for what pure Sangiovese in Montalcino means. The estate's own selection, BBS11, carries the name on. Brunello's rules, all Sangiovese and five years of ageing, six for a Riserva, descend from what this house was already doing.

The Greppo lies south-east of the town at roughly 500 metres, cooled by altitude. The style is pale, high-toned and acid-driven, aged in large old Slavonian casks with no new oak and built to be unapproachable young. The Riserva comes only from the oldest parcels and only in outstanding years, and old bottles are called back to the cellar to be topped up and recorked, so the library reaches into the nineteenth century. The Annata is the regular Brunello of the year, and the Rosso di Montalcino the younger wine.

In December 2016 the EPI group of the Descours family, which also owns Piper-Heidsieck, Charles Heidsieck and Rare Champagne, acquired the majority of the estate. Jacopo Biondi Santi's Castello di Montepo wines are a separate operation.

Ours is the Annata 2012 at $425, bin 18542.

components.name: Marchesi Antinori
components.explain:
Marchesi Antinori is the Florentine family that has traded wine without a break since 1385, when it entered the city's winemakers' guild. With the oenologist Giacomo Tachis it made Tignanello, from the Tignanello vineyard in the Chianti Classico hills: from the 1971 vintage, Sangiovese aged in small French barrels outside the Chianti rules, so it was sold as a table wine. From 1975 the white grapes left the blend and Cabernet came in. Wines like it drove the creation of the IGT tier in 1992.

Ours is Tignanello 2010 at $720, sixteen years old. Solaia, its Cabernet-led sister from the same hillside, is on the list in magnum.

card.front: What made Antinori's Tignanello a Super Tuscan?
card.back: From the 1971 vintage it was Sangiovese aged in small French barrels outside the Chianti rules, later with Cabernet, so it was sold as table wine. Ours is the 2010.

producer.who: Marchesi Antinori, the Florentine wine family behind Tignanello and Solaia

producer.history:
Marchesi Antinori is a Florentine family that has traded wine without a break since 1385, when it entered the city's winemakers' guild. It is a merchant house first, many estates under one family name, from Chianti Classico and Badia a Passignano to Guado al Tasso on the coast at Bolgheri.

Its modern fame rests on wine made outside the rules of its day. Tignanello comes from the vineyard of that name on the Santa Cristina estate, between Florence and Siena inside the Chianti Classico zone. From the 1971 vintage Antinori aged its Sangiovese in small French barrels and sold it as a humble table wine, because it could not be called Chianti Classico; with the 1975 vintage the obligatory white grapes left the blend and Cabernet came in. The oenologist was Giacomo Tachis, who also made Sassicaia, with the counsel of Émile Peynaud. Solaia, first made in 1978 from an adjoining, south-facing plot, inverts the recipe: Cabernet-led with a little Sangiovese. Wines like these drove the creation of the IGT tier in 1992.

Tignanello is Sangiovese-led and Solaia Cabernet-led; reversing them is the standard error.

Ours is Tignanello 2010 at $720, bin 17913, now sixteen years old. The list also prints Solaia 2012 in magnum at $2230.
facts: A Florentine family trading wine without a break since 1385, when it entered the Florentine winemakers' guild.
Tignanello, from the 1971 vintage, was barrique-aged Sangiovese sold as table wine because it broke the Chianti rules.
With the 1975 vintage the white grapes left Tignanello's blend and Cabernet came in.
Giacomo Tachis, who also made Sassicaia, was the oenologist, with Émile Peynaud's counsel.
Solaia, first made in 1978 from an adjoining plot, is Cabernet-led; Tignanello is Sangiovese-led.
Tignanello and Solaia are labelled Toscana IGT, not Chianti Classico DOCG; the IGT tier came with the 1992 Goria law.
Ours: Tignanello 2010, $720, bin 17913. The list also prints Solaia 2012 in magnum, $2230, bin 29663.
notes: Say teen-yah-NEL-loh, ahn-tee-NOR-ee. Present it as one of the first Super Tuscans, from one of Italy's oldest wine families, with sixteen years on it.
Guests ask if it is a Chianti. The honest answer: it grows in the Chianti Classico hills but carries the Toscana label because it broke the old rules.
Never swap Tignanello and Solaia: Tignanello is Sangiovese-led, Solaia Cabernet-led and on our list only in magnum.
A sixteen-year-old bottle can carry sediment: the sommelier checks and decants it.
Sassicaia is not an Antinori wine, though the families are related; Ornellaia was founded by Lodovico Antinori, Piero's brother, and is a separate estate.
producer.sayIt: Tignanello is Antinori's Sangiovese with Cabernet, one of the first Super Tuscans: cherry, cedar and tobacco at sixteen years.
askKitchen: Has the Tignanello 2010 been checked for condition, and who decants it?

components.name: Masseto
components.explain:
Masseto is pure Merlot from a single hill of blue clay at Bolgheri, on the Tuscan coast. The clay holds water through the hot coastal summer, which is why Merlot behaves there as it does nowhere else in Tuscany; the Codex calls it Italy's answer to Pétrus. The vineyard was first planted by Tenuta dell'Ornellaia, the estate Lodovico Antinori founded in 1981, and Masseto's first vintage was 1986. It is now run as a separate estate with its own cellar, and it is labelled Toscana IGT, not Bolgheri DOC.

Ours is the 2011 at $1080, fifteen years old. The list prints it under Tenuta dell'Ornellaia, with 2015, 2016 and 2020 beside it.

card.front: What makes Masseto special?
card.back: It is pure Merlot from a single hill of blue clay in Bolgheri, first planted by Ornellaia, first vintage 1986. The clay keeps the vines watered through the summer. Ours is the 2011.

producer.history:
Masseto is a single hill of blue clay at Bolgheri, on the Tuscan coast, and the wine of that name is pure Merlot from it. The clay holds water through the hot coastal summer, which is why Merlot behaves there as it does nowhere else in Tuscany. The Codex calls it Italy's answer to Pétrus, and the proof that soil, not variety, drove the Bolgheri revolution.

The hill was part of Tenuta dell'Ornellaia, the estate Lodovico Antinori founded in 1981, whose own wine, Ornellaia, is a Bordeaux blend led by Cabernet Sauvignon. Masseto's first vintage was 1986. It is now run as a separate estate with its own cellar, though our list still prints it under Tenuta dell'Ornellaia. It is aged in French oak and labelled Toscana IGT; it has never taken an appellation of its own. The Codex lists it among the non-Bordeaux icons sold through La Place de Bordeaux, that city's merchant network, beside Opus One and Almaviva.

Ours is the 2011 at $1080, bin 27143. The list also prints the 2015 at $1225, the 2016 at $1300 and the 2020 at $1045: the youngest costs less than ours, so ring by vintage.

components.name: Castello Banfi
components.explain:
Castello Banfi is a very large estate in the south-west of Montalcino, in Tuscany, assembled from 1978 by the Mariani family of New York, American wine importers. The Codex treats it as the case of American capital reshaping an Italian denomination, and its clonal research gave Montalcino modern Sangiovese selections.

Banfi also makes Montalcino's older wine. Before Brunello, the town was famous for Moscadello, a sweet white from Moscato Bianco traded well beyond Tuscany; it took its own DOC in 1984. Florus is Banfi's late harvest Moscadello: honey, apricot and candied orange.

Ours is Florus 2011 at $60, the value bottle with the Blackberry Trifle and the Pineapple Tarte Tatin. Summus and Stilnovo, two Banfi reds, are on the list too.

card.front: What is Banfi's Florus?
card.back: A late harvest Moscadello di Montalcino from Moscato Bianco: the sweet wine Montalcino made before Brunello. Banfi, founded in 1978 by the American Mariani family, makes it.

Castello Banfi is a very large estate in the south-west of Montalcino, near Sant'Angelo Scalo, south of Siena. The Mariani family of New York, American wine importers, assembled it from 1978, and the Codex treats it as the examinable example of American capital reshaping an Italian denomination. Its clonal trial plantings gave Montalcino some of its modern Sangiovese selections. The house style is commercially scaled and technically exact: riper, rounder Brunello, with French oak for the top Riserva, Poggio all'Oro, and a single-vineyard Brunello, Poggio alle Mura, from around the castle itself.

Banfi also makes Montalcino's older wine. For centuries before Brunello, the town's famous wine was Moscadello, a sweet white from Moscato Bianco, traded well beyond Tuscany; it took its own DOC in 1984 and survives in still, frizzante and late harvest forms. Florus is Banfi's late harvest Moscadello: honey, apricot, candied orange and orange blossom.

Ours is Florus 2011 at $60, bin 192345, the value bottle with the Blackberry Trifle and the Pineapple Tarte Tatin. The list also prints two Banfi reds among the Super Tuscans: Stilnovo 2023 at $45 and Summus 2020 at $165.

components.name: Opus One
components.explain:
Opus One is the Oakville estate founded by Robert Mondavi and Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Château Mouton Rothschild, the first serious partnership between a Bordeaux first growth proprietor and a New World producer. Its first vintage was 1979, released in 1984 together with the 1980, and its own winery was completed in 1991. It is its own winery, not a Robert Mondavi bottling.

It makes one grand vin, a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with the other Bordeaux grapes, aged in new French oak: cassis and cedar, polish before power. Overture is the second wine.

Guests ask for it by name. We study two: the 2015 half-bottle, two or three glasses for a couple, and the 2010, sixteen years old and silky, for the Chateaubriand. Ring by vintage and size: the list prints many of each.

card.front: Who founded Opus One, and what was its first vintage?
card.back: Robert Mondavi and Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Château Mouton Rothschild, in Oakville. The first vintage was 1979, released in 1984 together with the 1980.

producer.who: Opus One, the Oakville estate of the Mondavi and Mouton Rothschild partnership
producer.where: Oakville, Napa Valley, California
producer.founded: 1979, the first vintage, by Robert Mondavi and Baron Philippe de Rothschild
producer.history:
Opus One is the partnership that told the world Napa had arrived. Robert Mondavi, whose Oakville winery of 1966 led the valley's reinvention, and Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Château Mouton Rothschild, the Pauillac first growth, agreed at the end of the 1970s to make one wine together: the first serious joint venture between a Bordeaux first growth proprietor and a New World producer. The Codex reads it as the commercial consequence of the Paris tasting, when European houses began to treat Napa as a place to invest.

The first vintage was 1979, released in 1984 together with the 1980, and it was priced from the start at a level no Californian bottle had attempted. The estate is in Oakville, with vineyards that include land beside the historic To Kalon vineyard, first planted by H.W. Crabb in 1868, and a purpose-built winery completed in 1991. Opus One is its own winery and brand, not a Robert Mondavi bottling, and it is even sold through La Place de Bordeaux, the city's merchant network.

The wine is a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with the other Bordeaux grapes, aged in new French oak: Bordeaux proportion applied to Napa fruit, cassis and cedar, polish before power. Overture is the second wine. Our list runs from half-bottles to a six litre bottle; we study the 2015 half-bottle and the 2010.

components.name: Harlan Estate
components.explain:
Harlan Estate is Bill Harlan's attempt to build a Bordeaux first growth in Napa. He bought land in the western hills above Oakville in 1984 and planted on the slopes, deliberately off the valley floor; the first commercial vintage was 1990, held back until 1996. With Screaming Eagle it defines Napa's cult era: tiny production, a mailing list and very high prices.

The wine is a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend aged in new French oak, dense and built for decades. The Maiden is the second wine; BOND and The Mascot, both on our list, are the same family's separate labels.

Wine Spectator named our Harlan Estate vertical when it described the cellar for the Grand Award of 2021. The list prints ten vintages; ours to study is the 2006, twenty years old.

card.front: What did Bill Harlan set out to build above Oakville?
card.back: A Napa estate on the Bordeaux first growth model: hillside Cabernet, land bought in 1984, first commercial vintage 1990. BOND and The Mascot are separate family labels.

producer.who: Harlan Estate, Bill Harlan’s hillside estate above Oakville

producer.history:
Harlan Estate is Bill Harlan's answer to a question: could Napa build an estate on the model of a Bordeaux first growth? He bought land in the western hills above Oakville in 1984 and planted it deliberately off the valley floor, on the slopes. The first commercial vintage was 1990, held back and released in 1996, and by the Codex the 1994 was the breakthrough. With Screaming Eagle it marks the start of Napa's cult era in the 1990s: tiny production, a mailing list, very high scores and the prices that followed.

The wine is a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with the other Bordeaux grapes, aged in new French oak: dense hillside fruit worked into espresso, graphite and tobacco, with tannin built for decades rather than early charm. The Maiden is the second wine. The same family stands behind BOND, which bottles Cabernet from single hillside vineyards, and Promontory, separate labels and never Harlan wines; The Mascot, from the family's younger vines, is on our list beside BOND.

When Wine Spectator described our cellar for the Grand Award of 2021, it named the dozens of verticals on the list, Harlan Estate among them. Our list prints ten vintages, from 2003 to 2015; ours to study is the 2006, twenty years old.

components.name: Screaming Eagle
components.explain:
Screaming Eagle is the defining name of Napa's cult era. Jean Phillips bought a small property on the eastern side of the Oakville valley floor in 1986; the first vintage, 1992, was made by Heidi Barrett and released in 1995. Production runs to hundreds of cases, sold through a mailing list, and the fame rests on scarcity and scores, not on any classification.

Second Flight is the second wine of the same estate, renamed The Flight from the 2015 vintage. Ours is the 2012, a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc: cassis, plum, black olive and spice, plush yet savoury.

The estate wine itself is not on our list, so never present this bottle as it. The printed list files it with the red blends, not the Cabernets: bin 181131.

components.name: Dominus Estate
components.explain:
Dominus is the Napa estate Christian Moueix created; its first vintage was 1983. His Libourne family is long associated with Pétrus and with Trotanoy in Pomerol, whose 1946 is on our list, and Dominus is the standing example of a European hand in California.

It is a single vineyard, Napanook, a gravelly bench at Yountville first planted in the nineteenth century; Napanook is also the name of the second wine. Though Pomerol is Merlot country, Dominus is Cabernet-led, with Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot: savoury and dusty, firm, with no sweetness on the finish.

Ours is the 2014, twelve years old: blackcurrant, graphite, tobacco and dried herbs. Offer it to the Bordeaux lover; the 2001 is printed at nearly the same price, so ring by vintage.

components.name: Heitz Cellar
components.explain:
Heitz Cellar was founded in St. Helena in 1961 by Joe and Alice Heitz, and Joe Heitz showed that a Napa vineyard's name could carry a wine. From the 1966 vintage he bottled Cabernet from Martha's Vineyard, Tom and Martha May's vineyard in Oakville, among the first vineyard-designated Cabernets in California. The 1970 was one of the six California reds at the Paris tasting of 1976.

Martha's Vineyard is famous for mint and eucalyptus over cassis, a classic blind tasting cue, and it is released only after years in the cellar.

Ours is the 2009, seventeen years old: blackcurrant, cedar, mint and earth, the tannin softened. The list runs from 1997 to 2017 and in magnums, so ring by size and vintage.

card.back: It was one of California's first vineyard-named Cabernets, from the 1966 vintage, grown in Tom and Martha May's Oakville vineyard, with a signature note of mint and eucalyptus.

components.name: Shafer Vineyards
components.explain:
Shafer Vineyards is the Stags Leap District estate John Shafer founded in 1972, on the east side of the Napa Valley. Its flagship, Hillside Select, is a selection of the estate's terraced hillside blocks rather than a single named vineyard, and one of the most sought after Cabernets in Napa. The style is warm and plush, cocoa and black cherry, framed by the district's fine tannin; the Chardonnay, Red Shoulder Ranch, is grown in Carneros.

One Point Five, our wine, is named for John Shafer and his son Doug: a generation and a half. The 2023 is black cherry, blackberry, dark chocolate and violet, rich and velvety. Stags Leap District takes no apostrophe; Stag's Leap Wine Cellars is a different winery.

card.front: Why is Shafer's Cabernet called One Point Five?
card.back: It is named for the founder, John Shafer, and his son Doug: a generation and a half. Stags Leap District Cabernet, a step below Hillside Select.

components.name: Caymus Vineyards
components.explain:
Caymus Vineyards is the Rutherford winery the Wagner family founded in 1972: the clearest example of the ripe, plush Napa style, and among the most widely sold serious Napa Cabernets in America. The name comes from the Rancho Caymus land grant; Caymus is a producer, not an appellation.

The Napa Valley Cabernet draws fruit from across the valley: black cherry, cassis, cocoa and vanilla, soft and generous young, and dry, though it tastes rich. Special Selection is the reserve, from the best lots and aged longer in oak.

We study both: the Napa Valley 2023 for the Roost Burger and the Special Selection 2018 for a celebration. Belle Glos, on our list, is a Wagner family Pinot Noir label, not a Caymus wine.

card.front: How is Caymus Special Selection different from the Napa Valley Cabernet?
card.back: It is the reserve, from the best lots and aged longer in oak: the same plush style, fuller and longer.

components.name: Joseph Phelps Vineyards
components.explain:
Joseph Phelps Vineyards was founded in 1973 in St. Helena, in the Napa Valley, by Joseph Phelps, a building contractor from Colorado. Its flagship is Insignia, first made in 1974 and one of California's first proprietary Bordeaux-style blends: a wine sold under its own name rather than a grape's, led by Cabernet Sauvignon with the other Bordeaux grapes, the mix changing with each vintage. It came more than a decade before the Meritage name existed. The style is polished and ripe: cassis, graphite, cedar and sweet oak over a broad Napa core.

We hold Insignia across vintages: the 2011 in half-bottle, the anchor among our red halves, and the 2013 in the celebration tier, with more on the list up to a 2015 magnum.

components.name: Chappellet
components.explain:
Chappellet is the estate that Donn and Molly Chappellet founded on Pritchard Hill, in the eastern hills of the Napa Valley, in 1967, a year after Robert Mondavi broke ground at Oakville. They were pioneers of that slope, there long before the cult producers now associated with it. Pritchard Hill is not an appellation, so the label says Napa Valley. The steep, rocky vineyards give firm Cabernet with dried herb and red currant.

Our bottle is the Mountain Cuvée 2024, the friendliest of the three Chappellet reds on our list: a Cabernet-led Bordeaux-style blend from the estate and other Napa vineyards, its mix changing every year, soft and ready now, and our Napa red under $100.

components.name: Frog's Leap
components.explain:
Frog's Leap is John Williams's winery in Rutherford, in the middle of the Napa Valley; Larry Turley, later of Turley Wine Cellars, was its co-founder. It is known for farming organically and for dry farming: the vines get no irrigation and send their roots deep for water, a deliberate choice in a West where irrigation is routine. The wines are balanced and lower in alcohol than many Napa reds.

The Estate Rutherford Cabernet comes from its own vineyards on Rutherford's valley floor, home of the dusty tannin André Tchelistcheff called Rutherford dust. Ours is the 2021, fresh and savoury, with the 2020 and a 1991 also on the list: Napa for the guest who wants it fresh rather than heavy.

card.front: What makes Frog's Leap different in Napa?
card.back: It farms organically and dry farms, giving its Rutherford vines no irrigation, and its wines are fresher and lower in alcohol than many Napa reds.

producer.history:
Frog's Leap is John Williams's winery in Rutherford, in the middle of the Napa Valley. Larry Turley, later the man behind Turley Wine Cellars, was its co-founder.

It is known for two choices in the vineyard. It farms organically, and it dry farms: the vines get no irrigation and must send their roots deep for water. Across much of the American West vines are irrigated as a matter of course, so a dry-farmed Napa vineyard is a deliberate stand. The wines are balanced and lower in alcohol than many Napa reds, made for the table.

Rutherford sits beside Oakville on the valley floor north of Yountville, the historic heartland of Napa Cabernet, and its Cabernet is known for what André Tchelistcheff called Rutherford dust, a dusty, cocoa-like texture in the tannin rather than a kind of soil. The Estate Rutherford Cabernet comes from Frog's Leap's own vineyards there: red and black currant, cherry, dusty earth and dried herbs, with fresh acidity and fine tannin.

Our list holds Frog's Leap in depth: the Estate Rutherford 2021 and 2020, a 1991 printed on both the Cabernet and the Merlot pages, and the Napa Valley Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay. The 2021 is the sweet spot bottle for a guest who finds big Napa too much.

components.name: Silver Oak Cellars
components.explain:
Silver Oak Cellars was founded in 1972 by Justin Meyer and Ray Duncan, and it has one rule: it makes only Cabernet Sauvignon, in a Napa Valley and an Alexander Valley bottling, aged only in American oak and rested in bottle before release. American oak gives the vanilla, coconut and dill that make the style so recognisable: ripe blackberry and black cherry, sweet spice and a smooth texture. Guests often ask for it by name.

The Alexander Valley wine, from Sonoma, is the softer and earlier drinking; the Napa Valley, our bottle in the 2020, is the firmer. With the Roost Burger's short rib and bacon, or a steak, it has the weight to match.

components.name: Cakebread Cellars
components.explain:
Cakebread Cellars is a Rutherford winery, in the heart of the Napa Valley, founded in 1973 by Jack and Dolores Cakebread. Its Napa Valley Chardonnay is a long-time restaurant favourite and one of the Napa names guests know best: ripe pear, apple and citrus with a touch of vanilla from some oak, round and polished, with fresh acidity.

It is our anchor among the Napa Chardonnays, the 2023, with the 2024 also on the list at the same price. Pour it with the buttery plates of the house: the pecan fish, the crab claws, the BBQ lobster and the poussin with its mustard cream. For a guest who wants no oak at all, steer to the Louis Michel Chablis.

components.name: Kosta Browne
components.explain:
Kosta Browne, of Sebastopol in Sonoma County, was founded by Dan Kosta and Michael Browne, two restaurant workers who started making wine with tip money they had saved, and it grew into one of California's most sought-after Pinot Noir houses. The style is ripe, plush and polished: black cherry, raspberry, cola and baking spice with a silky texture and French oak.

Its core wines come from the Sonoma Coast and the foggy Russian River Valley; Gap's Crown is a single vineyard in the windy Petaluma Gap. Ours is the Sonoma Coast 2021, with the 2020 and two half-bottles also on the list: a server's story with a rich Pinot for duck, pork, salmon or mushrooms.

components.name: Broadbent
components.explain:
Broadbent is a label rather than a lodge. Bartholomew Broadbent is a British wine merchant and Madeira specialist, the founder of Broadbent Selections and an importer of Madeira into North America, and he bottles Madeira under his own name. Wine Spectator lists the Broadbent Madeiras under Justino's, one of the island's producers.

His single cask bottlings are drawn from one cask of one harvest, so each is a little different. Ours is the Malvasia 2009, aged in old 650 litre oak casks and bottled in 500 ml. Malvasia, or Malmsey, is Madeira's sweetest style, kept tangy by the island's high natural acidity: coffee, caramel, toffee and orange peel. The list also prints a drier Single Cask Verdelho 1997.

Madeira needs no decanting and keeps for months once opened.

card.back: Bartholomew Broadbent, a Madeira specialist and importer, bottles it under his name. A single cask is one cask of one harvest: ours is Malvasia 2009, the sweetest style.

Broadbent is a label rather than a lodge on the island. Bartholomew Broadbent is a British wine merchant and Madeira specialist, the founder of Broadbent Selections and an importer of Madeira into North America, and he bottles Madeira under the Broadbent label. Who makes each wine is a question for the sommelier: Wine Spectator lists the Broadbent Madeiras under Justino's Madeira Wines.

Madeira is the fortified wine of the Portuguese island of Madeira, out in the Atlantic. After fortification it is warmed, quickly in heated tanks or slowly in casks in the warm lofts of the lodge, the slow way kept for the finest wines. Heat and air turn it amber, give it caramel, coffee and nuts, and make it long lived and stable once opened. Its classic styles are named for grapes, from Sercial, the driest, through Verdelho and Bual to Malvasia, or Malmsey, the sweetest, all held up by high natural acidity.

Broadbent's single cask bottlings come from one cask of one harvest. Ours is the Malvasia 2009, aged in old 650 litre oak casks and bottled in 500 ml: coffee, caramel, toffee and orange peel, sweet and tangy. The list also prints a Single Cask Verdelho 1997, a drier style.

components.name: Henriques & Henriques
components.explain:
Henriques & Henriques is a historic Madeira house whose history dates to 1850, based at Câmara de Lobos on the island's south coast. Its name is best known for the drier styles, Sercial and Verdelho.

Its Founder's Solera 1894 is the oldest date on our list. A solera blends wine across casks over the years, so the date is when the solera began, not a single harvest. The producer and its importer say this one was begun in 1894 and closed in 1899, and describe it as Malvasia: sweet, dark amber with gold and green, with dried fruit, spice, honey and old wood. Our list prints Verdelho, the medium-dry style, so the grape is for the sommelier to confirm.

Never call 1894 a vintage. The sommelier presents this bottle; it needs no decanting.

card.front: What does 1894 mean on the Henriques & Henriques Founder's Solera?
card.back: The year the solera began, not a single harvest; the producer says it was closed in 1899. It is described as Malvasia, though our list prints Verdelho.

The Codex places it at Câmara de Lobos, on the island's south coast, and records it as one of the few Madeira houses with substantial vineyards of its own on an island of smallholders. Its reputation, the Codex adds, was built on the drier styles, Sercial and Verdelho, with a strong 15 Year Old range, and it is a dependable source of Terrantez, a near-extinct noble grape.

Its Founder's Solera 1894 is the oldest date on our list and the highest-priced fortified wine we sell. A solera blends wine across casks over the years, drawing from the oldest and refreshing it with younger wine, so the date is when the solera began, not a single harvest. The producer and its importer describe this one as begun in 1894 and closed in 1899.

They describe it as Malvasia, sweet, at about 20 percent alcohol: dark amber with gold and green, with dried fruit, spice, honey and old wood. Our list prints it as Verdelho, the medium-dry style, so the grape is a question for the sommelier, who presents this bottle at the table.

components.name: Mas de Valériole
components.explain:
Mas de Valériole is a family estate in the Camargue, the delta where the Rhône meets the Mediterranean, about ten miles south of Arles, and its vineyards are cooled by the Mediterranean wind. Its rosé, Vé, is sold as IGP Méditerranée, not under a Provence appellation.

Vé, a Provençal expression meaning look at that, is pale and dry: Caladoc, a cross of Grenache and Malbec, with Merlot and Marselan, pressed straight off the skins and kept fresh in steel. It tastes of raspberry and ripe citrus with a salty finish.

Our list prints the 2025 as a bottle at $50 and a magnum at $85, the friendliest priced big bottle on the list: two bottles’ worth, ten to twelve glasses, for a table that is sharing.

components.name: Famille Durand
components.explain:
Our Sauvignon Blanc by the glass carries the Durand name and comes from the Loire Valley. The house’s glass page prints Famille Durand, Val de Loire, 2024; the Binwise list prints Domaine Durand, Loire Valley, 2025. Which Durand estate makes it, and where, is not confirmed: more than one Loire grower trades under the name, and the well-known Domaine Durand of Cornas is a Rhône estate that makes no Sauvignon at all.

So say what the label says and no more. Val de Loire names the region and no village, so call it a Loire Sauvignon Blanc and not Sancerre unless the label says otherwise. It is crisp and herbal, grapefruit and cut grass, and at $14 it is among the least expensive glasses we pour, the first pick with the Eggs Sardou.

card.back: The menu prints Famille Durand, Val de Loire, 2024, and Binwise Domaine Durand, 2025; which Durand is not confirmed. It names no village, so call it a Loire Sauvignon Blanc, not Sancerre.

More than one unrelated Loire grower trades under the Durand name, and the well-known Domaine Durand of Cornas, in the Rhône, makes Syrah and no Sauvignon Blanc, so it is not this wine. What the guide does give is how it tastes and why it is poured. Fermented in steel with no oak, as the guide described the 2025, it is bone-dry and zippy: grapefruit, cut grass and a flinty note. Artichokes make most wines taste oddly sweet or metallic; a dry, herbal Sauvignon Blanc survives them, which is why it is the first pick with the Eggs Sardou.

So the server reads the label, says Loire Sauvignon Blanc, and never says Sancerre unless the label does.

components.name: Domaine Henri Gouges
components.explain:
Domaine Henri Gouges is the family domaine most often named first in Nuits-Saint-Georges, the town that gives the Côte de Nuits its name. Henri Gouges was a leader of the movement to bottle wine at the domaine and of the drive that produced the appellation contrôlée system. Most of its vines lie in the town’s premiers crus: Les Saint-Georges, Les Vaucrains, Les Pruliers and the Clos des Porrets-Saint-Georges, which it owns alone. It also makes a rare white from a white mutation of Pinot found in its own vines.

The wines are firm, earthy and slow, built to age. The domaine is farmed organically and run by the fourth generation of the family. We pour its village Nuits-Saint-Georges in a half-bottle and Les Pruliers Premier Cru 2016, both for the duck.

producer.where: Nuits-Saint-Georges, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
producer.history:
Domaine Henri Gouges is the family domaine that Burgundy lovers name first in Nuits-Saint-Georges, the town that gives the Côte de Nuits its name. It carries the name of Henri Gouges, a leader of two causes that shaped modern Burgundy: bottling wine at the domaine, and the drive that produced the appellation contrôlée system.

Its vines are concentrated in the premiers crus of Nuits: Les Saint-Georges, the vineyard that gave the town half its name, Les Vaucrains, Les Pruliers on the south side of the town, and the Clos des Porrets-Saint-Georges, which the domaine owns alone. Nuits-Saint-Georges has no grand cru, and the village has asked for Les Saint-Georges to be promoted; where that request stands is a question for the sommelier. The domaine also makes a rare white from La Perrière, from a white mutation of Pinot found in its own vines, not from Chardonnay.

The style is firm, earthy and slow, built for a decade in bottle. The domaine is farmed organically and run by the fourth generation, Grégory and Antoine Gouges, by the domaine’s own account as of October 2026. Our half-bottle is its village wine and Les Pruliers 2016 its premier cru, both poured for the duck.

components.name: Domaine Faiveley
components.explain:
Faiveley is one of Burgundy’s great family wine houses, founded in 1825 and based in Nuits-Saint-Georges. It is both a domaine, farming its own vines, and a maison, which also bottles wine from bought fruit.

It is one of the largest vineyard owners in Burgundy, from Mercurey in the Côte Chalonnaise to the grand crus of Gevrey-Chambertin and the Corton hill, where its Clos des Cortons Faiveley is the only grand cru whose official name carries a family surname. Long known for firm reds, the house has made finer, more aromatic wines since Erwan Faiveley took over in 2005. Our Bourgogne Rouge 2022 is the value red Burgundy for the duck.

components.name: Domaine Jean Grivot
components.explain:
Domaine Jean Grivot is a family domaine in Vosne-Romanée, the most celebrated red wine village of the Côte de Nuits, and one of its reference names. Its vines run from village wines through Vosne-Romanée and Nuits-Saint-Georges premiers crus such as Les Beaux Monts and Les Boudots to three grand crus: Clos de Vougeot, Echézeaux and its flagship, Richebourg.

The wines are classical and firm, with moderate new oak. Étienne Grivot’s work with the consultant Guy Accad in the late 1980s, and the domaine’s later step back toward clarity, is a classic Burgundy case study. As of October 2026, Mathilde Grivot, of the next generation, has run it since 2017. We carry its Les Charmois Nuits-Saint-Georges 2013 and the Echézeaux Grand Cru 2011.

Its vines run from village wines through a long list of Vosne-Romanée and Nuits-Saint-Georges premiers crus, among them Les Beaux Monts, Les Suchots and Les Boudots, to three grand crus: Clos de Vougeot, Echézeaux and Richebourg, its flagship.

components.name: Domaine Tollot-Beaut
components.explain:
Domaine Tollot-Beaut is a family domaine based in Chorey-lès-Beaune, in the Côte de Beaune. It is known for ripe, generous, fruity reds with a touch of new oak, wines that are welcoming young.

Its range climbs like a map of the northern Côte de Beaune: its home village of Chorey-lès-Beaune, Aloxe-Corton, the Beaune premier cru Clos du Roi, the Savigny-lès-Beaune premier cru Les Lavières, and two grand crus on the Corton hill, the red Corton Bressandes and the white Corton-Charlemagne. Our Les Lavières 2019 is the sweet spot bottle for the Eggs Owen: ripe red cherry and raspberry, a little spice and toast, supple tannin.

components.name: Maison Joseph Drouhin
components.explain:
Maison Joseph Drouhin is one of the great family houses of Beaune, founded in 1880, with cellars under the town. It is both a merchant and a grower, with its own vineyards across the Côte d’Or and in Chablis, farmed organically and biodynamically, and its style puts elegance before weight.

Its signature is the Clos des Mouches, a premier cru on the slope above Beaune, where Drouhin owns the largest share and makes the wine in red and white. In 1987 Robert Drouhin bought land in Oregon’s Dundee Hills, founding Domaine Drouhin Oregon. Our Clos des Mouches 2015 is a red Burgundy anchor: red and black cherry, rose and spice, silky tannin.

components.name: Domaine Georges Roumier
components.explain:
Domaine Georges Roumier is a family domaine in Chambolle-Musigny, founded in 1924, and one of the most sought-after names in Burgundy. Its wines are drawn fine and cool: red currant, crushed rock and rose, with restrained oak and a stony finish. Its grand crus, among them Bonnes-Mares and a sliver of Musigny, and its premier cru Les Amoureuses are hard to find anywhere.

The Clos de la Bussière is a walled premier cru in neighbouring Morey-Saint-Denis that Roumier owns alone, a monopole, and it shows a darker, earthier side of the house than its Chambolle-Musigny wines. Ours is the 2014, the celebration bottle for the Blackened Tofu.

components.name: Alain Graillot
components.explain:
Alain Graillot founded his domaine in Crozes-Hermitage in 1985 and did as much as anyone to make the appellation serious. Crozes-Hermitage is the largest appellation of the Northern Rhône, the land around the hill of Hermitage, and Graillot's vines lie on its stony Chassis plain south of Tain.

The domaine ferments its Syrah with whole bunches and raises it in neutral wood, not new oak, for peppery, olive-scented wines that age far better than the name suggests. La Guiraude is a selection made only in stronger vintages.

Our Crozes-Hermitage 2015 has eleven years: blackberry and olive, black pepper and smoked meat, the most food-friendly kind of Syrah on our Rhône pages.

producer.history:
Alain Graillot founded his domaine in Crozes-Hermitage in 1985 and did as much as anyone to raise the name of the appellation. Crozes-Hermitage is the largest appellation of the Northern Rhône: the land around the great hill of Hermitage, not a lesser plot on it. Much of it lies on the Chassis plain south of Tain, a flat terrace of rounded stones over alluvium that took nearly all of the appellation's growth after the 1950s.

Graillot's vines are on that stony plain, and the domaine is based at Pont-de-l'Isère. The Codex names him with Combier as the growers who work the plain to a very high standard, the proof that a Crozes from the flat land can be serious.

The domaine's method is whole bunches, fermented with the stems, and neutral wood rather than new oak: Syrah that is peppery and taut, with olive and cool dark fruit, and that ages far better than the appellation's reputation suggests. The range takes in a white Crozes-Hermitage from Marsanne and Roussanne, a Saint-Joseph from across the river and, in stronger vintages only, a selection called La Guiraude.

Our 2015 has eleven years: blackberry and olive, black pepper and smoked meat, medium body and fine tannin, an anchor of our Rhône pages.

components.name: André Perret
components.explain:
André Perret's domaine is at Chavanay, in the south of the Condrieu appellation, where his family grew orchards; he took over from his father in 1982 and is counted among the masters of Viognier.

Condrieu is a small appellation of steep granite slopes in the Northern Rhône, the home of Viognier, and its wine is dry and white. components.name: René Rostaing
components.explain:
René Rostaing's domaine is at Ampuis in Côte-Rôtie, the roasted slope at the northern end of the Rhône, and dates from 1971. It grew from parcels that came from Albert Dervieux-Thaize and Marius Gentaz-Dervieux, so Rostaing bottles both hillsides: the perfumed Côte Blonde, and La Landonne on the firmer Côte Brune.

The style is fine-boned and transparent rather than powerful. Ampodium, formerly Cuvée Classique, is the estate blend of many parcels across the appellation.

Our Ampodium 2012 has fourteen years: blackberry, violet, black olive and pepper, silky and fragrant, the perfumed side of Syrah for lamb and duck.

René Rostaing's domaine is at Ampuis, the village beneath the steep terraces of Côte-Rôtie, the roasted slope at the northern end of the Rhône valley, where Syrah grows at its most perfumed. The Codex dates it to 1971. It grew from parcels that came to René Rostaing from two Côte-Rôtie growers of an older generation, Albert Dervieux-Thaize and Marius Gentaz-Dervieux, including vines on the Côte Blonde and in La Landonne.

That is what makes the name useful: Rostaing bottles both sides of the appellation. The Côte Blonde, on lighter, sandier soil, gives perfume; La Landonne, on the iron-rich schist of the Côte Brune, gives structure. Guigal bottles a La Landonne too: the lieu-dit is shared, the wine is not. The house style is transparent and fine-boned rather than powerful, with older oak and gentle extraction.

Ampodium, once called Cuvée Classique, is the estate blend, drawn from many parcels across the appellation. Our 2012 has fourteen years: blackberry, violet, black olive, smoked meat and pepper, silky and fragrant, with a long, savoury finish. The list also carries the Côte Blonde, La Landonne and the Condrieu La Bonnette.

components.name: Auguste Clape
components.explain:
The Clape family domaine, carrying Auguste Clape's name, is the reference producer of Cornas: the wine other Cornas is measured against. Cornas is a small, steep granite amphitheatre at the south of the Northern Rhône, and its red may be Syrah only.

The domaine's old terraces above the village, chiefly Reynard, La Côte, Patou and Sabarotte, go into one Cornas, made traditionally with whole bunches in old foudres and no new oak. Renaissance is the younger-vine cuvée, not a grander one.

Our Cornas 2016 has ten years: blackberry, violet, pepper and smoke, with firm tannin opening. Decant it about an hour ahead.

card.front: Which Cornas is the benchmark, and how is it made?
card.back: Auguste Clape's: old granite terraces blended into one Cornas, with whole bunches, old foudres and no new oak. Renaissance is the younger vines. Ours is the 2016.

producer.history:
The Clape family's domaine in Cornas carries the name of Auguste Clape, and it is the reference producer of the appellation, the Cornas other growers are measured against.

Cornas is a small, steep granite amphitheatre at the south of the Northern Rhône, on the west bank across from Valence, and its red is Syrah only: the appellation permits no white grape at all. The Clape vines are old terraces on the slopes above the village, chiefly Reynard, La Côte, Patou and Sabarotte, blended into a single Cornas.

The method is traditional: whole bunches, old foudres and no new oak, and the wine goes unfiltered. Young it is black and savage; with age it turns to smoke, olive and iron. Clape holds the classical seat in Cornas, where Thierry Allemand is the reformer, and frames the appellation's argument with the destemming, new-oak school.

Besides the Cornas, the family makes Renaissance, the younger-vine cuvée, a white Saint-Péray from the neighbouring appellation, a Côtes du Rhône and Le Vin des Amis, a simple Vin de France red. Our 2016 has ten years: blackberry, black cherry, violet, pepper and smoke, with firm tannin opening.

components.name: Domaine Jean-Louis Chave
components.explain:
The Chave family has grown vines since 1481 and is the grower most associated with the hill of Hermitage. The domaine is at Mauves, across the Rhône from the hill at Tain-l'Hermitage.

Chave holds parcels across the hill's named sectors, Les Bessards, Le Méal, L'Ermite, Péléat and Les Rocoules, and blends them into one Hermitage rather than bottling each alone: the blending case against Chapoutier's parcel wines. The white is Marsanne with a little Roussanne, and Cuvée Cathelin is a selection made only in chosen vintages.

Our Hermitage 2013 has thirteen years: blackberry, cassis, smoke and iron, deep and very long. Collectors ask for it by name.

card.front: How does Chave make its Hermitage, and how does that differ from Chapoutier?
card.back: Chave blends parcels from across the hill, Les Bessards, Le Méal, L'Ermite and others, into one Hermitage; Chapoutier bottles several sectors separately. Ours is the 2013.

The Chave family has grown vines since 1481, the date the Codex gives, and Domaine Jean-Louis Chave is the grower most associated with the hill of Hermitage. The domaine is based at Mauves, on the west bank, across the Rhône from the hill at Tain-l'Hermitage, with old Saint-Joseph terraces at Mauves and Tournon.

Hermitage is a single hill above the river at Tain, its sectors on granite and on clay, and its Syrah is among the longest-lived red wines of France. Chave holds parcels across its named sectors, Les Bessards, Le Méal, L'Ermite, Péléat and Les Rocoules, and blends them rather than bottling each alone, on the principle that each supplies something the others cannot. That is the blending case against Chapoutier, which bottles several sectors as separate parcel wines.

The white Hermitage is Marsanne with a little Roussanne, one of the few whites that can outlive the reds. In chosen vintages only, the domaine makes Cuvée Cathelin, a selection named for the painter Bernard Cathelin, whose design is on its label. J.L. Chave Sélection is the négociant label, not the domaine.

Our Hermitage 2013 has thirteen years: blackberry, cassis, violet, smoke and iron, deep and firm, with a very long finish. Collectors ask for Chave by name, and the sommelier decants it.

components.name: E. Guigal
components.explain:
E. Guigal is the family house of Ampuis, founded in 1946 by Étienne Guigal, and so dominant in Côte-Rôtie that its style is taken for the appellation's. Its three single-vineyard Côte-Rôties are the La La's: La Mouline, first made in 1966, La Landonne in 1978 and La Turque in 1985, each raised around forty-two months in new oak.

La Mouline is a terraced amphitheatre on the Côte Blonde, its Syrah fermented with around a tenth Viognier: the most perfumed of the three. La Landonne, on the Côte Brune, is all Syrah.

Our La Mouline 2012 has fourteen years: violet, raspberry, bacon and spice, silky and long.

card.front: Name Guigal's three La La's, and the one that is all Syrah.
card.back: La Mouline, on the Côte Blonde with a little Viognier, and La Landonne and La Turque, both on the Côte Brune. La Landonne is all Syrah. Ours is La Mouline 2012.

producer.who: E. Guigal, the Ampuis family house behind the La La's of Côte-Rôtie
producer.where: Ampuis, Côte-Rôtie, Northern Rhône, France
producer.founded: 1946, by Étienne Guigal
producer.history:
E. Guigal is the family house of Ampuis, founded in 1946 by Étienne Guigal, who had worked at Vidal-Fleury, an older Ampuis house, before setting up on his own. His son Marcel Guigal took the house on and built its single-vineyard wines, and in 1984 the family bought Vidal-Fleury itself. In 2001 it added the Grippat and de Vallouit vineyards, and it owns the Château d'Ampuis.

Guigal is so dominant in Côte-Rôtie that its style is often taken for the appellation's. Its range runs from a widely sold Côtes du Rhône to the auction room, and at the top stand three single-vineyard Côte-Rôties that collectors call the La La's: La Mouline, first made in 1966, La Landonne in 1978 and La Turque in 1985. Each is picked late and raised around forty-two months in new oak, far longer than the appellation's habit.

La Mouline is a terraced amphitheatre on the Côte Blonde, where Viognier grows among the Syrah and is fermented with it, around a tenth of the wine; it is the most perfumed and silky of the three. La Landonne is all Syrah from the Côte Brune, and La Turque, also on the Côte Brune, carries a smaller share of Viognier.

Our La Mouline 2012 has fourteen years: violet, raspberry and blackberry, bacon and spice, with a long, fine finish.

components.name: Domaine Raspail-Ay
components.explain:
Domaine Raspail-Ay is a family estate in Gigondas, the Southern Rhône village under the Dentelles de Montmirail, the jagged limestone ridge whose slopes give Grenache a firmer, fresher red than the plain below. Gigondas has been a cru in its own right since 1971, so the label carries no Côtes du Rhône name.

Its red is Grenache-led with Syrah: ripe red and black cherry, garrigue herbs and pepper, with firm but rounded tannin. Our list prints the 2021 twice, a full bottle at $115 and a 375 ml half-bottle at $55. The half is the one to offer with the Petite Filet Mignon: two or three glasses, the same region a step deeper than the tasting's Côtes du Rhône.

Vineyards climbing toward that ridge make a Grenache red firmer and fresher than the plain below, which is why Gigondas is the usual suggestion for a guest who finds Châteauneuf-du-Pape too heavy.

Gigondas was promoted from Côtes du Rhône Villages to a cru of its own in 1971, and its red must still rest on Grenache. The Raspail-Ay red follows the village pattern: Grenache-led with Syrah, ripe red and black cherry, garrigue herbs and pepper, with firm but rounded tannin and a warm finish.
