components.name: Château Rayas
components.explain:
Château Rayas is the Reynaud family's estate in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, and the cult name of the appellation. Where most Châteauneuf blends several grapes over hot round stones, Rayas makes its red from Grenache alone, grown on sand in cool parcels shaded by pine woods, with very low yields, and raises it in old wood with no new oak. The result is pale, perfumed and silky, so often taken for red Burgundy when tasted blind that the comparison has become its signature.

The family also makes Pignan, a named parcel of the same estate, the Côtes du Rhône of Château de Fonsalette and La Pialade, and Château des Tours in Vacqueyras. Ours is the 2011, at $1200 the cult bottle of our Rhône pages.

card.front: What makes Château Rayas unlike other Châteauneuf-du-Pape?
card.back: It is all Grenache, grown on sand in cool, pine-shaded parcels and raised in old wood: pale, perfumed and silky, often mistaken for red Burgundy.

producer.who: Château Rayas, the Reynaud family's estate in Châteauneuf-du-Pape
producer.where: Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Southern Rhône, France

producer.history:
Château Rayas is the Reynaud family's estate in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, dated by the Codex to 1880, and it is the appellation's great exception. Most Châteauneuf is a blend grown over hot, round stones; Rayas lies in the cool, wooded north-east of the appellation on sand and clay, without galets, and its red is Grenache alone.

Sand, the shade of the surrounding pine woods and very low yields give a wine so pale and perfumed that it is regularly mistaken for red Burgundy when tasted blind. It is raised in old wood, with no new oak and no pretence of power: kirsch, incense and red fruit rather than the dark warmth of its neighbours. Rayas is why examiners say Châteauneuf need not be a blend and need not be dark.

Jacques Reynaud ran the estate until his death in 1997, and his nephew Emmanuel Reynaud followed him; our wine list of October 2026 names Emmanuel as the hand behind Rayas and Château des Tours.

The family's other wines are on our list too: Pignan, a named parcel of the same estate; Château de Fonsalette and La Pialade, both Côtes du Rhône; and Château des Tours in Vacqueyras. Rayas itself appears in three vintages. Ours is the 2011, fifteen years old, translucent and silky.

components.name: Domaine La Tour Vieille
components.explain:
Domaine La Tour Vieille is a domaine of Collioure, on the Côte Vermeille in Roussillon, where terraced schist drops almost into the Mediterranean at the Spanish frontier. Those terraces give two appellations: dry Collioure, and Banyuls, the sweet red whose fermentation is stopped with grape spirit so the grape's own sugar stays in the wine. The current Reserva blends Grenache Noir, Grenache Gris and Carignan.

The domaine bottles Banyuls in two styles. Rimage is the early-bottled vintage style, fresh black fruit. Reserva, a Catalan spelling, is a blend of years aged the oxidative way, with air, which turns it to dried fig, walnut, caramel and coffee.

Ours is the Reserva, the dinner tasting's dessert pour with The Snickers: Banyuls with chocolate is the classic match.

card.front: What kind of Banyuls is the La Tour Vieille Reserva on the dinner tasting?
card.back: A sweet fortified Grenache led blend from the Collioure terraces, aged the oxidative way: dried fig, walnut, caramel and coffee. The Rimage is the young fruit style; ours is the Reserva.

producer.who: Domaine La Tour Vieille, the Collioure domaine behind the dinner tasting's Banyuls
producer.where: Collioure, Côte Vermeille, Roussillon, France
producer.history:
Domaine La Tour Vieille is a domaine of Collioure, on the Côte Vermeille, the rocky coast of Roussillon where the Pyrenees meet the Mediterranean at the Spanish frontier. It is the work of Christine Campadieu and Vincent Cantié, who brought together their families' vines on the steep schist terraces between Collioure and Banyuls-sur-Mer.

Those terraces are too steep for any machine and are laced with stone channels that carry the storm water off. From the same slopes come two appellations: dry Collioure, and Banyuls, a vin doux naturel; the grower decides at harvest which to declare. For Banyuls the fermentation is stopped by adding neutral grape spirit of at least 96 percent, so the grape's own sugar stays in the wine. A Banyuls must be at least half Grenache noir; Banyuls Grand Cru needs three quarters and thirty months in wood, a recipe rather than a better site.

La Tour Vieille bottles Banyuls in two moods. Rimage is the early-bottled vintage style, fresh black fruit. Reserva, the Catalan spelling, is non-vintage and aged the oxidative way, in contact with air, which turns it to dried fig, walnut, caramel and coffee.

Ours is the Reserva, poured as the 4 oz dessert wine of the dinner tasting with The Snickers. Its sweetness and gentle tannin meet chocolate without turning bitter, which is why Banyuls is the classic chocolate wine.
facts: Banyuls comes from steep schist terraces in four communes of the Côte Vermeille: Banyuls-sur-Mer, Collioure, Port-Vendres and Cerbère.
The same terraces make dry red Collioure; the grower decides at harvest which wine to declare.
Banyuls is a vin doux naturel: neutral grape spirit of at least 96 percent, at 5 to 10 percent of the volume, stops fermentation.
A Banyuls must be at least 50 percent Grenache noir; Banyuls Grand Cru needs 75 percent and 30 months in wood.
Rimage is the early-bottled vintage style of Banyuls; the oxidative style takes on coffee, walnut and dried fig.
Our Reserva is printed NV, a blend of years, and Reserva is a Catalan spelling, not the French Réserve.
Our Reserva is the dinner tasting's dessert pour, 4 oz with The Snickers, and is not on the by-the-glass list.
Banyuls suits chocolate because its oxidative Grenache has cocoa-like notes and gentler tannin than young Vintage Port.
The current NV Reserva page lists 80 percent Grenache Noir, 15 percent Grenache Gris and 5 percent Carignan; confirm the restaurant lot before treating these figures as its analysis.
notes: Say lah TOOR vee-AY, bahn-YOOLS, reh-ZAIR-vah. The final s of Banyuls is sounded.
Lead with dried fig, caramel and coffee; fresh black cherry describes a Rimage, not our Reserva.

Like Port, Banyuls is fortified during fermentation to retain grape sugar. This Reserva is a Roussillon blend aged oxidatively; do not promise that all Banyuls is softer or less alcoholic than all Port.
Guests ask for a glass outside the tasting: whether it is poured à la carte, and at what price, is a sommelier question, so promise nothing.
Never quote a founding year for the domaine; none is confirmed here.
producer.sayIt: To close, La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva: a sweet fortified blend from Roussillon, with dried fig, caramel and coffee notes alongside chocolate.
askKitchen: Is the Reserva poured à la carte, at breakfast and at dinner, and at what price for 2 to 3 oz?
Is the bottle we pour the Reserva, aged oxidatively, and not the Rimage?

components.name: Riveyrac
components.explain:
Riveyrac is the name on old vintages of Rivesaltes, a vin doux naturel of Roussillon, near Perpignan. The wines come from the cooperative cellar of Salses-le-Château in the Pyrénées-Orientales, founded by eight growers in 1909, by retailers' accounts.

Ours is Grenache and Grenache Gris, whose fermentation was stopped with grape spirit to keep its sugar; nothing sweet is ever added. The old wines then age for decades in old casks, where air turns them amber and nutty. It is not Muscat de Rivesaltes, a separate and fresher Muscat wine.

Ours is the 1975, fifty-one years old: caramel, walnut, quince, marmalade and coffee. With the Bananas Foster it tastes like the sauce itself.

card.front: What is the Riveyrac 1975 on our dessert list?
card.back: A Rivesaltes from Roussillon: fortified Grenache and Grenache Gris aged for decades in old casks, from the Salses-le-Château cooperative cellar. Caramel and walnut, our bottle for the Bananas Foster.

producer.history:
Riveyrac is the name on a run of old vintage Rivesaltes, a sweet fortified wine of Roussillon. By retailers' accounts, the wines come from the cooperative cellar of Salses-le-Château in the Pyrénées-Orientales, near Perpignan, founded by eight growers in 1909.

Rivesaltes is a vin doux naturel. The grapes are fermented, and neutral grape spirit is added partway to stop the yeast, so the grape's own sugar stays in the wine; nothing sweet is ever added. The old wines are then aged for decades in old casks, where slow contact with air turns them amber and nutty. That oxidative vocabulary, ambré, tuilé, hors d'âge and rancio, belongs to Rivesaltes, Maury and Banyuls alike.

Our bottle is the 1975, which those retailers sell as La Cuvée des Aigles: Grenache and Grenache Gris, about 15.5 percent, and fifty-one years old. It tastes of caramel, walnut, quince, marmalade and coffee, sweet with a delicate acidity.

It is not Muscat de Rivesaltes, a separate and lighter appellation of Muscat. On our list the Riveyrac is the bottle for the World Famous Bananas Foster: butter, brown sugar and rum meet caramel and nuts.

Our list prints it at $190 under bin 193312, a bin also printed for Marco de Bartoli's Bukkuram 2008.

Guests ask whether it is still good. The honest answer: sweet fortified wines aged with air last for decades, and caramel and nuts are what it should taste of.

components.name: R. López de Heredia
components.explain:
R. López de Heredia Viña Tondonia is one of the oldest houses in Rioja, founded in 1877 at Haro, the wine town of Rioja Alta, and the Codex's anchor for traditional Rioja. It bottles its estate vineyards as separate wines, Viña Tondonia, Viña Bosconia, Viña Cubillo and the white Viña Gravonia; Tondonia is a vineyard, not the company.

The house works slowly: fermentation in old wooden vats, years in old American oak barrels from its own cooperage, no filtration and long rests in bottle, so the reds arrive pale, savoury and mature.

Viña Cubillo, our Crianza 2016, is its youngest red: dried cherry, strawberry and leather, soft enough for the Roost Burger. The list also carries Viña Gravonia, the aged white.

card.front: What is Viña Cubillo, and who makes it?
card.back: The youngest red of R. López de Heredia, Haro's great traditional house, founded in 1877: a Crianza aged about three years in old American oak. Ours is the 2016.

producer.history:
R. López de Heredia Viña Tondonia is one of the oldest bodegas in Rioja, founded in 1877 at Haro, the wine town of Rioja Alta; the R. is for Rafael López de Heredia, its founder. The Codex sets it among the nineteenth-century foundings that gave Rioja its great houses and their Bordeaux technique: after Marqués de Murrieta and Marqués de Riscal, and two years before CVNE.

The Codex makes it the anchor for traditional Rioja. It bottles its estate vineyards as separate wines: Viña Tondonia, Viña Bosconia and Viña Cubillo among the reds, and Viña Gravonia, a white the Codex ties to the Zaconia vineyard. Tondonia is a vineyard, not the company, and Tondonia and Bosconia are different wines from different sites, not quality tiers.

Everything is slow: fermentation in old wooden vats, long ageing in old American oak barrels made in the bodega's own cooperage, fining with egg white, no filtration, and years more in bottle before release. The reds arrive pale and mature; the whites are deliberately oxidative, a style examiners use to tell intent from fault.

Viña Cubillo is the youngest red, a Crianza of Tempranillo with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo, aged about three years in barrel. Our 2016 is ten years old: dried cherry, strawberry, leather and gentle spice, light in tannin, with lively acidity.

components.name: CVNE (Compañía Vinícola del Norte de España)
components.explain:
CVNE, the Compañía Vinícola del Norte de España, is a historic Rioja house in the railway station quarter of Haro, founded in 1879 by the brothers Eusebio and Raimundo Real de Asúa. Its name is spoken Cune, KOO-nay, because the V of the old lettering was read as a U.

The company keeps its cellars apart: CVNE and Imperial at Haro in Rioja Alta, and Viña Real near Laguardia in Rioja Alavesa. Imperial and Viña Real are different subzones, not quality tiers, and the Imperial line is bottled as Reserva and as a Gran Reserva made only in selected years.

Our bottle is the Imperial Reserva 2018: Tempranillo with a little Graciano and Mazuelo, cherry, plum, sweet spice and leather, polished and savoury. The list also carries the CVNE Gran Reserva and the Viña Real Gran Reserva.

card.front: Why is CVNE said KOO-nay, and what is Imperial?
card.back: The V in its old lettering was read as a U, so CVNE became Cune. Imperial is its classic Rioja Alta label from Haro; ours is the Imperial Reserva 2018.

producer.history:
CVNE stands for Compañía Vinícola del Norte de España, the Northern Spanish Wine Company. It was founded at Haro in 1879 by the brothers Eusebio and Raimundo Real de Asúa, in the railway station quarter, the Barrio de la Estación, where Haro's great bodegas gathered beside the line to ship their wine. The initials are spoken Cune, KOO-nay, because the V of the old lettering was read as a U, and labels also print it Cune.

The Codex teaches CVNE as one company with two subzones and separate cellars: CVNE and Imperial at Haro in Rioja Alta, and Viña Real near Laguardia in Rioja Alavesa. Imperial and Viña Real are different places, not quality tiers. Monopole, a Viura white, is one of Spain's oldest white wine brands.

The style is classical, oak-aged Rioja: red fruit, cedar and spice, each cellar kept to its own subzone. Imperial is the Rioja Alta line, bottled as Reserva and as a Gran Reserva made only in selected years.

Our Imperial Reserva 2018 is Tempranillo with a little Graciano and Mazuelo, aged in oak and then in bottle before release: red and black cherry, plum, sweet spice and leather, medium to full, polished and savoury.

components.name: Dominio de Pingus
components.explain:
Dominio de Pingus is the Ribera del Duero estate the Danish winemaker Peter Sisseck founded in 1995, on old bush vines of Tinto Fino, the local Tempranillo, at La Horra, farmed biodynamically. Its flagship, Pingus, first made in 1995 in tiny amounts, is Spain's modern cult wine; the Codex credits Sisseck with making La Horra's old vines the reference parcels of the region.

Flor de Pingus is the second wine, from a wider set of La Horra parcels. PSI is a separate project that buys and revives growers' old-vine fruit; it is not declassified Pingus.

Our Flor de Pingus 2022 is young, dark and concentrated: blackberry, black cherry, liquorice and graphite, dense but fresh. Decant it an hour ahead for steak or lamb.

card.front: Who founded Dominio de Pingus, and what is Flor de Pingus?
card.back: The Danish winemaker Peter Sisseck, in 1995, with old Tinto Fino vines at La Horra in Ribera del Duero. Flor de Pingus is the estate's second wine; ours is the 2022.

producer.history:
Dominio de Pingus was founded in 1995 by Peter Sisseck, a Danish winemaker, in Ribera del Duero, the high-altitude Tempranillo country along the Duero in Castilla y León. He built it on old bush vines of Tinto Fino, the Ribera name for Tempranillo, at La Horra, farmed biodynamically, with very low yields and gentle handling of whole berries; the Codex places the winery downstream, at Quintanilla de Onésimo.

Pingus itself, first made in 1995 and produced in tiny amounts, is Spain's modern cult wine. The Codex says Sisseck's arrival made La Horra's old bush vines the reference parcels of Ribera del Duero and created the market for Spanish cult wine, in a region that had been granted its denomination only in 1982.

Flor de Pingus is the second wine, from a wider set of La Horra parcels, farmed the same way; the October card says both wines are aged in French oak. PSI is a separate project again, buying and reviving old bush-vine fruit from growers; it is not declassified Pingus.

Our Flor de Pingus 2022 is four years old: a deep, inky purple, with blackberry, black cherry, liquorice and graphite, ripe and dense in tannin, with a fresh line. It wants an hour in the decanter and a big piece of beef or lamb.

components.name: Vega Sicilia
components.explain:
Vega Sicilia is the estate at Valbuena de Duero, in Ribera del Duero, that the Codex dates to 1864. Bordeaux varieties have grown there since the nineteenth century, which the Codex gives as the reason Ribera del Duero permits Cabernet Sauvignon, and the estate was making its red long before the region was granted its denomination in 1982.

Único, the flagship, is Tinto Fino with Cabernet Sauvignon, aged in casks of several sizes and then in bottle, and released around a decade after the harvest. Valbuena 5° is released in its fifth year; Único Reserva Especial blends several vintages and carries no year.

Our Único 2009 is layered and fresh: dark cherry, plum, cedar, tobacco and sweet spice. It is a celebration bottle; involve the sommelier.

card.front: What makes Vega Sicilia Único different from other Spanish reds?
card.back: Its patience: Tinto Fino with Cabernet Sauvignon, aged in casks and bottle and released around a decade after harvest, from an estate dated to 1864. Ours is the 2009.

producer.history:
Vega Sicilia stands on the Duero at Valbuena de Duero, in Ribera del Duero, on the high plateau of Castilla y León. The Codex dates the estate to 1864, and Bordeaux varieties have been planted there since the nineteenth century. The Codex gives that as the reason Ribera del Duero permits Cabernet Sauvignon, and it means Vega Sicilia was making a Bordeaux-influenced red long before the region was granted its denomination in 1982.

Its signature is patience. The wines age for years in casks of several sizes and ages and then in bottle, so they are released resolved: released when ready, not when due, as the Codex puts it. Único, the flagship, is Tinto Fino, the local Tempranillo, with Cabernet Sauvignon, held around a decade before release. Valbuena 5° comes from the same estate and is released in its fifth year. Único Reserva Especial is a blend of several vintages sold without a year, and Alión is a separate winery, not a Vega Sicilia cuvée.

Our Único 2009 is seventeen years old: deep garnet, dark cherry, plum, cedar, tobacco and sweet spice, fine tannin and lively acidity, with a very long finish. The list also carries the Reserva Especial and two vintages of Valbuena 5°.

components.name: Raúl Pérez
components.explain:
Raúl Pérez is a winemaker from Bierzo, the mountain valley of north-west Spain beside Galicia. By the Codex, his family's old vines are at Valtuille de Abajo, the family bodega he came from is Castro Ventosa, and he bottles under his own labels, Ultreia and La Vizcaína, with projects in Ribeira Sacra, Rías Baixas and Monterrei. The Codex calls him the consultant behind much of the Atlantic Spain revival.

His style is restless and experimental: old foudres for Mencía, long lees ageing for whites, low sulphur.

Our Ultreia Godello 2021 is textured and saline: lemon, pear and almond with a herbal edge, the value white for the Gulf Fish en Papillote. Ultreia is an old pilgrims' greeting on the road to Santiago.

card.back: A Bierzo winemaker the Codex places behind much of the Atlantic Spain revival. Ultreia, an old pilgrims' greeting, is his own label; ours is the Ultreia Godello 2021, a textured, saline white.

producer.history:
Raúl Pérez is a winemaker from Bierzo, a mountain valley in the north-west of Castilla y León, beside Galicia and on the pilgrim road to Santiago de Compostela. The Codex places his family's old vines at Valtuille de Abajo and names Castro Ventosa as the family bodega he came from.

Under his own labels, Ultreia and La Vizcaína, which are labels and not separate wineries, he bottles Bierzo from old vines, and his projects reach into Ribeira Sacra, Rías Baixas and Monterrei. The Codex calls him the consultant behind much of the Atlantic Spain revival, and names him, with Descendientes de J. Palacios, as a leader of Bierzo's 2017 classification of villages, parajes and classified vineyards.

His style is restless and experimental: old foudres for Mencía, extended lees ageing for whites, low sulphur and a readiness to take aromatic risks. Among his wines are El Pecado, from very steep river terraces in Ribeira Sacra, and Sketch, an Albariño of which some is aged submerged in the sea.

Godello is the white grape of this corner of Spain. Our Ultreia Godello 2021 is gold, textured and round yet fresh: lemon, pear and almond with a saline, herbal edge. The list also carries Ultreia La Claudina, El Pecado, two La Vizcaína Bierzo reds and Encinas, made with Antoine Graillot.

components.name: Do Ferreiro
components.explain:
Do Ferreiro is a grower in the Val do Salnés, the coolest and most maritime corner of Rías Baixas, whose small granite parcels lie around Meaño; the Codex names the grower Gerardo Méndez. Ferreiro is Galician for blacksmith.

Its Cepas Vellas, old vines, comes from a plot of Albariño the Codex reports as more than two hundred years old, and it is the Codex's reference for old-vine Albariño and for the case that Rías Baixas can make textured whites that age.

Our Cepas Vellas 2018 has years in bottle: lemon, white peach and sea spray with a savoury, stony depth, textured and long. It is the bottle for the Creole Caesar and the grand cousin of our Albariño by the glass.

card.front: What does Cepas Vellas mean on the Do Ferreiro label?
card.back: Old vines, in Galician: a plot of Albariño in the Val do Salnés that the Codex reports as over two hundred years old. Ours is the 2018, textured and saline.

The estate is the Codex's reference for old-vine Albariño, and for the case that Rías Baixas can make textured, ageworthy whites rather than only aromatic ones. Its style is low-intervention: texture and salt rather than aromatic lift. Here, as is traditional across the region, the vines are trained high on pergolas to fight the Atlantic damp.

components.name: La Cigarrera
components.explain:
La Cigarrera is a sherry bodega in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the seaside town at the mouth of the Guadalquivir where Manzanilla is made. Manzanilla is fino-style sherry that may only be aged in Sanlúcar: the cool, humid Atlantic air keeps the flor, a living veil of yeast, thick through the year, so the wine stays pale, light and saline.

La Cigarrera's Manzanilla is Palomino from a solera, so it carries no vintage. Cigarrera is Spanish for a woman who makes cigars.

Ours is the half-bottle, bone dry: green apple, chamomile, almond, bread dough and a salty sea breeze. It is the half for the Turtle Soup, which is finished with aged sherry.

card.front: Why is La Cigarrera Manzanilla the half-bottle for the Turtle Soup?
card.back: It is bone dry sherry from Sanlúcar de Barrameda, aged under flor: salty, nutty and light. The soup is finished with aged sherry, so a dry sherry beside it repeats that flavour and cuts the richness.

producer.who: La Cigarrera, a Manzanilla bodega in Sanlúcar de Barrameda

producer.history:
La Cigarrera is a sherry bodega in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the seaside town at the mouth of the Guadalquivir river, facing the Atlantic in Andalucía. Sanlúcar is one of the three towns of the sherry triangle, with Jerez de la Frontera and El Puerto de Santa María, and the only one where Manzanilla may be aged.

Manzanilla is fino-style sherry from the Palomino grape, grown on white albariza soil. It ages under flor, a living layer of yeast on the surface of the wine, and Sanlúcar's cool, humid sea air keeps that veil thick all year, so the wine stays pale and light and takes on a salty tang. It is fortified, but delicate. It comes from a solera, tiers of casks topped up with younger wine, so the bottle carries no vintage.

Cigarrera is the Spanish word for a woman who makes cigars; why the bodega carries the name is a question for the sommelier.

Our La Cigarrera Manzanilla comes in a half-bottle: pale straw and bone dry, with green apple, chamomile, almond, bread dough and a salty sea breeze. Opened, it fades within days, so it is kept iced and poured in small measures.

components.name: Bodegas Barbadillo
components.explain:
Bodegas Barbadillo is a sherry house in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the seaside town at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, best known for Manzanilla, the dry, salty sherry that may only be aged there.

Its Pale Cream is a different thing: a light, pale sherry in the fino style that is then gently sweetened. Cream and Pale Cream are sweetened blends, unlike the naturally sweet Pedro Ximénez.

In the glass it is pale gold: apricot, honey, almond and vanilla with a salty, nutty edge, medium sweet. Served chilled, it is a first pick for the Cheese Board and an easy aperitif, though too lightly sweet for the bread pudding.

card.front: What is Barbadillo Pale Cream, and when do we pour it?
card.back: A pale, fino-style sherry gently sweetened, from a Sanlúcar house best known for Manzanilla. Serve it chilled as an aperitif or with the Cheese Board; it is too light for the bread pudding.

producer.history:
Bodegas Barbadillo is a sherry house in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the seaside town at the mouth of the Guadalquivir river in Andalucía, in the south-west of Spain. The house carries the Barbadillo name and is best known for Manzanilla, the light, dry, salty sherry that may only be aged in Sanlúcar, where the cool, humid Atlantic air keeps the flor thick through the year.

Most sherry begins dry, from the Palomino grape grown on white albariza soil. Sweet sherry is made in two ways: from naturally sweet grapes, Pedro Ximénez dried in the sun or Moscatel, or by sweetening a dry wine, which is what Cream and Pale Cream sherries are.

Barbadillo's Pale Cream is the light version: a pale sherry made in the fino style and then gently sweetened; how it is sweetened is a question for the sommelier. By the house's October 2026 notes, the pale cream style dates from the 1970s.

In the glass it is pale gold and silky: apricot, honey, almond and vanilla with a faint salty, nutty note, medium sweet, with a soft, long finish. Served chilled it is the friendly sweet sherry, before dinner or with the Cheese Board and the spiced nuts. It is too lightly sweet for the bread pudding, which wants a sweeter wine.

components.name: Pierre Sparr
components.explain:
Pierre Sparr is an Alsace house whose family story starts in the village of Sigolsheim, dated by the house to 1680. Pierre Sparr took over in the early 1900s and, by the house's account, was one of the pioneers of estate bottling in Alsace; he rebuilt after the Second World War destroyed Sigolsheim and its vineyards. Since 2009 the name has belonged to the Cave de Beblenheim, a growers' cooperative.

Our glass is its Crémant d'Alsace Brut Rosé: all Pinot Noir, as the appellation requires for a rosé, made by the traditional method and aged at least 18 months on its lees. Call it Crémant or French sparkling rosé, never Champagne; the list also carries Sparr's Mambourg and Schoenenbourg grand crus.

card.front: Why is Pierre Sparr's Crémant rosé all Pinot Noir? What do we call it?
card.back: Crémant d'Alsace rosé may be made only from Pinot Noir. Call it Crémant or French sparkling rosé, made the Champagne way in Alsace, never Champagne.

producer.who: Pierre Sparr, the Alsace house behind our sparkling rosé by the glass
producer.where: Sigolsheim, the family's village, and Beblenheim, home of the cooperative that took the house over in 2009; Haut-Rhin, Alsace, France
producer.founded: 1680, as the house dates the Sparr family; one guide says 1634
producer.history:
The Sparr name in Alsace goes back to 1680, the year the house gives for Jean Sparr in the village of Sigolsheim; some sources call it the founding, others his birth, and one guide dates the family's vines to 1634. In 1785 François Pierre Sparr enlarged the vineyards, and Charles Sparr later built up the trade and the ageing of the wines.

Pierre Sparr, who gave the house its name, took over in the early 1900s at about twenty and, by the house's account, became one of the pioneers of estate bottling in Alsace. In the Second World War Sigolsheim and its vineyards were destroyed; Pierre rebuilt, and his sons René and Charles enlarged the vineyards and opened European markets.

In 2009 the house was taken over by the Cave de Beblenheim, a cooperative founded in 1952 near Riquewihr, which keeps the Pierre Sparr name; the house now stands on the cooperative's street in Beblenheim, and its importer describes fruit from member growers. The range still includes grand cru wines from the Mambourg, the south-facing slope of Mount Sigolsheim, and the Schoenenbourg between Riquewihr and Zellenberg.

At Brennan's the Sparr is the pink bubbles by the glass: a Crémant d'Alsace Brut Rosé, all Pinot Noir, made by the traditional method and aged at least 18 months on its lees by the importer's sheet. The list also carries Sparr's Mambourg and Schoenenbourg grand crus from 2020.

In 2009 the house was taken over by the Cave de Beblenheim, a cooperative founded in 1952, which keeps the Pierre Sparr name.
The Crémant d'Alsace Brut Rosé is 100 per cent Pinot Noir, aged at least 18 months on its lees by the importer's sheet.

notes: Say pee-AIR SHPAR, Sparr rhyming with car, and kray-MAHN for Crémant. Call it Crémant or French sparkling rosé, never Champagne.
Since 2009 the house has belonged to the Cave de Beblenheim cooperative, as of October 2026. Do not call it a family estate today; ownership can change.

Say dry rather than a sugar figure: the published dosage figures disagree, and one is above the brut ceiling.

components.name: Cesarini Sforza
components.explain:
Cesarini Sforza is a sparkling wine house in Trento, in the Italian Alps, founded in 1974 by Count Lamberto Cesarini Sforza and a small group of friends. Its first traditional method wine came in 1976, and it counts itself among the pioneers of the Trento DOC, sold as Trentodoc. Its emblem is an eagle, the coat of arms of the city, and since December 2019 it has belonged to the Cavit group.

Our bottle is the Rosé Brut at $55: mostly Chardonnay with a little Pinot Noir from hillside plots, rested on its lees for about three years, dry and bright with small red berries. Say Trentodoc or Italian sparkling rosé, never Champagne or Prosecco.

card.front: Who founded Cesarini Sforza, and where?
card.back: Count Lamberto Cesarini Sforza and friends, in Trento in 1974. It makes Trentodoc by the traditional method; our Rosé Brut is mostly Chardonnay with a little Pinot Noir.

Cesarini Sforza takes its name from Count Lamberto Cesarini Sforza, who founded the house in Trento in 1974 with a small group of friends. The house's first Metodo Classico, made from selected Chardonnay and Pinot Nero vineyards, followed in 1976, and it is counted among the pioneers of the Trento DOC, sold as Trentodoc.

Its emblem is an eagle, which is also the coat of arms of the city of Trento, and its long-aged Aquila Reale Riserva, a Chardonnay Blanc de Blancs, carries the eagle's name.

The house has belonged to larger Trentino groups for most of this century: managed by the La Vis cooperative group from 2001, it was bought by the Cavit group in a December 2019 restructuring. It marked fifty years in 2024.

Our bottle is the Rosé Brut, mostly Chardonnay with a little Pinot Noir from hillside plots (the producer has given 85 and 15), aged on its lees for 36 months by the house's own page. At $55 it sits in the list's Selections Under $100, and it is the first pick for the Popcorn Shrimp at the Roost Bar.

components.name: Ferrari of Trento
components.explain:
Ferrari is Trento's best known sparkling house, founded in 1902 by Giulio Ferrari, who learned the Champagne method in Épernay and is credited with being the first to plant Chardonnay widely in Italy. Having no children, he passed the house in 1952 to Bruno Lunelli, a Trento wine merchant, whose family has run it since, by the house's own pages. It makes only Trentodoc, the traditional method sparkling wine of Trento, and it is no relation to the cars.

We pour the Rosé Brut, $95, 60 per cent Pinot Noir and 40 per cent Chardonnay, and the Brut in half-bottle, $60, all Chardonnay. Say Trentodoc or Italian sparkling wine, never Champagne.

card.front: Who founded Ferrari of Trento, and is it linked to the cars?
card.back: Giulio Ferrari, in 1902, after learning the Champagne method in Épernay. No link to the cars; the Lunelli family has run it since 1952.

producer.history:
Ferrari was founded in 1902 by Giulio Ferrari, who had worked in Épernay, in the heart of Champagne, and learned how traditional method sparkling wine was made. Convinced that his home region of Trentino suited Chardonnay, he is credited with being the first to plant it widely in Italy. In 1906 his wine won a gold medal at the International Exhibition in Milan, its first official recognition.

Giulio Ferrari had no children. In 1952 he chose as his successor Bruno Lunelli, a Trento wine shop owner, who went deep into debt to buy a company then making about 9,000 bottles a year. Bruno's sons led its growth, and the family's third generation leads it today, by the house's own pages.

Ferrari makes only Trentodoc, the traditional method sparkling wine of Trento, and it is no relation to the cars: Ferrari was the founder's surname. In 2021 it was named the official toast of Formula 1.

We pour two wines. The Rosé Brut, $95, is 60 per cent Pinot Noir and 40 per cent Chardonnay by the house's sheet, at least 20 months on its lees, and the first pick for the Crawfish Meat Pies. The Brut half-bottle, $60, is all Chardonnay. The list also carries Perlé Bianco 2017.

components.name: Jansz Tasmania
components.explain:
Jansz makes sparkling wine at Pipers River, in the cool north-east of Tasmania, the island south of mainland Australia. It is named for the explorer Abel Janszoon Tasman. The venture began in 1986 between Heemskerk Wines and the Champagne house Louis Roederer, and its first sparkling wine followed in 1989. The Hill-Smith family of Yalumba bought it in 1998 by most accounts.

The house's non-vintage is the Premium Cuvée, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; our list prints Premier Cuvée Brut 2022 at $65, so read the label. It is crisp citrus and green apple with a touch of brioche: say Tasmanian sparkling wine, never Champagne.

card.front: What links Jansz to Champagne?
card.back: It began in 1986 as a venture between Heemskerk Wines and the Champagne house Louis Roederer at Pipers River, Tasmania. Roederer was a partner then, not the owner today.

producer.who: Jansz Tasmania, the sparkling wine house at Pipers River, begun with Louis Roederer
producer.where: Pipers River, north-east Tasmania, Australia
producer.founded: 1986, as a venture with Louis Roederer; the vineyard was planted in 1975
producer.history:
Jansz is named for the Dutch explorer Abel Janszoon Tasman, who sighted the island in 1642. Its vineyard at Pipers River, in the north-east of Tasmania, was established in 1975 and first carried the name Heemskerk, after Tasman's ship.

In 1986 Heemskerk Wines and the Champagne house Louis Roederer, which had recognised how closely the Tasmanian climate resembled Champagne's, joined forces there to make sparkling wine; one source dates the partnership to 1982. In 1989, by one account, the estate made Tasmania's first sparkling wine by the traditional method. The Hill-Smith family, owners of Yalumba, bought the label and vineyard in 1998 by most accounts and renamed it Jansz Tasmania.

Pipers River is cool and close to the sea: breezes off the Bass Strait keep winters mild and summers cool, so the grapes ripen slowly and keep their acidity. Jansz calls its approach méthode Tasmanoise, to stress the island rather than imitate Champagne, though the method is the same second fermentation in bottle.

The house's non-vintage is the Premium Cuvée, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from several Tasmanian vineyards. Our list prints Jansz Premier Cuvée Brut 2022 at $65, the first pick for the Creole Spiced Nuts, so the sommelier should confirm which bottling is in the cellar.

components.name: Jean-Philippe Fichet
components.explain:
Jean-Philippe Fichet is a grower in Meursault, not to be confused with Domaine Fichet of Igé, whose Château London is the dinner tasting white. He began in 1981, lost his best fruit sources in the 1990s, a piece of Meursault-Perrières among them, and rebuilt from scratch on long-term leases, so that by 2000 he farmed a fine set of sites. His Meursaults all come from named village vineyards; he has no premier cru in the village, only a small parcel of Puligny’s Les Referts.

The style is taut and mineral, clarity over richness. Our Bourgogne Blanc 2023 comes from old vines in the village of Meursault and, by his importer’s sheets, is raised in tank rather than barrel. At $95 it is our white Burgundy anchor under $100.

producer.history:
Jean-Philippe Fichet is a grower in Meursault, the village famous for rich, nutty white Burgundy. He began in 1981, but in the 1990s he lost his best fruit sources, among them a piece of Meursault-Perrières, for want of long-term contracts; one account says the Perrières went in 1996, when its owner died.

He rebuilt from scratch. By 2000 he had pieced together a new domaine on carefully negotiated long-term leases, fermage and métayage, parcel by parcel. His Meursaults all come from lieux-dits, named village vineyards such as Les Chevalières, on the same slope as the premiers crus. By his importer’s account he has no premier or grand cru in Meursault itself, but a small parcel of the Puligny-Montrachet Premier Cru Les Referts, with vines in Monthelie and Auxey-Duresses too.

He farms by lutte raisonnée, reasoned farming, and by his importer’s sheet avoids chemical fertilisers, herbicides and pesticides and harvests by hand; importers describe the house style as mineral expression, texture and clarity over richness. By the same sheets, his Bourgogne Blanc comes from three parcels in the village of Meursault, with vines over 50 years old on average, fermented in steel and raised in cement tank; a separate Vieilles Vignes is aged longer in barrel.

He is a different grower from Domaine Fichet of Igé in the Mâconnais, maker of the Château London Mâcon-Igé on our dinner tasting.

components.name: Thierry et Pascale Matrot
components.explain:
Matrot is an old Meursault family. Joseph Matrot, grandson of vineyard owners in Puligny-Montrachet, settled in Meursault at his wife’s family domaine in 1914; his grandson Thierry started there in 1976 and, with his wife Pascale, gave the wines their present label from 2009. Their daughters Elsa and Adèle joined in 2008 and 2010 and took over from their father with the 2016 vintage.

By its merchant’s account the vines have been farmed organically since 2000. The whites ferment slowly in barrel with little new oak and are bottled just before the next harvest. Our bottle is the Bourgogne Blanc 2022 in a half-bottle, $45: two or three glasses of a Meursault family’s Chardonnay, fresh and lightly nutty, for one or two guests with the crab claws.

card.back: The Matrot family of Meursault: the label of Thierry and Pascale Matrot, whose daughters Elsa and Adèle took over with the 2016 vintage. Farmed organically since 2000, by its merchant.

producer.history:
The Matrot story in Meursault begins in 1914, when Joseph Matrot, the grandson of vineyard owners in Puligny-Montrachet, settled at his wife’s family domaine in the village. His grandson Thierry Matrot, Pierre Matrot’s son, started at the domaine in 1976 and, by one account, moved it away from chemical fertilisers as he did.

A 2015 visit found the family’s vines in three structures, the heirs of Joseph Matrot, Pierre Matrot, and Thierry and Pascale Matrot. Before 2009 the wines were known as Domaine Pierre Matrot; from 2009 every bottle leaving the cellars, older stock included, carried the names of Thierry and his wife Pascale.

The next generation is already at work. Elsa Matrot, with a degree in oenology, joined her parents in 2008; her sister Adèle, with a master’s in wine business, followed in 2010, and the two took over from their father with the 2016 vintage.

By one merchant’s account the vineyards have been farmed organically since 2000, without certification when it wrote. The whites ferment long and slowly in barrel with little new oak and are bottled just before the next harvest; the reds are made without stems. Beyond our half-bottle, the range climbs to the Meursault premiers crus Charmes, Perrières and Blagny and to Puligny’s Les Chalumeaux and Les Combettes.

components.name: Raymond Dupont-Fahn
components.explain:
Raymond Dupont-Fahn is a small family domaine near Meursault. Hachette and its merchants place it at Tailly, a little village on the plain just south of Meursault, though other Hachette entries name a Dupont-Fahn domaine at Monthélie. Its pride is Les Tillets, a village lieu-dit at the top of the Meursault slope, one of the highest vineyards in the village, with rocky topsoil.

The family’s other known wine, Chaumes des Perrières, comes from rocky land beside Perrières that was classed as Bourgogne after topsoil was added. Our Les Tillets 2022, $175, is Meursault at a sweet spot price: rich and nutty, with that high-slope lift, the sweet spot bottle for the BBQ lobster.

card.back: Les Tillets sits at the top of the Meursault slope, one of the village’s highest vineyards, on rocky topsoil. Raymond Dupont-Fahn, a small family estate near Meursault, makes it.

producer.history:
Domaine Raymond Dupont-Fahn is a small family estate near Meursault. Hachette and two merchants place it at Tailly, a little village on the plain just south of Meursault; other Hachette entries describe a Dupont-Fahn domaine at Monthélie, next door, and whether that is the same business is not settled. Merchants date the estate to 1975, but they disagree on which grandfather made the first purchase and on how many generations have run it since, so the honest line is a small family domaine.

Its best-known wine is Les Tillets. The vineyard is a lieu-dit, a named village site, at the top of the Meursault slope: one of the highest in Meursault, with rocky topsoil, and its height gives the wine an unusual freshness. By its merchant, the 2022 is all Chardonnay with about a fifth new oak, from a family that favours early harvests, organic farming and no chaptalisation.

The other story guests enjoy is Chaumes des Perrières. By the merchants’ accounts, the family’s rocky land on the boundary of Perrières and Sous le Dos d’Ane was judged too thin in the 1970s, and the INAO allowed 20 cm of topsoil to be spread on it; neighbouring growers objected, and the parcel was declassified from Meursault to Bourgogne.

components.name: Bitouzet-Prieur
components.explain:
Bitouzet-Prieur is a traditional family domaine in Volnay with vines in Meursault, two families joined by the marriage of Vincent Bitouzet and Annie Prieur; the Prieurs came from Meursault. By a 2016 report their son François, the sixth generation, was at the domaine.

The family are known as arch traditionalists: native yeasts, mostly used barrels and wines that are seldom open on release and reward patience. By the same report, Meursault makes up about two fifths of what they make. Our Les Corbins 2020, $210, comes from a small plot north of the village, just below the premier cru Les Plures, and arrives with a few years in bottle: creamy and nutty, the sweet spot bottle for the Poussin à la Moutarde.

card.front: Where is Bitouzet-Prieur based, and why does our Meursault Les Corbins taste rounder?
card.back: In Volnay, with vines in Meursault: a very traditional family, native yeasts and mostly used barrels. Our Les Corbins 2020 has several years in bottle, so it tastes creamy and nutty.

Bitouzet-Prieur joins two old Côte de Beaune families. The names came together with the marriage of Vincent Bitouzet and Annie Prieur, and the domaine is based in Volnay with holdings in Meursault. The Prieurs, on the maternal side, came from Meursault; importers tell the early history of the Bitouzet side in different ways, so its dates are best left alone at the table.

By a 2016 report, Vincent stopped the use of herbicides across the domaine in 1992 and 1993, the vines are farmed organically and picked by hand, and his and Annie’s son François, the sixth generation, was at the domaine. Meursault then made up about 40 percent of the wine.

The family are known as arch traditionalists: native yeast fermentations, mostly used barrels, and wines that are seldom open on release and reward a few years in bottle. Les Corbins, our bottle, is by its merchant a small plot north of Meursault village, just below the premier cru Les Plures, planted between 1974 and 1987. The 2020 spent 16 months in barrel, a fifth of them new.

components.name: Domaine Paul Pillot
components.explain:
Domaine Paul Pillot is a family estate in Chassagne-Montrachet. One merchant’s history traces the family’s vines there to 1900; Paul Pillot took charge in 1968, and his son Thierry, the fourth generation, has run the domaine since 2004 by most accounts, with his sister Chrystelle leading the vineyards. Its Chassagne premiers crus include the Clos Saint-Jean, the Grandes Ruchottes and Caillerets.

Our bottle is the Saint-Aubin Premier Cru Le Charmois 2022, $215. Saint-Aubin is the hillside village behind Puligny and Chassagne, and Le Charmois lies on the east-facing slope bordering Chassagne’s Les Chaumées, from vines over 50 years old with little new oak: crisp, chalky Chardonnay, the sweet spot bottle for the crab claws.

card.back: Domaine Paul Pillot, a Chassagne-Montrachet family estate. Le Charmois is a Saint-Aubin premier cru on the slope bordering Chassagne: crisp, chalky Chardonnay at a gentler price.

Domaine Paul Pillot is a family estate in Chassagne-Montrachet. One merchant’s history traces the family’s vines in the village to 1900, when a cooper turned to growing grapes; other sources begin the story with Paul Pillot himself.

Paul Pillot took charge in 1968 and expanded the holdings, which include the Chassagne premiers crus Clos Saint-Jean, Grandes Ruchottes and Caillerets. His son Thierry joined in 1999 and has run the domaine since 2004 by most accounts, 2007 by one; Thierry’s sister Chrystelle joined a few years later, and the fourth generation splits the work, Chrystelle in the vineyards and Thierry in the cellar. Thierry also has a small négoce label of his own, listed separately on our wine list.

The vines lie mostly in Chassagne-Montrachet, Saint-Aubin and Santenay, with small parcels in neighbouring villages. Both of the family’s Saint-Aubin vineyards sit on the east-facing hillside bordering the Chassagne premier cru Les Chaumées, cut off from the rest of Saint-Aubin by a small valley. Le Charmois, our bottle, comes from vines over 50 years old on marl and limestone soils rich in iron, raised with only about a tenth new oak, so the wine stays crisp and chalky: Chassagne’s neighbour at a gentler price.

components.name: François Carillon
components.explain:
François Carillon comes from one of Puligny-Montrachet’s old families: a Jehan Carillon appears in the village archives in 1520, and a Carillon grower is recorded in 1632. François worked at the family domaine from 1988. When his father, Louis Carillon, retired, the vines were divided between François and his brother Jacques, and 2010 was François’s first harvest under his own name.

He farms without herbicides, a reasoned approach rather than a certified organic one, and keeps new oak low, so the wines read as precise, balanced and mineral rather than powerful. Our bottle is his village Puligny-Montrachet 2022, $275: citrus, white peach and hazelnut with Puligny’s chalky tension, the celebration bottle for the crab claws.

The Carillons are one of the old families of Puligny-Montrachet. A Jehan Carillon appears in the archives in 1520, and a Carillon viticulteur is recorded in 1632; by the family’s account the craft has passed from father to son since, and one source counts François as the sixteenth generation.

François worked at the family property from 1988. When his father, Louis Carillon, retired, the vineyards were split between François and his brother Jacques, and each set up a domaine of his own: 2010 was François’s first harvest under his name. His share was mostly premier cru and village Puligny, and his vines now reach across Puligny-Montrachet, Chassagne-Montrachet and Saint-Aubin.

He farms with a reasoned approach and careful soil work, without herbicides since 1992 by one source; no organic certification was found for his estate. In the cellar he uses new oak sparingly, by one account never more than 15 percent even on the top wines, and reviewers describe precision, balance and minerality over power.

His Puligny holdings include Les Enseignères, a village lieu-dit just across from the grand cru Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet, and the premiers crus Les Folatières, Les Perrières and Champ Gain. Our bottle is his village Puligny-Montrachet.

components.name: Domaine Roulot
components.explain:
Domaine Roulot is a Meursault family estate whose modern fame was built by Guy Roulot. From the 1950s he bottled named village vineyards, lieux-dits such as Les Luchets and Les Tessons, on their own, and his 1973 Meursault Charmes came second among the whites at the 1976 Judgment of Paris. After his death in 1982, Ted Lemon, the first American to run a Burgundy domaine, and then Franck Grux made the wines, until Guy’s son Jean-Marc, a stage and film actor, took over in 1989.

Jean-Marc has farmed organically since he took over, and his wines are known as taut and precise rather than buttery. He also plays Marcel, the winemaker, in the film Back to Burgundy. Our village Meursault 2022 is $500 on the list, a measure of how sought-after the name is.

card.back: Domaine Roulot, with Guy Roulot’s 1973 Meursault Charmes. His son Jean-Marc, an actor, took over in 1989 and makes taut, precise Meursault; our village Meursault is his.

producer.history:
The Roulot family is long established in Meursault, and the domaine’s modern reputation was built by Guy Roulot. From the 1950s he bottled individual village lieux-dits on their own, named vineyards such as Les Luchets and Les Tessons. His 1973 Meursault Charmes finished second among the whites, behind Château Montelena’s 1973, at the 1976 Judgment of Paris.

When Guy died in 1982, his son Jean-Marc was starting a career as a stage and film actor. The wines were made first by Ted Lemon, the first American to run a Burgundy domaine, who went on to found Littorai, and then by Franck Grux, until Jean-Marc took over in 1989. He never quite gave up acting: in Cédric Klapisch’s film Back to Burgundy, released in 2017, he plays Marcel, the estate’s winemaker, and he was the film’s technical consultant.

Jean-Marc has farmed organically since 1989, and later biodynamically. When the vineyards of Domaine René Manuel were shared between Roulot and Lafon, he took the Clos des Bouchères. His wines are known as taut and precise rather than buttery: Meursault in its leaner, stonier voice.

components.name: Domaine Coche-Dury
components.explain:
Domaine Coche-Dury of Meursault makes some of the scarcest and most coveted white wine in the world. Léon Coche began buying vines in Meursault, Auxey-Duresses and Monthélie in 1923; his grandson Jean-François, Georges’s son, took over in the early 1970s and added his wife Odile Dury’s name. Robert Parker’s praise in the 1980s made it famous, and their son Raphaël Coche has made the wines since his father retired in 2010.

The style rests on long lees ageing in barrel with regular stirring, which gives the struck-match, flinty edge over citrus and a saline finish. Our Bourgogne Blanc 2022, $690, is the estate’s regional white, from parcels scattered through its Meursault vines by a merchant’s account: priced for its scarcity, not its appellation.

card.front: Why does a Coche-Dury Bourgogne Blanc cost more than most Meursault?
card.back: Scarcity: Coche-Dury is one of the most coveted white Burgundy estates, and even its regional white is hard to find. Raphaël Coche has made the wines since 2010, in the flinty, reductive style.

producer.history:
Domaine Coche-Dury began in 1923, when Léon Coche started buying parcels in Meursault, Auxey-Duresses and Monthélie. His vines passed to his children, his son Georges among them.

Georges’s son Jean-François took over in the early 1970s, 1972 or 1973 by different accounts, and married Odile Dury, whose name was added to the estate’s; one account dates the marriage to 1975. In the 1980s Robert Parker’s praise made him famous, and Coche-Dury became the reference for a reductive style of white Burgundy: long ageing on the lees in barrel, regular bâtonnage and a struck-match, flinty edge over citrus and a saline finish. Sotheby’s notes that recent vintages show a gentler struck match and gunflint.

Their son Raphaël Coche joined full time in the late 1990s and took over the winemaking when his father retired in 2010. In a Decanter profile he argues that everything in Meursault is under-classified, a village with no grand cru at all.

The domaine farms small parcels across Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet, Auxey-Duresses, Monthelie, Volnay and Aloxe-Corton, with the Meursault premiers crus Perrières, Caillerets and Genevrières, village lieux-dits such as Les Rougeots and a fraction of Corton-Charlemagne. By a merchant’s account, the Bourgogne Blanc comes from parcels scattered through its Meursault vines, some planted in the 1930s, on clay and limestone.

components.name: Trimbach
components.explain:
Trimbach is one of the old family houses of Alsace. It was founded in 1626 by Jean Trimbach at Riquewihr, later settled at Ribeauvillé, and the family counts thirteen generations. Its labels print F.E. Trimbach or simply Trimbach, and our list prints both: it is one house.

Trimbach also makes Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer, including its Réserve Personnelle tier and, in the right years, Vendanges Tardives: late-picked wines whose minimum sugar is set in the grapes at harvest, not in the bottle, so how sweet each one tastes varies.

Our pairings use four Trimbach wines: the Riesling Réserve 2020, our reference dry Riesling; Clos Sainte Hune 2007; a mature Pinot Gris Réserve Personnelle; and a Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives from the same year.

card.front: How would you introduce Trimbach at the table?
card.back: Trimbach, a family house in Alsace since 1626, famous for bone dry, long-lived Riesling; Clos Sainte Hune is its legend.

Its two most famous Rieslings come from grand cru ground, and their labels have traditionally not said so. Clos Sainte Hune is the family's own plot inside the Rosacker grand cru at Hunawihr, on limestone and dolomite; the house built its reputation long before the grand crus were drawn, so the name of the clos has carried the weight. Cuvée Frédéric Emile comes from the Geisberg and Osterberg slopes above Ribeauvillé and has been sold as plain Alsace.

components.name: Domaine du Pélican
components.say: doh-MEN doo pay-lee-KAHN; van ZHOHN; ar-BWAH
components.explain:
Domaine du Pélican is the Jura estate of the d'Angerville family, whose Domaine Marquis d'Angerville in Volnay is one of the great names of Burgundy: Sem d'Angerville was one of the growers who forced estate bottling and helped build the appellation system in the 1930s. The family founded the Jura estate in 2012, and it is a separate property, at Arbois.

The Pélican range on our list shows both faces of the Jura: the Grand Curoulet Chardonnay and the Savagnin Ouillé, topped up and fresh; a sparkling S°; two reds; and the Vin Jaune 2016, the bottle in our pairings, chosen to mirror the aged sherry that finishes the turtle soup.

card.front: How would you introduce Domaine du Pélican at the table?
card.back: Domaine du Pélican is the Jura estate of the d'Angerville family of Volnay: a Vin Jaune, nutty and savoury, aged over six years untopped.

producer.where: Arbois, Jura, France
producer.founded: 2012, by the d'Angerville family of Volnay
producer.history:
Domaine du Pélican is the Jura estate of the d'Angerville family, whose Domaine Marquis d'Angerville in Volnay is one of the great names of Burgundy: Sem d'Angerville was one of the growers who forced estate bottling and helped build the appellation system in the 1930s. The family founded the Jura estate in 2012, and it is a separate property, at Arbois.

Arbois is the Jura's largest appellation and was among the first French appellations, granted in 1936. The Jura makes its whites two ways. Ouillé wines are topped up in barrel like any other white. Sous voile wines are left untopped, so a veil of yeast grows on the surface and gives a nutty, savoury, sherry-like tang.

Vin Jaune is the purest sous voile wine: Savagnin alone, aged in cask without topping up for at least six years and three months, sixty months of it under the veil, and sold only in the squat 62 cl clavelin. It is never fortified; it finishes at ordinary table-wine strength.

The Pélican range on our list shows both faces of the Jura: the Grand Curoulet Chardonnay and the Savagnin Ouillé, topped up and fresh; a sparkling S°; two reds; and the Vin Jaune 2016, the bottle in our pairings, chosen to mirror the aged sherry that finishes the turtle soup.

Vin Jaune must be sold in the 62 cl clavelin, said to be what remains of a litre after the long ageing.
Vin Jaune is never fortified; it finishes at ordinary table-wine strength.
Ouillé means topped up: the Pélican Savagnin Ouillé is a fresh Savagnin, not aged under the veil.
Our list carries six Pélican wines: a sparkling S°, the Grand Curoulet Chardonnay, the Savagnin Ouillé, the Vin Jaune and two reds.

Guests ask whether Vin Jaune is sherry. The honest answer: no, it is an unfortified dry white, aged under a veil of yeast much as fino ages under flor.
Link it to the Volnay Clos des Ducs on our list: one family, two regions. Never say the Pélican is made in Burgundy.
Serve it cool, not cold, as its card says; it keeps for days once opened, so a table need not finish it.
Do not explain the name Pélican or name the family member who founded it until the sommelier confirms; no source says.
producer.sayIt: Domaine du Pélican is the Jura estate of the d'Angerville family of Volnay: a Vin Jaune, nutty and savoury, aged over six years untopped.
askKitchen: The list prints the Vin Jaune 2016 at 750 ml, but Vin Jaune is sold only in the 62 cl clavelin: which bottle do we hold?

components.name: C.H. Berres
components.explain:
C.H. Berres is a family estate at Ürzig on the Middle Mosel, and its Old Vines Riesling is our Riesling by the glass. The importer's notes place the grapes near Ürzig, picked by hand.

Ürzig is the Mosel's odd one out. Where Wehlen and Graach upstream grow Riesling on blue-grey slate, Ürzig's famous slope, the Würzgarten or spice garden, is red rock: red slate and red volcanic sandstone. Its wines are broader and more perfumed, with spice and orange peel rather than green apple.

card.front: How would you introduce C.H. Berres at the table?
card.back: Our Riesling by the glass, from the Berres family of Ürzig on the Mosel: light, racy and a touch sweet, lovely with spice.

Ürzig is the Mosel's odd one out. Where Wehlen and Graach upstream grow Riesling on blue-grey slate, Ürzig's famous slope, the Würzgarten or spice garden, is red rock: red slate and red volcanic sandstone. Its wines are broader and more perfumed, with spice and orange peel rather than green apple.

The 2022, by the importer's technical sheet, carries 20.7 grams of sugar a litre at 11.5 per cent alcohol, with 6.7 grams of acidity, and spent four months on its lees; the winemaker calls it a rich and modern, semi-sweet Riesling. The 2021 carried 18.9 grams. That is off-dry to semi-sweet, above both legal ceilings for halbtrocken, yet balanced by racy acidity, and it is exactly why the wine cools spice.

No source confirms the family's founding date or its generations, so the estate is best presented as a family estate of Ürzig and no more.

components.name: Weingut Dr. Hermann
components.explain:
Weingut Dr. Hermann is a family estate at Erden on the Middle Mosel, and it gives us two sweet Rieslings from the two famous red-rock villages of that stretch of river.

Our half-bottle of Erdener Prälat Auslese 2014 is, by one retailer's sheet, a gold capsule wine picked at 124 Oechsle with half the fruit touched by noble rot, at 8 per cent alcohol, and made only in 375 ml. The Kranklei is a Spätlese Goldkapsel from 2018. The gold capsule is a grower's own mark for a richer selection within one Prädikat, not a legal grade. The list also prints an Erdener Herzlei Spätlese Goldkapsel.

components.name: Weingut Stein
components.explain:
Weingut Stein is a small estate in the village of Alf on the Mosel. As of October 2026, its importers describe it as run by Ulrich Stein, known as Ulli, who has reclaimed steep slate vineyards that others had given up.

Its range is built on Riesling across the dryness scale, and our list shows it: Kabinett and Spätlese Trocken from the Palmberg, a Kabinett Trocken printed Alfer Holle 1900, and two feinherb wines, the Weihwasser and the Palmberg-Terrassen. Trocken is the legal word for dry. Feinherb has no legal definition at all: growers use it for wines just off dry, and it covers a wider range than halbtrocken, which the law caps.

In our pairings the two Stein wines are value bottles with a touch of sweetness: the Weihwasser for the gumbo's spice, the Palmberg-Terrassen for the duck confit waffle.

card.back: Weingut Stein, a small grower in Alf on the Mosel who rescues steep slate vineyards: Riesling just off dry, crisp and juicy.

components.name: Gainey Estate Vineyards
components.explain:
Gainey, said GAY-nee, is a family estate in Santa Barbara County, on California's Central Coast. The house wine list places it in both the Santa Ynez Valley and the Sta. Rita Hills, farming cool Sta. Rita Hills fruit for its Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, and its Chardonnays have carried either appellation on the label.

The Sta. Rita Hills are the cold western end of the Santa Ynez Valley. The valleys there run east to west, unusual on the Pacific coast, so ocean wind and fog pour straight inland and the season stays long and cool. The appellation was approved in 2001, and it is written Sta. Rita Hills to avoid a conflict with Chile's Santa Rita, so a server always says Santa Rita Hills in full.

card.front: How would you introduce Gainey Estate Vineyards at the table?
card.back: The Gainey Chardonnay from Santa Barbara County: creamy, with lemon curd and baked apple, kept fresh by the ocean-cooled hills.

producer.history:
Gainey, said GAY-nee, is a family estate in Santa Barbara County, on California's Central Coast. The house wine list places it in both the Santa Ynez Valley and the Sta. Rita Hills, farming cool Sta. Rita Hills fruit for its Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, and its Chardonnays have carried either appellation on the label.

The Sta. Rita Hills are the cold western end of the Santa Ynez Valley. The valleys there run east to west, unusual on the Pacific coast, so ocean wind and fog pour straight inland and the season stays long and cool. The appellation was approved in 2001, and it is written Sta. Rita Hills to avoid a conflict with Chile's Santa Rita, so a server always says Santa Rita Hills in full.

That climate is the point of our glass. The Chardonnay is creamy, with lemon curd and baked apple, but the cool hills keep its acidity bright: California richness without heaviness. It is our California Chardonnay by the glass, $17 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, printed on the list of 3 October 2026 as Gainey Estate Vineyards Sta. Rita Hills 2023, and the guide's first pick for the Louisiana Oysters, the Pecan Gulf Fish and the Poussin à la Moutarde. Au Bon Climat and Sandhi are our bottles from the same hills.

components.name: Sandhi
components.explain:
Sandhi, said SAHN-dee, is a Santa Barbara County winery founded by the sommelier Rajat Parr with the winemaker Sashi Moorman. It is known for fresh, restrained Chardonnay: California fruit in a Burgundian style rather than the ripe, buttery and oaky kind. The house wine list calls it lean and mineral.

Ours is the Sta. Rita Hills 2021 at $75, bin 13382: lemon, white peach and a little hazelnut, fresh but creamy, with bright acidity. The list also prints the Central Coast 2023 at $60, La Rinconada 2020 at $150 and Sanford & Benedict 2013 at $120. It is the value bottle for the Pecan Gulf Fish, and the Chardonnay for a guest who likes the grape but not a heavy one.

components.name: Au Bon Climat
components.explain:
Au Bon Climat, said oh bohn klee-MAH, was founded in Santa Barbara County in 1982 by Jim Clendenen, who held to a cool, restrained, food-first line, with no chase for ripeness. He was a pioneer of Burgundian-style Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in California and helped put Santa Barbara on the map. Clendenen died in 2021.

The list prints a long run of Au Bon Climat: Isabelle Pinot Noir, named for the founder's daughter, in three vintages; Knox Alexander; Hildegard, a richer white blend; and Nuits Blanches au Bouge Chardonnay, some in magnum. Ours is the Sanford & Benedict Chardonnay 2021 at $95, bin 143431: lemon curd, pear and hazelnut with a little toast, rich but fresh, with bright acidity. It is the value bottle for the Poussin à la Moutarde.

components.name: Ken Wright Cellars
components.explain:
Ken Wright Cellars is in Carlton, a small town in the northern Willamette Valley of Oregon, the state's heartland for Pinot Noir. Ken Wright is known above all for bottling Pinot Noir vineyard by vineyard, so that each hillside and soil can be tasted side by side; the house wine list says he helped Oregon think that way.

Our list prints a long run: Canary Hill and Freedom Hill 2021 at $150, Canary Hill and Shea in magnum at $300, and Carter and McCrone in half-bottles. Ours is the Willamette Valley Pinot Noir 2024, bin 148412, $72 on the list of 3 October 2026: his valley-wide blend across his vineyard sources, young and bright. It is red cherry, raspberry, forest floor and a little spice, light to medium in body with low tannin and fresh acidity, and it is the value pairing for the Blackened Tofu, where a tannic red would turn bitter against the blackening spice.

card.back: Ken Wright, known for Oregon Pinot Noir vineyard by vineyard: this is his Willamette Valley blend, bright cherry and forest floor, gentle with spice.

components.name: Kumeu River
components.explain:
Kumeu River is the estate the Brajkovich family founded at Kumeu, west of Auckland on New Zealand's North Island, and a benchmark for New Zealand Chardonnay. Its story is part of a larger one: Croatians from Dalmatia came to New Zealand from the 1890s to dig kauri gum, and many turned to vines on the clay of West Auckland. The Brajkovich family began at San Marino in 1944, the winery now called Kumeu River.

Ours is the Estate Chardonnay 2022 at $95, bin 12123, blended from vineyards around Kumeu: lemon, white peach and hazelnut, gently creamy, with a fine, mineral finish. The list also prints Coddington 2022 at $155 and Kumeu Village 2022, printed Hawke's Bay, at $50.

card.back: Kumeu River, founded by the Brajkovich family near Auckland: one of New Zealand's great Chardonnays, lemon, white peach and gentle cream.

Michael Brajkovich became New Zealand's first Master of Wine, and the estate has proved its place in blind tastings in London, where its Chardonnays were poured beside top white Burgundy. components.name: Charles Lafitte
components.explain:
Charles Lafitte is younger than some of its labels suggest. The Vranken-Pommery group, founded in 1976, dates the brand to 1983, when the first Charles Lafitte Champagnes reached the European market; the brand’s own story dates the Lafitte name to 1848 and to Jean-Baptiste Lafitte.

The 1834 it has traded on belongs to another family. In 1834 François André Goulet began making Champagne, and Charles Lafitte later succeeded the house of George Goulet, in 2003 by one source. Its 1834 cuvée name recalls that Goulet date, not the year Charles Lafitte began.

card.back: With this course, Charles Lafitte Brut: a crisp, dry Champagne from the Pommery family of houses, to wake the palate up.

components.name: Krug
components.explain:
Joseph Krug was born in Mainz, on the Rhine, in 1800, by one account, and learned Champagne at the house of Jacquesson before founding his own house in Reims in 1843. His founding idea, set down in a red notebook the house still keeps, was to make the finest Champagne every year, whatever the harvest, rather than depend on one vintage. That idea lives on in the Grande Cuvée, the multi-vintage blend at the heart of the house.

The fifth generation of the family created Krug Rosé, first released in 1983 after years of work. Krug also makes vintage wines and two walled single-vineyard wines, Clos du Mesnil from Chardonnay and Clos d’Ambonnay from Pinot Noir, both on our list.

card.front: How would you introduce Krug at the table?
card.back: Krug Grande Cuvée blends wines from many years, each edition numbered; the house was founded in Reims in 1843 by Joseph Krug.

producer.history:
Joseph Krug was born in Mainz, on the Rhine, in 1800, by one account, and learned Champagne at the house of Jacquesson before founding his own house in Reims in 1843. His founding idea, set down in a red notebook the house still keeps, was to make the finest Champagne every year, whatever the harvest, rather than depend on one vintage. That idea lives on in the Grande Cuvée, the multi-vintage blend at the heart of the house.

Every base wine is first fermented in small oak casks, and each year the house builds a Grande Cuvée from a large library of reserve wines and releases it as a numbered edition, counted from the founder’s first blend. The 170th Edition, on our bottle list, blends 195 wines from twelve years, the youngest from 2014 and the oldest from 1998: 51 percent Pinot Noir, 38 percent Chardonnay and 11 percent Meunier, with reserve wines 45 percent of the blend. A Krug ID on the back label tells the story of each bottle.

The fifth generation of the family created Krug Rosé, first released in 1983 after years of work. Krug also makes vintage wines and two walled single-vineyard wines, Clos du Mesnil from Chardonnay and Clos d’Ambonnay from Pinot Noir, both on our list.

components.name: Billecart-Salmon
components.explain:
Billecart-Salmon was founded at Mareuil-sur-Aÿ in 1818, on the marriage of Nicolas François Billecart and Elisabeth Salmon, whose two names the house still carries. It is still run by the family, and two of its great wines are named for the founding couple: the Cuvée Nicolas François, its vintage prestige white, and the Cuvée Elisabeth Salmon, its vintage prestige rosé.

The style is finesse: pale, fresh and finely beaded, and the house is loved above all for its rosé. The Elisabeth Salmon 2009 is about 55 percent Pinot Noir and 45 percent Chardonnay, coloured with some 10 percent still red Pinot Noir and aged more than a decade on its lees. The Sous Bois ferments and ages its base wines in oak barrels, and Brennan’s pours a Sous Bois magnum labelled for its eightieth anniversary.

card.back: Billecart-Salmon, founded in 1818 on a marriage, is a family house prized for finesse; its 1959 was named Champagne of the Millennium.

components.name: Bollinger
components.explain:
Bollinger was founded at Aÿ in 1829 by Hennequin de Villermont, Paul Renaudin and a partner named Bollinger, Jacques in some sources and Joseph in others. By one account the house first traded as Renaudin Bollinger, with Villermont’s name kept off the labels. Queen Victoria granted it a Royal Warrant in 1884, and Lily Bollinger, who ran the house after her husband Jacques died in 1941, is credited with doubling its production.

Bond made it famous on screen. Bollinger first appears in Live and Let Die in 1973, a film shot partly in the French Quarter, and has been the films’ official Champagne since Moonraker in 1979, a partnership sealed with a handshake.

card.front: How would you introduce Bollinger at the table?
card.back: Bollinger is the Pinot Noir house of Aÿ, rich and toasty from oak and reserve wines, and Bond’s Champagne on screen since 1973.

components.name: Pommery and Louis Pommery
components.explain:
Pommery was founded in Reims in 1858 as Pommery & Greno by Alexandre Louis Pommery and Narcisse Greno, at first as a wool business; one source dates the firm to 1836. Widowed, Louise Pommery took control, sold the wool trade and gave the house to Champagne.

Louis Pommery is the group’s sparkling wine from California, on sale in American cities by 2017 and named for the house’s founder. It is made by the traditional method from grapes chosen across California; one source gives the Brut Rosé as 76 percent Chardonnay and 24 percent Pinot Noir. It is not Champagne.

card.front: How would you introduce Pommery and Louis Pommery at the table?
card.back: Pommery is the Reims house whose widow, Madame Pommery, made dry Champagne fashionable in 1874; Louis Pommery is its California sparkling cousin.

She built it twice over. Under Reims she bought some 120 Gallo-Roman chalk pits, the crayères, for her cellars, beneath an estate begun in 1868. And in 1874 she launched Pommery Nature, the first brut Champagne to succeed commercially, when most Champagne was very sweet; the dry style the English took to became the world’s taste. By one account the house sold in about 80 countries by her death in 1890.

Pommery has belonged to the Vranken-Pommery group since 2002. Its Brut Rosé Royal blends the three grapes in near-equal shares by a 2022 competition entry, and takes its colour, by a merchant’s account, from red wine of Bouzy Pinot Noir.

components.name: Bründlmayer
components.explain:
Bründlmayer is a family estate in Langenlois, the wine town of the Kamptal, the valley of the little Kamp river northwest of Vienna. It is the Kamptal's leading estate and a major holder on the Zöbinger Heiligenstein, the hill above Zöbing that anchors any talk of Austrian Riesling outside the Wachau.

We pour Bründlmayer at three levels: the Terrassen Grüner Veltliner, its classic, and the Heiligenstein Riesling, both in half-bottles, and the Alte Reben Grüner Veltliner from old vines. Further up the list are its two sparkling wines.

card.back: Bründlmayer, the leading family estate of Austria's Kamptal: dry, peppery Grüner Veltliner and stony Riesling from the famous Heiligenstein hill.

It is the Kamptal's leading estate and a major holder on the Zöbinger Heiligenstein, the hill above Zöbing that anchors any talk of Austrian Riesling outside the Wachau.

The Heiligenstein is unusual ground: Permian desert sandstone shot through with volcanic material, despite a name that means holy stone. Its Rieslings are dry, stony and spicy, while the Codex sets Bründlmayer's Grüner Veltliner on loess, with the Lamm among its sites. One Heiligenstein bottling, Lyra, is named for the lyre-shaped trellis used in that parcel, and the estate also makes serious traditional method sparkling wine.

Kamptal Riesling and Grüner Veltliner are usually dry, and these are. The Heiligenstein bottlings higher up our list carry Erste Lage, first site, a ranking begun by the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, a private growers' association formed around the Kamptal and Kremstal. The hill is shared, and our list also prints Heiligenstein Rieslings from Schloss Gobelsburg and Hirsch.

We pour Bründlmayer at three levels: the Terrassen Grüner Veltliner, its classic, and the Heiligenstein Riesling, both in half-bottles, and the Alte Reben Grüner Veltliner from old vines. Further up the list are its two sparkling wines.

components.name: Loimer
components.explain:
Loimer is an estate in Langenlois, the wine town of the Kamptal, the valley of the little Kamp river northwest of Vienna.

Langenlois is Bründlmayer's town too, and the two are separate estates. The Kamptal's great white grapes are Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, made dry. Grüner Veltliner is Austria's own white grape, known for a note of white pepper that growers call Pfefferl; the compound behind it is rotundone, the same one behind the spice of cool-climate Syrah.

The wine list describes Loimer as a biodynamic estate. Biodynamic farming follows the organic rules, with no synthetic sprays or fertilisers, and adds its own preparations and a calendar for work in the vineyard.

card.front: How would you introduce Loimer at the table?
card.back: Loimer's Lois is Grüner Veltliner from Austria's Kamptal: crisp, peppery and dry, green apple and lime, and lovely with artichokes.

components.name: Franz Hirtzberger
components.explain:
Franz Hirtzberger is a family estate at Spitz in the Wachau, the narrow, terraced gorge of the Danube west of Krems that makes many of Austria's greatest dry whites. Spitz lies upriver, in the western part of the valley.

Our Honivogl Smaragd 2022 is Grüner Veltliner at its grandest: ripe pear, quince, white pepper, honeyed spice and stone, rich and powerful yet dry. A separate Wachau grower, Mathias Hirtzberger, is also on the list; the list says only that he comes from the Hirtzberger family.

card.back: Franz Hirtzberger of Spitz, one of the Wachau's great names: the Honivogl Smaragd is Grüner Veltliner at its grandest, rich yet dry.

producer.history:
Franz Hirtzberger is a family estate at Spitz in the Wachau, the narrow, terraced gorge of the Danube west of Krems that makes many of Austria's greatest dry whites. Spitz lies upriver, in the western part of the valley.

The estate is one of the names that define the Wachau. Its two most famous vineyards are the Honivogl, its great Grüner Veltliner site, and the Singerriedel, the Riesling site the Codex pairs with Hirtzberger among the Wachau's leading rieds. Both are on our list as Smaragd.

Smaragd belongs to Vinea Wachau, the growers' association founded in 1983, which sorts its members' dry wines by ripeness: Steinfeder, the lightest, then Federspiel, then Smaragd, the ripest and fullest, at 12.5 per cent alcohol or more, named for the emerald lizard that suns itself on the terrace walls. The words are the association's trademarks, not Austrian law, and appear only on Wachau labels; its Codex Wachau forbids chaptalisation and concentration. Since the 2020 vintage the Wachau has also been a DAC.

Our Honivogl Smaragd 2022 is Grüner Veltliner at its grandest: ripe pear, quince, white pepper, honeyed spice and stone, rich and powerful yet dry. A separate Wachau grower, Mathias Hirtzberger, is also on the list; the list says only that he comes from the Hirtzberger family.
