components.name: Jean Foillard
components.explain:
Jean Foillard farms old Gamay vines at Villié-Morgon, in the Morgon cru of Beaujolais. With Marcel Lapierre, Jean-Paul Thévenet and Guy Breton he belongs to the group their American importer, Kermit Lynch, called the Gang of Four. They followed the oenologist Jules Chauvet back to whole bunches, native yeasts and little or no added sulphur at a time when much Beaujolais was industrial, and their Morgon became a root of the natural wine movement.

His name is tied to the Côte du Py, the hill at the heart of Morgon, whose decomposed schist sets it apart from the granite of most Beaujolais crus. Foillard also farms Corcelette, a sandier granite site that gives a lighter, more floral Morgon, and vines in Fleurie.

card.front: How would you introduce Jean Foillard at the table?
card.back: Jean Foillard is one of the Gang of Four who revived Beaujolais; his Côte du Py is dark cherry, violet and stone, served cool.

They followed the oenologist Jules Chauvet back to whole bunches, native yeasts and little or no added sulphur at a time when much Beaujolais was industrial, and their Morgon became a root of the natural wine movement.

His name is tied to the Côte du Py, the hill at the heart of Morgon, whose decomposed schist sets it apart from the granite of most Beaujolais crus. Foillard also farms Corcelette, a sandier granite site that gives a lighter, more floral Morgon, and vines in Fleurie.

In the cellar he uses a long, cool semi-carbonic maceration with indigenous yeasts and minimal sulphur, then ages the wine in old Burgundy barrels. The result is dark, savoury Gamay that keeps: a Morgon that can morgonner, the old verb for a wine that has taken on the kirsch and earth of age. His son, Alex Foillard, makes cru Beaujolais of his own.

Also bottles Morgon Corcelette, from sandier granite, lighter and more floral, and a Fleurie.
The Côte du Py is decomposed schist, not the granite of most Beaujolais crus, and many growers share the hill.
His son Alex Foillard makes his own natural-leaning cru Beaujolais; our list carries his Brouilly.

Serve it a touch cool, 55 to 60°F, in a Burgundy bowl. The magnum suits a party of six or more ordering a mix of fish and meat.
A guest who says they do not like Beaujolais usually means the nouveau. Say: this is a cru from one hill, a different wine.

components.name: Inglenook
components.explain:
Inglenook is one of the founding estates of the Napa Valley. Gustave Niebaum, a Finnish sea captain who had made his fortune in the Alaska trade, founded it at Rutherford in 1879, and before Prohibition it was the benchmark Napa estate, the reputation the valley later spent decades trying to recover. John Daniel Jr., of the founding family, ran it in the twentieth century until the sale of 1964, after which the famous name went onto everyday wine.

Our saved list offers Rubicon 2010 by the glass and bottle. Its Cabernet Sauvignon led blend brings blackcurrant, cedar, tobacco and earth as tasting cues; maturity does not guarantee soft tannin or sound condition. Assess the bottle before service.

Gustave Niebaum, a Finnish sea captain who had made his fortune in the Alaska trade, founded it at Rutherford in 1879, and before Prohibition it was the benchmark Napa estate, the reputation the valley later spent decades trying to recover. John Daniel Jr., of the founding family, ran it in the twentieth century until the sale of 1964, after which the famous name went onto everyday wine.

In 1975 the Coppola family bought part of the old estate, and from the 1978 harvest they made Rubicon, a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot, named for Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon. Francis Ford Coppola reassembled the Niebaum property over the years and bought back the Inglenook name itself only in 2011; in between, the labels read Niebaum-Coppola and then Rubicon Estate.

Rutherford is the heart of the valley, and the fine, dusty tannin of its Cabernet is Rutherford dust, André Tchelistcheff's phrase; Inglenook helped build its legend.

components.name: Duckhorn Vineyards
components.explain:
Duckhorn Vineyards was founded in 1976 by Dan and Margaret Duckhorn in St. Helena, in the heart of the Napa Valley. Its first vintage, the 1978, included a Merlot from the Three Palms Vineyard, and Merlot made its name at a time when few in America took the grape seriously.

Three Palms lies on a rocky alluvial fan on the valley floor near Calistoga, at the warm north end of the valley, and is named for three palm trees on the property. The stones drain well and keep the vines lean, which gives the wine concentration. In 2017 Wine Spectator named the Three Palms Merlot its Wine of the Year.

We pour five Duckhorn wines: the Three Palms Merlot 2020, the Napa Valley Cabernet 2022 in bottle and in magnum, and two half-bottles, the Napa Valley Merlot and the North Coast Sauvignon Blanc.

components.name: Chalk Hill
components.explain:
Chalk Hill is an estate in Sonoma County, named for the Chalk Hill area in the hills east of Windsor and south-east of Healdsburg, on the eastern edge of the Russian River Valley. The area also names a small appellation, shared by every grower inside it, and it is known for rich Chardonnay.

Ours is the 2021 in half-bottle, two or three glasses: at breakfast and lunch, the half-bottle for the pecan Gulf fish, a creamy wine for a creamy plate, with the lump crab and the cauliflower purée, and lovely with the crab and corn omelette and the crab claws. The Binwise list prints it as Chalk Hill Chardonnay Sonoma; whether its fruit is the estate's own Chalk Hill grapes or from wider Sonoma is for the sommelier to read off the label.

card.front: How would you introduce Chalk Hill at the table?
card.back: A half-bottle of Chalk Hill Chardonnay from Sonoma: creamy and round, ripe pear and a little toast, lovely with the crab on the pecan fish.

components.name: Ridge Vineyards
components.explain:
Ridge Vineyards was founded in 1962 high in the Santa Cruz Mountains, south of San Francisco, at Monte Bello, where Osea Perrone had built a winery in the 1880s. The vineyard climbs to about 800 metres on a limestone-bearing ridge above the San Andreas fault, and its Cabernet-led blend, Monte Bello, became one of America's great wines under Paul Draper, Ridge's longtime winemaker.

On 24 May 1976 the Monte Bello 1971 came fifth among the reds at the Paris tasting; thirty years later, at the anniversary re-tasting of 24 May 2006, held in London and Napa at once, it came first.

We pour six: Monte Bello 2012, the Estate Cabernet half from the Monte Bello vineyards, Lytton Springs in bottle and in half, Three Valleys, and Essence, a sweet late harvest Zinfandel made only in exceptional years.

card.back: Ridge makes Monte Bello, whose 1971 was fifth at Paris in 1976 and first at the 2006 re-tasting, and old-vine Zinfandel like Lytton Springs.

components.name: Dow’s
components.explain:
Dow's is one of the great Port houses of the Douro valley in northern Portugal. The Codex gives its founding year as 1798, and notes that Dow's is the brand while Silva and Cosens is the company behind it.

In 1882 a young Scot, Andrew James Symington, came to Porto to work for Graham's. He became a partner in Warre's and, in 1912, in Dow's. The Symington family runs Dow's today alongside Graham's, Warre's and Cockburn's, as of October 2026.

We pour two declared vintages: the 2000 in a half-bottle and the 1985, now forty-one years old.

card.front: How would you introduce Dow’s at the table?
card.back: Dow's, the Symington family's Port house, known for Vintage Port with a drier, firmer finish than most. We pour the 2000 in a half-bottle and the 1985.

producer.history:
Dow's is one of the great Port houses of the Douro valley in northern Portugal. The Codex gives its founding year as 1798, and notes that Dow's is the brand while Silva and Cosens is the company behind it.

In 1882 a young Scot, Andrew James Symington, came to Porto to work for Graham's. He became a partner in Warre's and, in 1912, in Dow's. The Symington family runs Dow's today alongside Graham's, Warre's and Cockburn's, as of October 2026.

Dow's home estate is Quinta do Bomfim at Pinhão, in the Cima Corgo, the heart of the Port vineyards, and the Codex adds Quinta da Senhora da Ribeira in the hotter Douro Superior. In years without a declaration, both are bottled on their own as single quinta Vintage Ports.

The house style is the thing to remember. Dow's Vintage Ports finish drier than most, firm and savoury, because the house leaves less sugar in the wine; Graham's, from the same family, is richer and sweeter. Dry here is relative: every Vintage Port is a sweet wine.

We pour two declared vintages: the 2000 in a half-bottle and the 1985, now forty-one years old.

components.name: Feist
components.explain:
Feist is one of the old Port names founded by merchants from abroad: two German cousins, H. and C.J. Feist, founded it in London in 1836. It opened in Oporto, the English name for Porto, in 1870, and was taken over by Barros in 1953, as the house's own page records.

The same page records that the Sogevinus group bought Feist in 2006; ownership can change. Feist is a small producer of vintage wines and is known mainly for ruby and tawny Ports, alongside its Late Bottled Vintage.

It is the value Port with chocolate on our list, poured with the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake and The Snickers.

producer.history:
Feist is one of the old Port names founded by merchants from abroad: two German cousins, H. and C.J. Feist, founded it in London in 1836. It opened in Oporto, the English name for Porto, in 1870, and was taken over by Barros in 1953, as the house's own page records.

The same page records that the Sogevinus group bought Feist in 2006; ownership can change. Feist is a small producer of vintage wines and is known mainly for ruby and tawny Ports, alongside its Late Bottled Vintage.

A Late Bottled Vintage is Port from a single year, bottled between the fourth and sixth year after the harvest, so it is ready far sooner than a Vintage Port. Most is filtered and pours clear; traditional unfiltered bottlings throw a deposit. Ours, the 2006, has had many more years in bottle since and is unusually mature for its kind: black cherry, plum, raisin and cocoa, sweet and supple.

It is the value Port with chocolate on our list, poured with the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake and The Snickers.

components.name: Graham’s
components.explain:
Graham's is one of the great Port houses of the Douro valley. The Codex gives its founding year as 1820 and its full name as W. and J. Graham's.

It was to work for Graham's that a young Scot, Andrew James Symington, came to Porto in 1882. He became a partner in Warre's and, in 1912, in Dow's, and in 1970 the Symington family bought Graham's itself. The family runs Graham's today beside Dow's, Warre's and Cockburn's, as of October 2026.

We pour two declared vintages: the 2000, still vigorous at twenty-six, and the 1983, mellowed into toffee and walnut. The list also prints a 1948 and a 1972, with no style named.

components.explain:

producer.history:
Domaine de l’Écu is at Le Landreau, in Muscadet Sèvre et Maine near Nantes, the western end of the Loire where the weather comes off the Atlantic. Muscadet is the appellation and Melon de Bourgogne the grape, and Sèvre et Maine names two small rivers that drain the heart of the vineyard.

The estate farms biodynamically and is long associated with Guy Bossard, an early champion of organic and then biodynamic farming in Muscadet. Its idea is simple and rare: the vines of one grape in one village are bottled by the rock beneath them. Granite gives the ripest and roundest wine, Gneiss the most floral, and Orthogneiss, a gneiss formed from an igneous rock such as granite, the tightest and most saline, the estate’s usual benchmark. Gneiss weathers into a poor, stony soil that holds almost no water, so the vines root deep and crop lightly. Many of the wines are made with little or no added sulphur.

That makes it the clearest teaching example in France of soil-named wines from a single grape, and a standing argument against Muscadet as a cheap category.

Ours is the Orthogneiss 2022 at $70, printed Domaine L’Ecu, the value bottle for the Creole Caesar. The estate’s Pinot Noir, Ange, sold as Vin de France, is on our red list at $135.

components.name: Domaine de la Pépière
components.explain:
Domaine de la Pépière is at Maisdon-sur-Sèvre, in Muscadet Sèvre et Maine near Nantes. Marc Ollivier founded it in 1984 and farmed organically from the start, and it became the estate that made Muscadet serious again.

Its secret is time. Ordinary Muscadet sur lie rests on its lees through one winter and is bottled the year after the harvest; Pépière took lees ageing far beyond the legal minimum, for salt, citrus pith and stony grip, with no oak and no fruit gloss. Its old vines on granite give the Clos des Briords, the bottling that made Muscadet collectable.

Ours is the Monnières-Saint Fiacre 2020 at $75, the value bottle for the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters. The list also prints it in magnum, and a Château-Thébaud 2019 magnum.

card.front: How would you introduce Domaine de la Pépière at the table?
card.back: Pépière made Muscadet serious again: this Monnières-Saint Fiacre is bone dry, salty and deep, the classic wine for raw oysters.

components.name: Damien Laureau
components.explain:
Damien Laureau is a grower in Savennières, the small appellation on the north bank of the Loire in Anjou, downstream of Angers. The sources here say little more about him: where his cellar stands, when he began and which parcels he farms are not confirmed, so none of it is told at the table.

Ours is L’Alliance 2022 at $75, the value bottle for the Turtle Soup: quince, beeswax, chamomile and toasted nuts, waxy and full, with a stony finish. Its nutty depth echoes the sherry in the soup and its acidity cuts the richness. How it is made is a question for the sommelier.

card.back: Savennières is the Loire’s great dry Chenin: Damien Laureau’s L’Alliance is waxy and nutty, and it loves the sherry in the turtle soup.

Damien Laureau is a grower in Savennières, the small appellation on the north bank of the Loire in Anjou, downstream of Angers. The sources here say little more about him: where his cellar stands, when he began and which parcels he farms are not confirmed, so none of it is told at the table.

The place says a great deal. Savennières is steep, dark schist with full southern exposure, poor rock and low yields, and it makes the most austere and long-lived dry Chenin Blanc in France, almost forbidding in youth; ten years usually turns the austerity into honey, quince and wet wool. Two named crus are carved out of it, Coulée de Serrant and Roche aux Moines. Savennières is dry, while the Coteaux du Layon across the river, from the same grape, is sweet.

Chenin’s very high acidity is what lets it age for decades, and a young Savennières opens with air.

Domaine des Baumard is a family estate at Rochefort-sur-Loire, in Anjou; the Codex dates it to 1955. It is the estate that carries both faces of Anjou Chenin Blanc, so it answers the appellation question from either side.

On the north bank it has parcels in Savennières, including the Clos du Papillon, a celebrated lieu-dit shared by more than one owner, for dry, taut Chenin. Across the river it has holdings in Quarts de Chaume, a tiny south-facing amphitheatre of schist above the Layon and the Loire’s only grand cru, for sweet wine. The Layon valley draws noble rot in the best years, and Chenin’s searching acidity carries great sweetness without turning cloying, which is why a sweet Layon still tastes fresh after decades.

The house style is technically precise and clean, with acidity preserved and sweetness carried lightly. The Clos Sainte Catherine is its Coteaux du Layon at moderate sweetness, a bridge between the dry and the botrytised styles.

components.name: Marquis d’Angerville
components.explain:
Domaine Marquis d’Angerville is the great family domaine of Volnay, the village known for the most perfumed, silky Pinot Noir of the Côte de Beaune. Its name belongs to Burgundy’s history as well as to its wine lists: Sem d’Angerville was one of the growers who forced estate bottling and helped build the appellation contrôlée framework in the 1930s.

In 2012 the family founded Domaine du Pélican at Arbois in the Jura, a separate estate whose Vin Jaune is also on our list. Our Clos des Ducs 2014, twelve years old, shows red cherry, rose and violet, with silky tannin.

Its name belongs to Burgundy’s history as well as to its wine lists: Sem d’Angerville was one of the growers who forced estate bottling and helped build the appellation contrôlée framework in the 1930s.

The domaine owns the Clos des Ducs, a walled premier cru beside the domaine in the village, and owns it alone, a monopole. Volnay has no grand cru, and the Clos des Ducs, with Taillepieds and Caillerets, is among the premiers crus argued to deserve promotion. Its other Volnay premiers crus include Champans and Frémiets, and it makes a white Meursault Premier Cru, Les Santenots.

It is farmed biodynamically, and the wines are pale, fine and aromatic, made with low extraction and little new oak: the model of Volnay as the elegant village.

components.name: Domaine de Durban
components.explain:
Domaine de Durban is an estate high above the village of Beaumes-de-Venise in the Southern Rhône. Beaumes-de-Venise, like Gigondas, lies under the Dentelles de Montmirail, a jagged limestone ridge whose name means the lace of Montmirail.

Beaumes-de-Venise is famous above all for its sweet Muscat, Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, a vin doux naturel: a wine whose fermentation is stopped with grape spirit, so that it keeps the grape's sweetness. Durban is known first for that Muscat. The wine we pour is the other side of the village: the estate's dry red, sold under the Beaumes-de-Venise name, one of the named crus of the Southern Rhône and an appellation separate from the sweet wine.

card.front: How would you introduce Domaine de Durban at the table?
card.back: The Durban is a dry red from a village famous for sweet Muscat: ripe Grenache and Syrah, peppery, with soft tannins.

components.name: Domaine de Châteaumar
components.explain:
Domaine de Châteaumar is a Southern Rhône estate, and the wine we know is its Cuvée Vincent, the red on the Traditional Breakfast at Brennan's: a 4 oz pour with the Petite Filet Mignon, included in the tasting, with no glass price on the list.

Its story is in the vineyard. The Cuvée Vincent comes from old Syrah, fifty year old vines by published accounts, on two parcels bordering Châteauneuf-du-Pape, about nine kilometres from Orange, farmed organically without certification. It is sold as Côtes du Rhône, the regional name, rather than Châteauneuf, and it is all Syrah, which is the talking point: in the Southern Rhône the reds are usually blends led by Grenache. An early guide called it Grenache-based; accounts of the 2016 and 2022 vintages describe it as all Syrah, so it is never called Grenache.

card.front: How would you introduce Domaine de Châteaumar at the table?
card.back: With the filet we pour Châteaumar's Cuvée Vincent: all Syrah from old vines beside Châteauneuf, juicy and peppery. It is sold as Côtes du Rhône.

components.name: Chapel Down
components.explain:
Chapel Down is based at Tenterden in Kent, in south-east England, where the first vines on the site were planted in 1977 by Stephen Skelton. At the start of the new millennium the English Wine Group was formed, by Decanter's account; one account names the Tenterden and Lamberhurst vineyards as the two it merged. That business grew into today's company.

It is now described as England's largest wine producer. Most of what it makes is sparkling wine by the traditional method, with still wines beside it; its Kit's Coty vineyard sits on the chalk of the North Downs, facing south.

card.front: How would you introduce Chapel Down at the table?
card.back: Chapel Down, from Tenterden in Kent, is one of England's largest wine producers; its rosé won Best in Show at Decanter in 2024.

components.name: Ridgeview
components.explain:
Ridgeview was founded in the mid 1990s by Mike and Chris Roberts at Ditchling Common in Sussex; the estate gives 1995, while Decanter and The Drinks Business give 1994, and the first commercial vintage was 1996. From the start Mike Roberts insisted on making only sparkling wine, and only from the Champagne grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.

The wines soon made the case. A RidgeView Merret Bloomsbury 2002 won the World Wide Trophy for Best Sparkling Wine at the 2005 International Wine and Spirit Competition, and in 2010 the Grosvenor Blanc de Blancs 2006 beat five Champagnes to the Decanter World Wine Awards International Trophy for sparkling wine over £10, which Decanter called the only time a wine from outside Champagne had won it. The wines take the names of London districts: Bloomsbury, Cavendish, Fitzrovia and Grosvenor.

card.front: How would you introduce Ridgeview at the table?
card.back: Ridgeview, founded at Ditchling in Sussex in the mid 1990s, makes only sparkling wine; Bloomsbury is Chardonnay-led, crisp, with a light toast.

components.name: Domaine Huet
components.explain:
Domaine Huet began on 27 November 1928, when Victor Huet and his wife Anna-Constance bought the Le Haut-Lieu property in Vouvray, on the Loire near Tours. Victor's lungs and nerves had been damaged in the First World War, and he came to Vouvray to recover. Their son Gaston was running the estate by 1937.

Gaston Huet spent five years in a German prisoner of war camp during the Second World War, yet over more than half a century he built the domaine's name and sat on national committees that shaped French wine. He added the walled Clos du Bourg in 1953 and Le Mont in 1957, the three vineyards behind the Huet name, all Chenin Blanc. He died in April 2002, aged 92.

Brennan's carries Huet across the list, from the Pétillant 2019 and Le Haut-Lieu Sec to the Clos du Bourg Demi-Sec 2015 and Le Mont Moelleux 2009.

card.front: How would you introduce Domaine Huet at the table?
card.back: Domaine Huet, founded in 1928, is Vouvray's great estate: three vineyards, all Chenin Blanc, made dry, gently sweet or sweet as the year allows.

components.name: Domaine Leflaive
components.explain:
Domaine Leflaive is the name many white Burgundy lovers think of first for Puligny-Montrachet. The family’s roots in the village go back to 1717 and a Claude Leflaive.

The modern domaine was the work of Joseph Leflaive, an engineer who had helped design the first French submarine. After phylloxera he came home, bought vines and buildings, replanted and began selling wine under the family name; the domaine dates its founding as we know it to 1920, and its own timeline puts its first bottles in the United States in the 1930s. His sons Vincent and Jo ran it after his death in 1953.

The holdings run from the Mâcon to the grands crus of Puligny, Chevalier-Montrachet among them, and include the Meursault Premier Cru Sous le Dos d’Ane, a parcel that, by the estate’s sheet, grew Pinot Noir, sold as Blagny, until 2002.

card.front: How would you introduce Domaine Leflaive at the table?
card.back: Domaine Leflaive is the great name of Puligny-Montrachet, farmed biodynamically; this is its Chardonnay from Verzé, pure, chalky and bright.

producer.history:
Domaine Leflaive is the name many white Burgundy lovers think of first for Puligny-Montrachet. The family’s roots in the village go back to 1717 and a Claude Leflaive.

The modern domaine was the work of Joseph Leflaive, an engineer who had helped design the first French submarine. His sons Vincent and Jo ran it after his death in 1953.

Vincent’s daughter, Anne-Claude Leflaive, co-managed the domaine from 1990 and ran it alone from 1994. She began biodynamic trials on one hectare in 1990 and had the whole domaine farmed that way by the late 1990s. In early 2004 the domaine bought vines at Verzé in the Mâconnais, farmed biodynamically from that first harvest. After her death in 2015, Brice de la Morandière, a great-grandson of Joseph, became managing partner.

The holdings run from the Mâcon to the grands crus of Puligny, Chevalier-Montrachet among them, and include the Meursault Premier Cru Sous le Dos d’Ane, a parcel that, by the estate’s sheet, grew Pinot Noir, sold as Blagny, until 2002.

Biodynamic trials began on one hectare in 1990; the whole domaine was farmed biodynamically by the late 1990s, 1997 being the date most often given.
The Verzé vines in the Mâconnais were bought in early 2004 and have been farmed biodynamically since; 2004 was their first harvest.
By its importer’s account, Pierre Morey and Dominique Lafon recommended the Verzé site, and its first grapes were made into wine in the Puligny cellars.

Chevalier-Montrachet, the estate’s grand vin in the Codex, lies on the steep upper slope; the domaine also holds Bâtard-Montrachet and Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet.
Domaine Leflaive is not Olivier Leflaive, a separate négociant house in the same village founded in 1984.

producer.who: Creekstone Farms
producer.where: Arkansas City, Kansas (founded in Campbellsburg, Kentucky)
producer.history:
Creekstone Farms began in 1995, when John and Carol Stewart set up a purebred Black Angus farm in Campbellsburg, Kentucky. Stewart was a cattle geneticist at heart: he developed his own Angus line, sold bulls, genetics and semen to ranchers, and at one point owned the highest-marbling bull in the breed.

In 2003 the company moved into processing, buying a processing plant in Arkansas City, Kansas, where it began processing its own Premium Black Angus cattle in May 2003. Its cattle-receiving facility was the first built from the ground up to the low-stress handling standards of Dr. Temple Grandin. After BSE was found in the US herd in December 2003, Creekstone asked in 2004 to test every animal it slaughtered, and when the USDA refused, it took the question to court.

Stewart announced his retirement in October 2006. Sun Capital Partners had owned the business since 2005, and in 2017 it sold Creekstone to the Japanese trading house Marubeni Corporation, which owns it today. The company still buys its cattle on verifiable Black Angus genetics rather than hide colour, and its Natural Black Angus line carries the Certified Humane label.

At Brennan's the name is printed on three plates: both hanger steaks and the tenderloin of the Roasted Chateaubriand.
facts: Founded in 1995 by John and Carol Stewart as a purebred Black Angus farm in Campbellsburg, Kentucky.
Processes its beef at a plant in Arkansas City, Kansas, bought in 2003; processing began there in May 2003.
Its cattle-receiving facility was the first built from the ground up to Dr. Temple Grandin's handling standards.
Cattle are bought on verifiable Black Angus genetics, not on black hide colour alone.
Owned by Japan's Marubeni Corporation since 2017, which bought it from Sun Capital Partners.
Its Natural Black Angus Beef has carried the Certified Humane Raised and Handled label since September 2015, verified by Humane Farm Animal Care.
In 2004 Creekstone asked to test every animal it slaughtered for BSE; the USDA refused and Creekstone went to court.
USDA Prime, printed on our breakfast hanger, is the top grade: young, well-fed cattle with abundant marbling.
notes: The menu prints Prime only on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak. Do not call the dinner hanger or the Chateaubriand Prime unless the kitchen confirms it.
Do not say every Creekstone steak here is Certified Humane: the label covers the Natural Black Angus line, and which programme the kitchen buys is not confirmed.
Guests ask whether the beef is local. The honest answer: it is Black Angus from Creekstone in Kansas, not a local farm.
If asked who owns it: Marubeni Corporation, the Japanese trading house, since 2017; John and Carol Stewart founded it in Kentucky in 1995.
The breakfast menu spells it Creekstone Farm; the company is Creekstone Farms.
Always take the guest's temperature on a hanger or the Chateaubriand; doneness is the guest's choice and the kitchen's craft.
producer.sayIt: Creekstone Farms is Black Angus beef from Kansas, a company founded as an Angus farm in 1995 and built around careful, low-stress handling of its cattle.

producer.where: Austin, Texas (packing at Springfield, Missouri)
producer.history:
Vital Farms began in 2007, when Matt O'Hayer started with 20 hens on a 27-acre farm near Austin, Texas. The idea was eggs from hens that genuinely live outdoors, and the company built its standard around pasture: each hen has at least 108 square feet of rotated pasture, where it forages for grasses, succulents and wildflowers. That is the same figure the Certified Humane pasture standard sets, and the eggs carry that certification.

Rather than keep one great company flock, Vital Farms works with a network of small family farms, now numbering in the hundreds. In 2017 it opened its own egg washing and packing plant in Springfield, Missouri, which it calls Egg Central Station, and a second Egg Central Station is being built in Seymour, Indiana.

The company went public on Nasdaq as VITL in July 2020 and is a Certified B Corporation. It sells butter as well as eggs.

On our menu the name appears once: the sunny-side-up egg on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, where the runny yolk meets the béarnaise.
facts: Founded in 2007 by Matt O'Hayer and headquartered in Austin, Texas.
It began with 20 hens on a 27-acre farm.
Pasture-raised: at least 108 square feet of rotated outdoor pasture per hen, the Certified Humane pasture standard.
The eggs come from a network of hundreds of small family farms.
Its own packing plant, Egg Central Station, opened in Springfield, Missouri, in 2017.
Listed on Nasdaq as VITL since July 2020, and a Certified B Corporation.
notes: The menu names Vital Farms only on the breakfast hanger. Do not say the eggs on the Hussarde, Sardou, Owen or Duck Confit Waffle are Vital Farms until the kitchen confirms.
Guests ask what pasture-raised means: at least 108 square feet of rotated outdoor pasture per hen, so the hens forage on grass.
Do not promise a yolk colour; it changes with the hens' diet and the season.
Any question about egg doneness or diet goes to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: The egg is Vital Farms, pasture-raised: every hen has at least 108 square feet of outdoor pasture.
askKitchen: Are all our eggs Vital Farms, or only the egg on the breakfast hanger?

producer.who: D'Artagnan's Rohan duck
producer.where: Raised in New York's Catskills; D'Artagnan is based in Union, New Jersey
producer.history:
The Rohan is D'Artagnan's own duck. D'Artagnan was founded in 1985 by Ariane Daguin and George Faison, who met working at a charcuterie shop in New York City. A farmer had the first domestically raised foie gras in the United States and needed someone to sell it, so the two started a company to do it, selling whole raw lobes to New York chefs. Daguin was born in Auch, in Gascony, the eldest child of the Michelin-starred chef André Daguin, and the company is named for the Gascon musketeer. It is based in Union, New Jersey.

D'Artagnan's blog introduced the Rohan in January 2012. It is a proprietary cross of several breeds, including the heritage Mallard and the Pekin, bred to approximate a style of duck found in Normandy and named for the family of dukes and princes of Rohan in Brittany. The birds are raised for D'Artagnan on a farm in New York's Catskills, cage-free and never given antibiotics, hormones or steroids, to 11 weeks, five weeks longer than the average factory duck. Daguin says the extra time deepens the flavour and improves the meat-to-bone ratio.

The result is rosy, tender, mild meat with a rich, buttery depth. Brennan's prints Rohan on the duck breast of the dinner tasting and on the confit leg of the Duck Confit Waffle.
facts: The Rohan is a proprietary D'Artagnan cross of several breeds, including the heritage Mallard and the Pekin.
Raised for D'Artagnan on a farm in New York's Catskills to 11 weeks, five weeks longer than the average factory duck.
Raised cage-free, never given antibiotics, hormones or steroids.
Named for the family of dukes and princes of Rohan, in Brittany; bred to approximate a style of Normandy duck.
D'Artagnan was founded in 1985 by Ariane Daguin and George Faison to sell the first domestically raised US foie gras.
Ariane Daguin is the eldest child of André Daguin, the Michelin-starred Gascon chef famous for foie gras.
D'Artagnan has its headquarters and distribution centre in Union, New Jersey.
notes: Say a special cross, not a breed; the guide's word breed is loose.
The menu prints Rohan, not D'Artagnan. If a guest asks, Rohan is D'Artagnan's duck, raised in New York's Catskills; whether we buy direct is not confirmed.
Never name a farm: no source names the farm that raises the Rohan, and Crescent Duck Farm on Long Island is a separate Pekin farm.
The tasting duck changes with the season: the pasted card has cane syrup peaches, the house website a hazelnut-crusted, 14-day dry-aged breast. Read tonight's card.
Duck breast is served rosy; take the guest's preference to the kitchen rather than promising a temperature.
producer.sayIt: Rohan is a special Mallard and Pekin cross raised in New York's Catskills, longer than most ducks, for rosy, tender meat.
askKitchen: Do we buy the Rohan direct from D'Artagnan or through a distributor?
Which duck course is on tonight: the cane syrup peaches or the hazelnut-crusted, dry-aged breast?
If the breast is dry-aged, for how long on the current course?

producer.who: Nueske's
producer.where: Wittenberg, Wisconsin
producer.history:
The Nueske story starts with Wilhelm and Wilhelmina Nueske, who emigrated from Prussia to Wisconsin in 1887 and brought their family recipes and their way of smoking over applewood. Two generations later, in 1933, Robert Carl Nueske, known as R.C., then 19, left his grandparents, parents, two brothers and a sister to work the family farm at Wittenberg, traded his plough for a delivery truck, and sold the family's smoked bacon, hams and sausages to the resorts of northern Wisconsin.

In the 1940s he bought a butcher shop and designed and built six smokehouses. The method has barely changed since: the bacon is smoked for about a full day over embers of real Wisconsin applewood logs, which gives a sweet, rounded smoke.

The company is still family owned and run, now in its third generation, with Tanya Nueske as chief executive; she says the family smokes the way her grandfather did. Besides bacon it smokes hams, poultry and sausages.

At Brennan's the name is printed on one dish, the dinner Succotash, where the smoky bacon meets the sweet glazed summer vegetables.
facts: Wilhelm and Wilhelmina Nueske emigrated from Prussia to Wisconsin in 1887, bringing the family recipes.
R.C. Nueske began selling the family's applewood-smoked meats in 1933, at 19, to resorts in northern Wisconsin.
In the 1940s he bought a butcher shop and designed and built six smokehouses.
The bacon is smoked for about 24 hours over embers of real Wisconsin applewood logs.
Third-generation family owned and run in Wittenberg, Wisconsin, with Tanya Nueske as chief executive.
notes: Nueske's is printed only on the dinner Succotash. Do not say the breakfast Thick-Cut Bacon, the children's bacon or the Roost Burger bacon is Nueske's until the kitchen confirms.
Say about 24 hours of applewood smoke, not at least 24; accounts range from 20 to 24 hours.
The Succotash has bacon in it, so mention it when a guest orders vegetables expecting no meat; any dietary question goes to the kitchen.
The pronunciation is contested; follow the house.
producer.sayIt: The bacon is Nueske's, a Wisconsin family smokehouse since 1933, smoked about a full day over real applewood.
askKitchen: Is the breakfast thick-cut bacon, and the bacon on the Roost Burger, also Nueske's?

producer.who: Grana Padano DOP, Consorzio di Tutela
producer.where: The Po Valley, northern Italy
producer.founded: 1954 (the Consorzio di Tutela)
producer.history:
Grana Padano traces itself to 1135 and the Abbey of Chiaravalle, a few kilometres south of Milan. Bernard of Clairvaux had chosen to reclaim the marshland there, and his Cistercian monks drained and farmed it. With more milk than they could drink, they made a hard cheese that kept, which they called caseus vetus, old cheese. Ordinary people named it for its texture instead: grana, grainy, and Padano, from the Po Valley.

The Consorzio di Tutela, which protects the name, was founded on 18 June 1954, uniting producers, refiners and merchants, and the European Union made Grana Padano a DOP in 1996. Every wheel, 24 to 40 kg, ages at least nine months; at nine months inspectors test it with a hammer, a needle and a probe, and only a wheel that passes is fire-branded. Some age beyond 24 months.

It is now the world's best-selling protected cheese, over 5.2 million wheels in 2022. Its rules are its own: it may be made in 32 provinces across five northern regions, the cows may eat silage, and lysozyme, a protein from egg white, may be used as a preservative. With its nine-month minimum it is a younger, milder and different cheese from Parmigiano Reggiano, not a lesser copy of it.
facts: The Consorzio dates the cheese to 1135 at the Abbey of Chiaravalle, south of Milan.
The monks called it caseus vetus, old cheese; grana means grainy, Padano means of the Po Valley.
The Consorzio di Tutela was founded on 18 June 1954.
The European Union recognised Grana Padano as a DOP in 1996.
Every wheel ages at least nine months and is tested with hammer, needle and probe before fire-branding.
It is the world's best-selling PDO cheese: over 5.2 million wheels in 2022.
It may be made in 32 provinces across five northern regions of Italy.
Its rules allow silage in the feed and lysozyme, an egg-white protein, as a preservative.
notes: Say Grana Padano is the Po Valley's protected hard cheese, younger and milder than Parmigiano Reggiano; never call it Parmigiano.
The menu names no maker or age; do not claim a particular maker or a 24-month wheel.
Lysozyme, an egg-white protein, is allowed in Grana Padano, though not every wheel uses it: any egg question on the Caesar or Shells & Cheese goes to the kitchen.
The monks of Chiaravalle make a good one-line story: a cheese born of drained marshland and spare milk, in 1135.
producer.sayIt: Grana Padano, the Po Valley's protected hard cheese, first made by Cistercian monks near Milan in 1135: nutty, grainy and a touch milder than Parmigiano.
askKitchen: Which Grana Padano do we buy, and how old is it?

producer.who: Mimolette, the Boule de Lille
producer.where: Lille and French Flanders
producer.history:
Mimolette is the French answer to Dutch Edam. The story told in France is that Louis XIV, under the mercantilist policies of his minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert, wanted a native cheese to replace the Edam the French were buying. Another telling has Colbert's embargo on foreign goods leaving the people of Flanders without their favourite Dutch-style cheese, so they made it themselves. Either way, it was made around Lille, and to tell it apart from Edam it was coloured, first with carrot juice and later with annatto, the seed that gives its blazing orange.

As it ages, cheese mites, which the French call little affineurs, are allowed onto the rind. They eat into the crust, leaving the grey, pitted, moon-like surface, and help the cheese ripen. In 2013 the American FDA detained about a ton of Mimolette because the mites exceeded six per cubic inch; the restriction was lifted in 2014.

Today a large maker is the Normandy cooperative Isigny Sainte-Mère, which began making Mimolette, also called Boule de Lille, in 1951 with master cheesemakers recruited from the north, and sells it from young to extra-mature at 24 months.
facts: Traditionally made around Lille, said to be created under Colbert's policies to replace Dutch Edam.
It was coloured first with carrot juice, later with annatto, to set it apart from Edam.
Cheese mites, the French little affineurs, work the rind and give its lunar surface.
In 2013 the FDA detained about a ton over mite levels above six per cubic inch; lifted in 2014.
It is also called Boule de Lille.
Isigny Sainte-Mère has made it since 1951, aged up to 24 months.
notes: Say mee-mo-LET: the orange French cheese from Lille, nutty and butterscotch-sweet as it ages.
The mite story delights some tables and puts others off; offer it only to the curious.
No maker or age is printed; never say Isigny Sainte-Mère or a particular age unless the kitchen confirms it.
The orange is annatto, a plant colouring, the same seed that turns some cheddar orange; dietary questions about the colouring go to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Mimolette, mee-mo-LET, the orange cheese of Lille, made in the seventeenth century to rival Dutch Edam, melted with Abita Amber.
askKitchen: Which Mimolette do we use, and how old is it?

producer.who: Marcona almonds of Spain
producer.where: Alicante, Spain, and the Mediterranean coast from southern Catalonia to Valencia
producer.history:
The Marcona is a Spanish almond variety native to the province of Alicante, and grown along the Mediterranean coast in southern Catalonia, Castellón and Valencia. It is called the queen of almonds. It is shorter, wider and rounder than the long almonds of commercial orchards, softer and sweeter, and it has almost none of the bitter edge an ordinary almond carries.

Its oldest work is in sweets. Marcona is the almond of turrón, the nougat of Alicante and Jijona, made in Jijona since at least the sixteenth century, and of marzipan. Jijona grinds the almond to a fine paste for its soft turrón; Alicante uses it whole and toasted in the hard one.

At the table, Marcona is the tapas almond: blanched to slip off the skin, roasted or fried in olive oil, and dusted with salt, so it eats rich and tender with a gentle crunch, and sits well beside Sherry and cheese.

At Brennan's it appears twice: in the gremolata on the Crab & Corn Omelette, and in the banana leaf of the Gulf Fish en Papillote, with olives, sorghum and crab.
facts: Marcona is a Spanish almond variety native to the province of Alicante.
It is shorter, wider and rounder than standard almonds, with almost no bitterness.
It is the traditional almond of turrón; Jijona turrón is recorded from at least the sixteenth century.
Jijona turrón grinds it to a paste; Alicante turrón uses it whole and toasted.
It is usually served blanched, roasted or fried in olive oil, and salted.
notes: Say Marcona as the round, sweet Spanish almond, the one Spain eats with Sherry.
No grower or packer is printed; do not name one.
Tree nut questions on the omelette or the en papillote go straight to the kitchen; never say a dish can be made without them unless the kitchen says so.
Whether ours are fried, roasted or raw is a lineup question.
producer.sayIt: Marcona almonds, the round, sweet almond of Alicante in Spain, buttery and tender, the one Spain eats with Sherry.
askKitchen: Are our Marcona almonds bought fried and salted, or do we toast them?

producer.who: Nocellara del Belice olives, Castelvetrano style
producer.where: Valle del Belice, south-western Sicily
producer.history:
What Americans call a Castelvetrano olive is, strictly, a way of preparing an olive. The variety is Nocellara del Belice, grown in the Valle del Belice in south-western Sicily, a dual-purpose olive pressed for oil and cured for the table. One of its table preparations is named for the comune of Castelvetrano in the valley, and olives treated that way are sold in the United States as Castelvetrano olives.

The method explains the taste. The olives are picked young and green and washed in a lye and water solution, which strips their natural bitterness completely in a matter of weeks; they are then kept in brine without fermenting. Skipping fermentation keeps the vivid emerald colour and leaves a mild, buttery, almost sweet olive with a crisp bite. The Sevillian method, by contrast, debitters partly and ferments, for a sharper olive.

In 1998 Nocellara del Belice was awarded a Protected Designation of Origin, and the variety now carries two: Nocellara del Belice DOP table olives and Valle del Belìce DOP extra virgin olive oil, which must be at least 70 per cent Nocellara.
facts: The variety is Nocellara del Belice, from the Valle del Belice in south-western Sicily.
Castelvetrano names a preparation, after the comune of Castelvetrano in the valley.
Awarded a Protected Designation of Origin in 1998.
Two DOP names: Nocellara del Belice table olives and Valle del Belìce olive oil, at least 70 per cent Nocellara.
Picked young and washed in lye, then brined without fermentation, keeping them bright green and mild.
The Sevillian method debitters only partly and ferments the olives.
notes: Say kah-stel-veh-TRAH-noh: the bright green Sicilian olive, buttery and mild, the one olive-shy guests often like.
Never call ours DOP unless the kitchen confirms the jar; the menu prints only Castelvetrano.
Warn that olives can carry stones unless the kitchen confirms they are pitted.
Guests sometimes ask whether the green means unripe: picked young, yes, and cured to remove bitterness.
producer.sayIt: Castelvetrano olives, the bright green Nocellara del Belice of western Sicily, cured young so they stay mild and buttery.
askKitchen: Are the Castelvetrano olives pitted, and are they DOP Nocellara del Belice?

producer.who: Girolamo Luxardo
producer.where: Torreglia, near Padua, Italy (founded in Zara, Dalmatia)
producer.history:
In 1817 Girolamo Luxardo moved to Zara, on the Dalmatian coast, as consular representative of the Kingdom of Sardinia. His wife, Maria Canevari, made rosolio maraschino at home, a cherry liqueur of the region, and in 1821 he founded a distillery to make it properly. Within eight years the Emperor recognised it as superior. Around 1905 the plant at Zara made the first Luxardo maraschino cherries, marasca cherries candied in their own syrup, and in 1913 Michelangelo Luxardo, the third generation, built a new distillery.

The war ended all of it. Allied bombing from November 1943 to October 1944 destroyed 80 per cent of Zara, and the factory with it. Pietro Luxardo and his brother Nicolò, with Nicolò's wife, were killed by Tito's partisans. Giorgio Luxardo, the only survivor of the fourth generation, fled across the Adriatic; the family story says he carried a single cherry sapling.

With Nicolò III of the fifth generation he re-founded the firm briefly in Venice, then at Torreglia in the Euganean Hills near Padua, where the first marasca orchard was planted in 1947. It now has 20,000 trees, the company is still family owned, and it marked 200 years in 2021.
facts: Founded in 1821 by Girolamo Luxardo in Zara, then Habsburg Dalmatia.
His wife Maria Canevari made rosolio maraschino at home before the distillery.
The first Luxardo maraschino cherries were made at Zara around 1905.
Allied bombing in 1943 and 1944 destroyed the Zara factory.
Giorgio Luxardo, sole survivor of the fourth generation, re-founded the firm at Torreglia near Padua.
The first marasca orchard at Torreglia was planted in 1947; it now has 20,000 trees.
The firm is still family owned and marked 200 years in 2021.
Luxardo marasca also goes into Sangue Morlacco, its cherry liqueur.
notes: The Cherries Jubilee prints Luxardo by name, but it was not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026: confirm with a manager that it is served before offering it.
Never say which Luxardo product is in the sauce until the kitchen tells you: Maraschino, Sangue Morlacco or the cherries in syrup.
The single sapling is a family story; tell it as a story, not a record.
Alcohol questions go to the kitchen: flaming does not remove all the alcohol.
producer.sayIt: Luxardo is the family cherry house founded in Zara in 1821 and replanted near Padua; its marasca cherry is the heart of this dessert.
askKitchen: Which Luxardo product goes into the sauce?
Which spirit is lit at the table?

producer.who: 'Nduja di Spilinga
producer.where: Spilinga, province of Vibo Valentia, Calabria
producer.history:
'Nduja comes from Spilinga, a hill town in the province of Vibo Valentia, at the toe of Italy. It was a poor family's sausage. After the winter slaughter the better cuts went to the landowners, and what was left, the fatty, less prized trimmings, was turned into something that would keep and feed a household.

The method is simple and bold: fatback, belly and shoulder trimmings minced very fine with dried Calabrian chilli, around a third of the weight, plus salt, packed into a natural casing, lightly smoked over local wood and aged for several months. The result is soft enough to spread like a pâté and melts into anything warm.

Where it came from is argued. One theory says the Aragonese brought it in the sixteenth century; another derives it from the French andouille, introduced when Joachim Murat ruled the Kingdom of Naples at the beginning of the nineteenth century. If that second theory is right, the 'nduja in our white beans and the andouille in our gumbo share a French ancestor, a pleasing thought for a New Orleans table, offered as a theory and no more.
facts: 'Nduja comes from Spilinga in the province of Vibo Valentia, Calabria.
It is fatty pork trimmings minced with dried Calabrian chilli, about a third of the weight.
It is cased, lightly smoked and aged for several months, and spreads like a pâté.
It began as a way to use the fatty cuts left after the better ones went to landowners.
One theory credits the Aragonese in the sixteenth century; another the French andouille under Joachim Murat.
notes: Say en-DOO-yah, and warn spice-shy guests: it carries a slow red-pepper heat.
The andouille link is a theory, a good one for New Orleans; say one theory is, never that it is fact.
No maker is printed; whether ours is Italian or American is a kitchen question.
Pork is in the beans; dietary questions go to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: 'Nduja, en-DOO-yah, the spreadable chilli pork sausage of Spilinga in Calabria, melted into the white beans under the lobster.
askKitchen: Whose 'nduja do we use, and is it rendered into the beans or dolloped on top?

producer.who: Burrata of Andria
producer.where: Andria, the Murgia, Puglia
producer.history:
Burrata is a fresh cheese of the Murgia in Puglia, made from cow's milk, rennet and cream: a pouch of mozzarella filled with shreds of curd soaked in cream. Its birthplace is the town of Andria, though the date is argued. Some place it about 1900, at the farm of the brothers Lorenzo and Vincenzo Bianchino; more recent records credit Lorenzo Bianchino of the Piana Padura farm with first making it in 1956.

The story told in Puglia is of a heavy February snowfall that kept Bianchino from the market. With milk that would not keep, he wrapped curd, scraps of mozzarella and the cream from the morning milking inside a skin of mozzarella, so nothing was wasted.

For decades it stayed a local fresh cheese that had to be eaten within days. In November 2016 Burrata di Andria became a protected geographical indication, an IGP, recognising the town's claim.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada it does what mozzarella does in a caprese: a cool, milky foil for raw Louisiana tomatoes, torn and served at room temperature.
facts: Burrata is a fresh cow's milk cheese of the Murgia in Puglia, mozzarella filled with cream-soaked curd.
Its birthplace is Andria; some date it to about 1900 at the Bianchino brothers' farm.
More recent records credit Lorenzo Bianchino of the Piana Padura farm, in 1956.
The story says a February snowfall kept him from market, so he used up curd and cream.
Burrata di Andria became a protected geographical indication in November 2016.
notes: Say boo-RAH-tuh: mozzarella with a creamy centre, from Andria in Puglia.
Never call ours Burrata di Andria IGP or Italian unless the kitchen confirms it; good burrata is also made in America.
Tell the snowstorm story as a story; the date itself is argued.
No meat is printed on the dish; vegetarian and dairy questions still go to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Burrata, boo-RAH-tuh, from Andria in Puglia: a pouch of mozzarella with a soft, creamy centre, beside our Creole tomatoes.
askKitchen: Where is our burrata made, Italy or America?

producer.who: Sherry, D.O. Jerez-Xeres-Sherry
producer.where: Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María, Cádiz, Spain
producer.history:
Sherry is the fortified wine of a triangle of towns in the province of Cádiz, in southern Spain: Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María. It is made mostly from the Palomino grape, in styles from pale, salty Manzanilla and fino to the darker Amontillado and oloroso, which age in contact with air and turn nutty and deep.

What makes Sherry is the way it ages, criaderas y solera. Barrels are stacked in tiers; wine for bottling is drawn from the oldest, which is topped up from the next oldest, and so on up to the youngest. Every bottle is a blend of many years, and the style stays the same from decade to decade. That ageing was long reserved to the three towns.

In 1933 Jerez became the first denominación de origen recognised under Spain's new wine law, D.O. Jerez-Xeres-Sherry, though Rioja, which set up its own in 1925, also claims to be first.

Brennan's has finished its turtle soup with sherry for a long time: its own published recipe calls for dry sherry and hard-boiled egg, and says the flavour is heightened by a touch of sherry. Tonight's menu prints aged Sherry, and which bottle the kitchen uses is a question for lineup.
facts: Sherry must come from the triangle of Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María.
D.O. Jerez-Xeres-Sherry, recognised in 1933, was the first under Spain's wine law; Rioja dates its own to 1925.
It ages by criaderas y solera, a tiered blend of young into old wine.
It is made mostly from Palomino, from Manzanilla and fino to Amontillado and oloroso.
Brennan's published turtle soup recipe calls for dry sherry and hard-boiled egg.
The wine list's Sherries are Barbadillo Pale Cream, Valdespino VOS Solera 1842 and La Cigarrera Manzanilla.
notes: Say aged Sherry, the nutty fortified wine of Jerez, lifts the soup at the end; do not name a bottle until the kitchen does.
Never say the soup uses a Sherry from the wine list; that is unconfirmed.
Tell guests who avoid alcohol that Sherry is in the soup; never promise it cooks off.
A guest who likes the note can be offered a glass of the list's Sherry alongside, checked with the sommelier.
producer.sayIt: Finished with aged Sherry from Jerez in southern Spain, nutty and dry, which cuts the richness of the turtle soup.
askKitchen: Which Sherry finishes the Turtle Soup, and is it added in the kitchen, at the pass or at the table?

producer.who: Madeira, the island's fortified wine
producer.where: Madeira, Portugal
producer.history:
Madeira is a Portuguese island in the Atlantic, discovered by the navigators João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira in 1419. The first settlers planted vines, and by the 16th century the island had a wine trade, its casks shipped across the Atlantic.

Those voyages made the wine. Casks carried across the equator in hot holds came back changed, concentrated, darker and more stable, and the islanders learned to reproduce the voyage at home. The wine is fortified with grape spirit, then aged either by canteiro, casks warmed by the sun in lofts for years, or by estufagem, tanks heated to at most 50°C for at least 90 days, a method pioneered in 1794 by Pantaleão Fernandes. The four noble grapes name the styles, from dry Sercial and medium-dry Verdelho to Bual and sweet Malmsey, from Malvasia.

Because it has already been heated and aired, Madeira keeps, for decades and even after opening, which made it the wine of the American colonies; the signers are said to have toasted the Declaration of Independence with it in 1776, a story often told but thinly documented.

In the kitchen that same caramel, walnut and sharp acidity reduces into a glaze for the broccolini on the Creole Hanger Steak.
facts: The island was discovered by João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira in 1419.
Heat in ships' holds crossing the equator improved the wine; makers learned to reproduce it.
Estufagem heats the wine to at most 50°C for at least 90 days, pioneered in 1794.
Canteiro ages casks warmed naturally by the sun for years.
Already heated and oxidised, Madeira keeps for decades, even after opening.
The four noble styles: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual and Malmsey, from dry to sweet.
The signers are said to have toasted the Declaration of Independence with Madeira in 1776; tell it as a story.
notes: Say the broccolini is glazed with Madeira, the Portuguese island wine that is heated as it ages, so it tastes of caramel and walnut.
Never say the glaze uses a bottle from the wine list; the cooking Madeira is not named.
Guests who avoid alcohol should know the glaze is made with wine; never promise it cooks off.
A guest who loves the note can be pointed to the list's Madeiras, Broadbent and Henriques & Henriques, through the sommelier.
producer.sayIt: Broccolini glazed with Madeira, the Portuguese island wine aged in heat, beloved of the American colonies: caramel, walnut, bright acidity.
askKitchen: Which Madeira, and which style, goes into the broccolini glaze?

producer.who: The Brennan's pastry kitchen (chocolate maker not named)
producer.where: 417 Royal Street, New Orleans
producer.history:
The Snickers is Brennan's grown-up version of the candy bar, and the menu prints it plainly: Bavarian milk chocolate, caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts, at $15. It appears on the dessert menu and as a choice on the Taste of Brennan's tasting menu, where a diner listing describes it as house made.

Bavarian, on a pastry menu, most often names a preparation rather than a place: a Bavarian cream, or bavarois, is a set custard lightened with whipped cream, between a mousse and a custard. Read that way, the line promises a milk chocolate Bavarian cream, not chocolate made in Bavaria. No public source names the chocolate the pastry kitchen melts into it, and no claim should be made about a maker.

The kitchen's pastry roots are real. Kris Padalino became executive chef in June 2025 after eight years at Brennan's as pastry chef and executive sous chef. Who builds The Snickers now, and with which chocolate, are questions for lineup.
facts: The menu prints Bavarian Milk Chocolate, Caramel Custard, Nougat Ice Cream, Roasted Peanuts, $15.00.
It also appears as a dessert choice on the tasting menu.
A diner listing calls it a house-made Snickers-inspired dessert on the Taste of Brennan's menu.
No public source names the chocolate maker.
Kris Padalino became executive chef in June 2025 after eight years as pastry chef and executive sous chef.
notes: Say a milk chocolate Bavarian cream, light and set, between a mousse and a custard.
Never say the chocolate comes from Bavaria or name a brand; neither is confirmed.
Peanuts are printed on the dish: dietary questions go to the kitchen before ordering.
Bavarian creams are usually set with gelatine; vegetarian questions go to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Our Snickers: a milk chocolate Bavarian cream, between a mousse and a custard, with caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts.
askKitchen: Which milk chocolate goes into The Snickers, and does Bavarian mean a Bavarian cream?
Is the Bavarian set with gelatine?

producer.who: Grand Isle Jewels
producer.where: Grand Isle, Jefferson Parish, Louisiana
producer.history:
Grand Isle is the barrier island at the southern edge of Jefferson Parish. Its oyster industry was about 150 years old when it failed in the 1980s.

The revival began in 2012, when Jules Melancon, a multigenerational oysterman, became the first permitted to farm oysters off-bottom there: seed grown in floating cages just below the surface instead of on the seabed. Others followed, working in the Grand Isle Aquapark, where ocean and estuary water mix and the salinity suits a briny oyster. Melancon died in 2023.

In April 2025 the Jefferson Parish Economic Development Commission, JEDCO, gathered eight of the island's growers under one regional brand, Grand Isle Jewels. The name nods to the island's pirate past and to Melancon himself. The brand sells to restaurants across the Southeast and Texas, and a distribution partnership with Inland Foods followed a market test of about 10,000 products.
facts: Grand Isle Jewels is a regional oyster brand launched by JEDCO, the Jefferson Parish Economic Development Commission, in April 2025.
Eight Grand Isle growers farm under the brand, in floating cages rather than on the seabed.
Jules Melancon brought off-bottom farming to Grand Isle in 2012; the brand's name honours him and the island's pirate past.
The island's oyster industry, about 150 years old, had failed in the 1980s before off-bottom farming revived it.
Seed oysters grow just below the surface in an aquapark chosen for temperature, water flow and salinity.
The growers describe the flavour as briny and bright, from the mix of ocean and estuary water.
Inland Foods tested about 10,000 Grand Isle Jewels products before expanding distribution across the Southeast and Texas.
notes: The menu prints Grand Isle Jewel; the brand is Grand Isle Jewels. Either is fine aloud.
Expect these to taste saltier and brighter than the cooked Louisiana Oysters: they are grown in briny water on purpose.
Do not name a single farm, or say the method was invented on Grand Isle; say the island revived its oysters by farming them off the bottom.
Raw shellfish questions go to the manager or the kitchen; point to the asterisk on the menu, never give a safety verdict yourself.
producer.sayIt: These are Grand Isle Jewels, farmed in floating cages off Louisiana's barrier island: briny, bright and served raw.
askKitchen: How many oysters come per order, and which Grand Isle farm or farms are they from tonight?
Do we buy them from the growers or through a distributor?

producer.who: Louisiana oyster leases and public reefs
producer.where: Louisiana coast, from the Mississippi delta west to Vermilion Bay
producer.history:
Louisiana leads the nation in oysters. Between 2003 and 2022 it landed about a third of all oysters in the United States, and in 2022 it produced more than seven million pounds of oyster meat.

Oystermen have long dredged from two kinds of water bottom: about 1.7 million acres of public reefs, which the state opens each season, and about 400,403 acres of private leases, beds that families rent from the state and tend themselves. For years the split was roughly even. Since about 2007, freshwater pouring onto the main public grounds east of the Mississippi has weakened those reefs, and private leases now give more than nine oysters in ten; in 2023 public reefs gave only 7.3% of landings.

The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission sets the public season each year from its biologists' stock assessment, usually opening in September, with market oysters for sale following. Gulf water is less salty than the Atlantic, partly thanks to the Mississippi, which is why Louisiana oysters are plump, mild and a little sweet.
facts: From 2003 through 2022 Louisiana landed 32.3% of the nation's oysters, more than any other state.
Louisiana has about 1.7 million acres of public oyster reefs and about 400,403 acres of private leases.
In 2023 private leases gave 92.7% of Louisiana's commercial oyster landings and public reefs 7.3%.
Since about 2007 freshwater has weakened the main public grounds east of the Mississippi River.
The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission sets the public season yearly from LDWF biologists' stock assessment.
Gulf oysters grow in less salty water than Atlantic ones, so they are milder, plumper and slightly sweet.
notes: Say Louisiana oysters, grown on the state's private leases and public reefs; do not name a bay, reef or family unless the kitchen tells you.
Guests from the East Coast often ask why these are cooked: Gulf oysters are large and mild, so New Orleans cooks them as often as it eats them raw.
If a guest wants a briny raw oyster, steer them to the Grand Isle Jewels.
Never promise the oysters in a cooked dish are local on a given night; the menu prints Louisiana, the source behind it is the kitchen's.
producer.sayIt: These are Louisiana oysters, big and mild from the Gulf, cooked in our New Orleans BBQ sauce.
askKitchen: Where are tonight's cooked oysters from, and how many come per order?

producer.who: Louisiana shrimpers
producer.where: Louisiana coast and the Gulf
producer.history:
Shrimp is Louisiana's most valuable commercial fishery and the state is first in the nation for shrimp landings: in 2012 nearly 102 million pounds came ashore, worth more than $146 million at the dock. About 5,500 licensed shrimpers work two species, the brown shrimp of the spring season, roughly May to July, and the white shrimp of the autumn season, from mid-August to mid-December. The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission opens and closes each area on its biologists' advice.

The fishery is old and many-voiced. By the 1880s the marshes south of New Orleans were dotted with villages on stilts where shrimp were dried on raised platforms for Asia, the Philippines and Hawaii; at the peak, between 1900 and 1915, there were at least 95. Most of the merchants were Chinese, and the fishermen were Filipino, Chinese, Japanese, Italian, Croatian, Isleño, Creole, Cajun, African American and Native American. Manila Village, built over the oyster reefs of Barataria Bay by Filipino fishermen led by Quintin de la Cruz, even had its own post office.

Today almost 90 percent of the shrimp eaten in America is imported, which is what makes the word Louisiana on a menu worth saying.
facts: Louisiana is first in the nation for commercial shrimp landings; in 2012 nearly 102 million pounds were landed.
Two species carry the fishery: brown shrimp, Farfantepenaeus aztecus, and white shrimp, Litopenaeus setiferus.
Brown shrimp season generally runs May to July; white shrimp season mid-August to mid-December.
Shrimp is Louisiana's most valuable commercial fishery, with about 5,500 licensed commercial shrimpers.
At the peak of shrimp drying, 1900 to 1915, the marshes held at least 95 platform communities.
Manila Village in Barataria Bay was founded by Filipino fishermen led by Quintin de la Cruz.
Almost 90 percent of the shrimp eaten in the United States is imported, which is why Louisiana on a menu matters.
Louisiana's Act 372 of 2019 requires a menu notice when a restaurant serves imported shrimp or crawfish.
notes: Use the menu's words: Louisiana shrimp on the Shrimp & Grits and the Roost Popcorn Shrimp, Gulf shrimp on the children's fried shrimp.
If asked brown or white, the honest answer depends on the season and the boat; ask the kitchen rather than guess.
Never say all our shrimp are Louisiana: the children's breakfast popcorn shrimp prints no origin.
A good story at the table: the Filipino and Chinese shrimp-drying villages of the marsh, more than a century ago.
producer.sayIt: It's wild Louisiana shrimp, from the state that lands more shrimp than any other in the country.
askKitchen: Are tonight's shrimp brown or white, and from which supplier?
Is the children's breakfast popcorn shrimp the same Louisiana shrimp?

producer.who: Louisiana blue crabbers
producer.where: Louisiana coastal marshes and bays
producer.history:
Louisiana runs the largest commercial blue crab fishery in the Gulf and in the United States, supplying about a quarter of all the blue crab caught in the country. In 2018 it landed 30.6% of the nation's blue crabs, and its 2024 harvest was 40 million pounds. The crab is trapped in the brackish marshes and bays where fresh river water meets the Gulf.

Most of that catch is cooked and picked by hand, and the meat is sold by grade. New Orleans seafood counters sell three: jumbo lump, backfin lump and claw. Lump is prized for its large, sweet white pieces that hold their shape on a plate, while claw meat, darker and sweeter, is what many home cooks put in stuffed crabs.

Brennan's prints Louisiana lump crab on the Pecan Gulf Fish and the Crab & Corn Omelette, Louisiana crab on the Gulf Fish en Papillote, and serves warm Louisiana Crab Claws as a starter. No picking house or crabber is named.
facts: Louisiana's commercial blue crab fishery is the largest in the Gulf and in the United States.
Louisiana supplies about a quarter of the blue crab harvested in the United States.
Louisiana landed 30.6% of all US blue crabs in 2018; its 2024 harvest was 40 million pounds.
New Orleans seafood counters sell picked crabmeat in three grades: jumbo lump, backfin lump and claw.
The menu prints Louisiana lump crab on the Pecan Gulf Fish and the Crab & Corn Omelette.
notes: Say Louisiana lump crab, as printed; it is the sweet, large-piece grade, already cooked and only warmed.
Louisiana catches more blue crab than any other state, which is a fair thing to say with pride.
Do not name a picking house or claim jumbo lump; the menu prints lump.
Shellfish questions always go to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: That's Louisiana lump crab, sweet hand-picked blue crab from the state that catches more of it than any other.
askKitchen: Which picking house supplies our lump and claws?

producer.who: Gulf commercial fishermen
producer.where: Gulf waters off Louisiana
producer.history:
Gulf fish on a New Orleans menu means the day's catch, not one species. The city's appetite runs to fish such as true American red snapper and black drum, which sell far above the national average here, and sheepshead, an estuarine fish of Louisiana's coast that is nearly all sold to restaurants and markets in the state.

Louisiana has worked to widen that list. In 1981 the legislature created the Louisiana Seafood Promotion and Marketing Board to promote the state's commercial catch, with particular attention to underused species.

Brennan's owner has a public record on Gulf seafood. After the 2010 BP oil spill Ralph Brennan testified before Congress about the damage to the Gulf seafood industry, and he advocates sustainable, local seafood sourcing in each of his restaurants. In New Orleans the Audubon Nature Institute runs GULF, a sustainable seafood programme founded in 2012 that works with restaurants and fisheries.
facts: Gulf fish means the day's catch from Gulf waters, not a fixed species.
True American red snapper and black drum sell far above average in the New Orleans area.
Nearly all commercially caught Louisiana sheepshead is sold to restaurants or markets in the state.
Louisiana created its Seafood Promotion and Marketing Board in 1981, with a focus on underused species.
Ralph Brennan testified before Congress on the Gulf seafood industry after the 2010 BP oil spill.
Audubon Nature Institute's GULF sustainable seafood programme was founded in 2012.
notes: Learn tonight's fish at lineup; every table will ask what the Gulf fish is.
You may say our owner, Ralph Brennan, is a public advocate for local Gulf seafood; do not claim any certification or partnership.
Never guess a species. If the kitchen has not said, offer to ask.
Redfish on the Véronique is its own fish with its own story; do not call it the Gulf fish of the day.
producer.sayIt: Gulf fish is the day's catch from the Gulf; let me tell you exactly which fish the kitchen has tonight and how it's cooked.
askKitchen: What is tonight's Gulf fish on the Pecan Gulf Fish, the en Papillote and the children's plate?
Is it from a Louisiana boat, and from which supplier?

producer.who: Redfish (red drum)
producer.where: Gulf of Mexico; farmed redfish mainly in Texas
producer.history:
Redfish, the red drum, was an important commercial and restaurant fish in Louisiana until 1988. Its fall began one March evening in 1980, when Paul Prudhomme served blackened redfish at K-Paul's in New Orleans; from 1983 he took it on pop-ups to New York and San Francisco, where people queued for hours. Kitchens all over the country copied it, and the Gulf was fished hard: 12.7 million pounds of red drum in a single year.

The stock fell, and Louisiana's Wildlife and Fisheries Commission closed the commercial redfish fishery in the late 1980s; sources give 1987 and 1988. In 1988 anglers were limited to five fish a day with only one over 27 inches, and there has been no commercial redfish fishing in Louisiana since.

The collapse also spurred red drum hatcheries and farms, partly to restock the Gulf, and Texas has led the nation in red drum farms. Louisiana law lets licensed dealers sell farm-raised red drum, or red drum legally caught and sold commercially outside the state, so the redfish on a Louisiana menu today is one or the other.
facts: Paul Prudhomme served blackened redfish at K-Paul's in March 1980 and set off a national craze.
In one year 12.7 million pounds of red drum were harvested from the Gulf.
Louisiana closed commercial redfish fishing in the late 1980s; sources date the ban to 1987 or 1988.
Louisiana's 1988 rules cut anglers to five redfish a day, only one over 27 inches; commercial redfish fishing has not returned.
Louisiana law lets licensed dealers sell farm-raised red drum, or red drum legally caught commercially outside the state.
Red drum farming grew from the 1980s collapse; in one national count Texas led with eight red drum farms.
notes: Redfish is the red drum: firm, mild, slightly sweet, with a black spot near the tail.
Never say ours is wild Louisiana redfish: Louisiana has had no commercial redfish fishery since the late 1980s.
The story guests enjoy: Prudhomme's blackening craze nearly fished redfish out, and the rules since brought it back.
Where ours comes from, farmed or another state's catch, is a chef question.
producer.sayIt: Redfish is the red drum, firm and mild; it is the fish Paul Prudhomme made famous, and here it stands in for the classic sole.
askKitchen: Is our redfish farm-raised, and from where?

producer.who: Louisiana crawfish farmers and Atchafalaya fishermen
producer.where: South Louisiana rice country and the Atchafalaya Basin
producer.history:
Louisiana grows nearly all of America's crawfish. Its crawfish ponds covered 120,654 acres in 1990 and about 225,789 acres in a recent count, against roughly 7,500 acres in the whole of the rest of the country.

More than half of that farming happens in rice fields. After the rice harvest in July and August the farmers flood the same fields as crawfish ponds, so the clay soil that suits rice gives a second crop in the cooler months. Farm-raised crawfish make up most of Louisiana's supply, about 80% by one count.

The rest is wild, trapped in the deeper water of the Atchafalaya Basin, the largest river swamp in the United States, which has historically given about 90% of the state's wild landings.

On the Roost menu the Crawfish Meat Pies come with a chive rémoulade. The menu does not print Louisiana, so whether the tail meat in them is Louisiana crawfish is a question for the kitchen; Louisiana law requires a menu notice when imported crawfish are served.
facts: Louisiana crawfish ponds grew from 120,654 acres in 1990 to 225,789 acres, against about 7,500 acres elsewhere in the US.
More than half of Louisiana's crawfish farming is done in rice fields flooded after the rice harvest.
Farm-raised crawfish are about 80% of Louisiana's crawfish industry by one count; the rest is trapped wild.
Wild crawfish are trapped in the Atchafalaya Basin, the largest river swamp in the United States.
About 90% of Louisiana's wild crawfish landings have historically come from the Atchafalaya Basin.
Louisiana's Act 372 of 2019 requires a menu notice when imported crawfish or shrimp are served.
notes: The menu prints Crawfish Meat Pies, not Louisiana crawfish; do not add the word until the kitchen confirms it.
A good line: most Louisiana crawfish grow in rice fields, a second crop after the rice harvest.
Shellfish questions always go to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Crawfish are Louisiana's own: most are raised in flooded rice fields, the rest trapped wild in the Atchafalaya swamp.
askKitchen: Is the crawfish tail meat in the meat pies from Louisiana, and is it farmed or wild?

producer.who: Louisiana snapping turtle
producer.where: Louisiana, from licensed turtle farms and collectors
producer.history:
Turtle soup has been eaten in Louisiana since the 1700s, and it is still on the menus of the old houses: Arnaud's, Commander's Palace, Mandina's, Felix's and Brennan's among them. At Brennan's the chefs use snappers, freshwater snapping turtles.

The rules on which snapper changed in 2004. The alligator snapping turtle, the great loggerhead once common in Louisiana markets, became off limits to commercial trappers when a Wildlife and Fisheries regulation took effect on 20 November 2004. Licensed turtle farmers may still sell alligator snappers hatched from their own breeding stock, and Commander's Palace uses farm-raised alligator snapper for a steady supply. The common snapping turtle could still be taken and sold by holders of a reptile and amphibian collection licence, by a 2017 account, and most of the state's turtle trade involves farm-hatched animals.

For cooks, Brennan's own published turtle soup recipe notes that fresh or frozen turtle meat can be bought from specialty markets and seafood dealers in and around New Orleans. Brennan's menu prints 100% turtle meat, which means the meat in the soup is all turtle, not stretched with veal or beef. It does not say which snapper or which supplier.
facts: Turtle soup has been eaten in Louisiana since the 1700s.
Louisiana banned commercial trapping of the wild alligator snapping turtle from 20 November 2004.
Licensed Louisiana turtle farmers may still sell alligator snappers hatched from their breeding stock.
Commander's Palace buys farm-raised alligator snapping turtle for a steady supply.
Most of Louisiana's turtle trade involves animals hatched on farms.
Brennan's published recipe says turtle meat can be bought from seafood dealers in and around New Orleans.
Our menu prints 100% turtle meat: no veal or beef stretches the soup.
notes: Say 100% turtle meat, exactly as printed, and explain it means no veal or beef in the soup.
Do not say farm-raised or name a species or supplier until the chef tells you; both farmed and licensed wild snapping turtle are legal in Louisiana.
Never the courtyard turtles: they are red-eared sliders, pardoned house mascots, and the chefs use snappers. Smile when guests joke about it.
For a hesitant guest, describe the taste: rich, meaty and savoury, like a deep, finely chopped stew.
producer.sayIt: It's 100% turtle meat, snapping turtle, in a rich Creole soup finished with spinach, grated egg and aged Sherry.
askKitchen: Which turtle is in our soup, alligator snapper or common snapper, and is it farm-raised?
Who supplies it?

producer.who: Leidenheimer Baking Company
producer.where: Simon Bolivar Avenue, New Orleans
producer.history:
George Leidenheimer came to New Orleans from Deidesheim in Germany and opened a bakery on Dryades Street in 1896. He began with the heavy, dense brown breads of home, but the city's customers of French descent preferred a light, airy loaf, so he turned to New Orleans French bread, with its crisp crust.
