In 1904 the bakery moved to Simon Bolivar Avenue, where it still bakes. Its bread is older than the po-boy itself, which dates to the late 1920s, yet it became the loaf most of the city's po-boy shops reach for, and Leidenheimer is now the largest and best-known po-boy bread maker in New Orleans. The dough is naturally fermented and hand-stretched to a 32-inch loaf, and the bakery also makes pistolets and muffuletta bread.

The family still runs it: Robert J. "Sandy" Whann IV, George Leidenheimer's great-grandson, is the fourth generation and runs it with his sister, Katherine. After Hurricane Katrina, when the city had no power or clean water, Whann kept the bread coming by sending his operations manager to bake in a friend's bakery in Chicago.
facts: Founded in 1896 by George Leidenheimer, an immigrant from Deidesheim, Germany, first on Dryades Street.
Moved in 1904 to Simon Bolivar Avenue, where it still bakes.
He switched from dense German loaves to the light, crisp-crusted New Orleans French bread.
Its bread predates the po-boy, which dates to the late 1920s.
The dough is naturally fermented and hand-stretched to a 32-inch loaf.
Run by Sandy Whann, the fourth generation and George Leidenheimer's great-grandson.
After Hurricane Katrina it kept baking in a friend's bakery in Chicago.
notes: Say the crisps are made from Leidenheimer, the city's po-boy bread; that turns a garnish into a piece of New Orleans.
The menu prints the name; no source says more about how Brennan's buys or makes the crisps, so how they are cut and toasted is a kitchen answer.
Guests often ask whether the bakery is still family run: yes, the fourth generation.
Never claim Leidenheimer invented the po-boy; its bread is older than the sandwich.
producer.sayIt: The crisps are made from Leidenheimer French bread, the po-boy loaf New Orleans has baked since 1896.
askKitchen: How are the Leidenheimer crisps made: sliced and toasted here, with butter or oil?

producer.who: Tien Dat tofu
producer.where: West Bank, Jefferson Parish (Marrero and Harvey addresses); co-op in New Orleans East
producer.history:
Tien Dat is a small local tofu maker, part of the VEGGI Farmers Cooperative, whose extra firm tofu reaches the city through the co-op. Tien Dat Tofu LLC is registered on the West Bank, with addresses in Marrero and Harvey, across the river from the French Quarter. The tofu is made fresh in small batches, sold as extra firm and in flavoured styles such as black mushroom, and lemongrass and red chilli.

VEGGI stands for the Village de L'Est Green Growers Initiative. Village de L'Est is the Vietnamese American community of New Orleans East, and the co-op was established there in 2011, across the street from Mary Queen of Vietnam Church, in the aftermath of the BP oil spill, when twelve growers and programme developers chose through a community forum to build jobs in urban agriculture. It is owned and run by its members.

The co-op sells herbs, vegetables, chilli oil and more at the Crescent City Farmers Market, but it is best known for its freshly made tofu. Printing the name on the Blackened Tofu ties Brennan's plate to that community.
facts: Tien Dat Tofu LLC is a Louisiana company with West Bank addresses in Marrero and Harvey.
The tofu is sold through the VEGGI Farmers Cooperative, made fresh in small batches.
VEGGI means Village de L'Est Green Growers Initiative, after the Vietnamese American community of New Orleans East.
The co-op was established in 2011, after the BP oil spill, and is member owned.
It sits across the street from Mary Queen of Vietnam Church.
Twelve growers and programme developers formed it through a community forum.
The co-op is best known for its tofu and sells at the Crescent City Farmers Market.
notes: Say it is made locally by a Vietnamese American maker and sold through a New Orleans East co-op.
If a guest asks 'made in New Orleans?', the honest answer: the co-op is in New Orleans East; the maker's registered address is across the river on the West Bank.
No source names the person who makes it or describes the method; do not invent a family story.
Ingredient and dietary questions about the tofu and the blackening butter go to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: The tofu is Tien Dat, made locally and sold through the VEGGI co-op, the Vietnamese American growers of New Orleans East.
askKitchen: Which Tien Dat style do we buy (plain extra firm?), and how does the house pronounce it?

producer.who: Two Brooks Farm
producer.where: Sumner, Mississippi (the Delta)
producer.history:
Two Brooks Farm sits at Sumner in the Mississippi Delta. Mike Wagner started it in 1992, and he is a ninth-generation farmer: his family counts an unbroken line of ten generations back to 1742. The farm grows about 2,000 acres of rice and 1,000 of soybeans.

What sets it apart is the birds. The farm lies on the flyway, and after harvest ducks and geese settle on the flooded fields. Wagner noticed his soil changing where they gathered and began cutting back on fertiliser; the birds now supply much of it, and no fungicides or insecticides go on the rice.

From that long-grain rice the family built a line of 14 products, rice, grits and flour among them, with the Original Mississippi Midlands Brown Rice Grits one of Wagner's favourites. His son Lawrence and daughter Abbey, the next generation, have helped widen the range, and the products reach restaurants through US Foods. In 2022 Wagner was named Mississippi's winner of the Swisher Sweets/Sunbelt Ag Expo Southeastern Farmer of the Year award.
facts: At Sumner, Mississippi, in the Delta; started in 1992 by Mike Wagner.
Wagner is a ninth-generation farmer; the family traces ten generations back to 1742.
Ducks and geese winter on the fields and supply much of the fertiliser.
No fungicides or insecticides are used on the rice.
A line of 14 products, including rice, grits and flour.
Mississippi's state winner of the 2022 Swisher Sweets/Sunbelt Ag Expo Southeastern Farmer of the Year award.
Son Lawrence and daughter Abbey, the next generation, help run the farm.
notes: Two Brooks is in Mississippi, not Louisiana; guests sometimes test this.
The duck and geese story is true and memorable: the birds help fertilise the rice.
Whether the grits are cooked with stock or butter is a kitchen answer.
Do not call the rice organic; the sources say reduced fertiliser and no fungicides or insecticides, not certified organic.
producer.sayIt: The rice grits come from Two Brooks Farm in the Mississippi Delta, a family rice farm where wintering ducks help fertilise the fields.
askKitchen: Which Two Brooks grits do we use, white or brown rice, and are they cooked with stock or butter?

producer.who: Mushroom Maggie's Farm (to be confirmed by the chef)
producer.where: St Francisville, Louisiana
producer.history:
Mushroom Maggie's Farm is the best-known Louisiana grower called Maggie's, and the likely source of the side the menu prints simply as Maggie's Mushrooms. No public source names Brennan's as a customer, so treat the link as likely, not settled.

The farm is in St Francisville, upriver from Baton Rouge. Maggie Long and her husband Cyrus Lester have owned and run it since 2018. Their start was hard: in 2017, in the first week of official operations, a propane hose burst while they were steaming fruiting blocks, the barn burned down and Lester was left with burns over seventy percent of his skin. They started again from nothing and spent the next year rebuilding, so 2018 became the farm's first real year.

Today the farm grows 1,200 to 1,500 pounds of mushrooms a week, at least eight kinds, among them lion's mane, oyster, pink trumpet, shiitake and chestnut. It supplies about twenty top New Orleans restaurants and many closer to home, and Maggie Long often works directly with chefs as they plan their menus.
facts: In St Francisville, Louisiana, run since 2018 by Maggie Long and Cyrus Lester.
Grows 1,200 to 1,500 pounds of mushrooms a week.
At least eight kinds, including lion's mane, oyster, pink trumpet, shiitake and chestnut.
Supplies about twenty top New Orleans restaurants.
A 2017 fire in the first week of operations destroyed the barn and badly burned Cyrus Lester; they rebuilt for 2018.
notes: The menu prints only 'Maggie's Mushrooms'; no source confirms the farm supplies Brennan's.
Until the chef confirms it, say 'local mushrooms'; once confirmed, name the farm and St Francisville.
Learn tonight's varieties and how they are cooked at lineup; varieties change.
Butter, stock and whether the side is vegetarian are kitchen answers.
producer.sayIt: Maggie's Mushrooms is our side of local speciality mushrooms; I'll tell you exactly which varieties the kitchen has tonight.
askKitchen: Are Maggie's Mushrooms from Mushroom Maggie's Farm in St Francisville?
Which varieties tonight, and how are they cooked (butter, stock)?

producer.who: Crystal hot sauce, Baumer Foods
producer.where: Reserve, Louisiana (founded on Tchoupitoulas Street, New Orleans)
producer.history:
In 1923 Alvin A. Baumer borrowed money from his future in-laws and bought Mill's Fruit Products, a small snow-cone syrup company on Tchoupitoulas Street. Tucked in a drawer was a recipe for a pepper sauce labelled Crystal Pure. Baumer renamed it Crystal Pure Louisiana Hot Sauce and began bottling it in the city.

For decades Baumer Foods was as much a maker of jellies, preserves and mustard as of hot sauce. From the 1940s it bottled Crystal on Tulane Avenue, where a neon sign of a chef stirring a steaming pot of strawberry jam became a local landmark. The flooding after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 ruined that plant and forced the company to drop its historic preserves, jellies and mustard; it moved upriver to Reserve, Louisiana, at the Port of South Louisiana, 9 feet above sea level.

The recipe is short: aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar and salt, giving a reddish orange sauce with medium heat. The company is still family owned, led by Alvin "Al" Baumer Jr.
facts: In 1923 Alvin A. Baumer bought Mill's Fruit Products on Tchoupitoulas Street, with the Crystal recipe included.
Made from aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar and salt.
Reddish orange with medium heat.
From the 1940s it was bottled on Tulane Avenue, under a neon sign of a chef stirring jam.
Flooding after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 ended the Tulane Avenue plant; production moved upriver to Reserve, Louisiana.
Still family owned, led by Alvin "Al" Baumer Jr.
notes: Describe the gastrique as sweet, tangy and gently spicy; Crystal reads tangy before hot.
The menu prints only 'Crystal Gastrique'; how sweet or hot tonight's batch is, ask the kitchen.
Do not quote factory sizes or gallons shipped; the published figures disagree.
producer.sayIt: The dip is a gastrique made with Crystal, New Orleans' own hot sauce since 1923: sweet, tangy, gently spicy.

producer.who: Abita Brewing Company
producer.where: Abita Springs, Louisiana
producer.history:
Abita Brewing was founded in 1986 by Jim Patton and Rush Cumming in downtown Abita Springs, on the Northshore of Lake Pontchartrain. Its first beer went on sale on 4 July that year in New Orleans and Mandeville, and it is described as the first craft brewery to open in the South.

Amber was one of the brewery's original beers, and the one that put it on the map. Patton wrote the recipes for the flagships, Amber, Turbo Dog, Purple Haze and the root beer among them, before selling his share in 1997. Amber is a Munich-style lager of pale and caramel malts with German Perle hops: smooth, malty and lightly caramel, at 4.5 percent and a low 17 IBU.

At Brennan's the Amber goes into the Mimolette fondue of the Shells & Cheese, where its malt and low bitterness suit a cheese sauce, and the dessert list pours Abita Root Beer in the Amarula float.
facts: Founded in 1986 by Jim Patton and Rush Cumming in Abita Springs, Louisiana.
Its first beer went on sale on 4 July 1986.
Described as the first craft brewery to open in the South.
Amber, one of its original beers, is a Munich-style lager with pale and caramel malts and German Perle hops.
Amber is 4.5 percent alcohol with a low 17 IBU.
Brennan's prints Abita Amber in the Shells & Cheese and pours Abita Root Beer in the Amarula float.
notes: The low bitterness is why it suits a cheese sauce: hops turn bitter as a sauce reduces.
The guide says the beer's alcohol is mostly but not entirely cooked off; tell guests who avoid alcohol and let the kitchen answer anything further.
Do not quote well depths or water ages; those figures came from a retailer only.
Do not say Amber was Abita's very first beer; sources disagree, and some say Golden came first.
producer.sayIt: The fondue is loosened with Abita Amber, brewed across the lake in Abita Springs since 1986, for a smooth, malty depth.

producer.who: Congregation Coffee Roasters
producer.where: 240 Pelican Avenue, Algiers Point, New Orleans
producer.history:
Congregation Coffee was started in 2015 by two partners who met while working at Cochon Butcher. The name is a local joke and a hope at once: a group of alligators is called a congregation, and the blends High Walk, Low Walk and Gallop are named for an alligator's gaits. Two years after the roastery began, the café opened in a Victorian storefront at 240 Pelican Avenue in Algiers Point, across the river from the French Quarter.

Brennan's was a customer long before it was an owner. By 2023 the restaurant had poured Congregation for seven years, and the buyer called them the best roasters in the city. When the company ceased operations that year while looking for new owners, it came under Brennan ownership, and in November 2023 the Algiers Point café and the wholesale roastery on Tchoupitoulas Street reopened, with a founder collaborating. A second café followed at Magazine Street and Jefferson Avenue.

So the coffee at Brennan's comes from a roaster in the family: the Traditional Breakfast tasting pours Brennan's Private Blend Congregation Coffee & Chicory beside the Bananas Foster, and the coffee list prints a Single Estate-grown Congregation Coffee, Roasted For Brennan's.
facts: Founded in 2015 by two partners who met at Cochon Butcher.
A group of alligators is a congregation; blends High Walk, Low Walk and Gallop are alligator gaits.
The flagship café is at 240 Pelican Avenue, Algiers Point.
It roasts at 1746 Tchoupitoulas Street; the second café is at Magazine Street and Jefferson Avenue.
Brennan's had served Congregation for seven years before it came under Brennan ownership in 2023.
Reopened in November 2023, with a founder collaborating.
The menus print a Brennan's Private Blend with chicory and a single estate coffee roasted for Brennan's.
notes: You can say the roaster is owned by the Brennan family and the blend is made for the house.
The chicory blend is the Traditional Breakfast pour; the single estate coffee's origin rotates, so read it from the coffee card. The chicory story itself lives on the chicory card.
Do not claim Congregation has always been a Brennan company; it was independent until 2023.
The alligator name story is true and guests enjoy it.
producer.sayIt: The coffee is Congregation, roasted across the river in Algiers Point; this chicory blend is roasted privately for Brennan's.
askKitchen: Which single estate origin is on the coffee card this week?

producer.who: Brennan's honey (source unconfirmed)
producer.where: Served at 417 Royal Street; where the honey comes from is not confirmed, so ask the kitchen
producer.history:
The Roost's Cheese Board prints Brennan's Honey beside three cheeses, a seasonal chutney and fruit and nut bread. The name says the honey belongs to the house, but no public source says where it comes from.

No source describes bees, hives or an apiary at 417 Royal Street; the only small residents the press describes in the courtyard are its turtles. The honey might come from the house's own hives, from a named Louisiana beekeeper bottling for Brennan's, or be a honey the kitchen finishes itself. None of those is confirmed, so until the chef answers at lineup, call it Brennan's honey and nothing more.

What a server can say with confidence is what the menu prints. The board belongs to the Roost Bar & Bubbles, at $24.00, and the honey is there for the same reason honey sits on any good cheese board: its sweetness sets off salty, sharp cheese, while the chutney adds fruit and acid and the fruit and nut bread gives crunch.
facts: The Cheese Board prints Brennan's Honey with three cheeses, seasonal chutney and fruit and nut bread, $24.
No public source names hives at Brennan's or a beekeeper supplying it, so its source is a lineup question.
The Cheese Board is on the Roost Bar & Bubbles menu.
Brennan's has stood at 417 Royal Street since Owen Brennan leased the building in 1954.
notes: Say 'Brennan's honey' exactly as printed; never say 'our own bees' or name a farm until the chef confirms.
If a guest asks where it comes from, say you will find out, and ask the kitchen.
Honey flatters salty, sharp cheeses; that is why it is on the board. Which three cheeses are on tonight is a lineup question.
producer.sayIt: The board comes with Brennan's honey, a seasonal chutney and fruit and nut bread, sweet, sharp and crunchy around three cheeses.
askKitchen: Where does Brennan's honey come from: house hives, a named beekeeper, or a private label?
Which three cheeses are on the board tonight?

producer.who: Louisiana Creole tomato growers
producer.where: St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes, below New Orleans, and Louisiana generally
producer.history:
Creole is a growers' word before it is a variety. Farmers in St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes traditionally sold their tomatoes as Creole, and said that ripening on the vine in rich alluvial river soil gave them a flavour no other Louisiana or American tomato had. In the early 1900s, before tomatoes carried variety names, fruit from St. Charles, St. John and St. James parishes was simply called Creole too.

The LSU AgCenter muddied the water in 1969, when researcher Teme Hernandez released a variety actually named Creole. It yielded poorly, less than six pounds a plant, was never common in St. Bernard or Plaquemines, and the AgCenter did not keep its seed. So a Creole tomato today is a Louisiana-grown tomato picked ripe, not one cultivar.

The city celebrates it every June at the French Market's Creole Tomato Festival, which began in 1985 to mark the start of the season and honours the farmers who grow them. The French Market itself has stood since 1791.
facts: St. Bernard and Plaquemines growers traditionally sold their tomatoes as Creole, crediting vine ripening and alluvial soil.
In the early 1900s tomatoes from St. Charles, St. John and St. James parishes were also simply called Creole.
LSU AgCenter researcher Teme Hernandez released a variety named Creole in 1969; its seed stock was not kept.
Hernandez's Creole yielded less than six pounds per plant and was never common in St. Bernard or Plaquemines.
The French Market's Creole Tomato Festival began in 1985 and is held every June.
The French Market in New Orleans has stood since 1791.
notes: Say Creole tomato means a Louisiana tomato picked ripe, not a single variety; the menu pairs them with Louisiana heirlooms.
Do not name a farm or a parish for tonight's tomatoes unless the kitchen tells you at lineup.
The tostada follows the summer season; if guests ask why it has gone, the tomatoes have finished.
Guests sometimes ask whether Creole tomatoes are a breed: the honest answer is that the word is older than the 1969 LSU variety and means local and vine-ripened.
producer.sayIt: Creole tomatoes are Louisiana's summer tomatoes, picked ripe in river soil, served raw here with heirlooms, burrata and smoked tomato water.
askKitchen: Who grows tonight's Creole and heirloom tomatoes, and from which parish?
How long will the Creole Tomato Tostada stay on this season?

producer.who: Louisiana cane syrup (Steen's of Abbeville is the best-known maker; the menu names none)
producer.where: Abbeville, Louisiana, on Bayou Vermilion (Steen's)
producer.founded: 1910 (Steen's)
producer.history:
Louisiana cane syrup is cane juice concentrated by long cooking in open kettles, with nothing taken out and nothing added. Slow Food lists traditional cane syrup on its Ark of Taste, the catalogue of heritage foods worth saving.

The name most Louisianans reach for is Steen's. In 1910 an early freeze hit Charley Steen's cane crop near Abbeville. Rather than lose it, he built a small mill and turned the frozen cane into a few barrels of syrup. By 1930 Charley and Elizabeth Steen and their children had built a larger mill in the heart of Abbeville, on the banks of Bayou Vermilion, and from the 1950s the yellow can became a fixture of Cajun and Creole kitchens. The mill is still run by the Steen family and still cooks in open kettles, which is why the label reads 100% Pure Cane Syrup.

Brennan's menu prints cane syrup on the peaches of the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast but names no maker, so Steen's is the story of the style, not a claim about the kitchen's bottle.
facts: Cane syrup is cane juice concentrated by long cooking in open kettles.
Traditional cane syrup is listed on Slow Food's Ark of Taste.
Steen's began in 1910 when an early freeze hit Charley Steen's cane crop and he milled it into syrup.
By 1930 Charley and Elizabeth Steen built a larger mill in Abbeville on Bayou Vermilion.
Steen's still cooks in open kettles and adds nothing, hence 100% Pure Cane Syrup on the label.
Molasses is what remains after sugar is crystallised out; cane syrup has nothing removed.
notes: Say Louisiana cane syrup; never say Steen's is on the plate unless the kitchen confirms it.
Guests often ask if it is molasses: no, it is lighter and sweeter, cane juice simply boiled down.
The duck course has appeared in two versions on the house's own pages; describe the one printed tonight.
Steen's makes a good story for curious guests: a 1910 freeze turned into a Louisiana staple.
producer.sayIt: The peaches are glazed in Louisiana cane syrup, cane juice simply boiled down, lighter and more buttery than molasses, against the rich duck.
askKitchen: Whose cane syrup glazes the peaches on the duck, Steen's or another maker?
Is tonight's duck the cane syrup peach version or the hazelnut-crusted version?

producer.who: Roasted chicory root, the New Orleans coffee tradition
producer.where: Grown mostly in France and Belgium; roasted and blended with coffee in New Orleans
producer.history:
Chicory is the root of a blue-flowered perennial, dug, cut, dried, roasted and ground. In 1806 the British blockaded the French coast and Napoleon answered with his Continental System, an embargo on British trade that lasted until 1814. Imported coffee grew scarce, chicory became the French substitute, and the French kept their taste for it after the embargo ended. The habit reached New Orleans with its French colonial ties.

New Orleans was ready for it. By 1840 the port was the second largest coffee importer in the United States. During the Civil War, from 1861, the Union naval blockade cut the port off, and Louisianans stretched what coffee they had with chicory. Smithsonian calls it a cost-saving workaround that stuck around for tradition's sake: the rest of the South dropped it, New Orleans did not.

Today most commercial chicory is grown in France and Belgium. At Brennan's it is in the New Orleans Style Coffee, a blend of chicory and dark roast, in the private blend poured on the breakfast tasting, and baked into the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.
facts: Chicory is the roasted root of a blue-flowered perennial plant.
Napoleon's Continental System, an embargo on British trade from 21 November 1806, made imported coffee scarce, and chicory filled the gap.
The French kept drinking chicory in their coffee after the Continental System collapsed.
By 1840 New Orleans was the second largest coffee importer in the United States.
From 1861 the Union naval blockade cut off the port, and Louisianans stretched coffee with chicory.
Most commercial chicory is grown in France and Belgium.
Brennan's prints chicory in its New Orleans Style Coffee, the breakfast tasting coffee and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.
notes: Chicory is not coffee: it is a roasted root blended with coffee for body and a roasty, bitter-chocolate depth.

The breakfast tasting blend is roasted by Congregation, which has its own card; the menu names no roaster for the New Orleans Style Coffee, and where the chicory is grown is not public, so name no country for ours.
The Civil War story is true but not the whole story: the French habit came first.
Caffeine questions go to the service note and the kitchen; do not guess decaf options.
producer.sayIt: Chicory is a roasted root, a French habit New Orleans kept through the Civil War blockade; it gives our coffee a roasty, chocolatey depth.
askKitchen: What proportion of chicory is in the New Orleans Style Coffee blend?
Is the coffee cake baked with the same Congregation chicory blend we pour?

producer.who: Louisiana native pecans
producer.where: Louisiana and the Mississippi valley; Oak Alley Plantation, St. James Parish, for the first grafted pecans
producer.history:
Louisiana is one of the few states where the pecan is native. The state holds between 19,000 and 21,000 acres of native trees, and their nuts tend to be small, flavourful and high in oil, unlike the larger improved varieties bred since. The LSU AgCenter runs the only university research station in the country devoted solely to pecans.

The improved pecan itself began in Louisiana. In the winter of 1846 or 1847, Antoine, an enslaved gardener at Oak Alley Plantation in St. James Parish, grafted pecan wood from a tree with large, thin-shelled nuts onto other trees. He grafted sixteen trees near the house, more were grafted later, and by the end of the Civil War in 1865 Oak Alley had 126 grafted trees in bearing. His nut, later named Centennial, won a prize at the 1876 Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia, and grafting made the pecan an orchard crop.

In New Orleans kitchens the pecan stands where the almond stood in French recipes. It runs right through Brennan's menus: the pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish, the oat and pecan crumble on the Baked Apple, the pecans on the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake and the pralines on the bread pudding.
facts: Louisiana is one of few states where pecans are native.
Louisiana has between 19,000 and 21,000 acres of native pecans.
Native pecans tend to be small, flavourful and high in oil compared with improved varieties.
The LSU AgCenter runs the only university research station in the United States devoted solely to pecans.
Antoine, an enslaved gardener at Oak Alley, grafted pecans in 1846 or 1847; by 1865 the plantation had 126 grafted trees.
Antoine's pecan, named Centennial, won a prize at the 1876 Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia.
notes: Pecans appear in four dishes; nut questions always go to the kitchen and the service note, never a verdict from you.
Do not claim our pecans are Louisiana-grown or native unless the kitchen confirms the supplier.
Antoine's story is a powerful one for interested guests; tell it plainly and with respect.
Say pih-KAHN, the common Louisiana pronunciation.
producer.sayIt: The pecan is native to Louisiana, and New Orleans cooks use it where French recipes used almonds, from the fish to the pralines.
askKitchen: Where do our pecans come from, and are they Louisiana or native pecans?

producer.who: The New Orleans praline and the pralinières
producer.where: The French Quarter, New Orleans
producer.history:
The praline began as a French sugared almond, named for César, duc de Choiseul, comte du Plessis-Praslin, whose chef made it. Early in the eighteenth century the Ursuline nuns are credited with bringing the candy to New Orleans.

The New Orleans praline is a different thing, and it was made by the city's Black women. They took the almond sweet, used the pecans that grew all around them and added milk or cream, turning a hard sugared nut into the soft, creamy patty the city knows.

In the mid to late nineteenth century, women called pralinières sold them on the streets of the French Quarter. Free women of colour and enslaved women alike made and sold them, and for Black women it was a way to earn their own money; some bought their own freedom and their families' with the proceeds. On Brennan's New Orleans Bread Pudding, pralines bring that history and a caramel crunch to the whiskey caramel and buttermilk ice cream.
facts: The praline is named for César, duc de Choiseul, comte du Plessis-Praslin, whose chef made sugared almonds.
The Ursuline nuns are credited with bringing the praline to New Orleans early in the eighteenth century.
The city's Black women made the pecan praline, adding milk or cream to thicken it.
Pralinières sold pralines on French Quarter streets in the mid to late nineteenth century.
Some pralinières bought their own and their families' freedom with their earnings.
notes: Locals say PRAH-leen; follow the house if a guest says it another way, and never correct them.
Whether our pralines are made in-house is not public; ask before saying housemade.
Nut and dairy questions go to the kitchen and the service note.
Credit the pralinières when a guest asks about the history; it is the true origin of the New Orleans style.
producer.sayIt: New Orleans pralines are pecans, brown sugar and cream, a candy the city's pralinières sold in the French Quarter; they crown our bread pudding.
askKitchen: Are the pralines on the bread pudding made in-house, and if not, by whom?

producer.who: Louisiana popcorn rice (the Della type, bred by the LSU AgCenter)
producer.where: LSU Rice Research Station, Crowley, Louisiana; milled across south Louisiana
producer.founded: 1909 (the LSU Rice Research Station)
producer.history:
Popcorn rice is Louisiana's own aromatic long grain. The Rice Research Station at Crowley opened in 1909 on a 60-acre farm, set up by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station with the USDA and now run by the LSU AgCenter, and it was the AgCenter that released Della, an aromatic long-grain rice bred for cooks who wanted a fluffy texture and a strong popcorn-like aroma. Della is tall, falls over easily and yields poorly, which is why it remains a speciality rather than a field staple. The aroma itself is 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the molecule that also scents basmati, jasmine and fresh popcorn.

The best-known retail example comes from the Conrad Rice Mill in New Iberia, founded in 1912 by Philip Amalus Conrad and the oldest independently owned rice mill in the United States still working. Its Konriko brand, named in the 1950s, sells Wild Pecan Rice, a Della-type brown popcorn rice that smells of roasted nuts. Mike Davis bought the mill in February 1975 and turned it towards speciality rice.

Brennan's prints popcorn rice under its Seafood Gumbo and names no mill, so Konriko is the story of the style, not the kitchen's bag.
facts: The Rice Research Station at Crowley opened in 1909 on a 60-acre farm, a joint Louisiana and USDA project now run by the LSU AgCenter.
The LSU AgCenter released Della, an aromatic long grain with a strong popcorn-like aroma.
Della is tall, lodges easily and yields poorly, so it stays a speciality rice.
Popcorn rice owes its aroma to 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, shared with basmati and jasmine.
The Conrad Rice Mill in New Iberia, founded in 1912, is the oldest independently owned US rice mill still operating.
Konriko's Wild Pecan Rice is a Della-type brown popcorn rice with a roasted-nut aroma.
notes: There is no popcorn and no pecan in popcorn rice or Wild Pecan Rice; the names describe the aroma.
Do not name Konriko or any mill as ours unless the kitchen confirms it.
If a guest notices a toasty smell as the gumbo lands, that is the rice.
Do not give a year for Della's release; sources place it only in the early 1970s.
producer.sayIt: The gumbo sits on Louisiana popcorn rice, an aromatic long grain bred at LSU that really smells of popcorn as it cooks.
askKitchen: Whose popcorn rice do we use under the gumbo?

producer.who: South Louisiana rice country
producer.where: The southwest Louisiana prairie, centred on Crowley, Acadia Parish
producer.history:
South Louisiana Rice Dressing carries its place in its name. Rice growing on the southwest Louisiana prairie began in earnest in the early 1880s, and by 1890 a record crop of 80 million pounds made Louisiana the leading rice state, overtaking South Carolina. Crowley, the seat of Acadia Parish, became the centre of the industry, its fields watered by canals and wells.

Between 1800 and 1920 the region changed from subsistence farming and open-range cattle country into the first mechanised commercial rice region in the world, and southwest Louisiana still holds nearly 500,000 acres of rice land.

That is why rice, not bread, is the stuffing of south Louisiana: rice dressing is cooked rice folded into browned meat and the holy trinity, a Sunday and holiday dish. Brennan's prints the side with no description and no rice brand, so the meats and the rice are questions for the kitchen.
facts: Rice growing in southwest Louisiana began in earnest in the early 1880s.
Louisiana's record 1890 crop of 80 million pounds made it the leading rice state, passing South Carolina.
Crowley, seat of Acadia Parish, became the centre of southwestern Louisiana's rice industry.
Southwestern Louisiana became the first mechanised commercial rice region in the world by 1920.
Southwest Louisiana holds nearly 500,000 acres of rice land.
notes: The side prints no description; confirm the meats with the kitchen before describing it.
Do not claim the rice is from a named mill or parish without the kitchen's word.
Guests ask how it differs from dirty rice; the honest answer is that it depends who you ask.
Meat and dietary questions go to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Rice dressing is south Louisiana's stuffing, rice from the prairie rice country folded with browned meat and the trinity; I'll confirm tonight's meats.
askKitchen: Which meats go into the South Louisiana Rice Dressing, and is there liver?
Which rice is it made with?

producer.who: LaPlace andouille, the Andouille Capital of the World
producer.where: LaPlace, St. John the Baptist Parish, Louisiana
producer.history:
Andouille in Louisiana is a River Parishes sausage. The Germans of the German Coast, upriver from New Orleans, brought a strong tradition of sausage making, with French, Acadian, Native American, Spanish and African influences alongside. The town that made it famous is LaPlace, which Governor Edwin Edwards proclaimed the Andouille Capital of the World in the 1970s.

Three LaPlace shops carry the name. Jacob's World Famous Andouille dates from 1928, when Nelson and Camille Jacob began selling smoked andouille from their Milesville home; Aaron Lion is its fourth-generation owner. Wayne Jacob's Smokehouse, no relation to Jacob's, opened in 1950, and Bailey's sits next door to Jacob's. Locals say Jacob's is the smokiest, Wayne Jacob's has the spice and the girth, and Bailey's sits in between. LaPlace andouille is, as one writer put it, thick as a wrist, brown as tobacco and steeped in pecan wood smoke.

The town has held an Andouille Festival every October since the first, on 28 and 29 October 1972. Brennan's prints andouille in its Seafood Gumbo, as in its published gumbo recipe, and names no maker.
facts: Governor Edwin Edwards declared LaPlace the Andouille Capital of the World.
Jacob's World Famous Andouille in LaPlace dates from 1928, begun by Nelson and Camille Jacob.
Wayne Jacob's Smokehouse, unaffiliated with Jacob's, opened in 1950.
Jacob's, Bailey's and Wayne Jacob's are the three LaPlace shops famous for andouille.
LaPlace andouille is steeped in pecan wood smoke.
The first LaPlace Andouille Festival was held on 28 and 29 October 1972.
German Coast settlers brought the sausage-making tradition to the River Parishes.
notes: The menu names no andouille maker; never say it is from LaPlace or Jacob's unless the kitchen confirms.
Andouille is pork; tell a guest who avoids pork that it is in the gumbo before they order.
Say ahn-DOO-ee.
Louisiana andouille is a smoked seasoning sausage, unlike the French andouille made from tripe; do not confuse them.
producer.sayIt: The gumbo's smoke comes from andouille, Louisiana's coarse smoked pork sausage, a River Parishes tradition centred on LaPlace.
askKitchen: Who makes our andouille, and is it from LaPlace?

producer.who: Tasso, the Cajun smokehouse seasoning meat
producer.where: Acadiana, south Louisiana
producer.history:
Tasso belongs to the boucherie, the communal hog butchering of Acadiana, where neighbours killed a pig together and shared every part. The boucherie gave the Cajun larder boudin, cracklin', andouille and tasso, and tasso was traditionally made from the last lean pieces: a seasoning meat, not a meal.

It is often called a ham, but the name misleads. Tasso is cut from the shoulder, not the hind leg. The shoulder is sliced across the grain into pieces about three inches thick, cured briefly in salt and sugar for only three or four hours, rinsed, rubbed with cayenne and garlic, and hot-smoked until cooked through. The smokehouse has its own Acadian French word, boucanière.

Cooks rarely eat tasso on its own. They dice it into jambalaya, stews and braised vegetables, where a little carries smoke, salt and heat through the pot. At Brennan's it seasons the Creole sauce of the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. The menu names no maker, so who smokes it is a question for the kitchen.
facts: Tasso is a smoked, spiced, cured south Louisiana meat cut from the hog's shoulder, not the leg.
The shoulder is cut about three inches thick and cured only three or four hours.
After curing it is rubbed with cayenne and garlic and hot-smoked until cooked through.
At a boucherie, tasso was made from the last lean pieces; it is a seasoning meat.
The boucherie gave the Cajun larder boudin, cracklin', andouille and tasso.
Boucanière is the Acadian French word for smokehouse.
notes: Call it a seasoning meat; if a guest says Cajun ham, explain it is shoulder, not leg.
Tasso is pork; flag it for guests who avoid pork before they order the Shrimp & Grits.
The menu names no maker; ask before claiming it is smoked in-house or bought from a named smokehouse.
TAH-so and TASS-oh are both heard; follow the house habit.
producer.sayIt: Tasso is Cajun smoked pork shoulder, spiced with cayenne and garlic, used a little at a time to season our Creole sauce.
askKitchen: Is our tasso smoked in-house, and if not, who makes it?

producer.who: Sazerac Rye, the Sazerac Company
producer.where: New Orleans company, headquartered in Metairie; distilled at Buffalo Trace, Frankfort, Kentucky
producer.founded: The Sazerac Company: 1869, from the Sazerac Coffee House of the 1850s
producer.history:
Sazerac Rye carries the name of a bar. In the 1850s the Sazerac Coffee House in New Orleans took its name from Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac, which by the company's account went into its house cocktail. Thomas H. Handy took over the coffee house in 1869, and as phylloxera ruined the European vineyards, rye whiskey took the cognac's place in the city's drink.

The bottle is the Sazerac Company's namesake straight rye, distilled at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, Kentucky, and bottled at 90 proof. It was once labelled 6 years old and now carries no age statement; the mash bill is not disclosed, and it shares its grain recipe with Sazerac 18 Year and Thomas H. Handy. Reviewers find it light bodied for a rye, with apricot, orange peel, caramel and vanilla over the pepper.

The company grew from Handy's firm, which also came to own Antoine Peychaud's bitters. It was reorganised as the Sazerac Company in 1919, rode out Prohibition as a grocery wholesaler, and in 1948 was bought by Magnolia Liquor, a New Orleans wholesaler founded by two partners; the family of one of them owns it still. It bought Herbsaint in 1949 and the distillery now called Buffalo Trace in 1992, and it remains privately held, headquartered in Metairie, with more than 500 brands. All three bottles of the Classic Sazerac are its own.

In 2019 it opened the Sazerac House at the corner of Canal and Magazine, a museum with a small still that makes Sazerac rye.
facts: Named, like the company and the cocktail, for the Sazerac Coffee House of the 1850s, itself named for Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac.
A 90 proof straight rye distilled at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, Kentucky; once labelled 6 years old, it now carries no age statement.
The mash bill is not disclosed; it shares its grain recipe with Sazerac 18 Year and Thomas H. Handy.
Reviewers taste apricot, orange peel, caramel and vanilla over rye pepper, in a light body.
A 100 proof Sazerac Rye and the 125 proof Sazerac Rye Full Proof are separate bottles.
The firm became the Sazerac Company in 1919 and has been privately owned since Magnolia Liquor, a New Orleans wholesaler, bought it in 1948.
The company bought the distillery now called Buffalo Trace in 1992.
The Sazerac House at Canal and Magazine opened in 2019, a museum with a small still making Sazerac rye.
The company also owns Peychaud's Bitters and Herbsaint, the other two bottles in the Classic Sazerac.
notes: Say Sazerac Rye is made by a New Orleans company and distilled at Buffalo Trace in Kentucky. The small still at the Sazerac House also makes some Sazerac rye; the standard bottle is the Kentucky one.
Guests ask whether the drink is named for the whiskey. Both the cocktail and the company take the name of the Sazerac Coffee House, which took it from a cognac.
Do not quote an age: the bottle carries none. Sazerac 18 Year, a 100 proof Sazerac Rye and Sazerac Rye Full Proof are different bottles.
If a guest asks who owns it: a privately held New Orleans family company. Name nobody.
A curious guest can visit the Sazerac House at Canal and Magazine; tours are generally free with a reservation, so suggest they check its own site.
producer.sayIt: Sazerac Rye comes from the New Orleans company named for the old Sazerac Coffee House; it is distilled at Buffalo Trace in Kentucky.
askKitchen: Is the Classic poured on the standard 90 proof Sazerac Rye, or another Sazerac bottling such as the 100 proof?

producer.who: Peychaud's Bitters, the Sazerac Company
producer.where: Created on Royal Street, New Orleans; made at Buffalo Trace, Frankfort, Kentucky
producer.founded: between 1849 and 1857, by the most careful account
producer.history:
Peychaud's Bitters began with Antoine Amédée Peychaud, a Creole apothecary from Saint-Domingue, the French colony that became Haiti, who kept his shop on Royal Street in New Orleans. The most careful account dates the bright red aromatic bitters that carry his name to between 1849 and 1857, though company tellings reach back to the 1830s. In an 1857 advertisement in the New Orleans Bee he listed the city bars that sold them, the nearby Sazerac House among them.

Hard times followed. Peychaud had to sell his Royal Street building in 1868. By one account he then licensed the formula to local pharmacists while compounding it for Thomas H. Handy of the Sazerac Coffee House; another dates Handy's purchase of the brand to 1873. Peychaud died in 1883. The bitters have belonged ever since to Handy's firm and the Sazerac Company that grew from it, the New Orleans company behind Sazerac Rye and Herbsaint.

It is a gentian based bitters, close to Angostura in kind but with a stronger anise aroma and a background of mint; the recipe is kept secret. It is bottled at 35 percent alcohol and made at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, Kentucky, and the Sazerac House at Canal and Magazine also makes some bitters.

The company sells a second version, Peychaud's Barrel-Aged, launched in 2014 and rested 140 days in Sazerac Rye barrels, which adds oak, vanilla and candied spice.
facts: Created between 1849 and 1857, by the most careful account, by Antoine Amédée Peychaud, a Creole apothecary from Saint-Domingue.
An 1857 advertisement in the New Orleans Bee listed the Sazerac House among the bars selling it.
Peychaud sold his Royal Street building in 1868; Thomas H. Handy came to own the brand in the 1870s, one source says 1873.
Gentian based, like Angostura, but with a stronger anise aroma and a background of mint.
Bottled at 35 percent alcohol and made at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, Kentucky.
Peychaud's Barrel-Aged, launched in 2014, rests 140 days in Sazerac Rye barrels, adding oak, vanilla and candied spice.
Antoine Peychaud lived from 1803 to 1883.
notes: His apothecary is believed to have stood at what is now 437 Royal Street, on Brennan's block. Say believed, and tell it only once lineup has cleared it.
Never say Peychaud invented the cocktail or the word: cocktail was defined in print in 1806, when he was a small child.
The Origin Story prints barrel-aged Peychaud's. A Sazerac Company bottling exists; whether ours is that one or aged by the bar is a lineup question, so say barrel-aged and no more.
Say born on Royal Street, made in Kentucky today. Never say it is made on Royal Street.
Thompson's Dream uses Bitter Truth Creole Bitters instead, a tribute to the same style; a guest who wants Peychaud's there is asking for a change to the drink.
producer.sayIt: Peychaud's is the red New Orleans bitters Antoine Peychaud created in his Royal Street apothecary in the 1850s.
askKitchen: Is the Origin Story's barrel-aged Peychaud's the Sazerac Company's Barrel-Aged bottling, or bitters aged by our bar?
May we tell guests that Peychaud's apothecary stood on our block of Royal Street?

producer.who: Herbsaint, the Sazerac Company
producer.where: New Orleans, where it was created
producer.history:
Herbsaint was born in New Orleans in 1934, just after the repeal of Prohibition, while absinthe was still banned in the United States, as it had been since 1912. Its makers were J. Marion Legendre and Reginald Parker, who had learnt absinthe making in France during the First World War.

Legendre first sold it as Legendre Absinthe, though it never held grand wormwood. Within months the Federal Alcohol Control Administration objected to the word absinthe, and he renamed it Herbsaint, from herbe sainte, the Creole name for wormwood. In time it became a usual rinse for the Sazerac, the city's own cocktail.

In June 1949 the Sazerac Company, the New Orleans firm behind Sazerac Rye and Peychaud's, bought J.M. Legendre and Co. In the mid-1950s the standard bottling became a different 90 proof recipe, and by the early 1970s it was the only Herbsaint made. In December 2009, for the brand's 75th anniversary, the company brought back Legendre's original 100 proof recipe as Herbsaint Original. Both are sold today, and the 90 proof remains the predominant bottling.

The company does not say where Herbsaint is made now, so it is described as born in New Orleans, not made there.
facts: Created in New Orleans in 1934 by J. Marion Legendre and Reginald Parker, as an absinthe substitute.
First sold as Legendre Absinthe; federal regulators objected to the word, and it became Herbsaint.
The name comes from herbe sainte, the Creole name for wormwood; Legendre's liqueur never held grand wormwood.
The Sazerac Company bought J.M. Legendre and Co. in June 1949.
The standard bottling is 90 proof; Herbsaint Original, Legendre's 100 proof recipe, returned in December 2009.
Absinthe was banned in the United States from 1912 until 2007.
notes: Say ERB-sant: the H is silent.
It is a rinse, not a pour: the guest gets the anise perfume without much of the flavour.
Call it New Orleans' own anise liqueur, born here in 1934. Where it is made today is not published, so never say it is made in the city.
Is it absinthe? No: it was made as a substitute while absinthe was banned. Thompson's Dream rinses with real absinthe, and the Origin Story uses one too.
Questions about what is in it go to the bar; never answer them from memory.
producer.sayIt: Herbsaint is New Orleans' own anise liqueur, created here in 1934 while absinthe was banned; it rinses the glass for aroma.
askKitchen: Do we rinse with the standard 90 proof Herbsaint or the 100 proof Herbsaint Original?

producer.who: Willett Distillery, Kentucky Bourbon Distillers
producer.where: Bardstown, Kentucky
producer.history:
Distilling runs back generations in the Willett family. John David Willett, born in 1841, was a master distiller, and his son A. Lambert Willett followed him into the trade. In 1936 Lambert and his sons, led by Thompson Willett, founded the Willett Distilling Company on the family farm outside Bardstown, with Thompson as founder and president. The first batch, about 30 barrels, was made on 17 March 1937. Old Bardstown bourbon followed in the 1940s.

The stills went quiet in the early 1980s, after a brief spell making ethanol during the energy crisis of the 1970s. On 1 July 1984 Thompson Willett's son-in-law bought the property and renamed the business Kentucky Bourbon Distillers, which for years bottled whiskey distilled elsewhere. Its Willett Pot Still Reserve bourbon, launched in 2008 in a bottle shaped from the original still's blueprints, began that way too.

After years of renovation the family started the distillery again in January 2012, and its first own rye, two years old, reached the market around 2015. The Family Estate 4-year rye is a small batch, hand bottled at barrel strength, so its proof changes from batch to batch; it runs far hotter and spicier than the 90 proof Sazerac Rye of the Classic.
facts: Founded in 1936 on the family farm outside Bardstown, with Thompson Willett as founder and president.
The first batch, about 30 barrels, was made on 17 March 1937.
The stills fell silent in the early 1980s; from 1984 the business ran as Kentucky Bourbon Distillers, long an independent bottler.
The family restarted the distillery in January 2012; its first own rye reached the market around 2015.
The Family Estate 4-year rye is a small batch, hand bottled at barrel strength; its proof varies from batch to batch.
Willett Pot Still Reserve came out in 2008 in a bottle shaped from the original still's blueprints.
notes: Thompson's Dream is the house's own name: no Willett bottle carries it and nothing published explains it. It may nod to Thompson Willett, the founder; offer that only as a guess.
Read the proof from today's bottle; barrel strength changes batch to batch, so never quote one from memory.
Willett bottled whiskey made elsewhere before 2012. Do not say where a particular bottle was distilled unless the label or the bar says so.
Name nobody from today's family or staff; say a family distillery in Bardstown since 1936.
Offer Thompson's Dream to the guest who loves the Classic: louder rye spice and more heat.
producer.sayIt: Willett is a family distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, since 1936; its barrel-strength rye makes Thompson's Dream bigger and spicier than the Classic.
askKitchen: What proof is the Willett 4-year rye we are pouring now?
Does the house tell a story behind the name Thompson's Dream?

producer.who: Rittenhouse Rye, Heaven Hill
producer.where: Bardstown and Louisville, Kentucky
producer.founded: 1934 (Rittenhouse); 1935 (Heaven Hill)
producer.history:
Rittenhouse Rye was first sold in Philadelphia in 1934, just after Prohibition, by Continental Distilling, and named for the city's Rittenhouse Square. In 1948 it was relaunched as a four-year-old bottled in bond rye, the form it keeps. Heaven Hill bought the brand in the 1990s, in 1993 by some accounts and 1999 by others, and moved its production from Pennsylvania to Kentucky.

Heaven Hill itself was founded at Bardstown in 1935 by a group of investors; in time five brothers of one family bought out the rest, and their descendants own and run the company still. On 7 November 1996 fire swept through its warehouses, and some 90,000 barrels burned. In 1999 it bought the Bernheim distillery in Louisville, where it has distilled since, while ageing and bottling stayed around Bardstown; a new Bardstown distillery filled its first barrel on 7 April 2025.

Bottled in bond means the spirit of a single distilling season, aged at least four years in a federally bonded warehouse and bottled at 100 proof. Rittenhouse is 51 percent rye, with corn and malted barley: a modern Kentucky recipe, lower in rye than the old Pennsylvania ryes it nods to.

Rumors are Flying prints Brennan's Barrel Aged Rittenhouse Rye. No public source says what that means: a barrel chosen for the house, or rye rested again in a cask of the bar's own. The bar holds that story.
facts: First sold in Philadelphia in 1934 by Continental Distilling and named for Rittenhouse Square.
Relaunched in 1948 as a four-year-old bottled in bond rye.
Heaven Hill bought the brand in the 1990s (sources give 1993 or 1999) and moved production from Pennsylvania to Kentucky.
Bottled in bond: one distilling season, at least four years in a bonded warehouse, bottled at 100 proof.
The mash bill is 51 percent rye; sources split the corn and malted barley differently.
Heaven Hill was founded at Bardstown in 1935 and is still family owned and run.
Since 1999 Heaven Hill has distilled at Bernheim in Louisville, ageing and bottling around Bardstown.
A fire on 7 November 1996 swept its Bardstown warehouses, and some 90,000 barrels burned.
notes: Say barrel-aged for Brennan's, and no more, until the bar gives the story: who aged it, in what cask, and for how long.
A barrel pick is a single barrel that a bar or shop chooses at the distillery and bottles under its own label. Ask whether ours is one, or rye rested again in our own cask.
Never say Brennan's distilled it: Heaven Hill makes Rittenhouse in Kentucky.
At 100 proof its rye spice holds up against the tart cherry and brown sugar.
Heaven Hill is family owned; name nobody from the family or the distillery.
producer.sayIt: Rumors are Flying uses Rittenhouse, a 100 proof bottled in bond rye from Heaven Hill in Kentucky, in a barrel-aged version for Brennan's.
askKitchen: What is Brennan's Barrel Aged Rittenhouse: a barrel picked for the house, or Rittenhouse rested again in our own cask?
Who aged it, in what cask, and for how long?

producer.who: Rabbit Hole Distillery
producer.where: Louisville, Kentucky
producer.history:
Rabbit Hole was founded in Louisville in 2012 by a former clinical psychologist who left the profession to distil whiskey. The name, by one account, comes from his wife's warning that the venture would take the family down a rabbit hole from which they could never return. She is a Louisville native and a bourbon lover who had drawn him from Scotch to bourbon, and Dareringer, the sherry-finished bourbon, is named in her honour.

In its first years the brand's whiskey was made at other distilleries while its own was designed and built. The distillery opened in May 2018 in downtown Louisville. In June 2019 Pernod Ricard USA agreed to buy a majority share, at a price never disclosed; at the time the founder kept most of his shares and stayed on to run the company.

Dareringer is a wheated Kentucky straight bourbon. It ages first in new charred American oak, then is finished in casks that held Pedro Ximénez, a dark and very sweet sherry, and it is bottled at 93 proof. The finish lays raisin and dried fruit richness over the bourbon's vanilla and oak, a richness that carries the smoke, the Angostura, the orange and the cherry of the Birdcage.
facts: Founded in Louisville in 2012 by a former clinical psychologist.
Its downtown Louisville distillery opened in May 2018.
Pernod Ricard USA agreed to buy a majority share in June 2019; the founder stayed on to run the company at the time.
Dareringer is a wheated straight bourbon finished in Pedro Ximénez sherry casks and bottled at 93 proof.
Dareringer is named for the founder's wife, a Louisville native who drew him from Scotch to bourbon.
By one account the brand name recalls her warning that distilling would lead the family down a rabbit hole.
notes: The menu pours the Birdcage only in the Roost. From the dining room, invite a whiskey lover there for it; whether one may be sent to a table is a question for the manager.
Say sherry-finished, never sherry-aged: the bourbon ages in new oak first, then rests in the sherry casks.
Name nobody from the founding family; say the founder, a former psychologist, and his wife.
If a guest asks, Pernod Ricard has held a majority of Rabbit Hole since 2019. Do not say who runs it today.
The house page does not say how the Birdcage is smoked: describe the aroma, and let the bar explain the method.
producer.sayIt: Dareringer is a Louisville bourbon finished in Pedro Ximénez sherry casks, rich with dried fruit under the Birdcage's smoke.
askKitchen: How is the Birdcage smoked, and with what wood?
May a Birdcage be sent from the Roost to a dining room table?

producer.who: Tullamore D.E.W., William Grant & Sons
producer.where: Tullamore, County Offaly, Ireland
producer.history:
Tullamore D.E.W. traces its start to 1829, when Michael Molloy founded a distillery at Tullamore in County Offaly, a site most likely chosen for the Grand Canal beside it. After Molloy's death in 1857 it passed in time to his nephew, Bernard Daly.

The letters belong to Daniel E. Williams, who lived from 1848 to 1921; most sources give his middle name as Edmund. By the brand's account he started at the distillery as a stable boy at 15, and he rose to run it as general manager and later came to own it. By one account he added his initials to the whiskey's name in 1887, and they spell dew as well.

The old distillery closed in the 1950s and the brand name was sold in 1965; for decades the whiskey was made at Midleton. In 2010 the Scottish firm William Grant & Sons bought Tullamore D.E.W., and on 17 September 2014 it opened a new distillery at Clonminch, just outside the town, the first new Irish distillery on a greenfield site in over a century.

The whiskey is triple distilled and blended from the three Irish styles: pot still, malt and grain. The result is light and smooth, which suits hot coffee and cream.
facts: Founded in 1829 at Tullamore, County Offaly, by Michael Molloy, beside the Grand Canal.
D.E.W. are the initials of Daniel E. Williams, 1848 to 1921, general manager and later owner; by the brand's account he started as a stable boy.
By one account Williams added his initials to the brand name in 1887.
The original distillery closed in the 1950s and the brand name was sold in 1965.
William Grant & Sons bought the brand in 2010 and opened a new distillery at Clonminch on 17 September 2014.
Triple distilled and blended from pot still, malt and grain whiskey.
The Buena Vista Cafe in San Francisco, where Irish coffee was recreated in 1952, has poured Tullamore D.E.W. since 2006.
notes: The menu prints Tullamore Dew; the bottle writes D.E.W. When a guest asks, the letters are the initials of Daniel E. Williams, who by the brand's account rose from stable boy to owner.
Sources spell his middle name Edmund, Edmond or Edward; Daniel E. Williams is the careful form to say aloud.
Do not say it has been made in Tullamore without a break since 1829: the old distillery closed in the 1950s and the new one opened in 2014.
It is owned by William Grant & Sons, the Scottish firm; name nobody from the company.
A good link to tell: the Buena Vista in San Francisco, which made Irish coffee famous in America, has poured Tullamore since 2006.
producer.sayIt: Tullamore D.E.W. is a triple distilled Irish whiskey from County Offaly; the letters are the initials of Daniel E. Williams.
askKitchen: Which Tullamore D.E.W. bottling goes into Brennan's Irish Coffee?

producer.who: Jade Liqueurs, distilled at Combier
producer.where: Saumur, Loire Valley, France
producer.history:
Jade Nouvelle-Orléans is the work of Jade Liqueurs, a company founded in 2000 by a New Orleans-born scientist and absinthe historian. He researched surviving pre-ban absinthes and the old methods of making them, aiming to recreate the spirit as it was before the bans of the early twentieth century, without the myths that had grown up around it. Nouvelle-Orléans was the first Jade absinthe; a specialist retailer dates it to 2004 and says the founder has personally produced every batch since.

It is made at the Combier distillery in Saumur, in the Loire Valley, chosen partly for its historic equipment: copper bain-marie alembics built in the 1870s and acquired from one of the original absinthe distilleries of Pontarlier, France. Wormwood and other plants are macerated in wine alcohol and distilled, and a second infusion of plants in the distillate gives the pale green colour. It is bottled at 68 percent.

The name is a tribute to the founder's home city and its nineteenth-century absinthe culture. Its sellers describe the style as rooted in the absinthes that made the Sazerac and the Absinthe Frappé famous: fresh, with a peppery spice.

At Brennan's it is printed only on the Origin Story, the top of the Sazerac ladder, beside Dudognon Cognac and barrel-aged Peychaud's.
facts: Jade Liqueurs was founded in 2000 by a New Orleans-born scientist; Nouvelle-Orléans was its first absinthe, dated by a specialist retailer to 2004.
Distilled at the Combier distillery in Saumur, in France's Loire Valley, never in New Orleans.
Made in copper bain-marie alembics built in the 1870s, acquired from one of the original absinthe distilleries in Pontarlier.
Wormwood and other plants are macerated in wine alcohol and distilled; a second infusion of plants gives the pale green colour.
Bottled at 68 percent alcohol.
Reviewers describe it as reverse-engineered from the botanicals and flavour profiles of the pre-ban absinthes of the early 1900s.
Its sellers say its style is rooted in the absinthes that made the Sazerac and the Absinthe Frappé famous.
notes: Say it as a French absinthe made as a New Orleans tribute: distilled in Saumur, in the Loire Valley, not in the city.
Name no one behind it: say the founder, a New Orleans-born scientist who researched the absinthes made before the ban.
Guests ask whether absinthe makes you see things. The honest answer: wormwood does not cause hallucinations, and absinthe has been sold legally in the United States again since 2007.
At 68 percent it is strong, but it perfumes the Origin Story; describe the aroma, floral wormwood and fennel, not the strength.
Whether the bar rinses the glass with it, as the Classic is rinsed with Herbsaint, is a lineup question; do not describe the build until it is confirmed.
producer.sayIt: Jade Nouvelle-Orléans is a French absinthe, distilled in Saumur as a tribute to New Orleans' nineteenth-century absinthe culture.
askKitchen: Is the Origin Story's glass rinsed with the Jade, as the Classic is with Herbsaint, or is the Jade added another way?

producer.who: St. George Spirits
producer.where: Alameda, California
producer.history:
St. George Spirits was founded in 1982 as an eau de vie distillery, making clear fruit brandies. Its founder was master distiller for 28 years before handing the role to his successor in 2010. In 2004 the company moved into a 65,000-square-foot aircraft hangar on the former Alameda Naval Air Station, where it still distils.

When absinthe returned to American shelves in 2007, once federal regulators accepted that a properly made one met the thujone limit, St. George had a recipe ready, developed over eleven years. The label office refused the label several times, objecting to the monkey on it and to the word Verte, before approving it in early December 2007. St. George Absinthe Verte went on sale on 21 December 2007, the first legal American-made absinthe in 95 years, and the first 1,800 bottles sold out in six hours.

It is built on brandy rather than the beet spirit of many absinthes. Wormwood, fennel and star anise are infused in the brandy and distilled; the distillate is then infused with mint, tarragon, Genovese basil, lemon balm, hyssop and stinging nettle, which give the green colour and a garden character. Star anise is itself a departure from the green anise of the classic European recipes. It is bottled at 60 percent.

At Brennan's it rinses the glass of Thompson's Dream, the first step up from the Classic Sazerac, in place of the Classic's Herbsaint.
facts: Founded in 1982 as an eau de vie distillery; the founder was master distiller for 28 years and handed the role on in 2010.
Since 2004 it has distilled in a 65,000-square-foot hangar on the former Alameda Naval Air Station.
St. George Absinthe Verte went on sale on 21 December 2007, the first legal American-made absinthe in 95 years.
The federal label office refused the label several times, objecting to its monkey and the word Verte, before approving it in December 2007.
The first 1,800 bottles sold out in six hours.
Wormwood, fennel and star anise are infused in brandy and distilled, then mint, tarragon, Genovese basil, lemon balm, hyssop and stinging nettle are infused.
Bottled at 60 percent alcohol, on a brandy base rather than beet spirit.
notes: Say American-made: Lucid, made in France, reached the American market first in 2007, so St. George is the first American-made absinthe after the ban, not the first absinthe.
In Thompson's Dream it takes the place of the Classic's Herbsaint rinse, so the drink smells greener and more herbal.
Name nobody at St. George: say the founder and the current master distiller.
Guests ask about hallucinations. The honest answer: wormwood does not cause them, and the ban-era stories are legend.
The monkey on the label is a good table detail: the federal label office objected to it before approving the bottle in 2007.
producer.sayIt: St. George Absinthe Verte, from Alameda, California, was the first American-made absinthe sold after the ban ended in 2007.

producer.who: The Bitter Truth
producer.where: Munich, Germany
producer.history:
The Bitter Truth was founded in Munich in 2006 by two working bartenders. Their first releases came out in August 2006, an Orange Bitters and an Old Time Aromatic Bitters, and the company grew into an award-winning range that includes recreations of historical styles, such as Jerry Thomas' Own Decanter Bitters, a blend of citrus, dried fruit, cloves, angostura bark and cinnamon.

Creole Bitters were new by 2010, when a review called them the newest in the range. They are made in the New Orleans style: bright red, led by anise and caraway, with fennel, cinnamon and a little pepper behind and a floral finish. They are sold at 39 percent alcohol.

The name says what they are and what they are not. Peychaud's, the red bitters of the Classic Sazerac, is a Sazerac Company brand; The Bitter Truth sells its New Orleans-style bitters as Creole Bitters. Retailers sell The Bitter Truth's as a natural substitute in a Sazerac, and one reviewer found them very similar to Peychaud's and arguably more aromatic.

At Brennan's they are printed only in Thompson's Dream, with Willett 4-year rye and the St. George absinthe rinse, where they take the place of the Classic's Peychaud's.
facts: Founded in Munich in 2006 by two bartenders.
Its first releases, in August 2006, were Orange Bitters and Old Time Aromatic Bitters.
Creole Bitters were the newest in the range in a 2010 review: New Orleans-inspired, anise and caraway, a floral finish.
Retailers also list fennel, cinnamon, cayenne and pink peppercorn; the bitters are bright red and 39 percent alcohol.
Sold as a natural substitute for Peychaud's in a Sazerac; one reviewer found them arguably more aromatic.
Peychaud's is a Sazerac Company brand name; The Bitter Truth sells its New Orleans-style bitters as Creole Bitters.
The range includes Jerry Thomas' Own Decanter Bitters, with citrus, dried fruit, cloves, angostura bark and cinnamon.
notes: Never call them Peychaud's: they are a German maker's Creole-style bitters, chosen for Thompson's Dream. The Classic and the Origin Story use Peychaud's.
Name nobody: say the two Munich bartenders who founded the company.
Guests ask why German bitters go into a New Orleans drink. The honest answer: they are made in the New Orleans style and sold for exactly this drink, the Sazerac.
Describe the effect: still red and anise-led, a little spicier and more aromatic than Peychaud's.
producer.sayIt: Bitter Truth Creole Bitters come from Munich: a red, anise-led tribute to the New Orleans style, in place of Peychaud's.

producer.who: House of Angostura (Angostura Holdings)
producer.where: Trinidad; begun in Angostura, Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolívar
producer.history:
Angostura bitters began with Dr Johann Gottlieb Benjamin Siegert, a German surgeon born in 1796 who served in Simón Bolívar's army and settled around 1820 in the town of Angostura, Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolívar. The company says he had perfected his Amargo Aromatico by 1824, as a medicine for soldiers; another account, citing an 1876 court case, says he began selling it that year and set up a distillery in 1830. The bitters took the town's name.

Dr Siegert died in 1870, according to Difford's Guide, and in 1875 the family business, J.G.B. Siegert & Hijos, moved to Port of Spain, Trinidad, amid unrest in Venezuela. It has stayed on the island, adding rum from 1947 through Trinidad Distillers Limited. In 1982 it was listed on the Trinidad and Tobago Stock Exchange as Angostura Holdings. Reports in 2025 named its largest shareholder as Rumpro, part of the CL Financial group, which has been in liquidation since 2017, with the government's National Investment Fund Holding Company second. The bitters marked their bicentennial in 2024.

The recipe is a trade secret, and the label names only gentian among the botanicals. The oversized label has a legend of its own, most often told as a mix-up between the founder's sons over the bottle and the label that was never corrected. The label still shows a medal from the 1873 Vienna World's Fair.

At Brennan's it seasons the Birdcage, a smoked Old Fashioned, and the menu prints it with a demerara sugar cube in the Champagne Cocktail.
facts: Created by Dr Johann Gottlieb Benjamin Siegert, born in 1796, a German surgeon in Simón Bolívar's army, at Angostura, now Ciudad Bolívar.
The company dates his formula, Amargo Aromatico, to 1824, made as a medicine for soldiers.
In 1875 the business, J.G.B. Siegert & Hijos, moved to Port of Spain, Trinidad.
The label names one botanical, gentian; the full recipe is a trade secret.
Stories differ on why the label is oversized; the usual one is a mix-up between the founder's sons over bottle and label, never corrected.
The label shows a medal from the 1873 Vienna World's Fair.
Rum came later, from 1947, through Trinidad Distillers Limited.
Listed in 1982 as Angostura Holdings; reports in 2025 named Rumpro, of the CL Financial group, the largest shareholder and the government's National Investment Fund second.
The bitters marked their bicentennial in 2024.
notes: Never confuse it with Peychaud's: Angostura, dark and clove-spiced, is in the Birdcage and the Champagne Cocktail; Peychaud's, red and anise-led, is the Sazerac's.
Guests ask whether it holds angostura bark. The honest answer: the bitters are named for the town, not the bark; published histories say the bark is not in them, and the recipe is secret.
The Champagne Cocktail prints Angostura with a demerara sugar cube; in the classic build the bitters soak the cube, which keeps bubbles rising. Confirm the house build at lineup.
The bitters are named for a town in Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolívar, and are made in Trinidad today.
The Birdcage's measure and how it is smoked are the bar's to confirm; say Angostura seasons it, nothing more.
producer.sayIt: Angostura is the classic aromatic bitters, made in Trinidad to a secret recipe begun in Venezuela in 1824.
askKitchen: Is the Champagne Cocktail's sugar cube soaked with Angostura before the Champagne goes in, and with how many dashes?

producer.who: Maison Dudognon
producer.where: Lignières-Sonneville, Grande Champagne, Cognac
producer.founded: 1776, the family's vines at Lignières-Sonneville
producer.history:
The Dudognon family has grown vines at Lignières-Sonneville, in Grande Champagne, Cognac's first cru, since 1776; one history says the present estate was bought in 1852. The vineyard, Le Davore, lies on a chalky hillside tucked away from the village. Paulin Dudognon brought the house its first formal recognition, a gold medal in 1898.

For generations the family supplied its eaux-de-vie to the large Cognac houses. Raymond Dudognon, born in 1927 into a line of distillers going back to Paulin, took over in 1946 and was the first to sell cognac under the family name; one account dates that change to 1970. Raymond died in 2002, having chosen one of his three daughters to succeed him. She runs the house with her husband and their son, and every source found still names the family as its owners.

It is a bouilleur de cru, a grower that distils only its own grapes. The family distils over a wood fire on two copper alembic stills, roughly 100 barrels a year, air-dries the oak for its casks for five years, and adds nothing to the cognac but water. The cognacs are sold by age: a 10-year bottling, a 15-year Napoléon, the 20-year Vieille Réserve and a 60-year cognac named for Paulin.

At Brennan's the Origin Story prints Dudognon Cognac without naming the bottling, so which one the bar pours is a lineup question.
facts: The family has grown vines at Lignières-Sonneville, in Grande Champagne, since 1776; one history says the present estate was bought in 1852.
Paulin Dudognon won a gold medal in 1898, the house's first formal recognition.
Raymond Dudognon, born in 1927, took over in 1946 and first sold cognac under the family name; he died in 2002.
A bouilleur de cru: it distils only its own grapes, over a wood fire on two copper alembic stills, roughly 100 barrels a year.
Water is the only thing added to the cognac.
Oak for its casks is air-dried for five years.
Sold by age: a 10-year, a 15-year Napoléon, the 20-year Vieille Réserve and a 60-year named for Paulin.
notes: Grande Champagne is Cognac's first cru, chalky country; it has nothing to do with the sparkling wine region.
The house is family run; name no living member. Say the family, or Raymond Dudognon's daughter and her family.
Which Dudognon goes into the Origin Story is not printed; never name an age until the bar confirms it.
Guests ask why cognac in a Sazerac. The New Orleans story is that the first Sazeracs were made on cognac and rye took over after phylloxera, so the Origin Story returns to the start.
Describe it as grower cognac: one family's own grapes, distilled and aged on the estate, nothing added but water.
producer.sayIt: Dudognon is a family estate in Grande Champagne, growing its own grapes since 1776 and adding nothing to its cognac but water.
askKitchen: Which Dudognon bottling goes into the Origin Story: the 10-year, the Napoléon, the Vieille Réserve or another?

producer.who: Daron Calvados, Maison Ferrand
producer.where: Pays d'Auge, Normandy, France
producer.history:
Daron is a Calvados Pays d'Auge from Maison Ferrand, a house from Cognac. Difford's Guide lists Ferrand as both producer and owner, and retailers describe the calvados as made under Ferrand's direction, bringing a Cognac house's distilling experience to the orchards of Normandy's Pays d'Auge. It is not a Christian Drouin calvados: Drouin is a separate family house in the same appellation. No public source found here names the Normandy distillery or the year the brand began.

Calvados is apple brandy from Normandy: cider, sometimes with some pear, distilled and aged in oak. Pays d'Auge is its most exacting appellation, which requires double distillation in copper pot stills. Daron's cider comes from Normandy cider apples, Bisquets, Bedan, Petit Joly and St Martin, with a little pear, distilled slowly in copper pot stills and aged in Limousin oak.

Fine is the entry-level bottling of the Daron range. Difford's gives it no age statement but says it is aged an average of five years in small oak casks, in warehouses with traditional earth floors. Tasting notes speak of baked apple, honey and warm spice, ginger and clove, with a fairly dry finish.

At Brennan's it is the base of To Each His Own, with Lillet Blanc and quince liqueur, a drink named for the 1946 song.
facts: Difford's Guide lists Maison Ferrand, a Cognac house, as Daron's producer and owner.
A Calvados Pays d'Auge: the appellation requires double distillation in copper pot stills.
The cider comes from Bisquets, Bedan, Petit Joly and St Martin apples, with a little pear.
Daron Fine is aged an average of five years in small oak casks, in warehouses with earth floors.
Difford's lists no age statement for the Fine, and notes Limousin oak.
Fine is the entry-level calvados of the Daron range.
Tasting notes: baked apple, honey, ginger and clove, with a fairly dry finish.
notes: Daron belongs to Maison Ferrand, not to Christian Drouin, which is a separate family calvados house in the Pays d'Auge.
Fine means the youngest grade, not a lesser one: fresh apple first, oak second, which suits a stirred aperitif drink.
Do not quote an age: Difford's gives no age statement for the Fine, though retailers say about five years.
If a guest likes it, the next brandy drink is the Origin Story, our Sazerac on Cognac.
Calvados is Normandy apple brandy, from Daron, dah-ROHN.
producer.sayIt: Daron Fine is Calvados from Normandy's Pays d'Auge, apple brandy double distilled in copper pot stills, from the Cognac house Maison Ferrand.

producer.who: Chartreuse, made by the Carthusian monks
producer.where: Aiguenoire distillery, near Voiron, in the French Alps
producer.founded: Manuscript 1605; Elixir 1737; Green Chartreuse 1764 by most accounts
producer.history:
Chartreuse is made by the Carthusians, the order of the Grande Chartreuse monastery in the French Alps. By the order's story, in 1605 the Maréchal d'Estrées, a marshal of Henry IV's artillery, gave the monks a manuscript recipe for an elixir of 130 plants. It was so hard to decipher that only by 1737 had the monastery's apothecary, Brother Jérôme Maubec, worked out a practical recipe for the Elixir. Most accounts date Green Chartreuse, a milder liqueur adapted from it, to 1764, though sources differ on who finished the work. It is bottled at 55 percent.

The monks have been driven out more than once. Expelled from France in 1903, they made their liqueur in Tarragona, in Spain, while the French state sold the Chartreuse name to a commercial company; in 1929 they were allowed to use the name again, and Tarragona kept distilling until 1989. Production later settled in Voiron and, since 2018, at a new distillery at Aiguenoire.

Only the monks know the full recipe. The dried plants are sorted, crushed and mixed at the monastery, then sent to the distillery. In 2021 the monks decided not to raise output, and a letter of January 2023 explained why: their life of solitude and prayer comes first. Output was held at about 1.6 million bottles a year, and every market went on allocation.

At Brennan's it is the herbal heart of Five Minutes More.
facts: Made by the Carthusian monks of the Grande Chartreuse to a secret recipe of 130 plants.
The order traces the recipe to a manuscript the Maréchal d'Estrées gave it in 1605.
By 1737 the monastery's apothecary, Brother Jérôme Maubec, had worked out a practical recipe for the Elixir.
Most accounts date Green Chartreuse to 1764; it is bottled at 55 percent alcohol.
The dried plants are sorted, crushed and mixed at the monastery, then sent to the distillery.
