Expelled from France in 1903, the monks distilled in Tarragona, Spain, and could use the Chartreuse name again from 1929.
Distilled at Aiguenoire since 2018; the Caves de la Chartreuse in Voiron opened as a visitors' centre.
A January 2023 letter confirmed the monks would not raise output, held at about 1.6 million bottles a year, to protect their monastic life.
Every market went on allocation; the United States was limited to 90 percent of its 2021 volume.
notes: Say it is made by monks, and mean it: the Carthusians still hold the recipe. Name no living monk; say the monks.
Guests ask why it is hard to find. The honest answer: the monks chose not to raise production, so it would not crowd out their life of prayer.
The 1605 manuscript is the order's own story. Tell it as their history: the Elixir by 1737, the Green by most accounts in 1764.
At 55 percent it is strong and a little carries a drink; how much goes into Five Minutes More is the bar's to say.
If asked about the green, say the colour is natural, from the plants; never say it is dyed.
Yellow Chartreuse is the gentler, sweeter sister; the menu prints the Green.
producer.sayIt: Green Chartreuse is made by Carthusian monks in the French Alps from 130 plants, to a recipe only they know.
askKitchen: If the Green Chartreuse allocation runs short, does Five Minutes More come off the list or change?

producer.who: Zamora Company, makers of Licor 43
producer.where: Cartagena, Spain
producer.history:
Licor 43, Cuarenta y Tres in Spanish, comes from Cartagena, in Spain. The brand tells a story of Carthago Nova, the ancient city there, where in 209 BC the Romans are said to have found a golden liqueur, liqvor mirabilis. That is the brand's legend, not history, but it is the idea the recipe is said to build on.

Commercial production began in 1946 in a small distillery in Cartagena, with the liqueur bottled by hand. The recipe is credited to three siblings of the founding family and a brother-in-law, and it is still a closely guarded secret: by one account only the family and the factory's director know it in full. The name is the number of ingredients, 43, and only a handful have been made public: vanilla, orange peel, lemon, coriander and tea.

It is often called the most popular liqueur in Spain. The brand belongs to Zamora Company, and its factory, just outside Cartagena, makes it from start to finish and houses a museum open for tours. It is bottled at 31 percent.

At Brennan's it rounds off Five Minutes More, with Green Chartreuse, Cathead mandarin vodka and lemon. The founding year is also the year Brennan's opened: a happy coincidence, never a connection.
facts: Commercial production began in Cartagena, Spain, in 1946, with the liqueur bottled by hand.
Named for its 43 ingredients; the recipe is a closely guarded family secret.
Only a few ingredients are public: vanilla, orange peel, lemon, coriander and tea.
The brand's legend ties it to liqvor mirabilis, a golden liqueur Romans are said to have found in Carthago Nova in 209 BC.
Often called the most popular liqueur in Spain.
Owned by Zamora Company; made from start to finish at its factory just outside Cartagena, which houses a museum.
Bottled at 31 percent alcohol.
notes: Say it as vanilla and citrus from Spain; the 43 is the count of ingredients, not the strength.
Guests ask what the 43 are. The honest answer: a secret; the brand has revealed only vanilla, orange, lemon, coriander and tea.
The Roman story is the brand's legend; tell it as legend, never as history.
1946 is the year Brennan's opened and the year of the songs on the list: a coincidence, never a link between the houses.
Name no one in the family; say the founding family.
producer.sayIt: Licor 43 is a golden Spanish liqueur from Cartagena, made since 1946 from 43 ingredients, led by vanilla and citrus.

producer.who: Lillet, a Pernod Ricard house
producer.where: Podensac, south of Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Lillet was founded in 1872 in Podensac, south of Bordeaux, by the brothers Paul and Raymond Lillet, wine and spirits merchants who took up distilling. Their early trade was mainly in fruit liqueurs. Their first wine aperitif came in 1887: Kina Lillet, its name joining the family's to quinquina, the cinchona bark that gives quinine.

The recipe is still about 85 percent wine and 15 percent fruit liqueurs and cinchona. For the Blanc the wine is Semillon, with some Sauvignon Blanc, and the liqueurs are made by steeping the peels of sweet oranges, from Morocco or Spain, and bitter oranges, from Haiti or Peru, in alcohol for several weeks. The blend is matured in oak casks in the Podensac cellars and bottled at 17 percent.

In 1986 Lillet Blanc replaced Kina Lillet: sweeter and less bitter. That is why a Vesper made today does not taste as it did when it was written. The family sold the business in 1985, and in 2008 it passed to a subsidiary of Pernod Ricard, which owns it today.

At Brennan's it appears twice: topped with sparkling wine and lemon in the Riviera, and beside Daron Calvados and quince liqueur in To Each His Own.
facts: Founded in 1872 in Podensac, south of Bordeaux, by the brothers Paul and Raymond Lillet.
Kina Lillet, the first wine aperitif, came in 1887; Kina is from quinquina, the cinchona bark.
About 85 percent wine and 15 percent fruit liqueurs and cinchona.
The Blanc's wine is Semillon, with some Sauvignon Blanc.
The liqueurs steep sweet and bitter orange peels in alcohol for several weeks.
Matured in oak casks in the Podensac cellars; bottled at 17 percent.
Lillet Blanc replaced the more bitter Kina Lillet in 1986.
Owned by a Pernod Ricard subsidiary since 2008.
notes: Say it as a French wine aperitif from near Bordeaux: orange, honey and blossom, served cold.
The Bubbles menu spells it Lilet in the Riviera; the bottle is Lillet, said lee-LAY.
Guests who know the Vesper may ask if ours is the original. The honest answer: today's Lillet Blanc is lighter and less bitter than the Kina Lillet it was written for.
Who owns it: Pernod Ricard, since 2008. Name no owner before that; say the founding family sold in 1985.
producer.sayIt: Lillet Blanc is a French aperitif from Podensac, near Bordeaux: Semillon wine with orange-peel liqueurs, light and gently bitter.

producer.who: L.N. Mattei, makers of Cap Corse Mattei
producer.where: Bastia, Corsica
producer.history:
Louis-Napoléon Mattei opened his first shop in Bastia, on Corsica, in 1872, selling cigars, coffee, wine and liqueurs. In 1874 he began distilling cédrat, the thick-skinned citron of Cap Corse, the island's northern peninsula, and in 1875 he made a medicinal wine with quinquina, the cinchona bark that gives quinine. Accounts differ on how he came to the bark: his importer says he found it on a voyage to the Caribbean; another source says he meant it against malaria.

The Blanc is a mistelle: Muscat and Vermentinu grape must kept from fermenting with neutral alcohol, so its sweetness is the grape's own. It is flavoured with cinchona, cédrat and other plants, fruits and spices, and bottled at 17 percent. The bark brings spice and gentle bitterness to the middle and finish; the cédrat brings citrus perfume and a silky texture.

Its American importer has long called the house family owned, with macerations, ageing and bottling done in house, by one report in the Borgo industrial zone. Monocle reports, though, that a Corsican drinks group, Groupe Boisson Corse, has since bought the house, revived the founder's recipe and taken output from about 80,000 bottles to about 400,000. On Cap Corse stands the Moulin Mattei, a windmill a later head of the house turned into an advertisement for the aperitif; the Conservatoire du Littoral bought it in 2004 and restored its 1930s look.

At Brennan's it plays the vermouth's part in the Spoonbill, with Hendrick's gin and chive oil.
facts: Louis-Napoléon Mattei opened his first shop in Bastia in 1872, selling cigars, coffee, wine and liqueurs.
In 1875 he made a medicinal wine with quinquina, cinchona bark, the source of quinine.
Cap Corse is Corsica's northern peninsula; cédrat, the Corsican citron, is a signature ingredient.
The Blanc is a mistelle of Muscat and Vermentinu grape must with neutral alcohol, with no added sugar.
Flavoured with cinchona, cédrat and other plants, fruits and spices; bottled at 17 percent.
Monocle reports that Groupe Boisson Corse, a Corsican drinks group, bought the house and relaunched it, reviving the founder's recipe.
The Moulin Mattei windmill on Cap Corse, once the brand's advertisement, was bought by the Conservatoire du Littoral in 2004.
Imported to the United States by Haus Alpenz; there is a Rouge as well as the Blanc.
notes: Say quinquina, kan-kee-NAH: a wine aperitif with cinchona bark. Our page calls it vermouth; strictly it is vermouth's cousin.
Guests ask if it has quinine. The honest answer: it is flavoured with cinchona bark, the source of quinine, for a gentle bitterness; the amount is not published.
Do not call it a Corsican wine: it is grape must held from fermenting with spirit, a mistelle.
Do not call it family owned: the importer's pages say so, but Monocle reports a sale to a Corsican drinks group.
The founder, Louis-Napoléon Mattei, may be named; name no one at the house today.
The page prints the Blanc; Mattei also makes a Rouge, so check the bottle before describing it.
producer.sayIt: Cap Corse Mattei is a Corsican quinquina: Muscat and Vermentinu with cinchona bark and Corsican citron, gently bitter, from a Bastia house founded in 1872.
askKitchen: Is the Spoonbill stirred like a martini, and in what proportion of gin to Cap Corse?

producer.who: Amarula, a Heineken Beverages brand
producer.where: Phalaborwa and Stellenbosch, South Africa
producer.founded: Spirit 1983; cream liqueur 1989
producer.history:
Amarula is made from the fruit of the marula tree, which grows wild in southern Africa. The first product was a clear marula spirit, bottled in 1983. Cream was added to the recipe and the cream liqueur reached shelves in 1989, first marketed that September by the Southern Liqueur Company, part of Distell. In 2023 Heineken Beverages acquired Distell, and with it the brand.

The harvest runs from about mid-January to March around Phalaborwa. The ripe fruit falls and is gathered by women from the local rural communities, then taken to Amarula's plant in Phalaborwa, where the flesh is separated from the hard stones. The pulp is kept cool so it cannot ferment on its own and goes to the cellars in Stellenbosch, where it is fermented much like wine. It is distilled twice, first in column stills, then in copper pot stills, aged two years in small oak barrels and blended with fresh cream. It is bottled at 17 percent.

Elephants love marula fruit, which is why one is on the label. The story that elephants get drunk on fallen fruit was challenged by a 2006 study, and scientists still argue about it.

At Brennan's it is the South Africa in Floating in South Africa, with housemade vanilla bean ice cream and Abita root beer.
facts: Made from the fruit of the wild marula tree of southern Africa.
A clear marula spirit came first, in 1983; the cream liqueur reached shelves in 1989.
Fallen fruit is gathered by women of local rural communities near Phalaborwa and destoned at the plant there.
The pulp is fermented like wine in Stellenbosch, then distilled twice, in column and then copper pot stills.
Aged two years in small oak barrels, then blended with fresh cream; 17 percent alcohol.
First marketed in 1989 by the Southern Liqueur Company, part of Distell; Heineken Beverages acquired Distell in 2023.
The elephant on the label is there because elephants love marula fruit.
The brand says it launched the Amarula Trust to keep meeting elephants beneath the marula trees.
A 2006 study argued elephants do not get drunk on marula; later work has reopened the question.
notes: Say it as a South African cream liqueur made from a fruit, the marula, not from whiskey.
Guests ask if the elephants get drunk. The honest answer: it is a famous story and scientists still argue; never tell it as fact.
Cream and milk questions on Floating in South Africa go to the service note and lineup; the menu prints a cream liqueur and ice cream.
Who owns it: Heineken Beverages, since 2023; before that it was Distell's brand.
producer.sayIt: Amarula is a South African cream liqueur made from the wild marula fruit, distilled, aged two years in oak and blended with cream.
askKitchen: Is Floating in South Africa built as a float, the Amarula over the ice cream before the root beer, or blended?

producer.who: Frangelico, a Campari Group brand
producer.where: Canale, Piedmont, Italy
producer.history:
Frangelico is a hazelnut liqueur from Piedmont, launched in 1978 by the Barbero family company, founded in 1891, and made in Canale, in the heart of the region's hazelnut country. Its name and look come from a legend: a hermit monk called Fra Angelico, said to have lived in the Piedmont hills. The older brand story placed him in the seventeenth century and never claimed he made liqueur, so it is told as legend. The bottle is shaped like a friar's habit, with a knotted cord that was tied by hand until 2003.

It is made from Tonda Gentile hazelnuts from the Langhe, a variety with protected status; the brand buys about 38 tons a year. The nuts are shelled, toasted and crushed, infused in alcohol and water, and distilled. The hazelnut distillate is blended with cocoa, vanilla and roasted coffee, rested, and bottled at 20 percent.

In 2010 William Grant & Sons bought Frangelico in a package with Tullamore Dew, then sold it later that year, with Carolans and Irish Mist, to Gruppo Campari, already the liqueur's global source. At the time the United States was its largest market, about half of sales.

At Brennan's it is in two coffee cocktails: the Espresso Martini, with Kahlua, and Ralph’s Coffee, with Nocello.
facts: An Italian hazelnut liqueur made in Canale, Piedmont, launched in 1978.
Named for a legendary hermit monk, Fra Angelico, said to have lived in the Piedmont hills.
The bottle is a friar's habit with a knotted cord, tied by hand until 2003.
Made with Tonda Gentile hazelnuts from the Langhe, about 38 tons a year.
Toasted, crushed hazelnuts are infused in alcohol and water and distilled, then blended with cocoa, vanilla and coffee.
Bottled at 20 percent alcohol.
Gruppo Campari bought it from William Grant & Sons in 2010.
In 2010 the United States was its largest market, about half of sales.
notes: Say it as toasted hazelnut and vanilla from Piedmont.
Tell Fra Angelico as legend; no source shows a monk ever made it.
Nut questions on the Espresso Martini and Ralph’s Coffee go to the service note and lineup: both carry Frangelico, and Ralph’s Coffee also carries Nocello.
Who owns it: the Campari Group, since 2010.
producer.sayIt: Frangelico is a toasted hazelnut liqueur from Piedmont, made with Tonda Gentile hazelnuts, in a bottle shaped like a friar's habit.

producer.who: Kahlúa, a Pernod Ricard brand
producer.where: Veracruz, Mexico
producer.history:
Kahlúa is a coffee liqueur first produced in Veracruz, Mexico, in 1936; one account credits the Pedro Domecq company with beginning its production. The name is usually explained as Veracruz Nahuatl for House of the Acolhua people; the Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails derives it instead from kahwa, the Arabic word for coffee. Neither is settled.

It was almost unknown until the early 1960s, when an American importer took the United States rights and promoted it hard, and sales took off. The Domecq business became part of Allied Domecq in 1994, and in 2005 Pernod Ricard acquired the brand, which it still owns.

It is made by blending roasted, ground arabica coffee with water and sugar cane spirit, adding vanilla and caramel, and resting the blend before bottling. The coffee and the cane are grown in Veracruz; sources disagree on where the blending is done, and Difford's Guide and the Oxford Companion place it in Mexico City. Long bottled at 26.5 percent, it was cut to 20 percent in 2003 or 2004, by differing accounts, and to 16 percent in some markets in 2021.

At Brennan's it is in the Espresso Martini, with chicory, vodka and Frangelico; the menu spells it Kahlua.
facts: First produced in Veracruz, Mexico, in 1936.
Roasted, ground arabica coffee is blended with water and sugar cane spirit, vanilla and caramel, then rested before bottling.
The coffee and the sugar cane are grown in the state of Veracruz.
Part of Allied Domecq from 1994; owned by Pernod Ricard since 2005.
The name is usually read as Nahuatl for House of the Acolhua people; another account derives it from kahwa, Arabic for coffee.
Once 26.5 percent, cut to 20 percent in 2003 or 2004, and to 16 percent in some markets in 2021.
Sales took off in the 1960s after an American importer took the United States rights.
The producer confirms Kahlúa contains caffeine; the finished drink total cannot be calculated without its measures and other coffee ingredients.
notes: Say it as Mexico's coffee liqueur, sweet and roasty with vanilla. The menu spells it Kahlua, without the accent.
The menu prints chicory, but its Kahlua contains caffeine. The total depends on the measures and any additional coffee; do not call the printed cocktail caffeine free.
Name no importer or founder; say an American importer made it famous in the 1960s.
Who owns it: Pernod Ricard, since 2005.
producer.sayIt: Kahlúa is Mexico's coffee liqueur, made since 1936 from Veracruz arabica, sugar cane spirit, vanilla and caramel.

producer.who: Toschi Vignola, makers of Nocello
producer.where: Savignano sul Panaro, near Modena, Emilia-Romagna, Italy
producer.founded: 1945 (the company)
producer.history:
Nocello is made by Toschi, a family company founded in 1945 in Vignola, near Modena, by two brothers. They began by preserving cherries in spirit, and the company still specialises in fruit in spirit, liqueurs and products for gelato. Its working headquarters are now at Savignano sul Panaro, close by.

Nocello is made from walnuts and hazelnuts. It is amber, sweet and rounded, with a balanced walnut flavour and tones of vanilla, and bottled at 24 percent; in 2004 it won a gold medal at the IWSC. In the United States its label reads Imitation Liqueur. Toschi has not published its method, so a server describes the taste, not a process.

It belongs to the walnut liqueur tradition of Emilia-Romagna, whose best-known member is nocino, the dark liqueur made by steeping green walnuts in alcohol; by custom the walnuts are picked around St John's Day, 24 June. Toschi makes a Nocino too. Nocello is the lighter, sweeter cousin.

At Brennan's it goes into Ralph’s Coffee, with dark roast coffee and chicory, Frangelico and whipped cream: a roasty, nutty after-dinner coffee.
facts: Made by Toschi, founded in 1945 in Vignola, near Modena, by two brothers.
Toschi began by preserving cherries in spirit; it makes fruit in spirit, liqueurs and gelato products.
Made at Savignano sul Panaro, the company's operational headquarters.
A walnut and hazelnut liqueur, sweet and rounded with vanilla tones, at 24 percent.
Won a gold medal at the IWSC in 2004.
Labelled Imitation Liqueur in the United States.
Its traditional cousin, nocino, steeps green walnuts picked by custom around St John's Day, 24 June.
notes: Say it as a sweet Italian walnut liqueur from near Modena.
Nut questions on Ralph’s Coffee go to the service note and lineup: it carries Nocello and Frangelico.
Do not call it nocino: nocino is the dark green-walnut liqueur; Nocello is Toschi's sweeter walnut and hazelnut liqueur.
If a guest reads Imitation Liqueur on the bottle, say that is the American label's wording; the bar can show the bottle.
The menu does not say who Ralph’s Coffee is named for; tell no story about the name.
producer.sayIt: Nocello is a sweet Italian walnut and hazelnut liqueur from Toschi, near Modena, amber, with soft vanilla tones.

producer.who: Pedro Ximénez, the sweet sherry style (bodega not printed)
producer.where: Jerez, Spain, with most PX grapes grown in Montilla-Moriles
producer.history:
Pedro Ximénez, PX for short, is both a white grape and the sweetest, darkest style of sherry. The grapes are left on the vine until very ripe, picked by hand and laid on straw mats to dry in the sun, a practice called asoleo. They shrink towards raisins, losing water and concentrating sugar, so the must is so dense that fermentation often stalls. The wine is fortified and aged until it is almost black and syrupy, tasting of raisin, fig and molasses.

Most PX grapes grow not in Jerez but in Montilla-Moriles. Jerez bodegas often buy PX must or wine from there and age and blend it in their own cellars, where it must rest at least two years before it may be called sherry. The Jerez rules allow PX only for sweet wines, and it also sweetens other sherries into cream styles.

Sherry itself, its towns, its solera and its denomination of 1933, has its own profile with the aged sherry of the Turtle Soup, so this one keeps to PX.

At Brennan's it gives Banane au Chocolat its dried fruit depth, under crème de banane and crème de cacao. The menu names no bodega. Casks that once held PX also finish the Rabbit Hole bourbon in the Birdcage.
facts: Pedro Ximénez is a white grape and the sweetest, darkest style of sherry.
Very ripe grapes are dried in the sun on straw mats, called asoleo, concentrating their sugar.
Most PX is grown in Montilla-Moriles; Jerez bodegas often buy the must or wine and age it.
To be called sherry, it must rest at least two years in the Jerez zone.
Jerez rules allow PX grapes only for sweet wines; PX also sweetens cream sherries.
Fortified and aged until almost black and syrupy, it tastes of raisin, fig and molasses.
notes: Say PX, the dark, raisiny sherry from sun-dried grapes.
The menu names no bodega; name none until the bar does.
Guests may have heard the grape came to Spain from Germany with a soldier. The honest answer: it is an old story, and no source found here supports it.
A link across the list: the Rabbit Hole Dareringer in the Birdcage is finished in Pedro Ximénez sherry casks.
producer.sayIt: Pedro Ximénez is Spain's sweetest sherry, made from sun-dried grapes: dark, syrupy, tasting of raisin and fig.
askKitchen: Which Pedro Ximénez sherry, from which bodega, goes into Banane au Chocolat?

producer.who: Pimento dram, the allspice liqueur of Jamaica
producer.where: Jamaica
producer.founded: An article of commerce since the 1850s
producer.history:
Allspice dram, called pimento dram in Jamaica, is rum in which allspice berries have been steeped, then sweetened. Allspice is the dried berry of the pimento tree; the Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails says its flavour recalls cloves, cinnamon and nutmeg, and records the dram as an article of commerce since the 1850s. Bottles were shown at the International Exhibition of 1862. In Jamaica the berry kept its Spanish name, pimiento, now pimento; the English called it allspice. It is no relation of the pimento pepper.

The National Museum Jamaica records that the liqueur became popular in Europe and North America in the early 1900s, when J. Wray & Nephew bottled and sold it. It appeared in drinks such as the Lion's Tail and was taken up by the tiki bars. Imports to the United States later stopped, and bartenders made their own.

The revival came in 2008 with St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram, made in Austria from Jamaican allspice berries, raw sugar and pot-stilled Jamaican rum for an American importer.

At Brennan's it gives For Sentimental Reasons its warm baking spice, under pear purée and sparkling wine. The menu names no brand, so which dram the bar pours is a lineup question.
facts: Allspice dram is rum steeped with allspice berries and sweetened, a Jamaican liqueur.
Its flavour recalls cloves, cinnamon and nutmeg, says the Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails.
An article of commerce since the 1850s; shown at the International Exhibition of 1862.
J. Wray & Nephew bottled and sold it in the early 1900s, by the National Museum Jamaica's record.
In Jamaica the berry is called pimento, from the Spanish; it is no relation of the pimento pepper.
St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram, made in Austria with Jamaican berries, raw sugar and pot-stilled rum, debuted in 2008.
notes: Say it as Jamaica's spiced rum liqueur: clove, cinnamon and nutmeg in one berry.
The menu names no brand; describe the flavour and let the bar name the bottle.
It is sweet spice, not heat: never call it pepper or say the drink is hot.
A little carries the drink: For Sentimental Reasons is pear and bubbles first, with the spice underneath.
producer.sayIt: Allspice dram is Jamaica's pimento dram: rum steeped with allspice berries, tasting of clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once.
askKitchen: Which allspice dram goes into For Sentimental Reasons: St. Elizabeth, another brand, or a house infusion?

producer.who: Chopin, Podlaska Wytwórnia Wódek Polmos
producer.where: Krzesk, near Siedlce, east of Warsaw, Poland
producer.founded: Distillery 1896; brand 1992 or 1993
producer.history:
Chopin is a Polish vodka named for the composer Frédéric Chopin, a favoured son of Poland. It is made by Podlaska Wytwórnia Wódek Polmos of Siedlce, east of Warsaw, at a distillery near the hamlet of Krzesk that has made vodka since 1896. The brand says its still of that year is one of the oldest remaining stills in Poland.

The brand dates from the early 1990s: sources give 1992 or 1993. When its founder bought the distillery itself is less clear: one account says 1993, another 2003. Chopin reached North America in 1997. The company calls itself family owned and run, now in its second generation, and Poland’s last family owned vodka brand.

Chopin is a single-ingredient vodka. Each bottling is made from one raw material, potato, rye or wheat, and distilled four times. The brand grows some of its ingredients on its own farmland and buys the rest from family farms near the distillery, and its water comes from an artesian spring beneath the grounds. The potato vodka, the best known bottling, uses Stobrawa potatoes, which retailers say are grown in Podlasie.

Potato vodka is fuller and creamier in texture than most grain vodkas, with a faint earthiness. Which Chopin goes into the Flamingo is a question for the bar.
facts: Named for the composer Frédéric Chopin, a favoured son of Poland.
Made by Podlaska Wytwórnia Wódek Polmos of Siedlce, at a distillery near Krzesk that has made vodka since 1896.
A single-ingredient vodka: each bottling is made from potato, rye or wheat alone and distilled four times.
The brand dates from 1992 or 1993 by different sources; the distillery purchase is dated 1993 or 2003. Chopin reached North America in 1997.
The brand says its ingredients grow on its own land or on nearby family farms, and its water comes from an artesian spring beneath the grounds.
The potato vodka uses Stobrawa potatoes, grown in Podlasie by retailers’ accounts.
Family owned and run, in its second generation; the company calls itself Poland’s last family owned vodka brand.
The brand calls its 1896 still one of the oldest remaining stills in Poland.
notes: The menu prints Chopin Vodka without a bottling. Chopin makes potato, rye and wheat vodkas, so confirm with the bar before you say potato.
Guests ask whether potato vodka tastes of potato. The honest answer: hardly; it is fuller and creamier in texture than most grain vodkas, with a faint earthiness.
Say SHOH-pan, like the composer. If asked who owns it: the founding family, now in its second generation. Name nobody.
Do not quote how many potatoes go into a bottle (seven pounds or five kilos by different sources) or how far away the farms are (20 or 15 miles).
If a guest asks about gluten with a potato vodka, promise nothing from the label: take the question to the bar and the kitchen at lineup.
producer.sayIt: Chopin is a Polish single-ingredient vodka, distilled four times at a family-owned distillery that has made vodka since 1896.
askKitchen: Which Chopin goes into the Flamingo: the potato vodka, or the rye or wheat?

producer.who: Monkey 47, Black Forest Distillers
producer.where: Near Loßburg, in the Black Forest, Germany
producer.founded: 2008; launched about 2010
producer.history:
Monkey 47 tells its own story through a British officer. By the brand’s account, Montgomery Collins, known as Monty, a Royal Air Force officer posted to Berlin after the Second World War, sponsored a monkey named Max at the Berlin Zoo. He left the air force in 1951, settled in the northern Black Forest and opened a guesthouse, Zum Wilden Affen, the Wild Monkey, where his Schwarzwald Dry Gin was the house drink until the 1970s. No archive or independent account of him has been found, so it is told as the brand’s story.

The modern gin began in 2008, when the founder, from a German brandy family, left a job at Nokia to recreate the recipe in the Black Forest. After more than 120 trial distillations the gin came to market, usually dated 2010. In January 2016 Pernod Ricard Deutschland agreed to buy a majority stake, and in March 2020 Pernod Ricard bought the rest, with the founder staying on as an adviser. The distillery near Loßburg, built in 2015, centres on a custom still from a German coppersmith.

The name holds the numbers: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol. About a third of the botanicals are Black Forest plants, among them spruce, lingonberries, elderflower, blackthorn and bramble leaves, and the citrus peels go in fresh. They macerate in molasses-based neutral spirit and spring water before distillation in small stills; the gin then rests in large earthenware vessels for about three months, is cut slowly with water and is bottled without chill filtration.
facts: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol give the gin its name; about a third of the botanicals come from the Black Forest.
Black Forest botanicals include spruce, lingonberries, elderflower, blackthorn and bramble leaves; the citrus peels are used fresh.
Botanicals macerate in molasses-based neutral spirit and spring water, about 36 hours by one account, before distillation in small stills.
The gin rests in large earthenware vessels, 90 or 100 days by different accounts, before slow dilution; it is not chill filtered.
By the brand’s account, the RAF officer Montgomery Collins opened the Zum Wilden Affen guesthouse in the Black Forest after leaving the air force in 1951.
The founder began recreating the recipe in 2008, over more than 120 trial distillations; the launch is usually dated 2010.
Pernod Ricard Deutschland agreed a majority stake in January 2016, and Pernod Ricard bought the rest in March 2020; neither price was disclosed.
The distillery near Loßburg was built in 2015 around a custom still made by a German coppersmith.
notes: Tell the Montgomery Collins story as the brand’s story: no archive or independent account confirming the officer, the guesthouse or the recipe was found.
Guests ask about the 47: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol. It is a strong, aromatic gin, which is why it still reads under the Champagne in the Flamingo.
The menu prints Monkey 47 Schwarzwald Gin; the bottle says Schwarzwald Dry Gin. Schwarzwald is German for the Black Forest.
If asked who owns it: Pernod Ricard, the sole owner since 2020 after buying a majority in 2016. Name nobody; the founder is said as the founder.
Do not call it a British gin: it is German, made in the Black Forest.
producer.sayIt: Monkey 47 is a Black Forest gin: 47 botanicals at 47 percent, a third of them from the forest, rested in earthenware before bottling.

producer.who: Hendrick’s Gin, William Grant & Sons
producer.where: Girvan, Scotland
producer.founded: 1999; the company 1887
producer.history:
Hendrick’s is a Scottish gin made by William Grant & Sons, the family-owned company William Grant founded in 1887, the year his Glenfiddich distillery began production, and still run by his descendants. The gin is made at Girvan, where the company built its grain distillery in 1963 under a great-grandson of William Grant.

That same great-grandson bought two old stills at auction in 1966: a Bennett still of 1860 and a Carter-Head still built in 1948 by John Dore & Co. By the company’s account, in 1988 he set a company distiller the task of making one spirit from both. After years of trials Hendrick’s launched in 1999: the gins of the two stills are blended, then essences of rose and cucumber are added. Because the rose and cucumber go in after distillation, it cannot be labelled a London Dry gin.

Eleven botanicals stand behind the rose and cucumber, among them juniper, orris root, chamomile, cubeb, elderflower, yarrow, caraway and lemon and orange peel. The rose is described as Bulgarian; the cucumbers come from Holland or Belgium. The name, by most accounts, was chosen by a member of the Grant family after Hendrick, a gardener who took particular care of the family’s roses.

On 1 October 2018 the company opened the Hendrick’s Gin Palace in the grounds at Girvan, with new still houses that doubled capacity and glasshouses of exotic botanicals.
facts: Made by William Grant & Sons, the family-owned company William Grant founded in 1887 and his descendants still run.
Distilled at Girvan, Scotland, where the company built its grain distillery in 1963.
Two stills bought at auction in 1966: a Bennett still of 1860 and a Carter-Head still of 1948.
Launched in 1999: the two stills’ spirits are blended, then essences of rose and cucumber are added.
Because rose and cucumber go in after distillation, Hendrick’s cannot be labelled a London Dry gin.
Eleven botanicals besides rose and cucumber, including juniper, orris root, chamomile, cubeb, elderflower, yarrow and caraway.
The rose is described as Bulgarian; the cucumbers come from Holland or Belgium, by one account.
The Hendrick’s Gin Palace opened at Girvan on 1 October 2018, doubling capacity, with glasshouses of botanicals.
Named, by most accounts, after Hendrick, a gardener who tended a Grant family rose garden.
notes: Say Hendrick’s is Scottish, made at Girvan by William Grant & Sons, the family company behind Glenfiddich.
Guests ask why it is not a London Dry: the rose and cucumber are added after distillation, which a London Dry may not do.
Name nobody from the company: say a great-grandson of William Grant, or the master distiller.
The still dates vary by source; if asked, quote the company’s own: the Bennett of 1860 and the Carter-Head of 1948.
In the Spoonbill the cucumber meets the chive oil and the rose meets the Cap Corse quinquina: say cool, green and floral.
producer.sayIt: Hendrick’s is a Scottish gin from Girvan, made in two old stills and finished with rose and cucumber; it launched in 1999.

producer.who: Gentilly Gin, Seven Three Distilling Co.
producer.where: 301 North Claiborne Avenue, Tremé, New Orleans
producer.history:
Seven Three Distilling Co. is a New Orleans craft distillery named for the city’s 73 officially recognised neighbourhoods, and it names its spirits after them: St. Roch Vodka, Bywater Bourbon, Marigny Moonshine, Irish Channel Whiskey, Black Pearl Rum and Gentilly Gin. A New Orleans husband and wife developed the brand while building a custom distillery, which opened in early 2017 in a warehouse at 301 North Claiborne Avenue, on the corner of Bienville Street, usually described as Tremé. Its first release was a run of 1,000 bottles of St. Roch Vodka, a neutral spirit redistilled and filtered for five days through copper, limestone and charcoal.

Gentilly Gin starts from the same neutral base. Juniper is joined by persimmon and elderflower, 17 botanicals in all, inspired by the traiteurs, the old faith healers of Louisiana. It is bottled at 87 proof, 43.5 percent. Tasters find elderflower, a little anise and vanilla on the nose, honeyed persimmon, ginger and juniper on the palate, and a peppery finish. A Barrel Reserve version rests in barrels before bottling.

Gentilly itself is one of the city’s old neighbourhoods. By the common account, in 1727 the colonists Mathurin and Pierre Dreux chose the natural levee along Bayou Sauvage for their plantation and named it after the French community they came from; one recent history argues the name began as Chantilly.
facts: Named for the city’s 73 officially recognised neighbourhoods; each spirit takes a neighbourhood’s name.
Opened in early 2017 at 301 North Claiborne Avenue, at Bienville Street, founded by a New Orleans husband and wife.
Its first release was 1,000 bottles of St. Roch Vodka, redistilled and filtered for five days through copper, limestone and charcoal.
Gentilly Gin starts from the vodka’s neutral base, with juniper, persimmon, elderflower and other botanicals, 17 in all.
The botanicals were inspired by the traiteurs, the old faith healers of Louisiana.
Bottled at 87 proof, 43.5 percent alcohol; a Barrel Reserve version is rested in barrels before bottling.
The range includes Bywater Bourbon, Marigny Moonshine, Irish Channel Whiskey, Black Pearl Rum and Whiskey Tree bourbons.
Gentilly takes its name, by the common account, from the French home of the colonists Mathurin and Pierre Dreux, who settled there in 1727.
notes: Say Gentilly Gin is made here in New Orleans, at Seven Three Distilling in Tremé.
Guests ask what Gentilly means: one of the city’s neighbourhoods, and the distillery names every spirit after one.
Never claim the persimmon or the elderflower is grown in Louisiana: no source says where the botanicals come from.
If asked who owns it: the New Orleans husband and wife who founded it, as the local business press reported. Name nobody.
A curious guest can visit: the distillery has a tasting room and tours, but hours change, so suggest they check before going.
producer.sayIt: Gentilly Gin is made here in New Orleans by Seven Three Distilling, named for one of our neighbourhoods, with persimmon and elderflower.
askKitchen: Is the OBX made with the standard Gentilly Gin or the Gentilly Gin Barrel Reserve?

producer.who: Cathead Distillery
producer.where: 422 South Farish Street, Jackson, Mississippi
producer.history:
Cathead Distillery was founded in 2010 by two friends and blues fans who had spent about eleven years working in South Carolina before coming home to Jackson, Mississippi. Mississippi passed statewide prohibition in 1907 and was the last state to repeal it, in 1966, and then only county by county; the founders had to help amend several old state laws before they could open. Cathead went to market in May 2010, and Visit Jackson and the company’s own releases call it Mississippi’s first legal distillery.

It began in Gluckstadt and moved downtown to 422 South Farish Street in 2015. The name is blues slang: the old blues players called each other cats, as a term of respect. The logo draws on the folk art of the Delta bluesman James Son Thomas, who sculpted cat heads from river clay, and the company has sent part of its sales to music nonprofits.

Cathead makes vodkas, Bristow Gin, a chicory liqueur called Hoodoo and Old Soul Bourbon in small batches. Its vodka is made in runs of 500 gallons or less, with some sweet corn in the grain for a crisp finish, and bottled at 80 proof. Beside the plain vodka come flavoured ones: honeysuckle, pecan, a bitter orange made with bitter orange and satsuma extracts, and a Satsuma Mandarin Vodka listed on the distillery’s shop pages, most likely the bottle the menu calls Cathead Mandarin Vodka. No source gives its proof or how it is flavoured; a canned Satsuma Mandarin vodka soda at 5 percent is a different product.
facts: Founded in 2010 in Jackson, Mississippi, by two friends and blues fans; it went to market in May 2010.
Visit Jackson and the company’s releases call it Mississippi’s first legal distillery.
Mississippi passed statewide prohibition in 1907 and was the last state to repeal it, in 1966; the founders helped amend old state laws to open.
Began in Gluckstadt and moved in 2015 to 422 South Farish Street, downtown Jackson, opening there on 12 December.
The name is blues slang: old blues players called each other cats, a term of respect.
The logo draws on the clay cat heads sculpted by the Delta bluesman James Son Thomas.
Its vodka is made in batches of 500 gallons or less, with some sweet corn in the grain, and bottled at 80 proof.
Flavoured vodkas include honeysuckle, pecan and bitter orange, made with bitter orange and satsuma extracts; a Satsuma Mandarin Vodka is listed on its shop pages.
It has sent part of its sales to music nonprofits, by one profile.
notes: Say Cathead Mandarin Vodka, as the menu prints it. The distillery has listed a Satsuma Mandarin Vodka, and a canned 5 percent vodka soda shares the flavour: confirm the bottle at lineup.
Say Mississippi’s first legal distillery, as the sources do, never simply the first distillery.
Guests ask about the name: blues slang, the old players’ word of respect for a fellow musician, and the logo is a bluesman’s clay cat head.
Do not claim the vodka is flavoured with Mississippi satsumas: no source says what the mandarin flavour is made from, or its proof.
If asked who owns it: two friends founded it in 2010; no source found names a later owner, so leave it there and name nobody.
producer.sayIt: Cathead comes from Jackson, Mississippi: the state’s first legal distillery, founded by two blues fans in 2010.
askKitchen: Which Cathead bottle goes into Five Minutes More: is it the Satsuma Mandarin Vodka, and at what proof?

producer.who: Volcán De Mi Tierra, Moët Hennessy
producer.where: Distillery NOM 1523, at the foot of the Tequila Volcano, Jalisco, Mexico
producer.history:
Volcán De Mi Tierra, the volcano of my land, is a tequila house born of a partnership between Moët Hennessy, the wine and spirits arm of LVMH, and a Mexican family whose lineage in Mexico goes back to the seventeenth century. By the brand’s story, a meeting between a family elder and LVMH executives raised the question of why the group had no tequila. The family owned land and a small distillery near the long-dormant Tequila Volcano in Jalisco; the partners chose the distillery, NOM 1523, revamped it and revived a brand the family had called Volcán. It has been described as the first 50:50 partnership LVMH had entered.

The tequila launched on 1 May 2017 with a Blanco and a Cristalino, a blend of añejo and extra añejo tequilas filtered clear, in eight American cities and Mexico. In October 2025 it was named the Official Tequila of Formula 1 under LVMH’s ten-year deal with the series.

The brand says the volcano’s ash left a soil rich in basalt and iron, which gives the tequila its taste. The agave comes from two terroirs: the highlands, at about 1,700 metres on iron-rich red clay, and the lowlands, at about 1,000 metres on dark volcanic soil that gives earthier, spicier notes. The Reposado rests in American and European oak, 135 days by one account and nine months by another, and is bottled at 40 percent: honey, dried fruit, toasted nuts, oak and vanilla.
facts: A 50:50 joint venture of Moët Hennessy, part of LVMH, and a Mexican family, described as the first such partnership LVMH entered.
Launched on 1 May 2017 with a Blanco and a Cristalino, in eight American cities and in Mexico.
Made at distillery NOM 1523 in Jalisco, at the foot of the long-dormant Tequila Volcano, on land the family owned.
Blends blue agave from the highlands, about 1,700 metres on iron-rich red clay, with lowland agave on dark volcanic soil at about 1,000 metres.
The brand credits the volcano’s ash with a soil rich in basalt and iron.
The Reposado rests in American and European oak; sources give 135 days or nine months.
Bottled at 40 percent; reviewers find honey, dried fruit, toasted nuts, oak and vanilla.
Named the Official Tequila of Formula 1 in October 2025, under LVMH’s ten-year deal with the series.
The Cristalino blends añejo and extra añejo tequilas, filtered to remove the colour.
notes: Say vol-KAHN; the menu prints Volcán Reposado Tequila, from the house Volcán De Mi Tierra.
Do not quote the ageing time: one source says 135 days, another nine months. Say rested in American and European oak.
Guests ask whether the volcano is real: yes, the long-dormant Tequila Volcano in Jalisco; the distillery stands at its foot.
If asked who owns it: Moët Hennessy, the LVMH wine and spirits house, half and half with a Mexican family. Name nobody.
Do not say highland agave only: the house blends highland and lowland agave.
producer.sayIt: Volcán is a tequila from the foot of Jalisco’s Tequila Volcano, made by Moët Hennessy with a Mexican family; the reposado rests in oak.

producer.who: Champagne Taittinger
producer.where: Reims, Champagne, France
producer.founded: 1734, as a Champagne trading house; the Taittinger family bought it in 1932
producer.history:
Taittinger traces its start to 1734, when Jacques Fourneaux began trading Champagne wines and worked with the Benedictine abbeys that owned some of the best vineyards. In the 1820s the firm became Forest-Fourneaux, and in 1932 Pierre Taittinger bought it and gave it his name; one source gives 1931.

In the years from 1945 to 1960 the house set up its cellars in the Gallo-Roman chalk pits beneath the site of the Saint-Nicaise abbey in Reims, where the wines still age. In 2005 the family sold its group to the American fund Starwood Capital Group; in 2006 a family-led bid, backed by the bank Crédit Agricole, bought the Champagne house back. A member of the family has been president since 1 January 2020.

Brut La Française is the house’s non-vintage Brut. Its mark is a high share of Chardonnay for a non-vintage blend, about 40 percent, with Pinot Noir and Meunier, which gives the light, fresh, elegant style the house is known for. One reviewer says it spends a year longer on its lees than the Brut Réserve, which ages at least three years.

At Brennan’s it tops the Flamingo in the Roost, and the same wine sits on the Birthday Bubbles list as a 3 litre double magnum.
facts: Traces its start to 1734, when Jacques Fourneaux began trading Champagne wines, working with Benedictine abbeys that owned top vineyards.
Pierre Taittinger bought the house, then called Forest-Fourneaux, in 1932 (one source says 1931), and it took the family name.
Its wines age in Gallo-Roman chalk pits beneath the site of the Saint-Nicaise abbey in Reims, where the house set up its cellars between 1945 and 1960.
Sold with the family’s group to Starwood Capital Group in 2005; in 2006 a family-led bid backed by the bank Crédit Agricole bought the Champagne house back.
Farms about 288 hectares of vines, across 37 crus by most accounts; one source gives 34.
Brut La Française is the non-vintage Brut: about 40 percent Chardonnay with Pinot Noir and Meunier, a high Chardonnay share for non-vintage Champagne.
One reviewer says La Française spends an extra year on its lees beyond the Brut Réserve, which ages at least three years.
Brennan’s lists La Française as a 3 litre double magnum on Birthday Bubbles, and Taittinger Prestige Rosé among the Bubbles rosé bottles.
notes: Say teh-tan-ZHAY. It is true Champagne, from Reims, so the word Champagne is right here: the Flamingo is the Roost drink that prints a Champagne house by name.
Guests ask whether Taittinger is still a family house. The honest answer: yes, the family runs it, after a short spell under an American fund in 2005 and 2006. Name nobody.
Do not quote the La Française blend as fixed: sources split the rest of it differently. Say about 40 percent Chardonnay, which is what makes it fresh and elegant.
Do not explain the name La Française: no source gives its meaning.
A guest who loves the Flamingo’s wine will find the same Taittinger La Française on the Birthday Bubbles list as a 3 litre double magnum; the sommelier handles the cellar side.
producer.sayIt: The Flamingo is topped with Taittinger La Française, a Chardonnay-led Champagne from a Reims house whose story begins in 1734.
askKitchen: Is the Flamingo always topped with Taittinger La Française, and what does the bar pour if it runs out?
How long does an opened bottle of La Française stay in service at the Roost Bar?

producer.who: Chandon, the sparkling wine house of Moët Hennessy (LVMH)
producer.where: Multiple countries and products; the cited U.S. Garden Spritz technical sheet identifies Argentina. Confirm the house bottle.
producer.founded: 1959 in Argentina; 1973 in California
producer.history:
Chandon is the international sparkling wine house developed beyond Champagne by the Moët group. Chandon California and Chandon Argentina are distinct origins. A brand family connection does not prove one origin or one production method.

The cited U.S. Garden Spritz technical sheet describes Argentine sparkling wine made with second fermentation and ageing in tank, then blended with a bitter orange component before bottling. Do not confuse that product with a Californian traditional method Brut.

Brennan's menu prints Chandon Brut sparkling wine and bitter orange liqueur, but does not establish whether the bar uses separate bottles or a ready to serve product. Confirm the current bottle, label and service.
facts: Chandon produces sparkling wine outside Champagne in multiple countries.
The cited U.S. Garden Spritz technical sheet identifies Argentina and second fermentation in tank, called Long Charmat.
In that product, the bitter orange component is blended with the wine before bottling.
A shared corporate history with Moët & Chandon does not make Chandon Champagne.
The saved Brennan's menu alone does not identify the product's country or fermentation method.
notes: Confirm whether the bar uses the prepared Garden Spritz or builds the drink from separate ingredients.
Read the current label before teaching its country, alcohol content or process; products can differ by market.
Use the menu's sparkling wine wording. Do not promise California or bottle fermentation.
The manufacturer’s serving suggestion is not confirmation of Brennan's glass, ice or garnish.
producer.sayIt: Our menu lists Chandon sparkling wine and bitter orange. I will confirm the exact bottle and preparation; it is sparkling wine rather than Champagne.
askKitchen: Which Chandon product and country does today's label show?
Is the drink built from separate ingredients or poured from a prepared bottle?
What are the confirmed measures, glass, ice and garnish?

producer.who: Elio Perrone, a family wine estate
producer.where: Castiglione Tinella, province of Asti, Piedmont, Italy
producer.founded: The family has made Moscato there since the end of the nineteenth century
producer.history:
Elio Perrone is a family estate in Castiglione Tinella, in the Moscato hills of the province of Asti in Piedmont. Sources say the family has made Moscato there since the end of the nineteenth century, over four generations. One profile dates the present generation’s taking over to 1989, when the son of the man whose name is on the label took the reins; another says the father retired in the late 1990s.

Moscato is the heart of the estate’s production. The family also farms vines at Isola d’Asti, where Barbera leads and Brachetto grows too, and the present generation created Bigaro, a blend of the two aromatic grapes made in the style of Moscato d’Asti.

Bigaro is its pink, softly sparkling wine: half Brachetto and half Moscato, crushed together and left a few days on the skins, with the fermentation stopped by filtering, so that it keeps some grape sugar and a light fizz at about 5 percent alcohol; one listing gives 7 percent for the 2024. Brachetto brings red berries and rose, Moscato brings peach and orange blossom, and the colour is salmon. Its importer lists it as Piedmont DOC, and it is served well chilled, as an aperitif or with fruit desserts.

In the OBX it tops Gentilly Gin, peach and lemon, adding fruit, a soft sweetness and a gentle sparkle.
facts: A family estate in Castiglione Tinella, in the Moscato hills of the province of Asti, Piedmont.
The family has made Moscato there since the end of the nineteenth century, over four generations, by the sources’ accounts.
One profile says the present generation took over in 1989; another says the father retired in the late 1990s.
The present generation created Bigaro, a Brachetto and Moscato blend made in the style of Moscato d’Asti.
Bigaro is half Brachetto and half Moscato, crushed together, left a few days on the skins, with fermentation stopped by filtering, leaving a light fizz and some sweetness.
About 5 percent alcohol on most listings; one listing gives 7 percent for the 2024.
Brachetto brings red berries and rose; Moscato brings peach and orange blossom.
A salmon-coloured, softly sweet, gently sparkling wine, listed by its importer as Piedmont DOC.
notes: Say bee-gah-ROH. Call it a sparkling wine, never Champagne or Prosecco: it is a softly sweet, low-alcohol pink from Piedmont.
Guests ask why the OBX drinks so lightly. The honest answer: the Bigaro is about 5 percent alcohol, far below Champagne, though the gin still makes it a full cocktail.
Do not say what the name Bigaro means: mottled has been suggested, but no source confirms it.
Elio Perrone is the name on the label and the estate is family run. Name nobody else.
A guest who likes Moscato d’Asti will recognise the style: grapey, floral and gently sweet.
producer.sayIt: The OBX is topped with Bigaro, a softly sweet, lightly sparkling pink from Piedmont, half Brachetto and half Moscato, about 5 percent alcohol.
askKitchen: Which vintage of the Bigaro is open, and what alcohol figure does its label print?

producer.who: Wölffer Estate Vineyard
producer.where: Sagaponack, Long Island, New York
producer.founded: 1987 or 1988, as Sagpond Vineyards; later renamed Wölffer Estate Vineyard
producer.history:
Wölffer Estate began with Christian Wölffer, a German-born investor who bought farmland at Sagaponack, on Long Island, from 1978, first for a horse farm. The original vineyard, acquired in 1988, had been a potato field. The winery was founded as Sagpond Vineyards in 1987 or 1988, by different accounts, and later renamed Wölffer Estate Vineyard, in 1997 by one account, when a new winery opened. Its winemaker came from Germany in 1992 and is now a partner. Christian Wölffer died on New Year’s Eve 2008 in Brazil, and the estate is owned and run by his children with that partner. It is known above all for its rosé.

Wölffer began making non-alcoholic drinks in 1996, with verjus. In 2021 it launched Spring in a Bottle, a non-alcoholic sparkling rosé made in Germany from a certified organic vineyard in Rheinhessen, with the alcohol and other volatiles gently removed at a low 77°F. It also sells Petite Rosé, a sparkling drink pressed from unripe grapes, and a still Summer in a Bottle Rosé Zero.

A dealcoholised wine is made as wine first and then stripped of its alcohol: by vacuum distillation at low temperature, by a spinning cone column, which takes off the lightest aromas first and blends them back, or by reverse osmosis through fine membranes. Wölffer does not say which method it uses.
facts: Christian Wölffer, a German-born investor, began buying farmland at Sagaponack, Long Island, in 1978, first for a horse farm.
Founded as Sagpond Vineyards in 1987 or 1988; renamed Wölffer Estate Vineyard later, in 1997 by one account, when a new winery opened.
The original Sagaponack vineyard, acquired in 1988, had been a potato field.
Christian Wölffer died on New Year’s Eve 2008 in Brazil; his children and the winemaker partner own and run the estate.
Wölffer began making non-alcoholic drinks in 1996, with verjus.
Spring in a Bottle, its non-alcoholic sparkling rosé, launched in 2021, made in Germany from a certified organic Rheinhessen vineyard.
Its alcohol is gently removed at a low 77°F; Total Wine and Wölffer list it at 0.0 percent, an earlier listing at 0.5.
Dealcoholised wine is fermented as wine first, then stripped of alcohol by vacuum distillation, a spinning cone column or reverse osmosis.
Wölffer also makes Petite Rosé, a sparkling non-alcoholic drink pressed from unripe grapes, and a still Summer in a Bottle Rosé Zero.
notes: The menu prints Wölffer Estate Zero Proof Sparkling Rosé, not a bottle name. Wölffer makes more than one sparkling zero proof rosé, so which is ours is a lineup question.
Guests ask whether it is truly zero. The honest answer: zero proof is not a legal term; listings give 0.0 percent and 0.5, so we read our label first.
If ours is Spring in a Bottle, it is real wine with the alcohol taken out, made in Germany for the Long Island estate. Do not call it a Long Island wine.
Any guest who must have no alcohol at all, for pregnancy, medication or recovery, gets the label and the bar, never a promise from the server.
Personality is the spirit-free twin of Rumors are Flying: tart cherry and brown sugar syrup over sparkling rosé.
producer.sayIt: Personality is built on a non-alcoholic sparkling rosé from Wölffer Estate, the Long Island winery known for rosé, with tart cherry and brown sugar.
askKitchen: Which Wölffer bottle is the base of Personality: Spring in a Bottle, Petite Rosé or another?
What alcohol figure does that bottle’s label print, so we know whether to say zero or non-alcoholic?

producer.who: Lyre’s
producer.where: Sydney, Australia, by business databases; one account says it began in Britain
producer.history:
Lyre’s makes non-alcoholic spirits, drinks built to taste like gin, whisky, rum, agave spirit and the rest without the alcohol. The company dates itself to 2019 and says it was founded to replicate the world’s most popular spirits in a non-alcoholic form. It was started by two Australians; one account calls it a British company at the start, while business databases place its head office in Leichhardt, Sydney.

The name comes from the lyrebird, the Australian bird famous for mimicking birdsong and every other sound, even a mobile phone. A co-founder has said the range is meant to be the most successful mimic of classic spirits, and a lyrebird in a top hat sits on the neck of each bottle.

The Agave Blanco lists water, natural flavours, agave syrup, citric acid, salt, a stabiliser and a preservative; Lyre’s says its flavours and distillates come from seeds, botanicals, fruits and spices. Its American page calls it simply non-alcoholic, and an Australian listing gives under 0.5 percent alcohol. Under United States federal rules for malt beverages and dealcoholised wine, non-alcoholic means under 0.5 percent, while alcohol free means no alcohol at all.

The range runs to 13 spirits, sold in over 60 countries. In March 2025 Amber Beverage Group added Lyre’s to its portfolio; one report calls it a partnership and another an acquisition.
facts: Founded in 2019, by its own account, to replicate the world’s most popular spirits in non-alcoholic form.
Started by two Australians; business databases place its head office in Leichhardt, Sydney, though one account calls it British at the start.
Named for the lyrebird, the Australian bird famed as a mimic; a lyrebird in a top hat sits on each bottle’s neck.
The Agave Blanco lists water, natural flavours, agave syrup, citric acid, salt, cellulose gum and potassium sorbate.
Its American page labels the Agave Blanco non-alcoholic; an Australian listing gives under 0.5 percent alcohol.
Under United States federal rules for malt beverages and dealcoholised wine, non-alcoholic means under 0.5 percent alcohol; alcohol free means none.
Lyre’s sells at least two agaves, the Agave Blanco and the Agave Reserva.
The range runs to 13 non-alcoholic spirits, sold in over 60 countries.
notes: Say LY-erz. Say non-alcoholic, never alcohol free or zero: Lyre’s labels it non-alcoholic, and an Australian listing gives under 0.5 percent.
The menu prints Lyre’s N/A Agave Tequila, but Lyre’s sells it as an agave spirit, not tequila. Say non-alcoholic agave.
Guests ask how it can taste like tequila. The honest answer: it is water built up with natural flavours, agave syrup and a little salt and acid, made to mimic one, as the lyrebird mimics.
Oh! What It Seemed to Be is the spirit-free twin of Old Buttermilk Sky, so a whole table can share the idea.
Pregnancy, medication or recovery questions go to the label and the bar; never promise zero.
producer.sayIt: Oh! What It Seemed to Be uses Lyre’s agave, an Australian non-alcoholic spirit named for the lyrebird, a famous mimic, with fig, lemon and cinnamon.
askKitchen: Is our Lyre’s the Agave Blanco or the Agave Reserva?
What alcohol figure does our bottle’s label print?

producer.who: Abita Root Beer, Abita Brewing Company
producer.where: Abita Springs, Louisiana, on the Northshore of Lake Pontchartrain
producer.founded: The root beer since the 1990s; the brewery 1986
producer.history:
Abita Root Beer is the soft drink of Abita Brewing, the brewery founded in 1986 in Abita Springs, on the Northshore of Lake Pontchartrain, across the lake from New Orleans. The brewery’s own story is told with the Abita Amber of the Shells & Cheese; this profile keeps to the root beer, which was among the founding brewer’s recipes for the flagships.

Abita has brewed it since the 1990s; press material of 2015 and 2016 says for over 20 years. It is hot brewed rather than cold mixed, with spring water from Abita Springs, herbs, vanilla and yucca, which makes the foam, and it is sweetened only with Louisiana cane sugar, which the brewery likens to the soft drinks of the 1940s and 1950s, before bottlers turned to corn sugar. The brewery describes it as naturally caffeine free.

It went into cans in 2015, when the brewery reported making more than 14,000 barrels of it a year. Abita has also launched a hard root beer, Bayou Bootlegger; the menu prints Abita Root Beer, the soft drink.

At Brennan’s it is the fizz in Floating in South Africa, with Amarula Cream Liqueur and housemade vanilla bean ice cream.
facts: Made by Abita Brewing Company of Abita Springs, Louisiana, founded in 1986; the brewery’s own story is told with the Abita Amber.
Hot brewed, not cold mixed, with Abita Springs spring water, herbs, vanilla and yucca, which makes the foam.
Sweetened only with Louisiana cane sugar, which the brewery likens to soft drinks of the 1940s and 1950s, before bottlers turned to corn sugar.
Described by the brewery as naturally caffeine free.
Brewed since the 1990s; the founding brewer’s recipes for Abita’s flagships included the root beer.
In cans since 2015, when the brewery reported more than 14,000 barrels of root beer a year.
Abita’s hard root beer, Bayou Bootlegger, is a different product from the soft drink on our menu.
notes: Say uh-BEE-tuh. It is a Louisiana root beer from across the lake, from the same brewery as the Abita Amber in the Shells & Cheese.
Guests ask whether the root beer has alcohol. Abita Root Beer is a soft drink; the alcohol in Floating in South Africa comes from the Amarula.
Do not confuse it with Abita’s hard root beer, Bayou Bootlegger: the menu prints Abita Root Beer.
Do not quote the depth of Abita’s well or the age of its water: those figures come from a retailer only.
Questions about the ice cream or the cream go to the service note and the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: The fizz is Abita Root Beer, brewed across the lake in Abita Springs with Louisiana cane sugar, vanilla and yucca for its creamy foam.
askKitchen: Is the Abita Root Beer poured from bottle or can?

producer.who: Egon Müller, the family estate of the Scharzhof on the Saar
producer.where: The Scharzhof, Wiltingen, Saar, Mosel, Germany
producer.founded: The Scharzhofberg was bought at auction in 1797 by Jean-Jacques Koch; it passed to the Müller family through his daughter's marriage
producer.history:
Egon Müller is the estate of the Scharzhof, a farmstead at Wiltingen on the Saar, the cold tributary that is part of the Mosel region. Above it rises the Scharzhofberg, a steep hill of blue Devonian slate most often called the finest ground on the Saar.

For centuries the hill belonged to a monastery in Trier. When the French revolutionary armies seized church land it was sold at auction, and in 1797 Jean-Jacques Koch bought it. It passed to the Müller family through his daughter's marriage.

The wines were served at royal courts, and before the First World War Scharzhofberger was among the most expensive wines in the world. The estate labels it simply Scharzhofberger, with no village name. Its fame rests on sweet Prädikat wines picked in repeated passes, very low in alcohol and very high in acid, and its Trockenbeerenauslese is counted among the most expensive white wines in the world.

The Saar ripens later and less surely than the main Mosel valley, which is why its great years are talked about for decades. Even the Kabinett, the lightest Prädikat, carries the house transparency: our Scharzhofberger Kabinett 2020, lightly sweet and low in alcohol, is a collector's wine at the lightest level.
facts: The Scharzhofberg belonged to a monastery in Trier until the French revolutionary armies seized church land.
In 1797 Jean-Jacques Koch bought the Scharzhofberg at auction; it passed to the Müller family through his daughter's marriage.
The Scharzhof stands at Wiltingen on the Saar, below the Scharzhofberg, a steep hill of blue Devonian slate.
The estate labels the wine simply Scharzhofberger, without the village name.
Scharzhofberger was served at royal courts and was among the most expensive wines in the world before the First World War.
The estate's Scharzhofberger Trockenbeerenauslese is counted among the most expensive white wines in the world.
The Saar is part of the Mosel region, not a separate one, and ripens later and less surely than the main valley.
Scharzberg is the Grosslage that borrows the name across much of the Saar; Scharzhofberger is the single vineyard.
notes: Say AY-gon MOO-ler, with lips rounded for the ü; Scharzhofberger is SHARTZ-hof-bair-ger.
Guests ask why a Kabinett costs $395. The honest answer: it is the lightest wine of perhaps the most sought-after Riesling estate in Germany, from one of the world's most famous vineyards.
Say lightly sweet and low in alcohol; never call it dry.
Say the leading owner on the Scharzhofberg, not the owner: other estates hold parcels of the hill too.
Do not quote hectares or name the head of the family today; no dated source confirms either.
producer.sayIt: Egon Müller's Scharzhofberger, from the Saar's most famous hill: one of the great Rieslings of the world, lightly sweet, weightless and electric.
askKitchen: Should the Scharzhofberger Kabinett 2020 be opened ahead, given its youth?

producer.who: Joh. Jos. Prüm, the Prüm family estate at Wehlen, usually called J.J. Prüm
producer.where: Wehlen, Middle Mosel, Germany
producer.founded: 1911, when the Prüm family holdings in Wehlen were divided
producer.history:
Joh. Jos. Prüm, usually called J.J. Prüm, is the benchmark estate of Wehlen on the Middle Mosel and the name most attached to the Wehlener Sonnenuhr. The estate as it stands dates from 1911, when the Prüm family's holdings in Wehlen were divided. Other Prüm estates exist, S.A. Prüm, Studert-Prüm and Dr. F. Weins-Prüm among them, so the full name matters.

The vineyard's name comes from the family too. In 1842 Jodocus Prüm built a sundial into the slate of the slope so that the workers on the hill could tell the time, and the ground took its name: Sonnenuhr means sundial. The slope is steep blue-grey Devonian slate, and the estate also holds vines in Graach, Zeltingen and Bernkastel.

The Prüm style is classical, fruity Mosel Riesling: feather light, lightly sweet and low in alcohol. Young bottles are often reductive and faintly spritzy, the house signature and not a fault, and they can seem closed for years before turning to honey, smoke and slate over decades. A gold capsule marks a finer selection within the same Prädikat.

On our list the estate gives the Wehlener Sonnenuhr Kabinett 2020 and, for a big table, the gold capsule Auslese 2015 in magnum.
facts: The Joh. Jos. Prüm estate dates from 1911, when the Prüm family holdings in Wehlen were divided.
In 1842 Jodocus Prüm built a sundial into the Wehlen slate so vineyard workers could tell the time; the vineyard took its name.
The estate bottles Wehlener Sonnenuhr, Graacher Himmelreich, Graacher Domprobst, Zeltinger Sonnenuhr and Bernkasteler Badstube, all from Devonian slate.
Young Prüm wines are often reductive and faintly spritzy, a house signature, then turn to honey, smoke and slate over decades.
Gold capsule and long gold capsule mark finer selections within one Prädikat; GKA on our list means Goldkapsel Auslese.
S.A. Prüm, Studert-Prüm and Dr. F. Weins-Prüm are separate estates; say Joh. Jos. or J.J. Prüm in full.
Sonnenuhr also names vineyards at Zeltingen and Brauneberg, among others, so the village name, Wehlener, carries the answer.
notes: Say PROOM and Wehlener Sonnenuhr VAY-len-er ZON-en-oor; Joh. Jos. is YOH-han YO-sef, or simply J.J. Prüm.
A young Kabinett may show a struck-match note and a little spritz: tell the guest it is the house style and that it opens with air.
Kabinett is the lightest Prädikat, lightly sweet and low in alcohol; never sell it as dry.
The magnum pours about twenty small dessert glasses, as its card says; offer it to a big table sharing dessert.
Do not name the family member running the estate today; no dated source names them.
producer.sayIt: J.J. Prüm, the legendary estate of Wehlen on the Mosel, from the sundial vineyard: feather-light Riesling, lightly sweet, that ages for decades.
askKitchen: Should the young Prüm Kabinett 2020 be opened ahead to let its reductive note clear?

producer.who: Château d'Issan, the Margaux third growth whose team makes our Moulin d'Issan
producer.where: Cantenac, Margaux, Médoc, Bordeaux, France; the Moulin d'Issan comes from its vines outside the Margaux appellation
producer.history:
Château d'Issan is a moated château at Cantenac, inside the Margaux appellation in the southern Médoc, ranked a third growth in the classification of 1855. Over its door is engraved its motto, Regum mensis arisque deorum: for the tables of kings and the altars of the gods. The house tells that wine from its land was served at the wedding of Eleanor of Aquitaine and Henry Plantagenet in 1152, the marriage through which Bordeaux later passed to the English crown, when Henry became king. It is a legend, and we tell it as one.

Not all of the estate's vines are entitled to the Margaux name. Some lie on low ground by the Gironde, outside the appellation, and their wine is labelled Bordeaux Supérieur. That is the Moulin d'Issan, grown on the estate, made by the d'Issan team, aged partly in new barrels and named for a ruined seventeenth century windmill: moulin is French for mill.

Our menu and the Binwise list head it a Cabernet Sauvignon blend; the château itself calls it Merlot led, and the mix changes with the vintage. Name both grapes and let the sommelier give the blend. It is our Bordeaux by the glass, the first pick for the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak.
facts: A third growth of the 1855 classification, at Cantenac inside the Margaux appellation.
A moated château; over its door is engraved the motto Regum mensis arisque deorum, for the tables of kings and the altars of the gods.
Estate legend says its wine was served at the wedding of Eleanor of Aquitaine and Henry Plantagenet in 1152; it is told as legend.
Moulin d'Issan is a Bordeaux Supérieur from d'Issan vines on low ground outside the Margaux appellation, grown on the estate and made by its team.
Moulin d'Issan is named for a ruined seventeenth century windmill; moulin is French for mill.
The château calls Moulin d'Issan Merlot led; our list heads it a Cabernet Sauvignon blend.
Blason d'Issan is the château's second wine, sold as Margaux, a different wine from the Moulin d'Issan.
notes: Say dee-SAHN and moo-LAN dee-SAHN; Margaux is mar-GOH. Never ISS-an.
Guests ask whether it is Margaux. The honest answer: a Margaux third growth makes it from its vines just outside the appellation, so the label says Bordeaux Supérieur.
Name both grapes, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon. The menu heads it a Cabernet blend and the château calls it Merlot led; the sommelier has the mix of the bottle open.
Tell the royal wedding of 1152 as the estate's legend, never as fact, and never call the Moulin the second wine: that is Blason d'Issan.
Read the label at lineup: the menu prints 2021 and the Binwise list 2023.
producer.sayIt: The Moulin d'Issan is made by Château d'Issan, a moated third growth in Margaux, from its vines just outside the appellation.
askKitchen: Which vintage is open tonight, the 2021 the menu prints or the 2023 on Binwise?
What is the blend of the vintage open: Merlot led, as the château describes it, or Cabernet led, as our list heads it?
Who owns and runs Château d'Issan today, if a guest asks?

producer.who: Château Talbot, a fourth growth of Saint-Julien
producer.where: Saint-Julien, Médoc, Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Château Talbot is a fourth growth of the 1855 classification in Saint-Julien, the village between Pauillac and Margaux known for balanced, elegant Cabernet. Its name is the best history lesson on our Bordeaux pages. It is named for John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, the English commander killed at the Battle of Castillon in 1453, the battle that ended English rule in Bordeaux and the last great battle of the Hundred Years' War. Shakespeare put him on stage as old Talbot.

The Cordier family has owned the estate since 1918. Its vineyard is a large inland block in the middle of Saint-Julien, with a white parcel set aside for Caillou Blanc, which is sold as Bordeaux Blanc because the Médoc's village appellations are for red wine only.

The red is Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and a little Petit Verdot, in a round, generous, approachable style: a dependable fourth growth of some size, as the Codex puts it. We carry the 2019, the sweet spot bottle for the Roasted Chateaubriand, and the list also prints a 1996.
facts: A fourth growth of the 1855 classification in Saint-Julien.
Named for John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, the English commander killed at the Battle of Castillon in 1453.
Castillon ended English rule in Bordeaux; Shakespeare put Talbot on stage.
Owned by the Cordier family since 1918.
Its vineyard is a large inland block in the middle of Saint-Julien.
Its white, Caillou Blanc, is sold as AOC Bordeaux Blanc, because the Médoc's village appellations are for red wine only.
Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and Petit Verdot, in a round, generous, approachable style.
notes: Say tal-BOH; Saint-Julien is san zhoo-LYAN.
Tell the name: the claret named for the English commander killed in 1453, when England lost Bordeaux. It is history, not legend.
Guests ask whether a fourth growth is lesser. The honest answer: the ranks follow the prices of 1855, and Talbot is generous and ready earlier than many.
The list prints a 2019 and a 1996: check the label and the bin, 33111 for the 2019, before you pour.
Name the Cordier family as owners with the date, since 1918; ownership can change.
producer.sayIt: Château Talbot is a Saint-Julien fourth growth named for John Talbot, the English commander killed at Castillon in 1453, when England lost Bordeaux.
askKitchen: Is the 2019 or the 1996 Talbot in the cellar tonight?

producer.who: Château Grand-Puy-Lacoste, a fifth growth of Pauillac
producer.where: Pauillac, Médoc, Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Château Grand-Puy-Lacoste is a fifth growth of the 1855 classification in Pauillac. Its vineyard is a single block on a gravel rise inland from the river; puy is the local word for such a rise, and two separate fifth growths carry it, Grand-Puy-Lacoste and Grand-Puy-Ducasse.

Our list and the Codex name the Borie family as its owners, as of October 2026, a name well known in Saint-Julien and Pauillac: Ducru-Beaucaillou, a Saint-Julien second growth, is also a Borie property, held separately by another member of the family. The second wine is Lacoste-Borie.

The Codex calls it pure, unfussy, Cabernet-dominant Pauillac, cassis and graphite with no cosmetic oak, a classicist's benchmark, and the trade often calls it one of the best values among the classed growths: a fifth growth that drinks above its rank. Our list carries it in six vintages, from 2003 to 2015.

The one to sell first is the 2008, eighteen years on: cassis and cedar, tobacco, earth and graphite, the firm tannin resolved. It is the celebration bottle for the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak at lunch, and it suits the Roasted Chateaubriand.
facts: A fifth growth of the 1855 classification in Pauillac.
A single block on a gravel rise inland from the river; puy is the local word for such a rise.
Owned by the Borie family, by our list and the Codex, as of October 2026; Ducru-Beaucaillou is a separate Borie property, held by another family member.
Its second wine is Lacoste-Borie.
Grand-Puy-Ducasse is a different fifth growth; the names are easily confused.
Pure, Cabernet-dominant Pauillac, cassis and graphite, often called one of the best values among the classed growths.
Our list prints six vintages, 2003 to 2015; the one to name is the 2008, bin 26123.
notes: Say grahn PWEE lah-KOST; Pauillac is poy-YAK.
Present it as honest, classic Pauillac that drinks above its fifth growth rank.
Guests ask whether a fifth growth is lesser. The honest answer: every growth is a classed growth, and the ranks follow the prices of 1855, not today’s glass.
Six vintages share the page: carry the bottle upright and check the label reads 2008.
Do not confuse it with Grand-Puy-Ducasse, a different fifth growth, or with Haut-Bages Libéral, beside it on our list.
Name the Borie family as owners only as our list and the Codex give it in October 2026; the year they took it on is not confirmed, and ownership can change.
producer.sayIt: Grand-Puy-Lacoste is classic Pauillac, a fifth growth that drinks above its rank: cassis, cedar and graphite.
askKitchen: Should the 2008 be decanted off its sediment, and how far ahead?
Since when has the Borie family owned Grand-Puy-Lacoste, if a guest asks?

producer.who: Château Pichon Longueville Comtesse de Lalande, Pichon Lalande for short, a second growth of Pauillac
producer.where: Pauillac, Médoc, Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Château Pichon Longueville Comtesse de Lalande, Pichon Lalande for short, is a second growth of the 1855 classification in Pauillac, across the road from Château Latour. It was once part of one great Pichon Longueville estate. In 1850 the estate was divided, and the share run by Virginie, Comtesse de Lalande, took her name; the other share is Pichon Longueville Baron, a separate second growth facing it across the road.

The Miailhe family bought it in 1925, and in January 2007 it was sold to the owners of Champagne Louis Roederer, whose Cristal is also on our list. Part of its vineyard lies inside the commune of Saint-Julien, yet the wine is sold as Pauillac.

It carries more Merlot than its neighbours, which gives a silky, floral style: rose, redcurrant and cream over a Pauillac frame, the gentlest of the super-seconds, as the Codex puts it. The second wine is Réserve de la Comtesse.

Our list carries it in several vintages, from a 1982 to a 2020 half-bottle. The one to sell first is the 2004, the celebration bottle for the Roasted Chateaubriand.
facts: A second growth of the 1855 classification in Pauillac, across the road from Château Latour.
Part of the Pichon Longueville estate divided in 1850; this share, run by Virginie, Comtesse de Lalande, carries her title.
Pichon Longueville Baron, the other share, is a separate Pauillac second growth.
