The Miailhe family bought it in 1925; it was sold in January 2007 to the owners of Champagne Louis Roederer.
Part of its vineyard lies inside the commune of Saint-Julien, yet the wine is sold as Pauillac.
It carries more Merlot than most Pauillac, which gives a silky, floral style.
Its second wine is Réserve de la Comtesse.
notes: Say pee-SHOHN lah-LAHND; most guests say Pichon Lalande or Pichon Comtesse.
Guests ask whether there are two Pichons. Yes: Baron and Comtesse, both Pauillac second growths. Ours is the Comtesse.
For a Champagne lover the link is Roederer: the owners of Cristal have owned it since January 2007; ownership can change.
Several vintages and a half-bottle share the page: ring in bin 26411 for the 2004 and check the label.
Never call it a first growth: it is a second growth, one of the super-seconds.
producer.sayIt: Pichon Lalande is the silky Pauillac, a second growth across the road from Latour, with more Merlot than its neighbours.
askKitchen: How long should the 2004 stand before it is decanted off its sediment?

producer.who: Château Suduiraut, a first growth of Sauternes at Preignac, Yquem's neighbour
producer.where: Preignac, Sauternes, Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Château Suduiraut is one of the premiers crus, the first growths, of Sauternes and Barsac, ranked beneath Yquem's Premier Cru Supérieur in the classification of 1855. The 1855 list named nine; there are eleven today, because two of them were later divided. It lies at Preignac, one of the five communes entitled to the Sauternes name, on a large estate next to Yquem. Its formal gardens are attributed to André Le Nôtre, the gardener of Versailles.

Sauternes is made from Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc left on the vine until noble rot, a mould brought by the autumn mists where the cold Ciron meets the Garonne, shrivels the grapes and concentrates their sugar; they are picked by hand in several passes. Suduiraut is Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc, aged in oak, and the Codex places it at the opulent end of Sauternes: candied apricot, honey and roasted pineapple, broad and rich, where Barsac is leaner.

The Codex names its second sweet wine Castelnau de Suduiraut and records a dry white sold under the initial S; what the estate bottles today, and who owns it, are for the sommelier.

We pour it twice, the 2016 in a half-bottle and the 2010 by the bottle, both for the New Orleans Bread Pudding, and both far below the price of Yquem.
facts: A Premier Cru Classé of Sauternes in 1855, beneath Yquem's Premier Cru Supérieur; the 1855 list named nine premiers crus, eleven today after two were divided.
At Preignac, one of the five Sauternes communes, on a large estate next to Château d’Yquem.
Its formal gardens are attributed to André Le Nôtre, the gardener of Versailles.
Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc from noble rot grapes, aged in oak; the Codex places it at the opulent end of Sauternes.
The Codex names Castelnau de Suduiraut as its second wine and records a dry white sold under the initial S.
Preignac gives rich Sauternes; Barsac, on more limestone, lighter and fresher: Suduiraut and Climens show the contrast on our list.
notes: Say soo-dwee-ROH. The Binwise list misspells it Suduirant; the château and its label are Suduiraut.
Two bottles: the 2016 half-bottle (bin 192321, $135) and the 2010 (bin 19142, $230). Ring by size and vintage; the Climens 2010 at $200 is a Barsac.
Guests ask how it differs from Yquem. The honest answer: a neighbour and a first growth, one rank below Yquem, the only Premier Cru Supérieur, at a far gentler price.
Never call it a Premier Cru Supérieur, and do not name an owner: ours is unconfirmed, and ownership can change.
Pour small, 2 to 3 oz, well chilled; recork and chill what is left, and ask the sommelier how long the house keeps an open bottle.
producer.sayIt: Suduiraut is a first growth of Sauternes, right beside Yquem: honeyed apricot and pineapple, made for our bread pudding.
askKitchen: How many days does the house keep an open Sauternes, half-bottle or full?
Who owns Suduiraut today, and since when? AXA Millésimes has been named, but no dated source confirms it.

producer.who: Château d'Yquem, the only Premier Cru Supérieur of Sauternes, the most famous sweet wine in the world
producer.where: Sauternes, Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Château d'Yquem stands on a hilltop in the commune of Sauternes. When the sweet wines of Sauternes and Barsac were ranked for the Paris Exposition of 1855, it was placed alone above every other estate as Premier Cru Supérieur, a rank created for it and never given to another.

The Lur-Saluces family held it from 1785, when it came to them through a marriage, for more than two centuries. Thomas Jefferson, the American minister in France who later became president, ordered it for himself and for George Washington. The Codex records LVMH as its owner since 1999; ownership can change.

Its reputation rests on refusal. The pickers pass through the vineyard again and again, taking only the berries noble rot has shrivelled, so each vine gives roughly a glass of wine, and in poor years there is no Yquem at all: none was released in 1972, 1974, 1992 or 2012, among others. The wine is Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc, aged in new oak, with an acidity that carries it for a century. From fruit picked before noble rot, or in a year without it, the estate makes a dry white, Y, called Ygrec, sold as Bordeaux Blanc and never as Sauternes.

We pour three: half-bottles of 2015 and 2016 at $450, and the 2007 by the bottle at $850; the list prints older vintages and a magnum too.
facts: The only Premier Cru Supérieur in the 1855 classification of Sauternes and Barsac, a rank held by no other estate.
A hilltop estate in the commune of Sauternes; the Lur-Saluces family held it from 1785, through a marriage, for over two centuries.
Thomas Jefferson ordered Yquem for himself and for George Washington.
Picked berry by berry in repeated passes; the yield is proverbially about a glass of wine per vine.
No Yquem was released in 1972, 1974, 1992 or 2012, among other poor years.
Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc, aged in new oak, with acidity that lets it age for a century.
Y, said ee-GREK, is the dry white, fermented dry on purpose and sold as Bordeaux Blanc, not Sauternes.
Owned by LVMH since 1999, as the Codex records; ownership can change.
notes: Say dee-KEM, and always Château d'Yquem with the d'. The sommelier presents the 2007.
Three bottles: halves of 2015 (bin 1926) and 2016 (bin 19271), both $450, and the 2007 (bin 192842, $850). Check the vintage on the label before presenting.
Guests ask why it costs so much. The honest answer: a rank of its own since 1855, berry by berry picking, about a glass a vine, and no wine in poor years.
Never claim a score or a vintage verdict; how each vintage is drinking is for the sommelier. It is never Château Yquem, nor a mere premier cru.
A half-bottle gives about four small pours: the way to offer a legend to a table that would never buy a full bottle.
producer.sayIt: Château d'Yquem is the most famous sweet wine in the world, ranked alone above every Sauternes in 1855 and picked berry by berry.
askKitchen: How is each of our Yquem vintages showing, the 2015 and 2016 halves and the 2007?
Which of the older Yquem vintages and the 2016 magnum on the list are in the cellar tonight?

producer.who: Château Climens, a first growth of Barsac, called the Lord of Barsac, made from Sémillon alone
producer.where: Barsac, Sauternes, Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Château Climens is one of the two premiers crus, the first growths, of Barsac in the 1855 classification of Sauternes and Barsac; the other is Coutet. Its admirers call it the Lord of Barsac, and sometimes the Yquem of Barsac.

Barsac is one of the five communes entitled to the Sauternes appellation and also holds its own, so its estates may label their wine Barsac or Sauternes; our list prints Climens as Barsac. Its ground is flatter, with more limestone beneath, the usual explanation for Barsac's lighter, more incisive style. Climens sits on a single plateau of red sand over limestone.

What sets it apart is the grape. Climens is planted entirely to Sémillon, with no Sauvignon Blanc at all, the cleanest proof that Sauvignon is optional in a Sauternes blend. It is picked by hand in successive passes for noble rot, vinified parcel by parcel, assembled late and aged in oak; the second wine is Cyprès de Climens. The estate has farmed biodynamically.

The Lurton family owned Climens from the 1970s until 2022, when a majority stake was sold to the Moitry family.

Ours is the 2010 at $200, the sweet spot bottle for the Lemon Tart: candied lemon, apricot and honey, sweet but lifted by Barsac's freshness.
facts: A Premier Cru Classé of Barsac in 1855; with Coutet, one of the two Barsac first growths.
Called the Lord of Barsac, and sometimes the Yquem of Barsac.
Planted entirely to Sémillon, on a single plateau of red sand over limestone: no Sauvignon Blanc at all.
Vinified parcel by parcel and assembled late; the second wine is Cyprès de Climens.
Barsac estates may label their wine Barsac or Sauternes; Sauternes from the other communes may not be called Barsac.
Farmed biodynamically, as of October 2026.
The Lurton family owned it from the 1970s; a majority stake passed to the Moitry family in 2022.
notes: Say klee-MAHNS, and say Barsac: our list prints it as Barsac, though it may legally say Sauternes.
The 2010 at $200 (bin 192821) sits beside the Suduiraut 2010 at $230: same year, different commune. Ring by bin.
Guests ask why only Sémillon. The honest answer: it is Climens's way; most neighbours add Sauvignon Blanc, and Climens shows Sémillon alone can be fresh.
If asked about farming, say the estate has farmed biodynamically and the sommelier can confirm practice since the 2022 sale; ownership can change, and never make a health claim.
Pour small and well chilled with the Lemon Tart: its citrus meets the lemon and the yuzu.
producer.sayIt: Climens is the Lord of Barsac, a first growth made from Sémillon alone: candied lemon and honey, sweet but fresh.
askKitchen: Does Climens still farm biodynamically since the 2022 sale, if a guest asks?

producer.who: Château Gilette, the tiny Preignac estate that holds its Sauternes for decades before release
producer.where: Preignac, Sauternes, Bordeaux, France
producer.history:
Château Gilette is a tiny estate at Preignac, one of the five communes of Sauternes, owned by the Médeville family as of October 2026. It was not classified in 1855, and its fame rests on something else: patience.

Where the classed growths on our list raise their Sauternes in oak barrels, Gilette keeps its finest wine, the Crème de Tête, the cream of the top, in small concrete vats for close to twenty years, never in oak, and releases it twenty years or more after the harvest. It reaches the bottle already mature: amber gold, with caramel and dried apricot, and still sweet and fresh.

The grapes are those of Sauternes, mainly Sémillon with some Sauvignon Blanc, shrivelled by noble rot; the exact blend is a question for the sommelier.

Ours is the 1989, thirty-seven years on, at $515, the celebration bottle with the Bananas Foster: crème brûlée, caramel, dried apricot and orange peel. When it was released, and how it is showing, are questions for the sommelier.
facts: A tiny estate at Preignac in Sauternes, owned by the Médeville family as of October 2026; not classified in 1855.
Its Crème de Tête stays in small concrete vats for close to twenty years and never touches oak.
Released twenty years or more after the harvest, so it reaches the table already mature.
Crème de Tête, the cream of the top, is the estate's top selection: mainly Sémillon, with some Sauvignon Blanc.
Our 1989 is amber gold: crème brûlée, caramel, dried apricot and orange peel, with freshness intact.
notes: Say zhee-LET. Show the label and the vintage: a 1989 Sauternes is the story itself.
Never call it a first growth or a classed growth: Gilette was not classified in 1855, and needs no rank.
Guests ask why it was aged so long. The honest answer: the estate holds its wine in concrete vats for about two decades before release; that is its tradition.
Pour after the Bananas Foster flambé, never near the flame; small pours, well chilled, the host last.
Do not give a release date, a vineyard size or the blend; the owning family can change. Ask the sommelier how the bottle is showing.
producer.sayIt: Gilette holds its Sauternes for about twenty years in concrete before release; this 1989 is caramel and crème brûlée with the flambé.
askKitchen: When was our Gilette Crème de Tête 1989 released, and how is it showing?
What is the Crème de Tête blend, and does it include any Muscadelle?

producer.who: Gaia Wines, the Greek house making Assyrtiko on Santorini and Agiorgitiko at Nemea
producer.where: Santorini, Greece, with a second operation at Nemea, Peloponnese
producer.history:
Gaia Wines is a Greek house founded in 1994 that runs two separate operations: old-vine Assyrtiko on the volcanic island of Santorini, and Agiorgitiko vineyards at Nemea in the Peloponnese. One name thus covers both of Greece's key answers, the island white and the mainland red.

Santorini lies in the Aegean, swept by constant, salt-laden wind. Growers weave the vines into low baskets, kouloura, that shelter the grapes, and because phylloxera never reached the island's volcanic pumice soils, the vines grow ungrafted on their own roots, many very old, renewed by layering a cane rather than replanting. Assyrtiko keeps ferocious acidity in the heat and tastes of lemon, salt and flint.

Gaia is technically exact and experimental. Its Thalassitis is one of the best-known Santorini names, and it has even aged bottles in the sea off the island. The Wild Ferment is named for its native-yeast fermentation; it is raised partly in a mix of steel, oak, acacia and ceramic, the house's argument for wood on Assyrtiko.

Ours is the Wild Ferment 2023 at $110, bin 1423, printed as Gai'a “Wild Ferment” Assyrtiko Santorini: lemon, salt, flint and white flowers, bone dry, with piercing acidity and a savoury depth. It is our anchor from Greece and the bottle for the Gulf fish en papillote.
facts: Founded in 1994, with two operations: old-vine Assyrtiko on Santorini and Agiorgitiko at Nemea, in the Peloponnese.
Thalassitis is the house's dry Santorini and one of the category's best-known names.
Thalassitis Submerged is aged in the sea off Santorini.
Wild Ferment is fermented with native yeasts and raised partly in steel, oak, acacia and ceramic.
Santorini's vines are trained low in kouloura baskets against the wind, on volcanic pumice soils phylloxera never reached.
Santorini and Nemea are separate PDOs under one producer, and Nemea is Agiorgitiko alone.
The list of 3 October 2026 prints it as Gai'a Wild Ferment Assyrtiko Santorini 2023, bin 1423, $110.
notes: Our wine card respells Gaia GUY-ah, but the Greek word is said nearer YEH-ah: settle the house's sound with the sommelier. Say ah-SEER-tee-koh and san-toh-REE-nee.
Mention the basket vines: guests love the image.
Say native yeasts and mixed vessels, not oaked: how much oak touches the 2023 is a lineup question.
Name no founder or owner: no source here names one.
Asked why it tastes salty: volcanic soil and sea air give Santorini whites a salty, flinty edge.
producer.sayIt: Gaia Wild Ferment Assyrtiko from Santorini: basket-trained volcanic vines and native yeasts, bone dry, salty and lemony, lovely with fish.
askKitchen: Does the 2023 Wild Ferment see oak or acacia in fermentation, and in what share?
Who founded Gaia? Leon Karatsalos and Yiannis Paraskevopoulos are recalled but unconfirmed: confirm before a server says either name.
How does the house say Gaia: GUY-ah, as our cards respell it, or nearer the Greek YEH-ah?

producer.who: Inniskillin, the Niagara winery that made Canadian icewine famous
producer.where: Niagara-on-the-Lake, Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Canada
producer.founded: 1975, by Donald Ziraldo and Karl Kaiser
producer.history:
Inniskillin, said in-ih-SKIL-in, was founded at Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ontario, in 1975 by Donald Ziraldo and Karl Kaiser. On 31 July 1975, as the house tells it, it received the first winery licence granted in Ontario since Prohibition.

Icewine made the name. The Niagara Peninsula lies between Lake Ontario and Lake Erie; the lakes temper the climate and the escarpment traps their air, yet the winters are reliably cold enough to freeze grapes on the vine. Under the VQA rules the grapes must freeze naturally on the vine at minus eight degrees Celsius or colder and be pressed while frozen; artificial freezing is forbidden. The water stays behind as ice, and only a few drops of sweet, concentrated juice run out.

In 1991 Inniskillin's Vidal Icewine 1989 won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in Bordeaux, the moment Canadian icewine arrived on the world stage. The house makes Vidal and Riesling icewines and a red one from Cabernet Franc, a style unusual outside Canada.

Ours is that red: the Cabernet Franc Icewine 2015 at $225, bin 192231, printed as Ice Wine, Niagara Penninsula VQA, 750ml. It is pale ruby, with strawberry, raspberry, red cherry and rhubarb, intensely sweet with vivid acidity, and the bottle for the Blackberry Trifle.
facts: Founded at Niagara-on-the-Lake in 1975 by Donald Ziraldo and Karl Kaiser.
On 31 July 1975 it received the first Ontario winery licence since Prohibition, as the house tells it.
Its Vidal Icewine 1989 won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in Bordeaux in 1991, the breakthrough for Canadian icewine.
VQA Icewine: grapes frozen naturally on the vine at minus eight Celsius or colder and pressed frozen; artificial freezing disqualifies.
Cabernet Franc Icewine is the red style, unusual outside Canada.
The list of 3 October 2026 prints our 2015 at $225, bin 192231, as 750ml; icewine is commonly sold in 375 ml or smaller bottles.
notes: Say in-ih-SKIL-in and nye-AG-rah.
Confirm the bottle size before quoting it: the list prints 750ml, but icewine is usually smaller.
Very sweet: small pours at 46 to 50°F in a small dessert glass.
The Grand Prix d'Honneur was for the Vidal 1989, not for our Cabernet Franc: never transfer the award.
Name the founders; name no current owner, which can change.
producer.sayIt: Inniskillin's red icewine: Cabernet Franc frozen on the vine in a Niagara winter, from the house that made Canadian icewine famous.
askKitchen: Is our 2015 Cabernet Franc Icewine a 375 ml or a 750 ml bottle, as the list prints?
Is it poured by the glass with the Blackberry Trifle, or sold only by the bottle?

producer.who: Bouchard Père & Fils, one of the oldest houses of Beaune
producer.where: Beaune, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
producer.history:
Bouchard Père & Fils is one of the oldest wine houses in Burgundy. In 1731 Michel Bouchard, a cloth merchant, settled in Beaune; his son Joseph became his partner in 1746 and took over the whole business in 1750.

In 1820 Bernard Bouchard bought the Château de Beaune, a fifteenth-century fortress raised under Louis XI, and the family turned its underground galleries into ageing cellars. The Henriot family took the house over in 1995, and the house records a union with Artémis Domaines in 2022.

The Clos de la Mousse, our half-bottle, is one of the house's treasures in Beaune. The oldest trace of it dates to 1220, when Canon Edme de Saudon left it to the Chapter of Notre-Dame de Beaune. It was split up in the Revolution, and the Bouchard family bought it up plot by plot until the last piece came on 13 April 1872, completing all 3.36 hectares inside a stone wall that still stands. It has belonged to Bouchard alone ever since: a monopole, so every bottle of Clos de la Mousse is Bouchard's. The house's other Beaune monopole is the white Clos Saint-Landry.
facts: Michel Bouchard, a cloth merchant, settled in Beaune in 1731; his son Joseph became his partner in 1746.
In 1820 Bernard Bouchard bought the Château de Beaune and turned its underground galleries into ageing cellars.
The Château de Beaune is a fifteenth-century fortress built under Louis XI.
The Clos de la Mousse is first recorded in 1220, left by Canon Edme de Saudon to the Chapter of Notre-Dame de Beaune.
Bouchard completed the walled Clos de la Mousse, 3.36 hectares, with its last plot on 13 April 1872.
The Clos de la Mousse has belonged to Bouchard alone since 1872: a monopole.
The Henriot family took over the house in 1995; the house records a 2022 union with Artémis Domaines.
Bouchard's other Beaune monopole is Clos Saint-Landry, a white premier cru.
notes: Say boo-SHAR pair ay FEESS and Clos de la Mousse kloh duh lah-MOOSS. Every bottle of it is Bouchard's: that is the line.
Guests ask what a clos is: a vineyard enclosed by a wall, and this one's wall still stands.
Ownership is a dated fact (Henriot from 1995, Artémis Domaines from 2022) and can change; say a historic Beaune house.
Do not call it a grand cru; Beaune has none. It is a premier cru, in a half-bottle.
Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus, also on our list, is a named parcel of Beaune Grèves, a different wine.
producer.sayIt: Bouchard's Clos de la Mousse: a walled Beaune Premier Cru the house has owned alone since 1872, silky red cherry and violet.

producer.who: Maison Louis Jadot, one of the great houses of Beaune
producer.where: Beaune, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
producer.founded: 1859; the family bought the Clos des Ursules in 1826
producer.history:
Louis Jadot is one of the great négociant houses of Beaune. The Jadot family, who came from Belgium, bought their first vineyard, the Clos des Ursules in Beaune, in 1826, and Louis Henry Denis Jadot founded the house in 1859. Like most great Burgundy houses it both buys grapes and owns vineyards; wines from its own vines carry a Domaine name, such as Domaine des Héritiers Louis Jadot, which includes the Clos des Ursules.

In the twentieth century the Gagey family became its stewards: André Gagey joined in 1954 and ran the house from 1962, after Louis-Auguste Jadot died young. In 1985 Madame Jadot sold the house to the Kopf family, its longtime US importer. Jacques Lardière, long its head winemaker, joined the house in 1970.

Every Jadot label carries the head of Bacchus, the Roman god of wine, one of the best known emblems in wine. The range runs from Chablis to Beaujolais: by the Codex's records Jadot bought Château des Jacques in Moulin-à-Vent in 1996 and Domaine J.A. Ferret in Pouilly-Fuissé in 2008.

We pour three: the Beaune Premier Cru on the dinner tasting, with the Redfish Véronique, and half-bottles of Beaujolais-Villages and village Meursault. The wine list also carries a deep run of Jadot, from Chevalier-Montrachet Les Demoiselles to Musigny.
facts: The Jadot family bought the Clos des Ursules in Beaune in 1826; Louis Henry Denis Jadot founded the house in 1859.
André Gagey joined in 1954 and ran the house from 1962.
Madame Jadot sold the house in 1985 to the Kopf family, its longtime US importer.
Jacques Lardière, long the house's head winemaker, joined Jadot in 1970.
Every Jadot label carries the head of Bacchus, the Roman god of wine.
Domaine des Héritiers Louis Jadot on a label means estate fruit; the Clos des Ursules is one such wine.
The Codex records Jadot buying Château des Jacques in Moulin-à-Vent in 1996 and Domaine J.A. Ferret in Pouilly-Fuissé in 2008.
notes: Say loo-EE zhah-DOH, and Beaune as bohn. The Beaune Premier Cru is the dinner tasting red, with the redfish; it has no glass price.
Guests ask what the face on the label is: Bacchus, the Roman god of wine.
Jadot is a négociant and a grower: call it a great Beaune house that owns vineyards and buys grapes, never a single estate.
Do not confuse Louis Jadot with Louis Latour, another Beaune house.
Who runs Jadot now is a dated fact and can change; the house, its history and the emblem are the story to tell.
Confirm at lineup that it is tonight's redfish pour: the house website has shown a Jadot Beaune Bressandes Premier Cru 2022 for that course.
producer.sayIt: Louis Jadot's Beaune Premier Cru, from the great house of Beaune with Bacchus on every label: bright red fruit, silky, lovely with the redfish.
askKitchen: Which premiers crus make up our Jadot Beaune 1er Cru 2023, and is it a Maison or a Domaine bottling?
Can the Jadot Beaune be poured à la carte by the glass?

producer.who: Pol Roger, the family house in Épernay that was Winston Churchill’s Champagne
producer.where: Épernay, Champagne, France
producer.founded: 1849, by Pol Roger
producer.history:
Pol Roger founded his house in 1849, making his first sale that January by one account; most sources place the start at Aÿ, with the move to Épernay usually dated 1851. When he died in 1899 his sons Maurice and Georges took over, and in 1900 they adopted the hyphenated family name Pol-Roger by deed poll. The family still owns the house.

Winston Churchill first tasted Pol Roger in 1908 and remained a loyal customer for decades. In 1944, after the liberation of Paris, he met Odette Pol-Roger at the British Embassy in Paris, at a lunch by most accounts, and they became friends; he later named a racehorse Pol Roger, which won at Kempton Park in 1953. When he died in 1965 the house put a black border on the labels it shipped to Britain. Its prestige cuvée, Sir Winston Churchill, began with the 1975 vintage and was launched in magnum in 1984 at Blenheim Palace; its blend has never been published.

Our bottle is the Blanc de Blancs 2015, made only from Chardonnay grown in six grand cru villages of the Côte des Blancs: Oiry, Chouilly, Cramant, Avize, Oger and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger. It aged about six years in the house’s cellars before release.
facts: Founded in 1849 by Pol Roger, at Aÿ by most sources; the move to Épernay is usually dated 1851.
His sons Maurice and Georges adopted the surname Pol-Roger by deed poll in 1900, after their father’s death in 1899.
Winston Churchill first tasted Pol Roger in 1908 and became a friend of Odette Pol-Roger in Paris in 1944.
Churchill named one of his racehorses Pol Roger; it won at Kempton Park in 1953.
After Churchill died in 1965, Pol Roger put a black border on the labels it shipped to Britain.
Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill began with the 1975 vintage and was launched in magnum in 1984 at Blenheim Palace.
The Blanc de Blancs is Chardonnay from six Côte des Blancs grands crus: Oiry, Chouilly, Cramant, Avize, Oger and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger.
The 2015 Blanc de Blancs aged about six years in the house’s cellars; reviewers give its dosage as 7 g/L.
Still owned by the Pol-Roger family, as of October 2026.
notes: Say pohl roh-ZHAY.
Our bottle is the Blanc de Blancs, not the Churchill cuvée. The list also holds Sir Winston Churchill 2013 and 2015 and the Brut NV; name the wine you are pouring.
Sir Winston Churchill is Pinot Noir dominant and its blend has never been published: never quote percentages for it.
Say Pol Roger was Churchill’s Champagne from 1908; the cuvée named for him began with the 1975 vintage, after his death. The black border went on labels for Britain.
Family owned as of October 2026; ownership can change.
producer.sayIt: Pol Roger is the family house in Épernay that Winston Churchill loved; our Blanc de Blancs 2015 is pure grand cru Chardonnay.
askKitchen: For a guest who asks for Churchill’s Champagne, which Sir Winston Churchill do we offer first, the 2013 or the 2015?

producer.who: Laurent-Perrier, the Tours-sur-Marne house of Grand Siècle and the macerated rosé
producer.where: Tours-sur-Marne, Vallée de la Marne, Champagne, France
producer.founded: 1812, at Tours-sur-Marne
producer.history:
Laurent-Perrier dates from 1812, when a former cooper and bottler named Pierlot set up at Tours-sur-Marne, in the Vallée de la Marne. The business passed to his cellar master, Eugène Laurent; when Laurent died in 1887, his widow, Mathilde Emilie Perrier, took charge and joined her name to his, as Veuve Laurent-Perrier.

In 1939 the house, by then close to failing, was bought by Marie-Louise Lanson de Nonancourt (one source says 1938). Her son Bernard de Nonancourt, who had served in the Resistance and with General Leclerc’s 2nd Armoured Division, took charge in 1948 or 1949 and multiplied its sales many times over.

He gave the house its signatures: Grand Siècle, a prestige blend of several great vintages launched around 1959 or 1960 in a bottle modelled on a seventeenth-century design; the Cuvée Rosé of 1968, coloured by leaving Pinot Noir on its skins rather than by blending in red wine; and in 1981 the zero-dosage Ultra Brut, which one source calls a reintroduction. The group also owns Salon, bought in 1988 or 1989.

Our half-bottle is Harmony, the demi-sec. Retailers give about 45 percent Chardonnay, 40 percent Pinot Noir and 15 percent Meunier, and the house’s own copy a dosage of 40 g/L of cane sugar: gently sweet and made for dessert.
facts: Founded at Tours-sur-Marne in 1812 by a former cooper and bottler named Pierlot.
The name joins cellar master Eugène Laurent and his widow, Mathilde Emilie Perrier, who ran the house after his death in 1887.
Marie-Louise Lanson de Nonancourt bought it in 1939; her son Bernard de Nonancourt took charge in 1948 or 1949.
Bernard de Nonancourt served in the Resistance and with General Leclerc’s 2nd Armoured Division.
Grand Siècle, launched around 1959 or 1960, is a prestige blend of several vintages in a bottle copied from a seventeenth-century design.
The Cuvée Rosé, launched in 1968, takes its colour from Pinot Noir skins rather than from blending in red wine.
The zero-dosage Ultra Brut dates from 1981, long before the style was fashionable; one source calls it a reintroduction.
Retailers give Harmony as about 45 percent Chardonnay, 40 Pinot Noir and 15 Meunier; the house’s copy gives 40 g/L of cane sugar.
Laurent-Perrier has owned Salon, the one-wine house of Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, since 1988 or 1989.
notes: Say loh-RAHN peh-RYAY.
Harmony is sweet. Offer it with dessert or the Framboise French Toast; never pour it for a guest who asked for a dry toast.
Guests ask why demi-sec, half dry, tastes sweet. The honest answer: demi-sec names the sweeter style, and Harmony carries about 40 g/L of sugar, far more than a Brut.
The list also holds Grand Siècle Iteration No. 20, No. 24 and No. 25, and a Rosé magnum it prints as 1959; the Cuvée Rosé began in 1968, so check that year before quoting it.
Salon has belonged to the same group since 1988 or 1989, which makes Harmony and Salon the two ends of one group’s range on our list.
producer.sayIt: Laurent-Perrier is the Tours-sur-Marne house of Grand Siècle and the macerated rosé; Harmony is its gently sweet demi-sec, made for dessert.
askKitchen: The list prints a Laurent-Perrier Rosé Brut magnum as 1959 at $5000: what year is on the bottle, given the Cuvée Rosé began in 1968?
May we print Harmony’s blend, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, where its card leaves the grapes empty?

producer.who: Piper-Heidsieck, the Reims Champagne house behind our house Champagne
producer.where: Reims, Champagne, France
producer.founded: 1785, by Florens-Louis Heidsieck
producer.history:
Piper-Heidsieck was founded in Reims in 1785 by Florens-Louis Heidsieck, and the house tells that he presented his Champagne to Queen Marie Antoinette. His nephew Christian Heidsieck joined the firm, and Henri-Guillaume Piper was working in it in the founder’s lifetime, from about 1815 by one account. After Florens-Louis died in 1828 Christian ran the house; after Christian died, his widow married Piper, and the two names were joined in the nineteenth century. Charles Heidsieck and Heidsieck & Co Monopole are separate houses.

For its centenary in 1885 the house commissioned Fabergé to design a jewelled bottle. It was never made as drawn, but the idea lives on in the golden dress of Rare, first made from the 1976 harvest as Piper’s prestige cuvée and sold as its own house since 2018.

The Cuvée Brut is Pinot Noir-led, with Meunier and Chardonnay from more than a hundred crus, and reserve wines keep the house style steady. Essentiel is a separate Extra Brut cuvée; its technical figures vary by release and do not identify Brennan’s private label. At Brennan’s the house Champagne is a Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut labelled Brennan’s Essential; a 2024 NOWFE event page called it Brennan’s private-label Piper-Heidsieck, and which Piper cuvée fills the bottle is for the sommelier to confirm.
facts: Founded in Reims in 1785 by Florens-Louis Heidsieck, who, the house tells, presented his Champagne to Queen Marie Antoinette.
Henri-Guillaume Piper joined the firm in the founder’s lifetime, about 1815 by one account, and later married the widow of Christian Heidsieck, the founder’s nephew.
Charles Heidsieck and Heidsieck & Co Monopole are separate houses; only Piper-Heidsieck makes our house Champagne.
For its 1885 centenary the house commissioned a jewelled bottle design from Fabergé; the bottle was never made as drawn.
The Cuvée Brut blends Pinot Noir, up to about half, with Meunier and Chardonnay from more than a hundred crus, plus reserve wines.
Essentiel’s blend and technical figures vary by bottling. A standard cuvée sheet does not confirm the blend, dosage or lees age of Brennan’s private label.
A June 2024 NOWFE event at Brennan’s poured Brennan’s private-label Piper-Heidsieck Essential beside Charles Heidsieck and Piper’s Rosé Sauvage.
Rare, first made from the 1976 harvest as Piper’s prestige cuvée, has been sold as a separate house since September 2018.
notes: Say PIE-per HIDE-sek; the house’s own people say PEE-pair HIDE-seek, and either is understood. Never shorten it to Heidsieck: three houses share that name.
Say labelled for Brennan’s, not made for us. Which Piper cuvée is in the bottle, and its dosage, is for the sommelier to confirm.
Extra Brut means 0 to 6 grams of sugar per liter in the finished wine; Brut is less than 12. The ranges overlap, so neither label proves which bottle tastes drier.
The Birthday Bubbles magnum is Cuvée Brut, a different label from Brennan’s Essential Extra Brut. Confirm the actual bottlings before comparing sweetness or texture.
Tell the Marie Antoinette story as the house’s own: say the house tells it, not that it is proven history.
producer.sayIt: Our house Champagne is an Extra Brut from Piper-Heidsieck, labelled for Brennan’s: very dry, from a Reims house founded in 1785.
askKitchen: Is Brennan’s Essential Piper-Heidsieck’s Essentiel Extra Brut under our label, or a blend made for us, and what disgorgement date is on the back label?
Which glass price stands for the house Champagne, $28 on Binwise or $30 on the menus?
Is the Birthday Bubbles magnum the Piper-Heidsieck Cuvée Brut, as printed, and is it in stock?

producer.who: Rare Champagne, the prestige vintage house that began at Piper-Heidsieck
producer.where: Reims, Champagne, France
producer.founded: First vintage 1976, as Piper-Heidsieck’s prestige cuvée; its own house since 2018
producer.history:
Rare began as Piper-Heidsieck’s prestige cuvée. Its first vintage was 1976, a year of unprecedented heat in Champagne, and it has been declared since only in years of extremes, when, as the house tells it, nature unleashes its forces. Counts of its vintages differ from source to source, and by whether the rosés are included.

The bottle wears a golden dress of leaves. Its story starts with Piper-Heidsieck’s centenary in 1885, when Fabergé was commissioned to design a jewelled bottle that was never made as drawn; in the 1980s the Paris workshop Arthus-Bertrand refined the idea into the golden crown that wraps the lower part of the bottle.

In September 2018 Rare became its own house, labelled and sold apart from Piper-Heidsieck, and the third Champagne house of the group that then held Piper-Heidsieck and Charles Heidsieck.

The wine is Chardonnay-led. The 2013, by its technical sheet, is 70 percent Chardonnay and 30 percent Pinot Noir from eleven crus, seven grand cru and three premier cru, aged at least eight years on its lees with 9 g/L of dosage, a Brut. Brennan’s pours Rare by the glass under a Coravin Sparkling stopper, lists the 2013 by the bottle, and keeps older vintages and Rare Rosé in large formats.
facts: First vintage 1976, a year of unprecedented heat, made as Piper-Heidsieck’s prestige cuvée.
Declared only in exceptional years, which the house describes as years of extremes; counts of the vintages differ by source.
Labelled, marketed and sold as its own house since September 2018, then the third Champagne house of the group holding Piper-Heidsieck and Charles Heidsieck.
The golden leaf dress was refined by the Paris workshop Arthus-Bertrand in the 1980s, after an 1885 Fabergé bottle design for Piper-Heidsieck.
Rare 2013: 70 percent Chardonnay and 30 percent Pinot Noir from eleven crus, seven of them grand cru and three premier cru.
The 2013 spent at least eight years on its lees and carries 9 g/L of dosage, which makes it a Brut.
Our list also holds Rare 1998 in magnum, Rare 2008 in a 6 L, and Rare Rosé 2012 and 2014 in large formats.
notes: Say Rare as the English word; the French say RAHR. Read the vintage on the label before naming it: Binwise prints 2012 for the glass, the current glass page 2013.
Do not say every grape comes from grand cru sites: the 2013 drew on eleven crus, mostly grand and premier cru. Say great crus, Chardonnay-led.
Guests ask how a vintage this fine can be poured by the glass. The honest answer: the opened bottle sits under a Coravin Sparkling stopper that keeps it fizzy.
Never say Piper-Heidsieck makes it today: it began there and has been its own house since 2018.
Do not quote an exact count of vintages: counts differ by source and by whether the rosés are included. Say only in exceptional years.
producer.sayIt: Rare is a prestige vintage Champagne, Chardonnay-led, first made in 1976 and declared only in exceptional years; I can pour it by the glass.
askKitchen: Which Rare vintage is open by the glass tonight, 2012 or 2013?
How long does the bar keep an opened Rare under the Coravin Sparkling stopper before it is retired?
Can the Rare large formats (1998 magnum, 2008 Methuselah, Rare Rosé) be ordered ahead, and with how much notice?

producer.who: Champagne Drappier, a family house in the Côte des Bar
producer.where: Urville, Côte des Bar (Aube), Champagne, France
producer.founded: 1808, when the family settled at Urville
producer.history:
The Drappier family settled at Urville, in the centre of the Côte des Bar in the Aube, in 1808, and still runs the house there. This is Champagne’s far south, nearer Chablis than Reims, and Pinot Noir country. The house dates its Urville cellars to 1152 and to Saint Bernard and the monks of Clairvaux, who brought Pinot from Burgundy; it tells that as its own history.

The house dates the family’s Pinot Noir plantings at Urville to the early 1930s, and Pinot Noir leads its vineyard, about 70 percent by one source. In 1952 the house introduced the Carte d’Or, still known by its yellow label; one guide credits André and Michelle Drappier. André Drappier died in 2025, aged 99.

The house is known for using very little sulphur, for a Brut Nature with no dosage, and for very large bottles, up to the 30 litre Melchizedek.

Its most famous customer lived nearby. General Charles de Gaulle’s home, La Boisserie, was at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises, and from 1965 the family’s Pinot Noir Champagne was poured there. The house makes a Cuvée Charles de Gaulle, by one source created for the fiftieth anniversary of his appeal of 18 June 1940: 80 percent Pinot Noir, 20 percent Chardonnay.
facts: The Drappier family settled at Urville, in the Côte des Bar in the Aube, in 1808 and still runs the house.
The house dates its Urville cellars to 1152 and the monks of Clairvaux; it tells this as its own history.
Pinot Noir leads its vineyard, about 70 percent by one source; the house dates the family’s Pinot Noir plantings at Urville to the early 1930s.
Carte d’Or, with its yellow label, was introduced in 1952.
Carte d’Or is Pinot Noir-led with a little Chardonnay and Meunier; sources give between 75 and 90 percent Pinot Noir.
Charles de Gaulle, whose home La Boisserie was at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises, drank Drappier from 1965; a Cuvée Charles de Gaulle honours him.
Known for low sulphur and very large bottles: it fills the 30 litre Melchizedek and, by one account, is the only maker of the 27 litre Primat.
Our list carries the Carte d’Or in half-bottle and 6 L, the Brut Nature, and Grande Sendrée 2010 and 2012.
notes: Say drah-PYAY. A good answer to where is it from: the Côte des Bar, far south of Reims, Pinot Noir country.
Offer it to the guest who loves Pinot Noir or a fuller Champagne; the half-bottle suits two people at a birthday.
Tell the de Gaulle story as sourced: he lived near Urville and drank the family’s Champagne from 1965. Do not claim state dinners.
Do not quote the Carte d’Or blend as fixed: sources give 75 to 90 percent Pinot Noir. Say mostly Pinot Noir.
Binwise lists the Carte d’Or only as a 6 L; confirm the half-bottle is in stock before offering it.
Low sulphur is how the house works, not a health promise: send any sulphite question to the sommelier or the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Drappier is a family house in Champagne’s far south, Pinot Noir country; General de Gaulle, who lived nearby, drank it from 1965.
askKitchen: Is the Drappier Carte d’Or half-bottle in stock, since Binwise lists the Carte d’Or only as a 6 L?
Does the 6 L Carte d’Or need ordering ahead, and who opens it?

producer.who: Champagne Taittinger of Reims, the house of Comtes de Champagne
producer.where: Reims, Champagne, France
producer.founded: 1734, as a trading house; the Taittinger name since 1932
producer.history:
In the cellar, Taittinger’s story is told through Chardonnay. The house gives that grape a bigger part than most of the great houses do, and its prestige wine is all Chardonnay: Comtes de Champagne Blanc de Blancs, first made from the 1952 vintage, drawn in most years from the grand cru villages of the Côte des Blancs and made only in the best years.

The name comes from Reims history. The family bought the thirteenth century House of the Counts of Champagne, in the rue de Tambour, after it was bombed in the First World War, and restored it under the Ministry of Fine Arts. By tradition the counts, Thibaud IV among them, stayed there when they came to Reims for royal coronations, and the house still uses it for receptions.

The Prestige Rosé blends all three grapes, with 12 to 15 percent still red Pinot Noir for its colour, some of it, by one source, from the Montagne de Reims and Les Riceys. La Française, the non-vintage Brut that also tops the Flamingo, sits on Birthday Bubbles in a 3 litre double magnum, and the list carries it in a 12 litre and Comtes de Champagne 2011 in magnum.
facts: Comtes de Champagne Blanc de Blancs, Taittinger’s prestige wine, was first made from the 1952 vintage and is made only in the best years.
In most years Comtes de Champagne comes from the grand cru villages of the Côte des Blancs.
The family bought and restored the thirteenth century House of the Counts of Champagne in Reims after it was bombed in the First World War.
By tradition the Counts of Champagne, Thibaud IV among them, stayed in that house for royal coronations at Reims; Taittinger uses it for receptions.
Prestige Rosé blends Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier and takes its colour from 12 to 15 percent still red Pinot Noir.
Our list carries Comtes de Champagne 2011 in magnum and La Française up to a 12 litre bottle.
notes: Say TAT-in-jer, as most American guests do; the French say teh-tan-ZHAY, which the bar’s card uses. Either is understood.
The double magnum of La Française is the same wine that tops the Flamingo: a good bridge for a guest who loved the cocktail.
Prestige Rosé is dry, a Brut: offer it to the guest who wants a pink Champagne with a lighter, fresher touch.
Do not quote the Prestige Rosé blend as fixed: sources give Chardonnay anywhere from 30 to 50 percent. Say a blend of the three grapes, coloured with red Pinot Noir.
Comtes de Champagne Blanc de Blancs is the vintage Chardonnay; a Comtes de Champagne Rosé also exists and is a different wine. Read the label.
producer.sayIt: Taittinger is the Reims house that favours Chardonnay; its Prestige Rosé is dry and fresh, coloured with a little red Pinot Noir.
askKitchen: Does the Taittinger Prestige Rosé keep its Bubbles price outside Bubbles hours?
Can the 12 litre La Française be ordered, and with how much notice?

producer.who: Moët & Chandon, the Épernay house
producer.where: Épernay, Champagne, France
producer.founded: 1743, by Claude Moët
producer.history:
Moët & Chandon began in Épernay in 1743, when the wine trader Claude Moët set up Moët et Cie. His grandson Jean-Rémy Moët became a friend of Napoleon Bonaparte, who is said to have given him his own Cross of the Legion of Honour. In 1833 Pierre-Gabriel Chandon de Briailles, Jean-Rémy’s son-in-law, became a partner, and the house took the name Moët & Chandon.

The Impérial name, which the house dates to 1869 (others say the 1860s), honours Napoleon; our menus and cards print it Imperial, without the accent. Moët is one of the largest Champagne producers, and Dom Pérignon is its prestige cuvée.

Its rosés are made by blending separately made red and white still wines. The Imperial Rosé we pour at Bubbles, which Moët labels Rosé Impérial, is a Brut: by the house’s ranges, 40 to 50 percent Pinot Noir, 30 to 40 percent Meunier and 10 to 20 percent Chardonnay, with 20 to 30 percent reserve wines and about 7 g/L of dosage. The Nectar Imperial Rosé is a much sweeter wine, about 45 g/L by one listing, in the demi-sec range: a dessert Champagne, for the guest who likes it soft.
facts: Founded in Épernay in 1743 by the wine trader Claude Moët, as Moët et Cie.
Jean-Rémy Moët, his grandson, was a friend of Napoleon Bonaparte; the Impérial name honours the emperor.
The house became Moët & Chandon in 1833, when Pierre-Gabriel Chandon de Briailles, Jean-Rémy’s son-in-law, became a partner.
The house dates its Impérial to 1869; other sources say the 1860s or 1862.
The Imperial Rosé, Moët’s Rosé Impérial, by the house’s ranges: 40 to 50 percent Pinot Noir, 30 to 40 Meunier, 10 to 20 Chardonnay; about 7 g/L dosage.
Moët makes its rosé by blending separately made still red and white wines.
The Nectar Imperial Rosé carries about 45 g/L of sugar by one listing, in the demi-sec range: a sweet Champagne.
Our list also holds Grand Vintage 2015 and Grand Vintage Rosé 2012, both Extra Brut.
notes: Say moh-ET, sounding the t: moh-ET ay shahn-DOHN in full.
Never swap the two pinks: the Imperial Rosé at Bubbles is dry, a Brut; the Nectar Imperial Rosé on the bottle list is sweet, for dessert.
Moët writes Impérial with an accent; our menus and cards print Imperial. It is the same name.
Guests ask whether Moët is the best Champagne. The honest answer: it is the best-known house style, made for consistency; the sommelier can suggest a step up.
Tell Napoleon as friendship and homage; do not say the emperor owned or founded the house.
Whether the Imperial Rosé is sold outside Bubbles is a lineup question.
producer.sayIt: Moët & Chandon, founded in Épernay in 1743; its Impérial name honours Napoleon, a friend of the family. This rosé is dry.
askKitchen: Is the Moët Imperial Rosé Brut sold outside Bubbles at Brennan’s, and at what price?
With which desserts does the sommelier want the Nectar Imperial Rosé offered?

producer.who: Dönnhoff, a family estate at Oberhausen and the Nahe's most famous grower
producer.where: Oberhausen, Nahe, Germany; the Hermannshöhle lies in neighbouring Niederhausen
producer.founded: 1750, as the Codex records it
producer.history:
Dönnhoff is a family estate at Oberhausen on the Nahe, the small river valley between the Mosel and the Rhine. The Codex gives 1750 as its founding year. Helmut Dönnhoff is the grower who made the name known around the world, and the Codex records that Cornelius Dönnhoff has followed him.

The Nahe is its own region, not a corner of the Mosel or Rheinhessen, and its soils change from volcanic rock and porphyry to slate and sandstone, sometimes within one vineyard. Dönnhoff's Rieslings show that mix as stone and smoke rather than loud fruit: crystalline and precise, between the delicacy of the Mosel and the breadth of the Rheingau.

Two of its vineyards are on our list. The Oberhäuser Brücke is a tiny vineyard beside the old bridge over the Nahe, and the Dönnhoff family are its only owners; the Codex calls it the source of the estate's finest sweet wines and Eiswein. The Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle, in the next village, a steep site of slate and volcanic rock, is the vineyard most often called the Nahe's greatest, and Dönnhoff is its best known grower. The estate's dry wine from it is a Grosses Gewächs, the VDP's name for a dry wine from its top tier of sites.

We pour both vineyards as gold capsule Auslesen from 2023, in half-bottles. A Goldkapsel is the grower's own mark of a richer selection, not a legal category.
facts: A family estate at Oberhausen on the Nahe; the Codex gives its founding year as 1750.
Helmut Dönnhoff made the estate's name; the Codex records that Cornelius Dönnhoff followed him.
The Oberhäuser Brücke, a tiny vineyard beside the old bridge over the Nahe, is owned by the Dönnhoff family alone.
The Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle, on slate and volcanic rock at Niederhausen, is often called the Nahe's greatest vineyard; Dönnhoff is its best known grower.
The Nahe is its own German wine region, not part of the Mosel or Rheinhessen, with soils from volcanic rock and porphyry to slate and sandstone.
Goldkapsel, the gold capsule, is a grower's mark of a richer selection within the same Prädikat, not a legal category.
Our list also prints Dönnhoff's dry Hermannshöhle Grosses Gewächs 2023 and magnums of Hermannshöhle and of Brücke Spätlese.
notes: Say DURN-hoff; Oberhäuser Brücke OH-ber-hoy-zer BROO-kuh, Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle NEE-der-hoy-zer HAIR-mahns-hur-luh, Goldkapsel GOLT-kap-sel.
The list spells it Dönhoff with one n; the estate is Dönnhoff. Find the halves by bin: 32821 for the Brücke, 32843 for the Hermannshöhle.
Both are sweet. Point to the gold capsule when you present the bottle and say it marks a richer selection chosen by the grower, not a legal grade.
The Brücke for lemon and citrus desserts, the Hermannshöhle for the trifle and the cheese board; a half-bottle gives about four small dessert pours.
Only the Brücke is the family's alone. For the Hermannshöhle say best known grower, never owner.
If asked who makes it: Helmut Dönnhoff made the name and Cornelius Dönnhoff followed him. Say nothing more about the family today without the sommelier.
producer.sayIt: Dönnhoff, the Nahe's most famous family estate: gold capsule Auslesen from the Brücke and the Hermannshöhle, sweet, racy and bright.
askKitchen: How sweet does each 2023 Goldkapsel Auslese taste now, and which do you prefer with the cheese board?
May a single dessert pour be sold from a Dönnhoff half-bottle, or only the whole half?

producer.who: Weingut Keller, a family estate at Flörsheim-Dalsheim and one of Germany's most admired growers
producer.where: Flörsheim-Dalsheim, Wonnegau, Rheinhessen, Germany
producer.founded: 1789, as the Codex records it
producer.history:
Weingut Keller is a family estate at Flörsheim-Dalsheim, in the Wonnegau district of southern Rheinhessen. The Codex gives 1789 as its founding year.

Rheinhessen is Germany's largest wine region, and for decades its name meant cheap, sweet export wine. The Wonnegau, around Westhofen and Dalsheim, became the centre of its dry-wine revival, and Keller is the estate most associated with that turn. Its limestone and clay sites include the Dalsheimer Hubacker and, at Westhofen, the Morstein, the Kirchspiel and the Abtserde, with later vineyards on the Roter Hang at Nierstein.

Its fame rests on dry Riesling of extreme tension, low in alcohol for its concentration. Klaus Peter Keller's G-Max, which the Codex dates to 2001 and names for his grandfather Georg and his son Maximilian, is in the Codex's words the most sought-after dry German Riesling of the modern era, and its vineyard has never been disclosed.

In good years Keller also makes sweet wines from late harvest and botrytis grapes. PIUS is one of them: an Auslese blended from grape varieties that change with the vintage, by two retailers' accounts. Our list carries a deep run of Keller, from the dry Von der Fels to the Morstein and Hubacker Grosses Gewächs; PIUS is the half-bottle for dessert.
facts: A family estate at Flörsheim-Dalsheim in Rheinhessen; the Codex gives its founding year as 1789.
Rheinhessen is Germany's largest wine region; the Wonnegau, around Westhofen and Dalsheim, became the centre of its dry-wine revival.
Its sites include the Dalsheimer Hubacker and, at Westhofen, the Morstein, Kirchspiel and Abtserde, on limestone and clay.
G-Max, which the Codex dates to 2001, is named for Klaus Peter Keller's grandfather Georg and son Maximilian; its vineyard is undisclosed.
The house style is dry Riesling of great tension, low in alcohol for its concentration, with no obvious oak.
PIUS is a sweet Auslese of late harvest and botrytis grapes; the varieties change with the vintage.
Our list prints Keller's Von der Fels, Limestone Kabinett, Abts Erde Kabinett, RR Feinherb, Hubacker and Morstein Grosses Gewächs, and PIUS.
Grosses Gewächs is the VDP's name for a dry wine from a Grosse Lage, its top tier of sites.
notes: Say KELL-er, PIUS PEE-oos and Auslese OWS-lay-zuh.
The list files PIUS under Riesling and once prints it Riesling Auslese, but its grapes change by vintage. Say a sweet Auslese blend and leave the 2022's grapes to the sommelier.
Keller is a cult name and its wines are rare: treat the half-bottle as a find, about four small dessert pours, for the Pineapple Tarte Tatin.
Keller is the estate, not the German word for cellar, and not Kellerberg, the Wachau vineyard behind Emmerich Knoll's Riesling on the same list.
If asked who makes it: Klaus Peter Keller is the name behind its modern fame. Say nothing more about the family today without the sommelier.
producer.sayIt: Keller is Rheinhessen's cult family estate, famous for dry Riesling; PIUS is its sweet Auslese, honeyed apricot and pineapple, pure and bright.
askKitchen: Which grapes are in the PIUS 2022, and does its label say Riesling?
May a single dessert pour be sold from the PIUS half-bottle?

producer.who: Kracher, the Weinlaubenhof at Illmitz, Austria's great sweet wine estate
producer.where: Illmitz, Seewinkel, on the eastern shore of the Neusiedlersee, Burgenland, Austria
producer.history:
Kracher, properly Weinlaubenhof Kracher, is a family estate at Illmitz, between the village and the shore of the Neusiedlersee in Burgenland, Austria's easternmost region, on the Hungarian border. The corner of the lake around Illmitz is the Seewinkel, flat land dotted with shallow salt ponds.

The lake is wide and very shallow. In autumn, mist rises off it and the pools around it in the morning and the afternoon sun burns it away, a rhythm that brings noble rot to the grapes almost every year, which is rare anywhere in the world.

Alois Kracher made the estate's sweet wines world famous from the late 1980s until his early death in 2007. Its great wines are the numbered Trockenbeerenauslesen, released each vintage in two lines: Zwischen den Seen, without new oak, for pure fruit, and Nouvelle Vague, in new barrique, for spice and toast. The estate made Welschriesling, a grape unrelated to Riesling, a serious sweet wine grape. As of October 2026, his son Gerhard runs the estate; that can change.

Our bottle is lighter than those: the Cuvée Auslese 2017, Welschriesling with Chardonnay, fermented and matured in stainless steel to stay fresh. Pear, quince, mandarin, passion fruit and orange blossom honey, creamy, with fresh acidity.
facts: Weinlaubenhof Kracher lies between the village of Illmitz and the shore of the Neusiedlersee, in Burgenland.
Autumn mist off the shallow lake and its pools, burned off by afternoon sun, brings noble rot almost every year.
Alois Kracher made its sweet wines world famous from the late 1980s until his early death in 2007.
His son Gerhard runs the estate, as of October 2026.
Its numbered Trockenbeerenauslesen come in two lines: Zwischen den Seen without new oak, Nouvelle Vague in new barrique.
Welschriesling, the estate's great sweet grape, is unrelated to Riesling.
Our Cuvée Auslese 2017 blends Welschriesling and Chardonnay, fermented and matured in stainless steel; sources disagree on the proportions.
The list prints it as Alois Kracher Auslese Burgenland 2017, in 750 ml.
notes: Say KRAH-ker, Illmitz ILL-mits, Burgenland BOOR-gen-land and Auslese OWS-lay-zuh.
The list prints Alois Kracher Auslese; our wine card calls it the Cuvée Auslese. Both mean bin 19234; confirm the label at lineup.
Bin 19234 is also printed for a Calera Viognier Doux and a Cinelli Colombini Vin Santo: fetch by name, not by bin alone.
Never call this Auslese a Trockenbeerenauslese or say it is aged in oak; it is the lighter, steel-kept style.
Do not give the Welschriesling and Chardonnay proportions; sources disagree. Who runs the estate can change: Gerhard Kracher ran it as of October 2026.
producer.sayIt: Kracher of Illmitz, Austria's great sweet wine estate by the Neusiedlersee: this Auslese is pear, mandarin and passion fruit, creamy and fresh.
askKitchen: Does our label read Cuvée Auslese, is the bottle 750 ml or 375 ml, and what is the 2017's grape split?

producer.who: La Miraja, the family estate in the castle of Castagnole Monferrato that makes our Barbera by the glass
producer.where: Castagnole Monferrato, Asti, Piemonte, Italy
producer.history:
La Miraja is a family estate in the hills of Asti, in Piemonte in north-west Italy. Its cellar is in the old castle of Castagnole Monferrato, whose armoury became a cellar in the 1400s.

Le Masche is its Barbera d'Asti, all Barbera from the Majole vineyard. The name recalls the masche, the spirits of local folklore believed to protect the vineyard. The producer's sheet describes native fermentation in steel tanks and at least twelve months in neutral oak, which keeps the fruit and acidity in front. That sheet is written for its Barbera d'Asti Superiore, a tier that must age 14 months, six of them in wood, and our menu prints Barbera d'Asti, so the sommelier confirms how this bottle was aged.

Barbera is Piemonte's everyday red: deep in colour, high in acidity and low in tannin, the opposite structure to Nebbiolo, its Piedmontese neighbour. Castagnole Monferrato is also the home of Ruchè, a different, aromatic red grape.

Ours is the 2023 at $16 a glass, new on the glass page of 3 October 2026 and our one Italian glass: dark cherry and plum, bright and juicy, the first pick for Maggie's Mushrooms.
facts: La Miraja is a family estate whose cellar is in the old castle of Castagnole Monferrato, an armoury that became a cellar in the 1400s.
Le Masche is all Barbera from the Majole vineyard; the name recalls the local spirits believed to protect the vineyard.
The producer's sheet, written for its Barbera d'Asti Superiore, describes native fermentation in steel and at least twelve months in neutral oak.
Barbera d'Asti is a DOCG with two tiers; the Superiore needs 14 months of ageing, six of them in wood.
Barbera is high in acidity and low in tannin, deep in colour: the opposite structure to Nebbiolo.
Castagnole Monferrato is also the home of Ruchè, a different, aromatic red grape.
Ours is the 2023 at $16 a glass, new on the glass page of 3 October 2026 and not on the Binwise list.
notes: Say lah mee-RAH-yah, leh MAHS-keh, bar-BEAR-ah DAHS-tee. Le Masche is the wine's name; La Miraja is the producer.
Present it as our one Italian glass: a juicy Piemonte red with bright acidity and soft tannin, for a guest who wants red at lunch without weight.
Guests ask what Le Masche means. The honest answer: the masche are spirits of local folklore, said to watch over the vineyard. Keep it light; it is a story, not a claim about the wine.
Never promise how long it spent in oak: the producer's sheet is for its Superiore, so the sommelier confirms this bottle.
It is printed by the glass only, so a bottle request goes to the sommelier. Do not confuse it with the Massolino Barbera d'Alba on the bottle list.
producer.sayIt: Our Barbera comes from a castle cellar in Piemonte: dark cherry, bright and juicy, soft tannin, lovely with the mushrooms.
askKitchen: Is Le Masche poured tonight, is the 2023 open, and does the label read Barbera d'Asti or Barbera d'Asti Superiore?

producer.who: Giuseppe Quintarelli, the great traditionalist of Valpolicella, in the hills above Negrar
producer.where: Negrar, Valpolicella Classico, Veneto, Italy
producer.history:
The Quintarelli estate is in the hills above Negrar, a commune of the Valpolicella Classico zone near Verona, and it dates from 1924. Giuseppe Quintarelli, called Bepi, born in 1927, ran it from the early 1950s until his death in 2012 and became the benchmark traditionalist of Valpolicella. The Codex names him with Guigal and López de Heredia as a producer so dominant that his house style reads as the region's own.

His method was patience. The grapes were dried for months on racks and in crates in drying lofts, the appassimento, and the wines aged for years in large Slavonian casks and were released late, the Amarone many years after the harvest. In vintages he thought unworthy he declared no Amarone and bottled the fruit as Rosso del Bepi instead. Alzero, made the same way from Cabernet grapes, cannot be called Amarone. His hand-written labels became part of the legend, and his family carries the estate on.

Recioto della Valpolicella, the sweet ancestor of Amarone, is made the same way but stopped while still sweet; it became a DOCG in 2009.

Ours is the Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997 at $500, twenty-nine years old, the celebration bottle with the Blackberry Trifle.
facts: The estate above Negrar, in Valpolicella Classico near Verona, dates from 1924.
Giuseppe Quintarelli, called Bepi (1927 to 2012), ran it from the early 1950s; his family carries it on.
Grapes dried for months on racks and in crates, years in large Slavonian casks, and late release.
In years without a declared Amarone, the fruit goes into Rosso del Bepi.
Alzero is made from dried Cabernet grapes, bottled as IGT, and cannot be called Amarone.
Recioto is made from dried Corvina, Corvinone, Rondinella and other local grapes, stopped while sweet; Amarone is fermented dry.
Recioto della Valpolicella became a DOCG in 2009.
Ours: Recioto 1997, $500, bin 19321. The same bin is printed for Taylor Fladgate Quinta de Vargellas 1987.
notes: Say kwin-tah-REL-lee, reh-CHOH-toh, val-poh-lee-CHEL-lah. Present it as a true rarity: a sweet red from the legend of Valpolicella.
Guests ask if it is like Amarone. The honest answer: made the same way from dried grapes, but Recioto is left sweet and Amarone is dry.
Quintarelli's Amarone and Rosso del Bepi on our list are dry reds, not dessert wines; Amabile del Cere is the other sweet one.
Ring it by name: bin 19321 is also printed for a 1987 Port.
Say his family carries the estate on; do not name who runs it today.
producer.sayIt: Quintarelli's Recioto is a sweet red from dried grapes by the legend of Valpolicella: dark cherry, fig and chocolate, lovely with the Blackberry Trifle.
askKitchen: Bin 19321 is printed for both the Quintarelli Recioto 1997 and the Taylor Fladgate Vargellas 1987: which is right?
The list files Quintarelli Ca' del Merlo 2023 and 2024 under Italian whites: is that a white wine or a filing slip?
Which grapes are in our Alzero 2007: the Codex says Cabernet Franc; does the label agree?

producer.who: Paul Hobbs, the California winemaker, and his Coombsville Cabernet
producer.where: Sebastopol, Sonoma County, with an estate in Coombsville, Napa Valley, California
producer.founded: 1991, by Paul Hobbs
producer.history:
Paul Hobbs is a winemaker's winery. Hobbs learned his craft making wine for others: at Robert Mondavi in the years of the first Opus One, then as winemaker at Simi, and from the late 1980s as a consultant in Mendoza, before founding his own label in 1991, with its winery at Sebastopol in Sonoma County. He founded Viña Cobos in Mendoza, Argentina, and Crocus, a Malbec from Cahors, is his project with a local partner; both are on our list.

His Napa estate is in Coombsville, a horseshoe of low hills east of the city of Napa, open to San Pablo Bay. Bay air makes it one of the coolest corners of Napa: Cabernet there ripens later than Oakville's, on poor, free-draining ash and tuff from the long-collapsed Mount George volcano, and comes in fresher and higher in acid. The estate is named for Nathan Coombs, who founded the city of Napa.

Our list carries his single vineyard Cabernets, the Nathan Coombs Estate and Beckstoffer Dr. Crane from St. Helena. The dinner tasting pours the Coombsville Cabernet Sauvignon 2021 with the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast: dark fruit, cocoa and firm structure, young enough to want air.
facts: Paul Hobbs founded his winery in 1991 at Sebastopol, Sonoma County, as the winery tells it.
Before 1991 he worked at Robert Mondavi in the first Opus One years, then as winemaker at Simi, and consulted in Mendoza from the late 1980s.
His Napa estate is in Coombsville and is named for Nathan Coombs, the founder of the city of Napa.
Coombsville is open to San Pablo Bay: one of Napa's coolest corners, where Cabernet ripens later than in Oakville, by the Codex.
Its soils are ash and tuff from the long-collapsed Mount George volcano, free-draining and poor, by the Codex.
The list prints his Nathan Coombs Estate 2014 and 2015 and Beckstoffer Dr. Crane Vineyard 2015 from St. Helena.
He founded Viña Cobos in Mendoza, and Crocus in Cahors is his project with a local partner; both are on our list.
Our Coombsville 2021 is printed only as a 4 oz pour, with the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast on the dinner tasting's $120 wine pairing.
notes: Say KOOMZ-vil: the b is silent. Hobbs is HOBZ.
It is the dinner tasting's Cabernet, the fourth course's 4 oz pour with no glass price; the Jadot Beaune before it is the other red. A glass on its own is a question for the sommelier.
The Nathan Coombs Estate on the bottle list is a different, single vineyard wine at a far higher price: never pour or ring one for the other.
Open or decant it 30 to 60 minutes ahead; at five years it is young and firm.
Describe the pairing to the garnish on tonight's printed card: the duck course has been printed two ways this year, and the wine is the same in both.
His winery is in Sonoma, so call him a California winemaker rather than a Napa one.
producer.sayIt: Paul Hobbs Cabernet from Coombsville, one of Napa's coolest corners: dark fruit and cocoa with real freshness, for the duck.
askKitchen: Is the bottle open tonight the Coombsville Cabernet or the Nathan Coombs Estate, and when is it opened for the tasting pours?
May a guest order the Coombsville Cabernet by the glass outside the pairing, and at what price?

producer.who: Chateau Montelena, the Calistoga estate whose Chardonnay won the 1976 Paris tasting
producer.where: Calistoga, at the northern end of the Napa Valley, California
producer.founded: 1882, by Alfred Tubbs; revived in 1972 by Jim Barrett
producer.history:
Chateau Montelena is a stone winery at the northern end of the Napa Valley in Calistoga, at the foot of Mount St. Helena. Alfred Tubbs founded it in 1882 and built the stone winery, and it was revived only in 1972, when Jim Barrett took it on.

On 24 May 1976, at a blind tasting in Paris organised by the British wine merchant Steven Spurrier and judged by leading French palates, Montelena's 1973 Chardonnay came first among the whites, ahead of the great white Burgundies; a Roulot Meursault Charmes 1973 came second. Stag's Leap Wine Cellars' 1973 Cabernet won the reds. The winemaker was Mike Grgich, who went on to found Grgich Hills, whose Violetta is on our list. It was the day the world took California seriously, and the film Bottle Shock told the story in 2008.

The house style for Chardonnay is restrained: orchard fruit and bright acidity, traditionally made without malolactic conversion, so there is no buttery sheen. The estate Cabernet, labelled Calistoga, is tight and slow to open, built for long ageing.

Ours is the Napa Valley Chardonnay 2023: green apple, lemon, pear and a little toast.
facts: Alfred Tubbs founded it in 1882 and built its stone winery; Jim Barrett revived it in 1972, as the Codex records.
At the Paris tasting of 24 May 1976 its 1973 Chardonnay came first among the whites, ahead of top white Burgundy.
The red flight went to Stag's Leap Wine Cellars' 1973 Cabernet; Montelena won with Chardonnay.
Mike Grgich made the winning wine and went on to found Grgich Hills.
A Roulot 1973 Meursault Charmes came second to Montelena in the white flight; Roulot's Charmes is on our list.
The Chardonnay is restrained, traditionally made without malolactic conversion: orchard fruit, no buttery sheen.
Calistoga became its own appellation long after the wine was famous; the estate Cabernet is labelled Calistoga.
The list of 3 October 2026 prints the Chardonnay 2023 at $175 and 2017 at $210, and the Calistoga Cabernet 2010 at $570 and 2022 at $195.
notes: Say shah-TOH mon-teh-LEE-nah.
Tell the Paris story as it stands: the 1973 Chardonnay, 24 May 1976. Ours is the same winery's Chardonnay, the 2023, not the winning wine.
Montelena won the whites, not the reds: the Cabernet winner was Stag's Leap Wine Cellars.
Guests may know the story from Bottle Shock, the 2008 film; it is a dramatisation, so tell the facts rather than the film.
Whether the 2023 was made without malolactic conversion is a lineup question; say restrained and bright, not a technical claim.
Say Jim Barrett revived it in 1972; name no current owner.
producer.sayIt: Chateau Montelena, whose 1973 Chardonnay beat the best of Burgundy in Paris in 1976: ours is the 2023, bright, balanced and lightly toasty.
askKitchen: Was the 2023 Chardonnay made without malolactic conversion, as the house style traditionally is?

producer.who: Grgich Hills Estate of Rutherford, founded by Mike Grgich, who made the Montelena Chardonnay that won in Paris
producer.where: Rutherford, Napa Valley, California; estate vineyards across Napa, from Rutherford and Yountville to Calistoga, Carneros and American Canyon
producer.history:
Grgich Hills Estate was founded in 1977 by Miljenko Grgich, known as Mike, with his partner Austin Hills: the Hills in the name is the partner, not a hillside. The winery is in Rutherford, in the heart of the Napa Valley.

The year before it opened, Grgich had made history. On 24 May 1976, at a blind tasting in Paris judged by leading French experts, the Chateau Montelena 1973 Chardonnay he made came first among the whites, ahead of great white Burgundy. The estate did not exist yet: he made the winning wine at Montelena, then founded his own house. Grgich was born in Croatia, and André Tchelistcheff, the great winemaker of Beaulieu Vineyard, was among those who guided him.

The estate's vineyards run across Napa, from Rutherford and Yountville to Calistoga and Carneros, and they are farmed organically. The house is known for Chardonnay kept lean and citrus driven, and for reds more savoury than sweet.

Our bottle is a rarity: Violetta, a late harvest dessert wine made only in rare years, when noble rot touches Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling and Gewürztraminer in its low-lying American Canyon vineyard. Ours is the 2012 in half-bottle, the pour for Bananas Foster.
facts: Founded in 1977 in Rutherford by Miljenko (Mike) Grgich with Austin Hills; Hills is the partner, not a hillside.
Grgich made the Chateau Montelena 1973 Chardonnay that came first among the whites at the Paris tasting of 24 May 1976.
The estate did not exist in 1976: the winning wine was made at Montelena.
Mike Grgich was born in Croatia.
Estate vineyards across Napa, including Rutherford, Yountville, Calistoga and Carneros, are farmed organically.
Violetta is a late harvest wine of Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling and Gewürztraminer touched by botrytis, from the low-lying American Canyon vineyard.
Violetta is made only in rare years, when noble rot touches the grapes.
The house style: lean, citrus driven Chardonnay and savoury reds.
notes: Say GUR-gich and vee-oh-LET-ah.
Never say Grgich Hills won the Paris tasting: Chateau Montelena did, with a Chardonnay Mike Grgich made there; he founded Grgich Hills the next year. Our list carries the Montelena Chardonnay too.
Violetta is sweet: pour small, well chilled, before the Bananas Foster is flambéed, and keep the bottle clear of the cart. Recork and chill the rest.

On the list of 3 October 2026 Grgich Hills Napa Valley is also printed on the Cabernet page (2021, $160) and the Zinfandel page (2020, $90, a bin shared with a Brunello): ring the Violetta by bin 19291.
Whom the name Violetta honours, and how to speak of Mike Grgich today, are questions for the sommelier.
producer.sayIt: Violetta is the rare dessert wine of Grgich Hills, founded by Mike Grgich, who made the Montelena Chardonnay that won in Paris in 1976.
askKitchen: What is the blend of the 2012 Violetta?
Whom is Violetta named for?
If a guest asks about Mike Grgich himself today, what should we say?

producer.who: Kongsgaard, the family winery of John Kongsgaard in the Napa Valley, famous for Chardonnay
producer.where: Napa Valley, California
producer.history:
Kongsgaard is the family winery of John Kongsgaard in the Napa Valley. Its Chardonnays are among the most sought after in California, made in small amounts in a rich style that is built to age in bottle like great white Burgundy. The top Chardonnay is The Judge, a rare bottle even among collectors.

The house is best known for Chardonnay, but the wine list counts its reds as just as serious: a dark, savoury, peppery Syrah and a deep, firm Cabernet. Production is small, and every bottle is a collector's choice.

Our list holds Kongsgaard in unusual depth. The Chardonnay comes in the 2015, the 2016 and the 2023, with The Judge 2023 beside them; the Cabernet and the Syrah each come in 2014 and 2016. The 2016 Chardonnay, ten years on, is the bottle with its own card: lemon curd, baked pear, hazelnut and honey with a smoky, savoury depth and a very long finish. It is the celebration bottle for the pecan Gulf fish, with the power for the pecan bordelaise and the lump crab, and grand with the BBQ lobster.

How this wine is made and aged is a question for the sommelier, and so is the story behind The Judge's name.
facts: Kongsgaard is the family winery of John Kongsgaard in the Napa Valley, as our wine card describes it.
Its Chardonnays are among the most sought after in California, made in small amounts.
The style is rich and long-lived, built to age in bottle like great white Burgundy.
The Judge is its rare top Chardonnay; our list prints the 2023.
It also makes a dark, peppery Syrah and a deep, firm Cabernet.
Our list prints the Chardonnay in 2015, 2016 and 2023, and the Cabernet and Syrah in 2014 and 2016.
notes: Say KONGZ-gard.
Kongsgaard Napa Valley 2016 is printed three times on the list of 3 October 2026: the Chardonnay at $280 (bin 123232), the Cabernet at $385 and the Syrah at $380. Say Chardonnay and ring by bin.
A guest who asks for The Judge by name means the rarer top Chardonnay, the 2023 at $950: check with the sommelier before you fetch it.
Serve it barely chilled so the layers show; it is ten years old, so pour it with some ceremony.
Do not describe how it is made or aged: no source here says, and the sommelier has it.
Family winery is how our wine card describes it; ownership can change, so if a guest asks who owns it, offer the sommelier.
producer.sayIt: Kongsgaard is one of the most sought-after Chardonnays in California, from a small Napa family winery; our 2016 has ten years in bottle.
askKitchen: How is the Kongsgaard Chardonnay made and aged?
What is the story behind the name The Judge?

producer.who: Niepoort, a family Port house of Dutch origin, famous for its Colheitas
producer.where: Vila Nova de Gaia, facing Porto, with Quinta de Nápoles in the Tedo valley, Douro, Portugal
producer.history:
Niepoort is a family Port house of Dutch origin, founded in 1842 in Vila Nova de Gaia, the riverside town facing Porto where the Port lodges stand. It has stayed in the same family for five or six generations, a small independent house beside the big firms founded by the British.

Niepoort is known above all for its Colheitas, tawny Ports from a single harvest aged for many years in cask, with the bottling date on the label as well as the harvest. The Codex also names it as effectively the only house that has kept Garrafeira alive: Port from one year, aged a few years in wood and then for years in large glass demijohns. Its Vintage Ports are deep and long lived, and the Codex calls the house style fresher and more transparent than the classic houses.

The name has also become one of the leading makers of Douro table wine; the Codex attaches Dirk Niepoort's name to that dry Douro revival, with wines such as Redoma and Batuta. Its Douro estate, as the Codex records it, is Quinta de Nápoles in the Tedo valley.

We pour two very different Niepoort wines: the Colheita 1997 in a half-bottle, amber and nutty, poured straight; and the Vintage Port 1987, aged in bottle, which must be decanted.
facts: Founded in 1842 in Vila Nova de Gaia by a family of Dutch origin, and family run for five or six generations.
Famous above all for Colheitas: tawny Port from one harvest, at least seven years in cask, with harvest and bottling dates on the label.
The Codex names Niepoort as effectively the only house keeping Garrafeira alive: years in wood, then at least eight years in glass demijohns.
The Codex records Quinta de Nápoles in the Tedo valley as its estate, with old field-blend parcels in the Cima Corgo.
A leading maker of Douro table wines; the Codex attaches Dirk Niepoort's name to the dry Douro revival, with Redoma and Batuta.
Our list prints Niepoort Vintage 1980, 1982, 1983 and 1987, a Colheita 1934, the Colheita 1997 half and a Garrafeira 1977.
Niepoort also makes Lagar de Baixo, a Baga red from Bairrada, on our list.
notes: Say NEE-port; Colheita is kol-YAY-tah.
Never mix the two: the Colheita is a tawny aged in cask, poured straight and a touch cool; the 1987 Vintage aged in bottle and is decanted off its crust.
Read both dates on the Colheita label to the guest: the 1997 harvest and the bottling date.
Who leads the house today is not dated in any source; say a family house of Dutch origin, and keep Dirk Niepoort for a guest who asks about Douro table wine.
No source says Niepoort declared 1987; call it Vintage Port 1987, never a declared year.
producer.sayIt: Niepoort, a family Port house of Dutch origin since 1842: famous for Colheitas, tawny Port from one harvest, and elegant Vintage Port.
askKitchen: What bottling date does our Niepoort Colheita 1997 half-bottle carry?
Was 1987 a declared Niepoort vintage, and may servers say so?
May the Niepoort 1987 be poured at breakfast and lunch with the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake?

producer.who: Taylor Fladgate, the historic Port house whose great estate is Quinta de Vargellas
producer.where: Vila Nova de Gaia, with Quinta de Vargellas in the Douro Superior and Quinta de Terra Feita in the Pinhão valley, Douro, Portugal
producer.history:
