Taylor Fladgate is one of the oldest Port houses: its story begins in 1692 with an English merchant, Job Bearsley. Outside the United States it is generally called Taylor's, as the Codex's own questions name it.

In 1893 it bought Quinta de Vargellas, a great estate in the Douro Superior, the hot, wild eastern end of the valley that runs to the Spanish border, beyond the Cachão da Valeira. Vargellas and Quinta de Terra Feita in the Pinhão valley are the two backbones of its Vintage Port blend.

Taylor's style is structure. The Codex calls it the reference for Vintage Port structure: firm, tannic and slow to mature, built to be kept rather than drunk young. In the best years the house declares a vintage. In good years when it does not declare, it bottles Vargellas on its own as a single quinta Vintage Port, which is still a true Vintage Port, from one estate, and not a second wine.

We pour both kinds: the declared Vintage Port 1977, forty-nine years old, and the Quinta de Vargellas 1987, from a year Taylor did not declare. Both have thrown a crust and must be decanted.
facts: Its story begins in 1692 with an English merchant, Job Bearsley.
It bought Quinta de Vargellas, in the Douro Superior beyond the Cachão da Valeira, in 1893.
In good years that are not declared, it bottles Quinta de Vargellas alone as a single quinta Vintage Port.
Quinta de Vargellas and Quinta de Terra Feita, in the Pinhão valley, are the two backbones of its Vintage blend, as the Codex records.
A declaration is made by the house itself; 1977 was a declared Taylor vintage and 1987 was not.
Our list prints Taylor Fladgate 1977 and 1994 and Quinta de Vargellas 1987.
notes: Say TAY-lor FLAD-gate, the d sounded; Quinta de Vargellas is KEEN-tah deh var-ZHEL-ash. Our wine card writes FLAG-ate, which drops the d.
A single quinta Vintage Port is still a Vintage Port, not a second wine: say from Taylor's finest estate, in a year the house did not declare.
Both throw a crust: they stand upright ahead, the sommelier draws the old corks and decants just before pouring.
Bin 19321 is printed for both the Vargellas 1987 and the Quintarelli Recioto 1997: ring the Vargellas by name and tell the sommelier about the clash.
If a guest asks why the label says Taylor Fladgate and not Taylor's, it is the name the house uses in the United States.
producer.sayIt: Taylor Fladgate, a Port house since 1692: its great estate, Quinta de Vargellas, gives our 1987; the 1977 is a declared classic.
askKitchen: Which bottle does bin 19321 ring: the Taylor Fladgate Vargellas 1987 or the Quintarelli Recioto 1997?
How far ahead should the Taylor Fladgate 1977 stand upright, and is it opened with tongs?

producer.who: Château Minuty, a cru classé estate at Gassin above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez
producer.where: Gassin, Saint-Tropez peninsula, Côtes de Provence, France
producer.founded: Bought by Gabriel Farnet in 1936
producer.history:
Château Minuty stands at Gassin, on the hills above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, with vineyards on the hills of Gassin and Ramatuelle. Gabriel Farnet bought the estate in 1936, and his descendants, the Matton family, made its name.

In 1955 Minuty was named one of the crus classés of the Côtes de Provence. That classification ranks estates rather than vineyards: 23 were named, the list has never been revised, and only 18 still hold the rank, because a title attaches to the property as it stood in 1955 and is lost if the estate is broken up or absorbed.

Its rosés are built on Grenache and pressed pale; pale is a style, not a sign of sweetness. Above the Prestige the estate makes the cuvées Rose et Or and 281.

Ours is the Prestige 2024, our rosé by the glass at $17: pale and dry, white peach, wild strawberry and citrus zest with a light mineral finish. It is the first pick with the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits and the Creole Tomato Tostada. Young rosé rolls over, so the vintage is read at lineup.
facts: Château Minuty stands at Gassin above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, with vineyards on the hills of Gassin and Ramatuelle.
Gabriel Farnet bought the estate in 1936; his descendants, the Matton family, built its name.
Named one of the crus classés of the Côtes de Provence in 1955: 23 estates, a list never revised, 18 surviving.
The 1955 rank attaches to the estate as it stood then, so holders only ever fall away.
Minuty’s current Prestige Rosé page lists Grenache, Syrah, Rolle and Cinsault without percentages. Exact 2024 proportions remain unconfirmed.
Rose et Or and 281 are the estate’s cuvées above the Prestige.
Our Prestige 2024 is the rosé by the glass at $17, first pick for the Shrimp & Grits and the Creole Tomato Tostada.
notes: Say mee nu TEE. Introduce Prestige as a pale, dry Côtes de Provence rosé. The Château estate’s classification is not a promise that every Minuty cuvée carries that classification.
Guests ask whether pale means sweet. The honest answer: no, the colour comes from a quick, gentle pressing, and the Prestige is dry.
Do not name an owner: who owns it today is not confirmed. Say the Matton family made its name, and remember ownership can change.
Read the vintage at lineup: young rosé rolls over, and the open bottle may already be the 2025.
It is not Whispering Angel, a different Provence estate sold by the bottle. Never swap one for the other.
producer.sayIt: Minuty Prestige is a pale, dry Provence rosé, with peach, strawberry and citrus notes, lovely with the shrimp and grits.
askKitchen: Is the open Minuty Prestige still the 2024, or has the 2025 arrived?
What vintage of Minuty Prestige is open, and does its technical sheet confirm the blend for that release?

producer.who: Château d’Esclans, the Provence estate behind Whispering Angel
producer.where: La Motte-en-Provence, Côtes de Provence, France
producer.founded: Bought in 2006 to make great rosé
producer.history:
Château d’Esclans lies in the Esclans valley at La Motte-en-Provence, in the hills behind the Riviera, with old Grenache and Rolle, the Provençal name for Vermentino. It was bought in 2006 by Sacha Lichine, son of the Bordeaux château owner and wine writer Alexis Lichine, with one aim: to make great rosé.

The name of its best known wine comes from the château’s chapel: above the altar is a carving of two cherubs that seemed to be whispering to each other, and the label of Whispering Angel carries a line drawing of them. Whispering Angel became the pale Provence rosé that popularised the style in America and created the volume luxury rosé category. It is blended from bought fruit as well as the estate’s own.

Above it the range climbs to Rock Angel, partly raised in oak, then Les Clans and Garrus, old-vine Grenache with Rolle fermented in large oak and priced against fine white Burgundy. As of October 2026 the estate is part of LVMH.

Ours is Whispering Angel 2024, $50 by the bottle: Grenache-led with Cinsault and Rolle, white peach, wild strawberry and citrus, dry and mineral, the value bottle for the Creole Tomato Tostada.
facts: Château d’Esclans lies in the Esclans valley at La Motte-en-Provence, in the Côtes de Provence hills behind the Riviera.
Sacha Lichine bought it in 2006 with one aim: to make great rosé.
Whispering Angel is named for two cherubs carved above the altar of the château’s chapel; the label shows them.
Whispering Angel popularised pale Provence rosé in America and created the volume luxury rosé category.
Whispering Angel is blended from bought fruit as well as estate fruit.
Garrus, old-vine Grenache with Rolle fermented in large oak, is priced against fine white Burgundy; Les Clans and Rock Angel sit between.
Rolle, one of the grapes in the blend, is the Provençal name for Vermentino.
The estate is part of LVMH, as of October 2026.
Ours is Whispering Angel 2024, $50, bin 10421, Grenache-led with Cinsault and Rolle.
notes: Say shah-TOH dess-KLAHN. Present Whispering Angel as the famous pale Provence rosé: dry, peach and strawberry, a guest favourite.
Guests ask about the name: two cherubs carved above the chapel altar seemed to whisper, and the label carries a drawing of them.
Never call it an estate-only wine: Whispering Angel is blended from bought fruit as well as the estate’s own. The estate’s grand rosé is Garrus.
Ownership can change: say the estate is part of LVMH, as of October 2026, and leave it there.
It is not our glass rosé: the Minuty Prestige is poured by the glass; Whispering Angel is sold by the bottle.
producer.sayIt: Whispering Angel from Château d’Esclans: the pale Provence rosé that popularised the style in America, dry and fresh, lovely with the tomatoes.
askKitchen: Is the Whispering Angel still the 2024 (bin 10421), and is it in stock tonight?

producer.who: Domaine Tempier, the Bandol estate Lucien and Lulu Peyraud took on in 1936
producer.where: Le Plan du Castellet, Bandol, Provence, France
producer.founded: Taken on by Lucien and Lulu Peyraud in 1936
producer.history:
Domaine Tempier is at Le Plan du Castellet near Bandol, on the Provençal coast between Marseille and Toulon. In 1936 Lucien Peyraud and Lucie Tempier, known to everyone as Lulu, took on her family’s farm. Lucien worked to have Bandol made an appellation of its own, granted in 1941, and he championed Mourvèdre, the late-ripening grape that needs the heat of this coast. Bandol red must still be at least half Mourvèdre and spend 18 months in wood.

Lulu’s Provençal cooking made the domaine a pilgrimage: it inspired Alice Waters of Chez Panisse, and the writer Richard Olney put it in a book, Lulu’s Provençal Table. She died in 2020 aged 102. A red cuvée on our list, Lulu et Lucien, carries the couple’s names.

The vines climb restanque terraces across Le Castellet, La Cadière and Le Plan du Castellet, and the great parcels, La Tourtine, La Migoua and Cabassaou, are bottled on their own. The reds are dark and savoury; the rosé, Mourvèdre with Grenache and Cinsault, is built to age.

Ours is the Bandol Rosé 2024 at $120: pale salmon, wild strawberry, blood orange and garrigue, dry and savoury, the classic bottle for the Creole Tomato Tostada.

producer.who: Domaine de Trévallon, the estate Éloi Dürrbach founded in the Alpilles
producer.where: Saint-Étienne-du-Grès, Alpilles, Provence, France
producer.founded: 1973, by Éloi Dürrbach
producer.history:
Domaine de Trévallon lies in the Alpilles, the limestone hills near Les Baux in Provence, at Saint-Étienne-du-Grès. In 1973 Éloi Dürrbach cleared limestone scrub there and planted the grapes he believed in: for the red, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah in roughly equal shares.

When the rules of the Les Baux-de-Provence appellation were finalised, they capped Cabernet Sauvignon at a small share of the blend, around a fifth. Dürrbach chose to leave the appellation rather than change a wine he had built over twenty years, so Trévallon has been sold ever since under a wider regional name, first Vin de Pays des Bouches-du-Rhône, now IGP Alpilles. It is the textbook case of a great wine outside the rules: the tier on a label reports conformity with a rulebook, never quality. The split was over grape variety alone; farming was never the quarrel in Les Baux, among the most organic appellations in France.

The red, aged in old wood, is herbal, ferrous and long-lived. The white is a small production, Marsanne-led with Roussanne, Chardonnay, Grenache Blanc and Clairette, the mix changing by vintage.

Ours is the white 2016 at $265: apricot, honey, fennel and Provençal herbs, the splurge bottle for the Gulf Fish en Papillote. The list also carries the white in 2019 and 2021, and the red in six vintages from 2012 to 2021.

Guests ask why the label says Alpilles. The honest answer: the founder’s blend broke the local appellation’s grape rules, so he left it; quality had nothing to do with it.
Trévallon is best known for its red; this is the rare white. The 2016 blend is a question for the sommelier.
Serve it barely chilled in a white Burgundy bowl and let it open; at ten years it is rich and textured.
A guest who likes the white may want the red: Cabernet and Syrah, savoury and long-lived, a step for a Bordeaux drinker.

producer.who: Pascal Cotat, a family grower in Chavignol, Sancerre
producer.where: Chavignol, Sancerre, Loire Valley, France
producer.history:
Pascal Cotat is a family grower in Chavignol, a village of the Sancerre appellation in the eastern Loire. There are two Cotat estates in Chavignol, Pascal’s and his cousin François’s, kept separate on family parcels.

Chavignol’s western slopes are Kimmeridgian marl, the chalky clay-limestone full of fossil oyster shells that surfaces again in Chablis, known locally as terres blanches. It ripens slowly and gives the broadest, most structured Sancerre. Les Monts Damnés, the damned mountains, is a very steep slope above the village, a lieu-dit rather than an appellation, worked largely by hand.

The Cotat family picks its Sauvignon Blanc ripe, and the wines are built to age. They can carry a trace of residual sugar, so the name Sancerre is no promise of bone dryness, and the Cotat pair is the standard proof that Sancerre is not always lean and herbaceous.

The rosé is Pinot Noir from a tiny parcel of old vines, fermented with native yeasts and aged in old casks. After a local dispute the parcel was declassified from the Sancerre appellation, so the wine is labelled by lot.

Our list prints both rosé lots, 2022 and 2024, La Grande Côte 2023 and Les Monts Damnés 2022. Ours are the Lot 2024 at $270 for the tostada and the Monts Damnés at $350 for the Caesar.

producer.who: Damien Martin, the father and son domaine at Davayé in the Mâconnais behind our red Burgundy by the glass
producer.where: Davayé, Mâconnais, Burgundy, France
producer.founded: 1982, by Robert Martin
producer.history:
Damien Martin is the name on the label of our red Burgundy by the glass, and behind it stands a father and son family domaine: Domaine Robert et Damien Martin, at Davayé in the Mâconnais, in southern Burgundy. Robert Martin founded it in 1982, and his son Damien runs it, as of October 2026.

The Mâconnais is above all white wine country, the southern home of Chardonnay, so this is a family’s red made for drinking rather than for the cellar: a Pinot Noir sold under the regional Bourgogne name, light and silky, with red cherry, raspberry and a touch of earth, light tannin and fresh acidity. The wine list calls it straightforward Bourgogne for everyday drinking, and that is its charm.

A Bourgogne label names the region, not a village or a vineyard, and no source here says where the grapes for this one grow; that is a question for the sommelier. At the table it is the gentle red: the first pick with the Blackened Tofu, and the red for a guest who wants one with a lighter plate or at breakfast.

producer.who: Domaine Saint Damien, the Saurel family's estate in Gigondas
producer.where: Gigondas, Southern Rhône, France
producer.founded: Farmed by the Saurel family since the early nineteenth century
producer.history:
Domaine Saint Damien is a family estate in Gigondas, the Southern Rhône village beneath the Dentelles de Montmirail. The Saurel family has farmed it since the early nineteenth century, and its vineyards have been certified organic since 2012.

La Louisianne, which retailers spell La Louisiane, comes from old vines on the middle terraces of Gigondas. It is about 80 percent Grenache with 15 percent Mourvèdre and a little Cinsault and Syrah, co-fermented with a long maceration in concrete, aged about twelve months in oak and bottled unfined and unfiltered. The name belongs to a lieu-dit, a named parcel; no source explains why the parcel carries it, so a Louisiana link is a question for the sommelier, never a story to tell.

The family bottles several Gigondas, and our list prints seven Saint Damien lines: Souteyrades, Vieilles Vignes, a cuvée named Clovis Saurel, and Les Prés, a white from Clairette. White Gigondas has been allowed only since the 2023 harvest, so Les Prés is one of the new wines of the cru.

At the table La Louisianne is the value bottle with the Petite Filet Mignon: ripe red and black cherry, garrigue and spice, generous, with soft tannin.

producer.who: Domaine du Pegau, the Féraud family's estate in Châteauneuf-du-Pape
producer.where: Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Southern Rhône, France
producer.founded: Named Domaine du Pegau in 1987; the Féraud family has farmed in Châteauneuf since the seventeenth century
producer.history:
Domaine du Pegau is the Féraud family's estate in Châteauneuf-du-Pape. The family has farmed there since the seventeenth century, but for generations sold most of its wine in bulk. Paul Féraud and his daughter Laurence gave the domaine its name in 1987, and the name of its main wine remembers the old way: the Cuvée Réservée was the share the family reserved to bottle themselves.

Pegau, which the Codex writes Pégaü, is the old Provençal word for a clay wine jug, one of them found in the papal palace at Avignon, and the jug is on the label. It is a name, not a place.

The style is proudly traditional. The Cuvée Réservée is about 80 percent Grenache with Syrah, Mourvèdre and other permitted varieties, not destemmed, fermented in cement and aged about two years in large old oak casks, without filtration. The result is the old Châteauneuf smell: kirsch and dried cherry with garrigue, leather and a savoury, hide-like note that traditionalists call terroir and modernists call a fault.

Above the Réservée sit Cuvée Laurence, the same wine given longer in wood, Cuvée da Capo, declared only in exceptional vintages, and Cuvée Inspiration, a very old-vine selection. Our list prints six Domaine du Pegau bottlings: the Réservée 2020 and 2021, a 2020 magnum and a 2016 double magnum, and Cuvée Laurence 2019 and a 2012 magnum.

Guests who know Châteauneuf may mention a leather or farmyard note. The honest answer: that savoury character is the house style, loved by its admirers; if a bottle smells wrong, bring the sommelier.

producer.who: Château de Beaucastel, the Perrin family's estate in Châteauneuf-du-Pape
producer.where: Courthézon, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Southern Rhône, France
producer.founded: Perrin family since 1909; the Beaucastel name is traced to the sixteenth century
producer.history:
Château de Beaucastel lies at Courthézon, in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, a large single block of vines on the galets, the round stones of the appellation. The Beaucastel name is traced to the sixteenth century, and the Perrin family has run the estate since 1909.

Beaucastel is the estate that actually plants all thirteen varieties the appellation permits, red and white, and it grows an unusually high share of old Mourvèdre, which plays a far larger role here than in its neighbours' wines. Mourvèdre wants heat and a long season and gives a savoury, meaty frame that ages slowly, which is why Beaucastel tastes of garrigue, leather and game over kirsch. It has farmed organically since about 1950. In the cellar it briefly heats the harvest before fermentation, a treatment almost nobody else in Châteauneuf uses, and raises the wine in large old foudres.

The estate keeps bottles of each vintage in its own cellar and releases back vintages as Oenothèque, labelled with the date the wine left the cellar. Our 2007 is one: it waited in the château's cellar until its release.

The family's reach goes further: Hommage à Jacques Perrin is the Mourvèdre-dominant top wine of great years, Coudoulet de Beaucastel is its Côtes du Rhône from across the road, and Beaucastel cuttings, imported to California in 1989, became the vineyard of Tablas Creek at Paso Robles.

Carry the 2007 upright, as a nineteen-year-old bottle may carry sediment; decanting is the sommelier's call. Expect it mature, savoury and silky.

producer.who: Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe, the Brunier family's estate on the La Crau plateau
producer.where: La Crau plateau, Bédarrides, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Southern Rhône, France
producer.history:
Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe stands on La Crau, a high plateau of Châteauneuf-du-Pape at Bédarrides. One of Claude Chappe's optical signal telegraph towers once stood there, on one of the highest points around, and the old tower gave the estate its name. Hippolyte Brunier planted vines on the plateau: in 1898 by the estate's own history, though the Codex prints 1891. The tower is long gone; the Brunier family still runs the estate, as of October 2026, and plays on the name: its younger wine is Télégramme.

La Crau holds the appellation's thickest bed of galets roulés, large round stones that store the day's heat and give the wine warmth and depth. The red, La Crau, is classical Châteauneuf: Grenache-led with real Mourvèdre and some Syrah, raised in large oak foudres, structured rather than sweet, and long lived.

The family's reach goes beyond the plateau: in 1998 the Brunier brothers and the importer Kermit Lynch bought Domaine Les Pallières in Gigondas.

On our list Vieux Télégraphe La Crau appears in five vintages. Ours is the 2014, twelve years old, the celebration bottle with the Creole Hanger Steak: warm fruit and soft tannin for the spice.

producer.who: Familia Torres, the Penedès wine family, and Pazo das Bruxas, its Albariño from Rías Baixas
producer.where: Rías Baixas, Galicia, Spain; the Torres family house is at Pacs del Penedès, Catalonia
producer.founded: 1870 for Familia Torres, as the Codex dates it
producer.history:
Pazo das Bruxas is Galician for the manor of the witches, and Galicia has a rich folklore of witches, the meigas. It is an Albariño from Rías Baixas, on the Atlantic coast of south-west Galicia, in Spain's green north-west corner, and it is made by Familia Torres, the wine family of Penedès in Catalonia.

The Codex dates the family house to 1870 and places it at Pacs del Penedès, with large holdings across Catalonia, in Penedès, Conca de Barberà and Priorat, and further estates elsewhere in Spain, in Chile and in California. Its most famous wine is Mas La Plana, a Penedès Cabernet Sauvignon whose 1970 vintage, by the Codex, came out ahead of top Bordeaux at the Paris Wine Olympiad of 1979, and the family has led the recovery of near-lost Catalan grape varieties.

The house's own list shows the family's reach: beside the Albariño by the glass it carries Torres wines from Penedès, Priorat and Ribera del Duero, among them Mas La Plana in four vintages, and Altos Ibéricos, the family's Rioja.

The Albariño is unoaked and bottled young: pale and bright, lemon and white peach with a saline, almost sea-spray snap. It is the first pick for the Creole Caesar and the Gulf Fish en Papillote, and it is kept iced, because the freshness fades as it warms.
facts: Pazo das Bruxas is Galician for the manor of the witches; in Galician the x is said sh.
The house wine list names Familia Torres as the maker; no record confirms where the grapes grow or that Torres owns vines in Rías Baixas.
The Codex dates Familia Torres to 1870 and places the family at Pacs del Penedès, in Catalonia.
By the Codex, Mas La Plana 1970, a Penedès Cabernet Sauvignon, came out ahead of top Bordeaux at the 1979 Paris Wine Olympiad.
The Codex credits Torres with leading the recovery of near-lost ancestral Catalan grape varieties.
The list of 3 October 2026 carries Torres wines from Penedès, Priorat and Ribera del Duero, and Altos Ibéricos, the family's Rioja.
Rías Baixas lies on the Atlantic coast of south-west Galicia, named for its rías, long sea inlets; Albariño covers almost all its vineyards.
The house menu prints Pazo das Brujas, the Castilian spelling; the Binwise list prints Pazo das Bruxas.
notes: Say PAH-tho dahs BROO-shas: in Galician the x is sh. Rías Baixas is REE-ahs BYE-shahs.
Lead with the family: a guest who knows the Torres name from Catalonia can be told this is the same family's Albariño from Spain's Atlantic coast.
Do not say Torres owns an estate or vineyards in Rías Baixas, and give no first vintage: accounts disagree on 2013 and 2014, and neither is confirmed.
Keep it iced and pour the guests first; its saline freshness fades as it warms. It is the still white offered with oysters.
A guest who loves it and wants a bottle can step up to Do Ferreiro's Cepas Vellas, old vine Albariño from the same coast.
producer.sayIt: Pazo das Bruxas, the manor of the witches: Albariño from Spain's Atlantic coast, made by the Torres family, lemony with a salty snap.
askKitchen: Which vintage of Pazo das Bruxas is open tonight, 2024 or 2025, and does the label name Familia Torres?
Does the back label say where in Rías Baixas the grapes grow, and does Torres own the vineyards or buy the fruit?

producer.who: La Rioja Alta S.A., the Haro house of the 890 and 904 Gran Reservas
producer.where: Barrio de la Estación, Haro, Rioja Alta, Rioja, Spain
producer.founded: 10 July 1890, by five families, in the station quarter of Haro
producer.history:
La Rioja Alta S.A. was founded on 10 July 1890 by five families in the Barrio de la Estación, the railway station quarter of Haro, where the town's great bodegas gathered beside the line. In 1904 it merged with Alfredo Ardanza's winery, and the house marked the union with a Reserva 1904, which became the Gran Reserva 904. Its other great Gran Reserva, the 890, marks the founding year. The first digit is dropped from both so that no one reads the number as a vintage.

The house is one of Rioja's great traditionalists. Its reds age for years in American oak barrels made in its own cooperage and are racked by hand from cask to cask, which gives the pale, sweetly spiced, long-aged style the Codex describes: coconut, dried strawberry and sandalwood. Viña Ardanza is its Reserva, a tier below the numbered Gran Reservas.

The 904 is about nine parts Tempranillo to one of Graciano, aged about four years in American oak and then for years in bottle before release; the 890 is declared only in exceptional years. Our 904 2015 is silky and savoury: dried cherry, strawberry, tobacco, vanilla, leather and sweet spice, with mellow tannin and a long finish. The list also carries the 890 2010.
facts: Founded on 10 July 1890 by five families in Haro's railway station quarter, as the house's own history tells it.
In 1904 it merged with Alfredo Ardanza's winery; the Reserva 1904 made to mark it became the Gran Reserva 904.
The 890 marks the founding year; the first digit is dropped so neither name is read as a vintage.
The 904 is about 90 per cent Tempranillo and 10 per cent Graciano.
Its reds age in American oak barrels from the house's own cooperage and are racked by hand from cask to cask.
Viña Ardanza is the house Reserva, a tier below the numbered Gran Reservas; the 890 is declared only in exceptional years, by the Codex.
A Rioja Gran Reserva has at least five years of ageing, at least two of them in oak.
The list of 3 October 2026 carries the 904 2015 and the 890 2010.
notes: Say lah ree-OH-hah AHL-tah; in English the wine is the nine-oh-four.
Present it as grand, classic Rioja: decant gently twenty minutes ahead, leaving the sediment, for the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, lamb or duck.
Guests ask whether 904 is the vintage. The honest answer: no, it marks the 1904 merger; ours is the 2015.
For a guest who wants more, the 890 2010 is the rarer Gran Reserva, declared only in exceptional years.
Leave the 2015's exact blend and barrel time to the sommelier, as the card does.
producer.sayIt: La Rioja Alta's 904, named for a merger in 1904: a Gran Reserva from Haro, silky Tempranillo with dried cherry, tobacco and spice.
askKitchen: What do the 904 2015 back label and technical sheet give for blend and months in American oak?
How does the sommelier want the 890 2010 offered beside the 904?

producer.who: Argyle, the Oregon sparkling wine house in Dundee, in the Willamette Valley
producer.where: Dundee, Willamette Valley, Oregon; vineyards in the Dundee Hills and the Eola-Amity Hills
producer.history:
Argyle began in 1987 in the town of Dundee, in Oregon's Willamette Valley, with one idea: that the valley's cool climate could make sparkling wine by the traditional method. Its own brochure names Rollin Soles as founder; other accounts call Soles and the Australian winemaker Brian Croser co-founders, with Soles arriving in the Yamhill Valley in 1985 on plans backed by Croser.

The first winery was a former hazelnut processing plant in Dundee, where the wines were made for nearly 30 years; it is now the Argyle Tasting House, and the NutHouse Pinot Noir takes its name from the building. In 1990 Cal Knudsen, who had been Dick Erath's partner, joined Argyle and brought his mature vineyard in the Dundee Hills, planted in the early 1970s. In 1996 Argyle bought land in the Eola Hills for its Lone Star Vineyard.

Croser's Australian company Petaluma bought Argyle in 2000 or 2001, by Prince of Pinot's two accounts, and Petaluma was itself taken over by Lion Nathan in 2001.

Sparkling wine has been Argyle's signature from the start. Our glass is the 2022 Brut, printed as Vintage Brut on the glass list; the bottle list adds the Extended Tirage, which the winery ages about a decade on its lees, and Julia Lee's Block, a Blanc de Blancs from the Knudsen Vineyard.
facts: Argyle was founded in 1987 in Dundee, Oregon, to make traditional method sparkling wine in the cool Willamette Valley.
The winery's brochure names Rollin Soles as founder; other sources call Soles and Brian Croser co-founders.
The original winery was a former hazelnut processing plant in Dundee, now the Argyle Tasting House.
Cal Knudsen joined in 1990, bringing his Dundee Hills vineyard, planted in the early 1970s; Julia Lee's Block comes from it.
Argyle bought land in the Eola Hills in 1996 for its Lone Star Vineyard.
Recent Vintage Brut blends are Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with a little Meunier; the 2019 was 63, 30 and 7 per cent.
The Extended Tirage Brut spends about a decade on its lees; the 2015 was disgorged in August 2025.
notes: Say ar-GYLE and wil-AM-it. It is Oregon sparkling wine, never Champagne, even though the Birthday Bubbles page files it under Champagne by the Glass.
The glass list prints Argyle Vintage Brut and the Birthday page Argyle Brut: both are the 2022 at $15.
Who founded it is told two ways: Rollin Soles in the winery's own brochure, Soles with Brian Croser elsewhere. Say Rollin Soles founded it with Brian Croser's backing.
Petaluma, Brian Croser's Australian company, bought Argyle around 2000 by Prince of Pinot's account. Ownership changes, so never volunteer who owns it today.
Confirm the 2022 blend with the sommelier before quoting any figures.
producer.sayIt: Argyle has made sparkling wine the Champagne way in Oregon's Willamette Valley since 1987; the 2022 Brut is crisp, with apple and citrus zest.
askKitchen: What is the blend of the Argyle 2022 Brut we pour?
Are the Extended Tirage and both Julia Lee's Block vintages in the cellar?

producer.who: Schramsberg Vineyards of Calistoga, and Mirabelle, its North Coast sparkling label
producer.where: Diamond Mountain, Calistoga, Napa Valley, California
producer.founded: 1862 by Jacob Schram; revived for sparkling wine in 1965 by Jack and Jamie Davies
producer.history:
Schramsberg's story has two beginnings. In 1862 Jacob Schram, a German immigrant and barber by trade, bought land on Diamond Mountain at Calistoga, at the north end of the Napa Valley, planted vines and had tunnels dug into the hillside, largely by Chinese labourers, to age his wine. Robert Louis Stevenson visited, in 1880 by the better supported account, and wrote about Schram in The Silverado Squatters, published in 1883. After Schram died in 1905 the winery faded and was sold in 1912.

In 1965 Jack and Jamie Davies bought the property to make sparkling wine by the traditional method. Their first wine, the 1965 Blanc de Blancs, is described as America's first commercial Chardonnay-based brut sparkling wine. In February 1972 President Richard Nixon served the Schramsberg Blanc de Blancs 1969 at the Toast to Peace in Beijing with Premier Zhou Enlai, and the winery says its wines have been poured by every administration since. The Davies family runs it, as of October 2026.

In 1992 Schramsberg introduced Mirabelle, its multi-vintage brut and brut rosé. The rosé is Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from cool North Coast sites in Carneros, the Sonoma Coast, Anderson Valley and Marin, and since 2022 each release carries a bottling number.

At Brennan's the Blanc de Blancs 2021 is a half-bottle on the list, and the Mirabelle Brut Rosé is the friendliest rosé bottle at Bubbles.
facts: Jacob Schram, a German immigrant and barber, bought land on Diamond Mountain in 1862 and had caves dug into the hillside.
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote about Schram's winery in The Silverado Squatters, published in 1883.
Jack and Jamie Davies bought the estate in 1965 to make traditional method sparkling wine; their first wine was the 1965 Blanc de Blancs.
The Blanc de Blancs is described as America's first commercially produced Chardonnay-based brut sparkling wine.
In February 1972 President Nixon served Schramsberg Blanc de Blancs 1969 at the Toast to Peace in Beijing with Premier Zhou Enlai.
Mirabelle, Schramsberg's multi-vintage brut and brut rosé, was introduced in 1992.
Mirabelle Brut Rosé is Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from Carneros, the Sonoma Coast, Anderson Valley and Marin; each release carries a bottling number.
notes: Say SHRAMZ-berg and meer-ah-BELL. Both are California sparkling wine, never Champagne.
Mirabelle is Schramsberg's own North Coast label, not a separate winery; it is on the Bubbles page, not the wine list.
The Toast to Peace wine was the Blanc de Blancs, the same wine as our half-bottle but the 1969 vintage: never say our bottle was poured for Nixon.
The Davies family runs Schramsberg, as of October 2026; that can change, so say it as of today.
No source gave the meaning of the name Mirabelle; if asked, offer to find out rather than guess.
producer.sayIt: Schramsberg revived an 1862 Calistoga estate in 1965, and its Blanc de Blancs was poured at the 1972 Toast to Peace in Beijing.
askKitchen: Which Mirabelle bottling is behind the Roost Bar now, and is it still $50 during Bubbles?
Is the J Schram 2009 in the cellar for a guest who wants the house prestige wine?

producer.who: Domaine des Comtes Lafon, the great Meursault estate behind our Clos de la Baronne
producer.where: Meursault, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
producer.founded: 1894, with the marriage of Jules Lafon and Marie Boch
producer.history:
Domaine des Comtes Lafon is one of the great names of Meursault. It began with a marriage: in 1894 Jules Lafon married Marie Boch, whose family had built the house and cellar at the Clos de la Barre in 1869. Jules bought plots in the best vineyards of Meursault and Volnay and a piece of Le Montrachet.

In 1923 he gave the harvest banquet that became the modern Paulée de Meursault, the November feast where growers share their best bottles; by one merchant’s account it grew from 35 friends to over 600 guests. Later the vines were worked by sharecroppers until his grandson René Lafon took over in 1956, and Dominique Lafon took over from his father in the mid 1980s. The domaine went organic in 1995 and biodynamic in 1998.

The holdings run from the village monopole Clos de la Barre around the house to the premiers crus Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes, Le Montrachet and the red Volnay Santenots-du-Milieu. In 1999 the family also bought an estate in the Mâconnais, Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon, a separate producer on our list.

Our Clos de la Baronne is a second walled vineyard in Meursault, owned entirely by the domaine. By its merchants, 2012 was its first vintage bottled on its own; before that it was kept for the family.
facts: The domaine began with the marriage of Jules Lafon and Marie Boch in 1894; the Boch family had built the Clos de la Barre house in 1869.
In 1923 Jules Lafon gave the harvest banquet that became the modern Paulée de Meursault, the November feast where growers share their best bottles.
René Lafon, Jules’s grandson, took over in 1956, when the vines were worked by sharecroppers.
Dominique Lafon took charge in the mid 1980s; the domaine went organic in 1995 and biodynamic in 1998.
The Clos de la Baronne is a walled monopole in Meursault, classed as village wine, which the domaine owns entirely.
By its merchants, 2012 was the first vintage of the Clos de la Baronne bottled on its own; before that it was kept for the family.
The holdings include Meursault Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes, the Clos de la Barre, a parcel of Le Montrachet and red Volnay Santenots-du-Milieu.
Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon, bought in Milly-Lamartine in 1999, is the family’s separate Mâconnais estate.
notes: Say lah-FOHN, and Clos de la Baronne kloh duh lah bah-RON.
Present it as a great Meursault name for a celebration: rich yet precise, ripe lemon, hazelnut and brioche.
The Clos de la Baronne is village Meursault, not a premier cru: say a walled vineyard the family owns entirely.
Do not confuse the Clos de la Baronne with the Clos de la Barre, the family’s other walled village vineyard, around the house.
Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon is the family’s Mâconnais estate, a separate wine at a gentler price; never pour one as the other.
producer.sayIt: Comtes Lafon is one of Meursault’s great estates; the Clos de la Baronne is their own walled vineyard, rich yet precise, for a celebration.
askKitchen: Is the Clos de la Baronne 2022 ready to drink, or should it be decanted?
